title: Dynamic Influence-Weighted Distillation for Single-IMU Activity Recognition
summary: Inertial sensors at multiple body locations can improve activity recognition, but requiring every sensor at inference increases the deployment burden. We study whether four synchronized IMUs available during training can improve a student that uses only the right-arm IMU during fitting and inference. A frozen four-IMU teacher provides logit and feature targets. Fixed-weight knowledge distillation applies each target with the same strength to every fitting sample, although the student may not benefit equally from them. We introduce dynamic influence weighting (DIW), which tests a one-step candidate update on separate fold-internal training participants. DIW then assigns separate sample-wise gates to the logit and feature losses. On WEAR, we evaluate 19 labels and 68,298 complete windows from 22 participants using subject-disjoint five-fold cross-validation. Pooled out-of-fold macro-F1 is 0.561820 for Supervised and 0.571623 for Fixed-weight KD. DIW reaches 0.638451, gains of 7.66 and 6.68 percentage points, respectively. It exceeds Supervised for 18 of 19 labels and 21 of 22 held-out participants. All three routes retain the same 80,915-parameter right-arm student at inference. Under this protocol, DIW converts training-only multi-position information into a stronger single-IMU model without changing deployed sensing or the student forward graph.

AI.tldr: Dynamic influence weighting (DIW) improves a single-arm IMU activity recognition model by distilling from a frozen four-IMU teacher, outperforming supervised and fixed-weight KD.
AI.motivation: Reduce deployment burden of multiple sensors at inference by leveraging training-time multi-position data to train a strong single-sensor model.
AI.method: A frozen four-IMU teacher provides logit and feature targets to a right-arm student. Fixed-weight KD applies each target equally. DIW learns per-sample gates by testing a one-step candidate update on fold-internal data, weighting both logit and feature losses on a per-sample basis.
AI.result: On WEAR with 19 labels, 68,298 windows, and 22 participants (subject-disjoint 5-fold CV), the right-arm student (80,915 parameters) achieves: Supervised macro-F1 0.561820, fixed-weight KD 0.571623, DIW 0.638451; gains of 7.66 and 6.68 percentage points over Supervised and fixed-weight KD, respectively. DIW outperforms Supervised for 18 of 19 labels and 21 of 22 participants.
AI.conclusion: DIW effectively converts training-time multi-location information into a stronger single-IMU model without altering the deployed sensing or the student architecture, improving performance across most labels/participants while maintaining the same inference graph.

title: GreenLeaf Law Embed Tiny: A Compact Embedding Model for Legal Domain Retrieval
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, IEEE dual-column format. Submitted to arXiv for preprint distribution
summary: We present GreenLeaf Law Embed Tiny, a 0.6B parameter embedding model for legal domain retrieval. GreenLeaf-Tiny achieves 75.11% on the Massive Legal Embedding Benchmark (MLEB) and 64.38% on MTEB(Law, v1),demonstrating competitive performance among models under 1B parameters. Our approach combines a two-stage training pipeline that first distills knowledge from a larger teacher model into a compact student architecture, then applies domain-specific fine-tuning with hard negative mining; a carefully curated dataset of 3.4 million query-passage pairs, including 150,000 human-curated samples across diverse legal jurisdictions; and an efficient inference architecture supporting multiple quantization levels (BF16, INT8, binary) enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments. We provide detailed analysis of our training methodology, architectural choices, and comprehensive evaluation across legal retrieval tasks. Our results demonstrate that domain-specific training with high-quality data can improve performance for specialized domain applications

AI.tldr: GreenLeaf-Tiny: a 0.6B parameter legal-domain embedding model built via teacher-student distillation with domain fine-tuning and hard negative mining; trained on 3.4M query-passage pairs (incl. 150k human-curated samples) and supporting BF16/INT8/binary quantization; achieves 75.11% on MLEB and 64.38% on MTEB(Law, v1) under 1B parameters.
AI.motivation: Address the need for efficient, high-performance legal-domain retrieval models that can run in resource-constrained environments, bridging the gap between large LMs and practical deployment.
AI.method: Two-stage training: (1) distill knowledge from a larger teacher into a compact student; (2) domain-specific fine-tuning with hard negative mining. Data: 3.4M query-passage pairs with 150k human-curated samples across diverse legal jurisdictions. Inference: architecture supports multiple quantization levels (BF16, INT8, binary) for efficient deployment.
AI.result: Achieves 75.11% on the Massive Legal Embedding Benchmark (MLEB) and 64.38% on MTEB(Law, v1), competitive among models under 1B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific training with high-quality data and distillation can yield strong performance for specialized domains; quantization enables deployment in resource-limited settings.

title: Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection: A Survey
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Big Data
summary: Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection (MMAD) detects rare abnormal events from heterogeneous data sources and is increasingly used in safety- and reliability-critical applications such as industrial inspection and cybersecurity. Yet the literature is fragmented across domains and modality combinations, and existing surveys usually group methods by architecture rather than by how abnormality is defined and separated in multi-modal settings. We survey MMAD from an assumption-driven perspective. We formalize the problem, identify five intrinsic characteristics underlying its core challenges, and organize prior work into two complementary paradigms. The first, normality-assumption methods, models regularity via representation learning, cross-modal alignment, and knowledge enhancement. The second, anomaly-assumption methods, sharpens decision boundaries through coarse-grained, structural, and semantic anomaly injection. We also investigate how foundation models are reshaping MMAD through scalable pretraining, flexible cross-modal transfer, and emerging reasoning capabilities. Finally, we compile representative benchmarks and evaluation protocols across domains and highlight open problems and future directions for robust, adaptive, and interpretable MMAD systems.

AI.tldr: A principled, assumption-driven survey of MMAD that organizes methods into two paradigms—normality-assumption and anomaly-assumption—while examining foundation models, benchmarks, and future directions.
AI.motivation: To address fragmentation of MMAD literature across domains and modalities by providing a formalized, assumption-based taxonomy and a unified perspective for how abnormality is defined and detected in multi-modal data.
AI.method: Formalize the MMAD problem, identify five intrinsic characteristics that define core challenges, and categorize prior work into two complementary paradigms (normality-assumption and anomaly-assumption); discuss the impact of foundation models; compile representative benchmarks and evaluation protocols.
AI.result: A cohesive taxonomy and synthesis of MMAD methods across modalities, highlighting the strengths and limitations of both paradigms, providing guidelines, benchmarking resources, and identifying open problems and future directions for robust, adaptive, and interpretable MMAD systems.
AI.conclusion: MMAD is progressing with two complementary paradigms that address different aspects of abnormality; scalable pretraining and cross-modal transfer from foundation models enhance capabilities; ongoing efforts should focus on robustness, adaptability, and interpretability, aided by standardized benchmarks and evaluation protocols.

title: ExFold: Unified Expert Folding for Training-Free MoE Prefill-Decode Acceleration
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity for strong quality while keeping per-token compute bounded through sparse expert activation. Yet low-latency MoE serving is increasingly challenging, because it spans two inference phases with fundamentally different bottlenecks: prefill is dominated by token-wise expert computation, whereas decode is constrained by memory traffic from the batch-wise activated expert set. However, existing training-free acceleration methods optimize only a single resource proxy, either the experts each token executes or the experts a batch activates, and either discard the excluded experts' contribution or leave it only implicitly approximated. In this paper, we propose ExFold, a unified training-free expert-folding framework for jointly accelerating MoE prefill and decode. ExFold casts both prefill and decode as one budgeted output-approximation problem: execute only a phase-specific constrained expert set while projecting the contribution of budget-excluded experts onto retained experts using calibrated scalar projectors. Motivated by the observation that many expert outputs are directionally aligned but differ in magnitude, ExFold calibrates a pairwise scalar-projector matrix on unlabeled data and uses it at inference time to fold excluded expert contributions into retained experts. Under this view, prefill acceleration becomes token-level Top-K folding, and decode acceleration becomes batch-level expert-pool folding. The two phases differ only in how retained experts are selected, while excluded contributions are recovered by one shared folding mechanism. We implement ExFold as a plug-and-play plugin in vLLM, with a lightweight expert-folding CUDA kernel, delivering up to 1.41x TTFT and 2.45x TPOT speedups while retaining about 99% of the original average quality.

AI.tldr: ExFold is a training-free, unified expert-folding framework for Mixture-of-Experts models that accelerates both prefill (token-level) and decode (batch-level) by folding excluded experts into retained ones using calibrated scalar projectors, achieving up to 1.41x TTFT and 2.45x TPOT speedups with ~99% quality retention.
AI.motivation: MoE models face two distinct inference bottlenecks: prefill (token-wise expert computation) and decode (memory traffic from batch-wise activated experts). Existing training-free accelerations optimize a single resource proxy and neglect the full contribution of excluded experts. A unified approach is needed to accelerate both phases without sacrificing model quality.
AI.method: Cast prefill and decode as a joint budgeted output-approximation problem. During each phase, select a constrained set of retained experts; fold the contributions of budget-excluded experts onto retained ones via a calibrated pairwise scalar-projector matrix learned on unlabeled data. This yields token-level Top-K folding for prefill and batch-level folding for decode, with a single folding mechanism for all excluded contributions. Implemented as a plug-in in vLLM with a CUDA kernel.
AI.result: Up to 1.41x speedup in TTFT and 2.45x speedup in TPOT, while preserving about 99% of the original average quality.
AI.conclusion: ExFold provides a practical, training-free, plug-in solution that unifies prefill and decode acceleration through a shared folding mechanism, delivering substantial latency reductions with minimal quality loss.

title: GaussVLA: Geometry-Aware Spatial Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models encode visual observations as flat 2D patch tokens that carry no intrinsic geometric structure, and augmenting them with dense monocular depth injects per-pixel scalar values that encode neither surface orientation nor geometric confidence. This leaves the policy with limited structured spatial reasoning for action prediction. We propose GaussVLA, a Mamba-based VLA that incorporates two custom modules: Gaussian Spatial Tokenizer (GST) to lift frozen semantic and depth features into compact 3D Gaussian tokens, pools geometrically salient regions with learned queries, and \emph{Depth-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT)} that performs structured, non-autoregressive geometric reasoning under language and flow-time conditioning. Across both simulation and real-world evaluations, GaussVLA demonstrates strong spatial-manipulation performance while remaining parameter-efficient. On LIBERO, it achieves 93.5% average success and 100.0% success on the Spatial suite with only 200M parameters, improving over SpatialVLA by 19.7% relative average success while remaining significantly more parameter-efficient.

AI.tldr: GaussVLA introduces two modules (GST and DA-CoT) to convert semantic+depth features into 3D Gaussian tokens and perform non-autoregressive geometric reasoning, yielding state-of-the-art, parameter-efficient spatial manipulation on LIBERO.
AI.motivation: VLA models use flat 2D patch tokens with depth, which lacks intrinsic geometry and structured spatial reasoning for manipulation tasks. There is a need for compact, geometry-aware representations and reasoning in VLA systems.
AI.method: Propose Gaussian Spatial Tokenizer (GST) that lifts frozen semantic and depth features into compact 3D Gaussian tokens and pools geometrically salient regions with learned queries; introduce Depth-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT) that conducts structured, non-autoregressive geometric reasoning under language and flow-time conditioning. The approach is Mamba-based and aims for parameter efficiency.
AI.result: GaussVLA achieves strong spatial manipulation performance across simulation and real-world tests. On LIBERO, it attains 93.5% average success and 100.0% success on the Spatial suite with only 200M parameters, improving SpatialVLA by 19.7% relative average success while remaining more parameter-efficient.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating GST and DA-CoT yields a geometry-aware VLA model that is both effective and parameter-efficient, offering a robust alternative to dense monocular depth-based approaches for spatial manipulation tasks.

title: Fusing Perceptual Vision Experts with Multimodal Large Language Models for Explainable Plant Disease Diagnosis: From Benchmark Imagery to Real-World Robotic Field Validation
summary: Accurate field plant disease diagnosis requires reliable fusion of uncertain and conflicting perceptual evidence. We present the Hybrid Hierarchical Multi-Agent Framework (H$^{2}$MAF), combining decision-level fusion of EfficientNet-B3 and ConvNeXt-Tiny with semantic arbitration by open-weight multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Gemma 4 E4B and Qwen3.5 4B, using structured JSON evidence to generate explainable diagnoses, risk levels, treatment urgency, and financial exposure. (H$^{2}$MAF) is evaluated on 14,364 images (1,370 test images) across PlantDoc (2,922 images, 27 classes) and two non-public, continuously captured Cornell robot-acquired field datasets: Stage 2 (20 GB; 4,215 images) and Stage 4 (40 GB; 7,227 images), covering Early Blight, Late Blight, and Septoria Leaf Spot under uncontrolled field conditions. On PlantDoc, Gemma improves accuracy from 63.9% to 68.5%, achieving +7.6 points on the 41.7% CNN-conflict subset. Cornell accuracies reach 99.3% and 98.9%, with only 1.7-4.1% disagreement, demonstrating conflict-dependent MLLM utility. The critical-risk error of gemma is 0.14-0.5 points, whereas Qwen overflags by 3.5-14.4 points. These results establish MLLM arbitration as a promising, yet calibration-dependent, approach for explainable agricultural AI and robotic field decision support. Github Link: https://github.com/Applied-AI-Research-Lab/Explainable-AI-Plant-Disease-Detection

AI.tldr: Hybrid Hierarchical Multi-Agent Framework (H2MAF) fuses EfficientNet-B3 and ConvNeXt-Tiny with open-weight multimodal LLMs (Gemma 4 E4B, Qwen3.5 4B) using structured JSON evidence to deliver explainable plant-disease diagnoses, risk, urgency, and financial exposure in field conditions.
AI.motivation: Address uncertainty and conflict in perceptual evidence for field plant-disease diagnosis by integrating CNN-based vision with semantic arbitration from multimodal LLMs to produce explainable, actionable outputs.
AI.method: Decision-level fusion of two CNN backbones (EfficientNet-B3, ConvNeXt-Tiny) fed into open-weight MLLMs (Gemma 4 E4B, Qwen3.5 4B) using structured JSON evidence. The MLLMs generate diagnoses, risk levels, treatment urgency, and financial exposure. Evaluated on 14,364 images from PlantDoc (1,370 test) and two Cornell robot-acquired datasets (Stage 2 and Stage 4). Diseases: Early Blight, Late Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot under uncontrolled field conditions.
AI.result: Gemma improves PlantDoc accuracy from 63.9% to 68.5%; +7.6 points on a CNN-conflict subset (41.7% of data). Cornell datasets achieve 99.3% and 98.9% accuracy with 1.7–4.1% disagreement. Critical-risk error for Gemma 0.14–0.5 points; Qwen overflags by 3.5–14.4 points. Demonstrates conflict-dependent utility of MLLM arbitration for explainable field AI and robotic decision support.
AI.conclusion: MLLM arbitration is promising for explainable agricultural AI but calibration-dependent. The approach shows strong performance gains and actionable explanations, with caveats related to model calibration and potential over/under-flagging by different LLMs.

title: Sequential Euclidean tree construction with exponential memory: distributional performance and worst-case guarantees
summary:
Let $p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_N$ be points of the unit ball of $\mathbb R^d$, processed in a prescribed order. We study the insertion cost $\sum_{i=1}^N\lVert p_i-x_{i-1}\rVert^α$, where each $x_{i-1}$ is computed from the previously observed points. The input-order path is sensitive to the input distribution but can repeatedly pay the diameter under adversarial input. The center star has controlled worst-case scale but ignores the observed sequence. We compress the past into one point through $x_0=p_0$ and $x_i=γx_{i-1}+(1-γ)p_i$, where $0\leqγ\leq1$. Thus $x_i$ is an exponentially weighted memory of the input, maintained with one $d$-dimensional point of working state.
  For independent uniform points, the stationary insertion length is nonincreasing in the usual stochastic order as $γ$ increases. If $d\geq2$ and $α>0$, every optimal constant parameter for $N$ insertions satisfies $1-γ_N^*=Θ(N^{-1/2})$. We determine its asymptotic constant and the resulting $\sqrt N$ correction, with explicit bounds in $d$ and $α$. For $α=1$, the leading expected tree length equals that of the center star and is strictly smaller than those of the endpoint constructions. For $α=2$, the minimizer is unique for $N\geq2$, with $1-γ_N^*=N^{-1/2}-\tfrac12N^{-1}+O(N^{-3/2})$.
  For arbitrary input sequences and fixed $0\leqγ<1$, the largest asymptotic mean cost is $(2/(1+γ))^α$ for $0<α\leq3$, strictly below the path value when $γ>0$. Among fixed nonnegative weighting rules whose contributing points have the same average distance in the input order from the most recent point, exponential weighting is within a factor smaller than $1.161^α$ of the best adversarial value in dimension at least two; this ratio tends to one as that average distance grows.

AI.tldr: Exponential memory (x_i = γ x_{i-1} + (1-γ)p_i) reduces online insertion costs in the unit ball; the optimal γ for N insertions scales as 1-γ_N^* = Θ(N^{-1/2}) in dimension d≥2 and α>0 with explicit constants, and exponential weighting is near-optimal against adversarial inputs across regimes; the work provides detailed comparisons to center-star, path, and endpoint constructions, and establishes bounds for fixed γ and arbitrary sequences, including special cases α=1 and α=2.
AI.motivation: To understand how summarizing the past with a single memory point affects insertion costs under both stochastic (i.i.d. uniform) and adversarial input sequences, and to quantify the trade-offs between adaptivity (memory) and stability (low sensitivity to order).
AI.method: Introduce an exponentially weighted memory: x_0=p_0, x_i=γ x_{i-1}+(1-γ)p_i with 0≤γ<1. Analyze i.i.d. uniform inputs in the unit ball (d≥2) to derive the stationary insertion length and optimal γ_N^*. Obtain asymptotics 1-γ_N^*=Θ(N^{-1/2}) with constants depending on d, α; evaluate α=1 and α=2 cases; compare with center-star, path, and endpoint constructions. For arbitrary input sequences and fixed γ, bound the largest asymptotic mean cost as (2/(1+γ))^α for 0<α≤3; compare fixed γ rules by ratio to best adversarial value and derive exponential weighting as near-optimal with factor <1.161^α; discuss behavior as average distance grows.
AI.result: Derived that for d≥2 and α>0, the optimal constant γ_N^* satisfies 1-γ_N^*=Θ(N^{-1/2}); determined the asymptotic constant and the √N correction, with explicit bounds in d and α. For α=1, the leading expected tree length matches that of the center star and is smaller than endpoint constructions; for α=2, the minimizer is unique for N≥2 and 1-γ_N^*=N^{-1/2}-1/2 N^{-1}+O(N^{-3/2}). For arbitrary inputs with fixed γ, the largest asymptotic mean cost is (2/(1+γ))^α (0<α≤3), strictly below the path value when γ>0. Among fixed nonnegative weighting rules with the same average input-order distance, exponential weighting is within a factor <1.161^α of the best adversarial value in dimension ≥2, approaching 1 as the average distance grows.
AI.conclusion: Exponential memory strikes a favorable balance between adaptivity and memory usage, achieving near-optimal insertion costs across stochastic and adversarial regimes. The results yield concrete asymptotics for optimal γ, show when the exponential rule matches or outperforms baseline constructions, and provide tight bounds and constants as functions of d and α that guide practical parameter choice.

title: VLM-based automatic multi-granularity graph representation of building layouts for design informatics
summary: Architectural floorplan images encode rich relational knowledge among functional spaces, which underpins design retrieval, knowledge-based reasoning, and BIM enrichment through the building lifecycle. However, it remains challenging to automatically construct task-adaptive graph representations for public buildings. To address this gap, we first define a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoGs) for public building layouts. Methodologically, we present a Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based automatic LoG construction through node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening. VLM-generated representations are systematically evaluated and tested in real-world tasks, using 147 academic library floorplans worldwide as a case study. Experiments showed VLM-generated graphs were broadly consistent with human-labeled graphs (matched node ratio >= 92%; 509.3 s per floor plan for three-LoG graph generation). Meso-grained graphs yield the best node-level zone prediction (Macro F1 = 0.647, at 65% of fine-grained complexity), while coarse-grained graphs are most effective for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman's \r{ho} = 0.610, at 16% of fine-grained complexity). By enabling scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout information from floorplan images, this study advances design informatics by converting plan images into knowledge representations, thereby enhancing the utilization of design information across the building life cycle.

AI.tldr: Proposes a multi-granularity Level-of-Graphs (LoG) framework and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) pipeline to automatically construct task-adaptive graphs from public building floorplans, validated on 147 academic library plans with high node-level match and granularity-dependent task gains.
AI.motivation: Public building floorplans lack scalable, annotation-free methods to derive task-adaptive graphs for retrieval, reasoning, and BIM integration across the building lifecycle.
AI.method: Define multi-granularity LoGs; develop a VLM-based automatic LoG construction pipeline including node identification, edge inference, text parsing, and graph coarsening; evaluate on 147 academic library floorplans to compare against human labels.
AI.result: VLM-generated graphs matched human-labeled graphs with node match ratio ≥ 92%; ~509.3 seconds per floor plan for three-LoG generation. Mesoscopic (meso) graphs maximized node-level zone prediction (Macro F1 = 0.647 at 65% fine-grained complexity); coarse-grained graphs best for graph-level layout quality evaluation (Spearman’s rho = 0.610 at 16% fine-grained complexity).
AI.conclusion: The approach enables scalable, annotation-free extraction of structured layout information from floorplans, converting images into knowledge representations and enhancing design information utilization across the building lifecycle.

title: When Does Frequency Decomposition Benefit Physics-Informed Neural Networks? A Preliminary Ablation Study
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) often have high-frequency and multi-scale features that neural networks struggle to approximate. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) build the governing equations directly into training, but suffer from spectral bias: they learn low-frequency components faster than high-frequency ones. Techniques such as Fourier feature embeddings and sinusoidal activations address this, but most studies assume they help across the board without checking which spectral regimes actually benefit. We introduce a dual-branch, spectrally-gated architecture (DBSG-PINN) that splits low- and high-frequency components into separate subnetworks joined by an adaptive gate, and use it to run a partially controlled ablation of frequency decomposition and spectral routing. We test this on five one-dimensional benchmark PDEs, ranging from smooth, single-scale problems to oscillatory, multi-scale ones. Frequency decomposition helps most on the spectrally complex benchmarks, cutting relative $L_2$ error by up to $59.2\%$ on a multimodal wave problem, but gives little benefit on smoother PDEs. On one benchmark (1D Wave), it performs substantially worse than a simpler fixed-combination variant. The gate's benefit scales with how spectrally rich the target solution is: the full model's advantage over the ablations is largest on multi-scale benchmarks and smallest (or negative) on single-scale ones, consistent with the gate exploiting frequency structure rather than acting as noise,though we do not directly visualize or quantify its spatial activations in this study. All results come from a single training seed across five 1D benchmarks, so we present this as an exploratory study meant to raise questions rather than answer them, and outline the additional seeds and benchmarks needed to test whether the pattern holds.

AI.tldr: A dual-branch spectrally gated PINN (DBSG-PINN) with low/high frequency subnetworks and an adaptive gate is tested as an exploratory ablation study across five 1D PDE benchmarks. Frequency decomposition helps on spectrally complex problems (up to ~59% relative L2 error reduction) but offers little to no benefit on smooth, single-scale PDEs; in one case (1D Wave) it underperforms a fixed-combination variant. The gate’s advantage scales with spectral richness; results are based on a single seed, highlighting the need for more seeds/benchmarks to validate patterns.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from spectral bias, learning low frequencies faster than high ones. While Fourier features and sinusoidal activations help, it is unclear which spectral regimes gain from frequency decomposition. The study aims to identify when spectral routing benefits PINNs and how adaptive gating interacts with frequency structure.
AI.method: Propose DBSG-PINN: two subnetworks dedicated to low- and high-frequency content, linked by an adaptive gate to form the final solution. Conduct a partially controlled ablation of frequency decomposition and spectral routing across five 1D PDE benchmarks (ranging from smooth to oscillatory/multi-scale). Compare full DBSG-PINN with ablated variants (e.g., fixed-combination, no gating). Use a single training seed for all experiments. Evaluate using relative L2 error across problems.
AI.result: Frequency decomposition reduced relative L2 error by up to 59.2% on a spectrally complex multimodal wave problem; little to no benefit on smoother PDEs. On 1D Wave, the method performed substantially worse than a simpler fixed-combination variant. The gate’s benefit grows with the spectral richness of the target solution; the full model has the largest advantage on multi-scale benchmarks and the smallest or negative advantage on single-scale ones. All results derive from a single seed, framing the work as exploratory and identifying the need for more seeds/benchmarks to test the pattern.
AI.conclusion: The gate likely leverages spectral structure rather than merely acting as noise. The study is exploratory and suggests conditions under which spectral routing helps PINNs, but more seeds and benchmarks are required to substantiate the observed patterns and generalize beyond the tested 1D problems.

title: ROS2 Connect: A new ROS2 over WAN Solution
comment: Proceedings of the 8th International Workshop on Robotics Software Engineering co-located with the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ROSE '26)
summary: The Robot Operating System 2 (ROS2) has become a widely adopted framework for the development of distributed robotic systems. However, its communication architecture, based on DDS and RTPS, relies on multicast discovery mechanisms that are typically unavailable in wide-area network (WAN) environments, making remote operation challenging. This work presents ROS2 Connect, a WebSocket-based communication framework that enables transparent and secure ROS2 interaction across routed networks without requiring modifications to network infrastructure or DDS configurations. The proposed client-server architecture supports bidirectional exchange of topics, services, actions, and system data while integrating authentication and access control mechanisms. Experimental evaluation over a real WAN connection demonstrates significantly lower latency, higher stability, and improved scalability compared to existing solutions, including DDS Router, rosbridge and Zenoh. Initial results show that ROS2 Connect provides a reliable foundation for teleoperation and distributed robotics applications over wide-area networks.

AI.tldr: ROS2 Connect offers a WebSocket-based bridge enabling secure, bidirectional ROS2 communication over routed networks, avoiding DDS/RTPS multicast requirements and infrastructure changes, and outperforming DDS Router, rosbridge, and Zenoh in WAN tests.
AI.motivation: Overcoming ROS2’s DDS/RTPS multicast discovery limitations in wide-area networks to enable remote operation and scalable distributed robotics without modifying network infra or DDS config.
AI.method: A client-server architecture using WebSocket to transparently exchange ROS2 topics, services, actions, and system data with integrated authentication and access control. No changes to DDS configurations or network infrastructure. Evaluation conducted on a real WAN connection, comparing latency, stability, and scalability against DDS Router, rosbridge, and Zenoh.
AI.result: Experimental WAN tests show significantly lower latency, higher stability, and improved scalability relative to the compared solutions. Initial results indicate that ROS2 Connect can serve as a reliable foundation for teleoperation and distributed robotics over WANs.
AI.conclusion: ROS2 Connect represents a promising approach to WAN-enabled ROS2 operation, offering secure, cross-network interoperability without DDS modifications and with favorable performance. Further work could explore broader scalability, security hardening, and deployment in diverse WAN topologies.

title: A Lightweight Multimodal Vision-Language Framework for Early-Stage Anatomical Green Fruit Classification in Commercial Orchards
summary: Accurate identification of early-stage apple fruitlet anatomical structures, including the calyx, fruitlet body, and peduncle, is essential for robotic thinning, crop-load management, and other precision orchard operations. This study presents a lightweight multimodal vision-language framework that adapts TinyCLIP for fine-grained fruitlet anatomy classification in complex orchard environments. A dataset of 600 high-resolution RGB images collected from Scilate and Scifresh apple orchards was converted into 224 x 224 image patches and annotated for three anatomical classes. Domain-specific language prompts, such as ``a photo of a class,'' were used to guide multimodal alignment between orchard imagery and horticultural structures. A sliding-window inference strategy with a stride of 112 pixels aggregates patch-level predictions into spatial heatmaps, enabling interpretable whole-image localization of fruitlet components relevant to robotic thinning. Patch-level evaluation on an NVIDIA T4 GPU achieved F1-scores of 0.95 for calyx, 0.98 for fruitlet, and 0.85 for peduncle, with a macro-F1 score of 0.93. Deployment-oriented optimization using ONNX and TensorRT enabled efficient inference on NVIDIA Jetson hardware, preserved accuracy under INT8 quantization, and supported model sizes of approximately 127-137 MB with millisecond-level patch inference. These results demonstrate that lightweight vision-language models can provide interpretable and edge-deployable perception for automated fruitlet analysis and future robotic thinning systems. The source code and implementation details are publicly available at https://github.com/WilliamBu1/A-Lightweight-Vision-Language-Model-for-Early-Stage-Fruitlet-Classification-in-Apple-Orchards.

AI.tldr: A lightweight TinyCLIP-based multimodal framework performs fine-grained apple fruitlet anatomy classification (calyx, fruitlet body, peduncle) using patch-based analysis and domain-specific prompts, producing spatial heatmaps for localization. Achieves high patch-level F1 scores (0.95–0.98; 0.85 for peduncle) and macro-F1 of 0.93, with ONNX/TensorRT edge deployment on Jetson and INT8 quantization; code available.
AI.motivation: Accurate, interpretable identification of early-stage fruitlet structures is crucial for robotic thinning and precision orchard operations in complex field environments. A lightweight, edge-deployable, multimodal approach could improve robustness over traditional vision methods.
AI.method: Adaptation of TinyCLIP for fine-grained fruitlet anatomy. A dataset of 600 high-resolution RGB images from Scilate/Scifresh orchards is patchified to 224×224 and annotated for calyx, fruitlet body, and peduncle. Domain-specific prompts (e.g., 'a photo of a class') guide vision-language alignment. A sliding-window inference (stride=112) aggregates patch predictions into spatial heatmaps for whole-image localization. Evaluation on NVIDIA T4 shows strong patch-level performance. Deployment uses ONNX/TensorRT with INT8 support, achieving small model sizes (~127–137 MB) and millisecond patch inference for edge devices.
AI.result: Patch-level F1: calyx 0.95, fruitlet 0.98, peduncle 0.85; macro-F1 = 0.93. Spatial heatmaps enable interpretable localization. Edge-friendly deployment: ONNX/TensorRT, INT8, Jetson-compatible with minimal latency and compact model size.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that lightweight vision-language models can deliver interpretable, edge-deployable perception for early-stage fruitlet analysis and robotic thinning systems, with publicly available source code.

title: SIMGUIDE: Procedurally Grounded Multi-Context Representations for Personalized Agent Planning
summary: Personalized AI agents overwhelmingly treat users as single entities: a flat profile concatenated into a prompt. This fails when the same person holds different priorities across life contexts -- and fails catastrophically when those priorities conflict. The core problem is not that agents lack information about users; it is that the format of user representations determines whether an agent can act on that information at all. We introduce SIMGUIDE, a method that structures user context into typed, domain-specific blocks called Sims and grounds each constraint with procedural examples drawn from past decisions. To evaluate this, we construct SIMBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks where the correct plan depends on which user context is active -- a property no existing benchmark tests. Declarative Sim constraints alone do not outperform retrieval-based personalization (RAG). Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG on GPT-4o (+7.9 Preference Adherence points, $p = 0.013$), and this advantage replicates on 100 $τ$-bench tasks across both GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet~4.5 ($p \leq 0.023$). At the parametric level, the same principle holds: training distribution dominates whether parametric adaptation succeeds at all. Task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves generation quality by 12.8 ROUGE-L points over the unadapted base model, and routing adapters by Sim type rather than user identity adds a further 7.3 points, robust to 28% routing error. Representation format -- not representation content -- is the first-order design variable.

AI.tldr: SIMGUIDE structures user context into typed, domain-specific Sims to ground constraints; introduces SIMBENCH with 47 tasks; procedurally grounded context outperforms retrieval-based personalization; parametric adaptation (LoRA, routing adapters) yields further gains; key insight: representation format, not content, is the primary design variable.
AI.motivation: Current personalized AI agents treat users as flat prompts, failing when different life contexts require conflicting priorities. A structured, domain-specific representation is needed to enable agents to reason and act on user constraints across contexts.
AI.method: Introduce SIMGUIDE with Sims: typed, domain-specific blocks of constraints grounded by procedural examples from past decisions. Build SIMBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 47 preference-conditioned planning tasks where active user context matters. Compare declarative Sim constraints to retrieval-based personalization (RAG). Evaluate with GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5; analyze parametric adaptation via LoRA fine-tuning and routing adapters by Sim type.
AI.result: Procedurally grounded Sims outperform RAG on GPT-4o (+7.9 Preference Adherence points, p=0.013) and replicate on 100 τ-bench tasks across GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (p≤0.023). Task-matched LoRA fine-tuning improves ROUGE-L by 12.8 points; routing adapters by Sim type add 7.3 points; robust to 28% routing error. Representation format—not content—emerges as the first-order design variable.
AI.conclusion: Structured, domain-specific user representations (Sims) are crucial for effective preference adherence and planning. The format of user context dominates performance gains and generalizes across models and tasks, suggesting a shift from flat prompts toward typed, procedural-grounded context blocks.

title: FAMPWQ: Fisher Information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization for Effective LLM Inference
summary: Recent years have witnessed remarkable achievements of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multiple domains, while the excessive resource requirements of LLMs hinder the deployment on resource-constrained devices. Although model quantization stands out as an effective approach, conventional quantization approaches typically incur severe performance degradation due to uniform bit-width or simple heuristic sensitivity evaluation. In this paper, we propose a novel Fisher information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization approach, i.e., FAMPWQ, which performs layer-adaptive weight quantization for effective LLM inference on commodity GPUs. First, we propose a system model with a novel Fisher information metric to measure the layer-wise sensitivity to quantization. Second, we propose a reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocator in FAMPWQ, which generates an adaptive bit-width allocation strategy based on the Fisher information sensitivity metric. Extensive experiments on 7 models and 5 benchmarks demonstrate that FAMPWQ significantly outperforms 7 baseline approaches in terms of PPL (up to 3.39 smaller), accuracy (up to 6.87% higher), and LLM-as-a-judge comparison (up to 76% win rate).

AI.tldr: Layer-adaptive mixed-precision weight quantization for LLMs guided by Fisher information and an RL-based bit-width allocator, achieving significant gains over baselines in perplexity, accuracy, and LLM-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLMs have high resource demands; uniform quantization degrades performance. A layer-aware, information-driven approach can reduce model size and compute with minimal accuracy loss on resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: Introduce FAMPWQ with a Fisher-information-based metric to quantify layer sensitivity to quantization. Use a reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocator to assign adaptive bit-widths per layer. System model integrates Fisher sensitivity and mixed-precision quantization. Evaluate on 7 models and 5 benchmarks.
AI.result: FAMPWQ outperforms 7 baselines on key metrics: perplexity reduced by up to 3.39x, accuracy increased by up to 6.87%, and LLM-as-a-judge win rate up to 76%.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, Fisher-information-guided mixed-precision quantization with RL-based bit-width allocation enables more accurate and efficient LLM inference on commodity GPUs, surpassing several baselines.

title: Extending Ground-Constraint LiDAR-IMU Calibration to Tilted Surfaces in a Continuous-Time Framework
comment: 8 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to Robotics & Automation Letters
summary: This paper presents a novel method that extends targetless LiDAR-IMU calibration for ground vehicles to non- flat environments. Calibration typically necessitates full exci- tation of the sensor rig, a requirement that is not fulfilled by ground vehicles in normal operation. To address the degenerate planar motion, state-of-the-art methods propose residuals that assume the colinearity of the gravity and physical surface normal vectors, restricting usage to cases where the ground is assumed flat. This paper proposes ground-plane residuals that do not require this assumption, and are applicable for planar motion on a tilted surface. Results are demonstrated on a dataset collected from a Husky ground vehicle, on the M2DGR dataset, as well as on an offroad vehicle dataset. Repeatability is shown to be improved both in tilted and flat-ground scenarios, with strong improvement demonstrated for the tilted case. The implementation and experiments are open-sourced at https://github.com/vkorotkine/licalib_tilted_ground.

AI.tldr: Extends targetless LiDAR-IMU calibration to non-flat environments by introducing ground-plane residuals that work with tilted planes, improving repeatability on tilted and flat ground; code available.
AI.motivation: Ground vehicle calibration suffers from degenerate planar motion in normal operation where prior methods assume gravity aligns with surface normals (flat ground). A method that handles tilted or non-flat ground improves calibration robustness.
AI.method: Introduce ground-plane residuals that do not rely on gravity–surface normal colinearity and are valid for planar motion on tilted surfaces, enabling targetless calibration in more realistic driving conditions.
AI.result: Validated on Husky, M2DGR, and offroad datasets; repeatability improves in tilted and flat-ground scenarios, with strong gains for tilted ground.
AI.conclusion: Ground-plane residuals enable robust, repeatable targetless LiDAR-IMU calibration in non-flat environments and tilted planes; implementation is open-source.

title: Synergising Local Geo-Environmental Characteristics with Spatial Context for Enhancing Landslide Susceptibility Mapping
summary: Data-driven methods are widely used in landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) because they can effectively model the complex relationships between landslides and geo-environmental conditions. Existing data-driven approaches generally follow two types of data representations. Pixel-based models focus solely on the geo-environmental characteristics of a specific landslide but neglect the influence of its surrounding environment. Patch-based models incorporate surrounding spatial context but may include pixels with weak or no spatial relevance to the target landslide location. To address this limitation, this study proposes a Local-Geo and Spatial Context Fusion (LGSCF) strategy, which synergises the geo-environmental characteristics of landslide points with their corresponding spatial context through a feature-wise modulation mechanism. We tested the LGSCF strategy by integrating it into several representative convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, creating nine different LGSCF-based models. The study area covers approximately 2644 km2 across Jenai and Sinyi Townships in Nantou County, Taiwan, and the dataset comprises 5332 landslide samples and an equal number of non-landslide samples. The results show that LGSCF-based models consistently outperform their original versions, achieving F1-scores up to 87.09% and AUC values up to 0.9472. Furthermore, the susceptibility maps produced by LGSCF-based models show that known landslides are more accurately concentrated in "very high" susceptibility zones with fewer misclassifications. These findings demonstrate that our fusion strategy can significantly improve the accuracy of landslide susceptibility mapping.

AI.tldr: A Local-Geo and Spatial Context Fusion (LGSCF) strategy is proposed to fuse landslide point geo-environmental features with surrounding spatial context via feature-wise modulation in CNNs, improving landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM). Nine LGSCF-based models outperform their baselines on 2644 km2 in Nantou County, with F1 up to 87.09% and AUC up to 0.9472; maps more accurately concentrate known landslides in very-high susceptibility zones.
AI.motivation: Pixel-based LSM models neglect surrounding environment; patch-based models include context but may include irrelevant pixels. A need exists to fuse local geo-features with spatial context in a discriminative, context-aware manner to enhance LSM accuracy.
AI.method: Introduce LGSCF (Local-Geo and Spatial Context Fusion) using a feature-wise modulation mechanism to combine geo-environmental features of landslide points with their spatial context. Integrate LGSCF into nine CNN architectures to create nine LGSCF-based models. Study area ~2644 km2 (Jenai and Sinyi Townships, Nantou County, Taiwan) with 5332 landslide and 5332 non-landslide samples. Evaluation via F1 and AUC; qualitative analysis of susceptibility maps.
AI.result: LGSCF-based models consistently outperform their original CNN counterparts, achieving F1-scores up to 87.09% and AUC values up to 0.9472. Susceptibility maps show known landslides concentrated in very-high zones with fewer misclassifications.
AI.conclusion: The fusion of local geo-environmental features with spatial context through a feature-wise modulation mechanism substantially improves landslide susceptibility mapping, demonstrating the effectiveness and generality of the LGSCF approach across multiple CNN architectures.

title: Reliable LLM-Powered Decision Engines for Large-Scale Supply Chain Operations: Architecture, Safety, and Performance Guarantees
summary: Current large-scale supply chains are highly uncertain, dynamic, and disruption prone that are challenging to serve up timely and resilient decisions through traditional rule-based and optimization-only systems. The increasing supply of heterogeneous data sources, such as transactional demand signals and unstructured disruption report, presents a chance of intelligent systems, which could reason, adapt and optimize at the same time. A hybrid architecture that combines large language models (LLMs) with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering is proposed in this paper as a performance of a Decision Engine, which is called LLM-Powered Decision Engine (LLM-DE). In comparison to purely data-driven or heuristic solutions, LLM-DE integrates semantic reasoning with LLM with a set of performance and safety guarantees that allow safe decision-making in large-scale supply chain processes. The suggested framework enables the end-to-end decision making such as demand forecasting, inventory optimization, and transportation routing and disruption mitigation. The findings affirm that language-based reasoning combined with optimization and formal constraints can be used to come up with not only smarter but also safer and more scalable supply chain decisions. This research provides a new architecture, a complete pipeline of algorithm, and a formulation based on mathematical constructs of the operational decision systems incorporating LLM. The proposed model offers a pragmatic and theoretical basis of the next-generation intelligent supply chain infrastructures that can be implemented to work dependably in the face of uncertainty and massive complexity.

AI.tldr: Proposes an LLM-powered decision engine (LLM-DE) that fuses LLM-based semantic reasoning with optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety filtering to enable end-to-end, safe, scalable supply chain decisions under uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Traditional rule-based/optimization-only systems struggle with uncertainty, data heterogeneity, and disruption; there is a need for reasoning, adaptation, and integrated decision-making over complex, data-rich supply chains.
AI.method: Hybrid architecture combining large language models with mathematical optimization, probabilistic forecasting, and safety-constrained decision filtering. It defines an end-to-end pipeline (demand forecasting, inventory optimization, routing, disruption mitigation) and provides a formal formulation and architecture for operational decision systems incorporating LLMs.
AI.result: Claims smarter, safer, and more scalable decisions by integrating semantic reasoning with optimization and formal constraints; offers a complete pipeline, algorithm, and mathematical formulation.
AI.conclusion: Presents a practical next-generation intelligent supply chain infrastructure with a principled balance of performance, safety, and scalability under uncertainty and large complexity.

title: MacroAgent: Regularity-Aware Macro Legalization with LLM-Agent-Designed Contour Algorithms
summary: Macros constitute a large part of the core area in modern very large-scale integration (VLSI) designs. Moreover, macro positions have a significant impact on the final quality of result (QoR), and macro legalization is typically the final step in determining the macro positions. However, existing approaches related to macro legalization either lack robustness or incur substantial computational costs or neglect the regularity between macros. To address these limitations, we introduce MacroAgent. The novel framework is a four-stage approach: clustering, contour generation, template matching, and inter-cluster refinement. We propose leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to discover multiple, effective heuristic regularity-aware contour algorithms. This framework successfully generates robust and effective algorithmic solutions for macro legalization. Compared with state-of-the-art macro legalization works, experimental results on TILOS and Chipyard benchmarks demonstrate a 2 to 8 fold improvement in layout regularity, a 3% to 5% reduction in routed wirelength with comparable congestion after global routing, and significantly better robustness with an acceptable runtime. Furthermore, end-to-end evaluation through Cadence Innovus place-and-route confirms that the regularity improvements translate into tangible PPA gains, including 2.9% lower routed wirelength and 68.3% TNS improvement over the DREAMPlace macro legalization baseline; it also achieves 1.8% lower routed wirelength when integrated into the Innovus macro placement flow.

AI.tldr: MacroAgent: a four-stage macro- legalization framework using LLM-discovered contour algorithms to improve layout regularity and PPA with robust performance and acceptable runtime.
AI.motivation: Macro legalization greatly impacts QoR in VLSI; current methods suffer from low robustness, high computational cost, or neglect macro regularity.
AI.method: Four-stage pipeline: clustering, contour generation, template matching, inter-cluster refinement. Leverages Large Language Models to discover multiple, effective regularity-aware contour algorithms. Evaluated on TILOS/Chipyard; compares against state-of-the-art macro legalization; integrates with Cadence Innovus for end-to-end P&R.
AI.result: 2–8× improvement in layout regularity; 3%–5% reduction in routed wirelength with comparable congestion after global routing; significantly better robustness with acceptable runtime. End-to-end PPA gains: 2.9% lower routed wirelength and 68.3% TNS improvement over DREAMPlace macro legalization baseline; 1.8% lower routed wirelength in Innovus macro placement flow.
AI.conclusion: MacroAgent demonstrates that LLM-guided, regularity-aware contour algorithms within a structured four-stage pipeline yield robust macro legalization with tangible PPA benefits across standard benchmarks and a commercial toolchain.

title: SkyDrive: Learning to Drive in a New City from Aerial Traffic Monitoring
summary: Autonomous driving has made remarkable progress through imitation learning with massive human demonstration data. However, a trained planner often degrades severely when applied to a new environment zero-shot, because of domain shifts in traffic regulations, road layout and driving behaviors. Therefore, adapting a trajectory planner to a new city typically requires resource-demanding local data collection with a vehicle sensor suite. In this work, we show that driving behavior can be learned from a scalable and efficient alternative. We introduce \emph{SkyDrive}, a framework that utilizes drone-based traffic monitoring to provide efficient supervision for autonomous driving agents in a new environment. While vehicle-based data collection logs the ego and its surroundings, an aerial platform naturally observes many road users simultaneously over an extended field of view. As a result, every vehicle can be a data source with grounded driving behavior, effectively scaling up the amount of supervision. Based on 137 hours of aerial traffic monitoring footage, we extract 650K driving samples and construct a benchmark for trajectory planners and motion predictors. Zero-shot experiments with multiple models reveal significant cross-city domain gaps, but many of them can be alleviated by limited supervision from the sky, e.g., 30 minutes of monitoring per location. Our findings show that aerial traffic monitoring is an efficient and scalable data source for adapting autonomous driving systems in new cities. Data and code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: SkyDrive uses drone-based traffic monitoring to provide scalable supervision for autonomous driving, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new cities. It builds a large aerial dataset (137 hours, 650k samples) and shows that limited sky supervision (around 30 minutes per location) can mitigate cross-city domain gaps. Data and code will be released.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving planners suffer from domain shifts when deployed in new cities; collecting vehicle-based data is expensive and time-consuming. A scalable, efficient supervision source is needed to adapt planners to different traffic regulations, road layouts, and driving behaviors.
AI.method: Leverage aerial traffic monitoring to observe multiple road users over a wide field of view. Extract driving samples from 137 hours of drone footage to build a large-scale dataset and a benchmark for trajectory planners and motion predictors. Evaluate zero-shot transfer across cities and study the effect of limited aerial supervision (e.g., ~30 minutes per location).
AI.result: The study reveals significant cross-city domain gaps in zero-shot transfer. Introducing limited aerial supervision substantially alleviates these gaps, improving adaptation. The dataset comprises 650k driving samples, enabling robust benchmarking for planners and predictors.
AI.conclusion: Aerial traffic monitoring is an efficient, scalable data source to adapt autonomous driving systems to new cities. The dataset and code will be publicly available, facilitating further research in domain adaptation and planner learning.

title: Targeting the Attention Heads Behind Object Hallucination in LLaVA
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the Actionable Interpretability Workshop, COLM 2026
summary: Vision-language models such as LLaVA-1.5-7B often hallucinate objects absent from the image when generating captions. We ask whether an interpretability diagnosis of this failure can guide a targeted fix, and we measure what that fix actually changes. We rank attention heads by how much their image attention drops around hallucinated object words, then screen the shortlist by ablating candidate heads and measuring the change in hallucination-token log probability, yielding a 32-head set. We restrict two interventions to these heads: a head-sliced LoRA adapter and an inference-time grounding controller. On 400 held-out COCO images, the combined method lowers CHAIRs (the fraction of captions with a hallucinated object) from 0.370 to 0.230 and CHAIRi (the fraction of hallucinated object mentions) from 0.156 to 0.096 (p < 0.001, paired sign-flip tests). Two controls sharpen attribution. A random-head LoRA control, matched layer-for-layer and trained identically, performs no better than the matched baseline on a separate 200-image control split, supporting the role of head selection rather than LoRA capacity. Under fixed decoding budgets, the CHAIR reduction persists and grows with budget (23% at 64 tokens to 58% at 128), arguing against a pure max-token or truncation artifact, although the method remains shorter and more conservative. The resulting behavior reduces unsupported object mentions while also lowering object recall (0.78 to 0.70). We present a diagnosis-to-intervention pipeline for object hallucination, and, more importantly, a controlled account of what acting on the diagnostic signal actually does: it localizes intervention sites with real, non-random leverage, reported as a behavioral profile rather than a single score.

AI.tldr: Interpretability-driven intervention to cure object hallucination in vision-language models by selecting influential attention heads and applying targeted fixes (head-sliced LoRA and grounding controller). Demonstrates causal leverage of a 32-head set, reducing CHAIR/CHAIRi on held-out COCO, with robust controls and budget-aware improvements; results indicate a diagnosist-to-intervention pipeline and a behavioral profile of intervention sites.
AI.motivation: To address object hallucination in image-captioning by establishing a causal link between diagnostic attention patterns and effective fixes, and to quantify what the intervention actually changes in model behavior.
AI.method: Rank image attention per head by the drop around hallucinated object words; ablate candidate heads to screen a 32-head shortlist by changes in hallucination-token log probability; apply two interventions on these heads: a head-sliced LoRA adapter and an inference-time grounding controller; evaluate on 400 held-out COCO images using CHAIR and CHAIRi metrics; include a random-head LoRA control and a matched-layer control on a separate 200-image split; test under fixed decoding budgets (64/128 tokens).
AI.result: CHAIR reduced from 0.370 to 0.230; CHAIRi reduced from 0.156 to 0.096 (p<0.001). Random-head control performs no better than baseline. With decoding budgets, CHAIR gains persist and grow (23% at 64 tokens to 58% at 128). Object recall decreases slightly (0.78 to 0.70).
AI.conclusion: Diagnose-to-intervention pipeline yields real leverage at localization sites; attribution controls confirm non-random effects; the approach provides a behavioral profile of where interventions work rather than a single-score metric, and demonstrates that targeted, interpretable interventions can meaningfully reduce hallucinations while revealing trade-offs.

title: AI-Powered Mental Health Chatbots in Africa: A Systematic Review and Culturally Adaptive Framework
summary: Mental health challenges in Africa remain under-addressed due to inadequate infrastructure, stigma, and a chronic shortage of professionals. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots are emerging globally as low-cost, accessible tools that can offer psychological support. This paper presents a systematic review of 52 empirical studies published between 2017 and 2025, critically analysing their cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance to African contexts. The findings demonstrate the potential of AI chatbots to improve accessibility, reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression, and expand psychosocial support, yet reveal limited African-specific adaptation. Most systems remain rooted in Western models and English-language designs, leaving critical gaps in local relevance, inclusivity, and sustainability. Based on the findings, the authors develop a Culturally Adaptive Digital Mental Health (CADMH) framework that integrates African cultural values, multilingual design, mobile-first optimisation, and ethical safeguards. The study highlights opportunities and barriers for integrating AI chatbots into African healthcare, offering guidance for research, practice, and policy.

AI.tldr: Systematic review of AI chatbots for mental health in Africa (2017-2025); finds Western/English bias; proposes CADMH framework for culturally adaptive design.
AI.motivation: To address Africa's under-addressed mental health via scalable AI tools and assess cultural/linguistic fit.
AI.method: Systematic review of 52 empirical studies from 2017-2025; critical analysis of cultural, linguistic, and infrastructural relevance; synthesis leads to framework.
AI.result: Evidence of potential to improve accessibility and reduce symptoms of anxiety/depression; but African-specific adaptation is limited; predominance of Western/English designs; CADMH framework proposed to address gaps.
AI.conclusion: AI chatbots can expand psychosocial support in Africa but require culturally adaptive, multilingual, mobile-first, and ethically safeguarded designs; policy-relevant guidance for integration.

title: CAT-GS: Balanced Multimodal Learning via Calibrated Gating and Fusion Surgery
comment: This article is accepted with minor revision in Neurocomputing Journal
summary: End-to-end training of multimodal neural networks often exhibits unstable neural dynamics characterized by three coupled failure modes that degrade learning: (i) modality imbalance, where one branch dominates gradient-based optimization; (ii) unstable gating, where noisy confidence cues induce erratic modality selection; and (iii) fusion interference, where modality-specific gradients conflict at the shared fusion layer. We propose CAT-GS (Calibrated, Adaptive, Thresholded Gating with Fusion Surgery), a neural dynamics-based optimization controller for intelligent computing applications. CAT-GS operates during backpropagation without modifying model architectures, fusion modules, or task losses. Through calibration of teacher-derived reliability via temperature scaling and EMA smoothing, CAT-GS stabilizes neural dynamics using a margin-thresholded policy to switch between warm-up dropout, weak-modality prioritization, and weak-biased blending, stabilizes gradient magnitudes under aggressive gating via capped gradient-budget renormalization, and applies fusion-only PCGrad to reduce destructive cross-modal interference at the primary shared bottleneck. We evaluate CAT-GS on audio--visual multimodal pattern recognition benchmarks (CREMA-D, AV-MNIST, and VGGSound), a tri-modal setting (UR-FUNNY), controlled synthetic data (CG-MNIST), and additional cross-domain benchmarks (AVE and CMU-MOSI). CAT-GS improves or matches fused multimodal accuracy against strong imbalance-aware baselines (including OGM-GE, G$^2$D, and UMT) across settings, and yields smoother gating behavior with fewer conflicting fusion gradients.

AI.tldr: CAT-GS is a dynamics-informed optimization controller that stabilizes end-to-end multimodal training without architecture or loss changes, improving fusion accuracy and reducing conflicting gradients.
AI.motivation: Multimodal networks commonly suffer from unstable training dynamics due to modality imbalance, unstable gating, and fusion interference, which hamper learning of cross-modal representations.
AI.method: Backprop-based controller using calibrated, adaptive, thresholded gating (margin-thresholded policy) with temperature scaling and EMA smoothing to estimate reliability; warm-up dropout, weak-modality prioritization, and weak-biased blending; capped gradient-budget renormalization to stabilize gradient magnitudes under gating; fusion-only PCGrad to mitigate cross-modal interference at the shared bottleneck; applied during backprop without modifying architectures or losses.
AI.result: CAT-GS achieves improved or matched fused multimodal accuracy across CREMA-D, AV-MNIST, VGGSound, UR-FUNNY, CG-MNIST, AVE, and CMU-MOSI versus strong imbalance-aware baselines (OGM-GE, G^2D, UMT); yields smoother gating and fewer conflicting fusion gradients across diverse benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: An effective optimization controller for multimodal training that stabilizes neural dynamics without architectural changes, delivering robust gains across datasets and settings.

title: Sequential Object Placement Optimization with Convex Decomposition
summary: Robotic object packing has been a core challenge for robotic deployment in logistics, industry, etc., due to the curse of dimensionality in combinatorial search and the difficulty of dealing with dynamic and contact constraints for irregularly shaped objects. Current heuristic and learning-based methods assume a limited spatial discretization resolution of space, and computation becomes extremely inefficient as discretization accuracy increases. In this work, we eliminate these assumptions by introducing SOPO-CD, a sequential optimization framework that frames object placement as a differentiable nonlinear optimization problem in a decomposed free space. We prove that placing a convex object inside a convex hull is essentially constraining the vertices of the object inside the convex hull. The constraints and their derivatives can be written in closed form and calculated within $200$ns. We implement a custom solver that achieves optimal placement within tightly constrained space in milliseconds; a $100 \times$ speedup compared to a classical grid search method. We generalize our framework to 2D Tangram, 2D Tetris, and 3D Bin Packing, and have demonstrated strong computational performance and packing utility. We also demonstrate solving a real-world Tangram puzzle online using an Allegro Hand and an Xarm.

AI.tldr: SOPO-CD reframes object packing as a differentiable nonlinear optimization in decomposed free space, achieving millisecond-level optimal placements and large speedups, with extensions to 2D Tangram/Tetris and 3D Bin Packing, including real-world robot demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Overcome the curse of dimensionality and discretization bottlenecks in combinatorial packing by providing a differentiable optimization formulation with closed-form derivatives for placement constraints.
AI.method: Sequential optimization framework; constraints that a convex object lies within a convex hull with closed-form derivatives; custom solver; derivatives computed in ~200 ns; 100x speedup vs grid search; generalizes to 2D Tangram, 2D Tetris, and 3D Bin Packing; real-world Tangram solving with Allegro Hand and Xarm.
AI.result: Shows strong computational performance and packing utility; optimal placements in tightly constrained spaces within milliseconds; reports a 100× speedup over grid search and real-world Tangram demonstration on robotic hardware.
AI.conclusion: SOPO-CD offers a fast, differentiable, scalable approach to rigid object packing, enabling real-time planning for complex shapes and combinations, with broad applicability to logistics, manufacturing, and interactive puzzle solving.

title: SHIFT-LLM: Distribution Shift Correction in Depth-Pruned LLMs
summary: Depth pruning removes entire Transformer blocks to reduce the inference cost of large language models, but disrupts the hidden-state distributions expected by downstream layers, leading to significant accuracy loss. We introduce SHIFT-LLM, a training-free post-pruning correction framework that inserts a Linear Residual Adapter (LRA) at each pruning site. Each LRA preserves the identity pathway of the original residual block and adds a lightweight affine residual correction. This correction is calibrated via closed-form least-squares regression on a small held-out set, without gradient computation, to approximate the missing residual update produced by the pruned block. Together with the preserved identity pathway, the resulting LRA output approximates the hidden state produced by the original block, thereby mitigating the distributional mismatch introduced by layer removal while avoiding the expensive attention and feed-forward computations of the removed blocks. The resulting LRAs support low-rank factorization and exact merging across consecutive pruned layers for additional compression, and combine naturally with parameter-efficient fine-tuning for further recovery beyond fine-tuning the pruned model alone. Experiments on five model families, six layer-selection criteria, and seven zero-shot benchmarks show that SHIFT-LLM consistently recovers accuracy lost to depth pruning across most configurations, achieving gains up to +15.7 points on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while requiring only a few hundred calibration samples and no gradient computation.

AI.tldr: A training-free post-pruning correction (SHIFT-LLM) mitigates accuracy loss from depth pruning by inserting Linear Residual Adapters at pruning sites, calibrated with closed-form least squares on a small held-out set, preserving the original residual pathway and enabling further compression and integration with PEFT.
AI.motivation: Depth pruning reduces inference cost but disturbs hidden-state distributions, causing significant accuracy loss. A lightweight, calibration-based correction is needed to recover performance without gradient-based retraining.
AI.method: Insert a Linear Residual Adapter (LRA) at each pruning site that preserves the identity path and adds an affine residual correction. Calibrate the affine parameters via closed-form least-squares on a small held-out set (no gradients). The LRA approximates the missing residual update from the pruned block. LRAs support low-rank factorization and exact merging across consecutive pruned layers and can be combined with parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across five model families, six layer-selection criteria, and seven zero-shot benchmarks shows SHIFT-LLM consistently recovers accuracy lost due to depth pruning, with gains up to 15.7 points on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using only hundreds of calibration samples and no gradient computation.
AI.conclusion: SHIFT-LLM provides a training-free, cost-efficient correction mechanism for depth-pruned LLMs that preserves the original residual path, enables additional compression, and complements parameter-efficient fine-tuning to recover pruned-model performance.

title: Measurement-Budget Allocation in Quantum Learning with Finite-Shot Generalization Guarantees
summary: On near-term quantum hardware, estimating a Born probability requires repeated circuit executions. A quantum learning experiment with a fixed measurement budget $B$ must therefore decide how many distinct training states $n$ to use and how many shots $S$ to allocate to each state. We study this tradeoff for binary quantum classifiers with fixed or independently selected measurement operators $M$, where the ideal score is $\Tr(Mρ)$. We prove a distribution-free generalization bound that separates the finite-sample and finite-shot contributions. The sample term scales as $\sqrt{d/n}$, while the shot term scales as $\sqrt{(\log n)/S}$; under the constraint $B=nS$, these two terms move in opposite directions. Minimising a conservative closed-form surrogate of the bound gives the allocation rule $\nstar = 2\sqrt{2dB/\log(2B/δ)}$ and $\Sstar = B/\nstar$. This surrogate has the same asymptotic scaling as the exact minimizer and yields a worst-case rate of $B^{-1/4}$. The guarantee is intentionally conservative, since it applies to the full class of binary quantum measurements. We complement the theory with PennyLane simulations using 2-qubit and 4-qubit variational quantum circuits on nine synthetic binary classification benchmarks. In all tested configurations, the one-sided empirical generalization gap remains below the theoretical bound. The result provides a conservative statistical guideline for allocating measurement budgets in finite-shot evaluation and pre-experimental planning for near-term quantum learning systems, complementing hardware-level scheduling and circuit-design considerations. Extending the guarantee to fully adaptive shot-noisy training remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: Principled budget allocation for finite-shot quantum learning: derive a distribution-free bound distinguishing finite-sample and finite-shot contributions, optimize a surrogate to obtain explicit n* and S* under B=nS, validate with PennyLane simulations, and discuss conservative guarantees and open problems for adaptive shot-noisy training.
AI.motivation: Provide a rigorous, model-agnostic guideline for how to allocate a fixed experimental budget B between the number of training states n and the number of shots per state S in binary quantum classifiers, to minimize generalization error.
AI.method: Derive a distribution-free generalization bound with sample term ~ sqrt(d/n) and shot term ~ sqrt((log n)/S). Under budget constraint B=nS, optimize a conservative closed-form surrogate of the bound to obtain explicit allocation n* and S*. Compare surrogate to exact minimizer. Validate via PennyLane simulations on 2- and 4-qubit variational circuits across nine binary classification benchmarks.
AI.result: Obtained explicit allocation rules: n* = 2 sqrt(2 d B / log(2B/δ)) and S* = B/n*. The surrogate shares the same asymptotic scaling as the exact solution and yields a worst-case rate of B^{-1/4}. The bound is conservative, applying to the full class of binary measurements. Empirical tests show the one-sided generalization gap remains below the bound in all configurations tested.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a conservative, actionable guideline for measurement-budget planning in near-term quantum learning, complementing hardware and circuit design. It also leaves open the extension to fully adaptive shot-noisy training.

title: Demystifying Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Language Models
comment: Link to website: https://minjang10.github.io/demystifying-rl-finetuning-web Link to code: https://github.com/sankarh-1/demystifying-rl-finetuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has emerged as a powerful framework for enhancing the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), enabling impressive reasoning, math, and coding capabilities. Yet for many researchers and practitioners, the principles behind classical RL remain a "black box". In this work, we deconstruct the RL post-training algorithm, investigating each step to clarify what is actually happening beneath the surface. By isolating the mechanics of RL with Verifiable Rewards in a controlled and simplified environment, we examine how RL outcomes are shaped by the base model's prior distribution, the granularity of the reward signal, the diversity of the prompt distribution, and model scale. We use the entropy of the policy's output distribution as a lens to compare the distributions learned through pretraining, SFT, and RL post-training, revealing how each stage shapes model certainty. Our investigation sheds light on how these choices interact to affect post-training success. For example, we show that the effect of so-called 'spurious rewards' depends on the prompt distribution used for post-training. We also provide insight into why the success of RL post-training depends on whether the base model already places sufficient probability mass on the desired behavior, linking it to the classical concept of exploration in RL. Ultimately, we provide this primer as a resource to those in the NLP community wishing to incorporate RL as a tool in their toolbox.

AI.tldr: A primer that demystifies RL post-training for LLMs by dissecting its steps in a controlled setting, showing how base model priors, reward granularity, prompt diversity, and scale shape outcomes; uses policy-entropy to compare pretraining, SFT, and RL post-training; highlights that spurious rewards depend on prompts and that success hinges on initial probability mass (exploration).
AI.motivation: To clarify the mechanics of RL post-training and provide a practical, verifiable framework for NLP researchers to understand when and how RL post-training yields benefits, bridging the gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: Systematically deconstruct RL post-training steps using a controlled environment with Verifiable Rewards. Analyze how base model priors, reward granularity, prompt distribution, and model scale influence outcomes. Use the entropy of the policy output distribution to compare pretraining, supervision fine-tuning (SFT), and RL post-training.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) RL post-training outcomes are shaped by the base model prior, reward granularity, prompt diversity, and model scale. (2) Policy-entropy trajectories reveal how pretraining, SFT, and RL post-training differently shape model certainty. (3) The impact of spurious rewards depends on the prompt distribution used. (4) RL post-training success aligns with whether the base model already assigns sufficient probability mass to the desired behavior, linking to exploration concepts in RL.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a practical primer for incorporating RL as a tool in NLP, offering a transparent frame to interpret RL post-training results, and guidance on when and how to design prompts and rewards for effective outcomes.

title: Control-Oriented Learning for Dynamic Tracking and Stability Analysis of Soft Pneumatic Actuators
summary: Soft pneumatic actuators offer inherent compliance and safe interaction but remain difficult to model and control because of their highly nonlinear, distributed dynamics. We present a control-oriented data-driven modeling and control framework that decomposes actuator behavior into a nonlinear static equilibrium model and a linear residual dynamics model identified using Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition with control (EDMDc). This representation enables feedforward compensation, task-space feedback control, and local closed-loop stability analysis through an augmented linear model.
