Experiments achieve approximately 1 mm root mean square error (RMSE) during low-speed (approximately 10 mm/s) trajectory tracking and below 10 mm RMSE at higher speeds (approximately 100 mm/s). The framework further achieves stable tracking of highly dynamic user-generated references with peak accelerations exceeding 25 m/s^2 while simultaneously performing real-time obstacle avoidance. Finally, the proposed stability analysis is experimentally validated by accurately predicting stable, marginal, and unstable operating regimes. These results demonstrate that structured, control-oriented learning provides an accurate and practical framework for soft actuator control.

AI.tldr: A data-driven control framework for soft pneumatic actuators that separates nonlinear static equilibrium from linear residual dynamics via EDMDc, enabling feedforward, task-space feedback, and stability analysis within an augmented linear model.
AI.motivation: Soft actuators offer safe, compliant interaction but are difficult to model and control due to nonlinear, distributed dynamics; a control-oriented, learnable representation is needed to enable accurate performance and stability guarantees.
AI.method: Modeling approach decomposes actuator behavior into a nonlinear static equilibrium model plus a linear residual dynamics model identified with Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition with control (EDMDc). This yields an augmented linear model for control, enabling feedforward compensation, task-space feedback, and a framework for stability analysis. Experimental validation includes trajectory tracking at low and high speeds, dynamic references with high accelerations, obstacle avoidance, and experimental stability regime prediction.
AI.result: Approximately 1 mm RMSE at ~10 mm/s; <10 mm RMSE at ~100 mm/s. Stable tracking with peak accelerations >25 m/s^2 and real-time obstacle avoidance. Experimental validation of stable, marginal, and unstable operating regimes.
AI.conclusion: Structured, control-oriented learning provides an accurate and practical framework for soft actuator control, enabling precise tracking and real-time safety features with stability guarantees.

title: RefLAM: A Reference-Grounded Line Annotation Pipeline for Historical Arabic Manuscripts
summary: Existing approaches to building line-level Arabic handwritten-text-recognition (HTR) training data either rely on fully manual annotation, which does not scale, or on automatic OCR-to-reference alignment methods not yet extended to multi-script, two-zone (main-plus-margin) manuscript layouts with a provable correctness guarantee. We present RefLAM (Reference-grounded Line Annotation for Manuscripts), a pipeline converting manuscript page images and clean transcriptions into validated, line-level ground truth without sacrificing human oversight. RefLAM couples a deep-learning page-segmentation model with a multimodal large language model (MLLM) for structured OCR and a diacritic-agnostic fuzzy alignment engine that grounds each OCR line in a contiguous span of the reference text, with a character-level confidence score in $[0,100]$. A perfect score is provably equivalent to character-for-character identity of the normalised strings (the Confidence-100 rule), verified with no counterexample across the released corpus. A reviewer can thus trust a perfect score, confirming most lines at a glance rather than retyping them, so annotation becomes triaged, with attention concentrated on uncertain alignments. Across 7 fully page-validated books we measured a 75$\times$ throughput gain over manual annotation (3,000 vs. 40 lines/hr); applying the same guarantee to 7 further books, we retained 16,533 confidence-100 main-text lines within one week, excluding sub-100 lines rather than manually correcting them. Using RefLAM, we release AraMS-28k: 14 historical Arabic manuscript books, 3,043 pages, and 27,971 main-text and 629 margin-line annotations with bounding boxes, layout labels, and insertion anchors for 191 margin entries (30.4%). We also finetune Muharaf-pretrained baselines (including HATFormer) on AraMS-28k and report CER results confirming its practical utility for downstream HTR training.

AI.tldr: RefLAM offers a scalable, validation-grounded pipeline for line-level Arabic HTR with a provable Confidence-100 alignment guarantee, leveraging page segmentation, an MLLM-based OCR structurer, and a diacritic-agnostic fuzzy aligner; it yields AraMS-28k and dramatic annotation throughput gains (75x) with improved downstream HTR baselines.
AI.motivation: Need scalable, correct line-level ground truth for Arabic manuscript HTR. Existing manual annotation is not scalable, and OCR-to-reference alignment methods lack proven correctness for multi-script, two-zone manuscript layouts.
AI.method: A deep-learning page-segmentation model identifies pages, an MLLM provides structured OCR, and a diacritic-agnostic fuzzy alignment engine grounds each OCR line to a contiguous span of reference text. A character-level confidence score [0,100] is produced; a Confidence-100 rule certifies exact character-for-character matches. Outputs include line bounding boxes, layout labels, and insertion anchors for margins.
AI.result: Achieves ~75x throughput improvement (3,000 vs 40 lines/hour) across 7 books; 16,533 Confidence-100 lines identified in a subsequent run over 7 more books within one week. Release AraMS-28k: 14 historical Arabic manuscript books, 3,043 pages, 27,971 main-text and 629 margin-line annotations with bounding boxes and anchors (191 margin entries). Fine-tuning Muharaf-pretrained baselines (including HATFormer) on AraMS-28k with CER improvements for downstream HTR.
AI.conclusion: RefLAM provides trustworthy, scalable annotation with minimal manual intervention, enabling high-quality HTR data creation and downstream model training, and resulting in a sizeable openly released dataset (AraMS-28k).

title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
summary: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

title: AFDBench: A Reasoning-First AI Scientist for NationalWeather Service Forecast Discussions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) hallucinate numerical values when generating high-stakes meteorological text, posing risks for weather communication. We present AFDBench, an AI meteorologist that generates professional Area Forecast Discussions (AFDs) by reasoning through structured AI weather forecast data from Google's WeatherNext 2. We introduce AFDBench, the first benchmark for evaluating generative meteorological reasoning, comprising 7,732 expert written discussions from 13 National Weather Service (NWS) offices paired with real AI weather forecast inputs, and three complementary metrics: Met-Align (numerical accuracy), Style-Align (professional dialect adherence), and Input-Grounding (fidelity to source weather data). Zero-shot evaluations reveal that open-source LLMs achieve low Style-Align (~0.33) and moderate Input-Grounding (~0.88), failing to write in the professional NWS register or faithfully use their input data. We apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with domain-specific rewards targeting temperature accuracy, synoptic correctness, and format compliance. On 1,033 held-out samples from two unseen NWS offices, GRPO nearly doubles Style-Align from 0.318 to 0.619 and improves Input-Grounding from 0.881 to 0.940, demonstrating that reinforcement learning teaches a 7B-parameter model to write like a professional meteorologist and faithfully interpret AI weather data.

AI.tldr: A study introduces AFDBench, a benchmark and RL-based framework to align LLM-generated meteorological discussions with professional norms and real forecast data, improving numerical accuracy, style, and data grounding.
AI.motivation: Address hallucinations and misalignment in LLMs when generating high-stakes meteorological text, ensuring professional tone and fidelity to input forecast data.
AI.method: Create AFDBench with 7,732 expert-written AFD-style discussions paired with Google WeatherNext 2 inputs; develop three metrics (Met-Align, Style-Align, Input-Grounding); perform zero-shot evaluations of open-source LLMs; apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with domain-specific rewards to train a 7B model; evaluate on 1,033 held-out samples from unseen NWS offices.
AI.result: Open-source LLMs underperform on Style-Align (~0.33) and have moderate Input-Grounding (≈0.88). After GRPO training, Style-Align improves from ~0.318 to ~0.619 and Input-Grounding from ~0.881 to ~0.940 on held-out data; numerical performance improved through reward-driven alignment.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning with domain-specific rewards enables a small 7B model to write in a professional meteorologist register and faithfully interpret AI forecast data, substantially closing the gap to expert performance and reducing hallucinated or misused data.

title: CRESSim-Neo: A Batched GPU Simulation Engine for Surgical Robotics and Robot Learning
summary: We introduce CRESSim-Neo, a batched GPU simulation engine for surgical robotics and robot learning. CRESSim-Neo combines position-based simulation of rigid bodies, deformable tissues, fluids, and strands with batched rendering, surgery-specific sensing, and a GPU-resident data pipeline. The engine supports applications including tissue manipulation, fluid suction, suturing, cable-driven robots, and ultrasound image synthesis. Direct access to physics and rendering buffers enables GPU-resident robot learning and zero-copy PyTorch integration using DLPack. We demonstrate CRESSim-Neo across rigid-body, deformable-body, and fluid simulation tasks, including vision-based and surgical robot-learning scenarios. On an NVIDIA RTX 4090, the engine achieves up to 2.03 million environment steps per second for 8192 parallel CartPole environments, and scales to batched surgical scenarios involving tissue deformation, fluid interaction, and ultrasound sensing. Overall, CRESSim-Neo provides a unified and scalable platform for surgical simulation, synthetic data generation, and surgical robot learning.

AI.tldr: CRESSim-Neo is a high-throughput, GPU-accelerated, batched simulation engine for surgical robotics that enables real-time physics, rendering, and learning with zero-copy PyTorch integration.
AI.motivation: There is a need for a unified, scalable platform to simulate complex surgical tasks (tissue manipulation, suturing, fluid handling) and generate synthetic data for vision and learning, including ultrasound sensing.
AI.method: Position-based simulation of rigid bodies, deformable tissues, fluids, and strands with batched rendering and a GPU-resident data pipeline. Direct access to physics and rendering buffers enables GPU-resident learning and zero-copy PyTorch integration via DLPack. Supports tissue manipulation, fluid suction, suturing, cable-driven robots, and ultrasound image synthesis. Demonstrated across rigid, deformable, and fluid tasks, including vision-based and surgeon-robot learning scenarios.
AI.result: On an NVIDIA RTX 4090, achieves up to 2.03 million environment steps per second for 8192 parallel CartPole environments, and scales to batched surgical scenarios with tissue deformation, fluid interaction, and ultrasound sensing. Demonstrations span rigid-body, deformable-body, and fluid simulations, plus vision-based and surgical-robot learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: CRESSim-Neo provides a unified and scalable platform for surgical simulation, synthetic data generation, and surgical robot learning.

title: Can You Trust Frozen Hematology Foundation Models under Acquisition Shift?
comment: Accepted at the HemaRAI 2026 workshop (MICCAI 2026 satellite event), oral presentation; to appear in MICCAI 2026 Satellite Events, LNCS, Springer. 25 pages (10 main incl. references + 15 supplementary), 4 figures. Project page: https://jaishrm07.github.io/hematology-fm-robustness/
summary: Frozen hematology foundation-model (FM) embeddings reach near-saturated in-domain white-blood-cell (WBC) accuracy, but clinical deployment demands reliability across scanners, sites, stains and preparation pipelines. We audit 15 frozen encoders (hematology, pathology, and general vision) across four public single-cell acquisition domains along two axes: accuracy robustness and calibration. In-domain linear-probe macro-F1 is saturated (0.98-0.997), yet cross-dataset macro-F1 drops 34-72% and rankings re-order: DinoBloom-L, the in-domain best, falls to 10th of 15 on the most-shifted target (MLL23) at the benchmark's shared 224-px input, behind RedDino and several general and pathology encoders. Rank transfer is probe-dependent: 1-NN retrieval is more stable on average than a source-fitted linear head (median $ρ$ 0.65 vs 0.45), but neither probe universally predicts target robustness. Calibration also collapses: source-trained probes are nearly calibrated in-domain (expected calibration error, ECE, 0.004) but confidently wrong off-domain (ECE 0.35), and source-fitted temperature scaling transfers poorly. We further audit pretraining exposure and identify MLL23 as DinoBloom's internal cohort; because DinoBloom's only held-out dataset is also our source domain, this benchmark cannot isolate exposure from scanner-associated shift. Label-free adaptation and marginal-entropy-based model selection appear safe under balanced evaluation but fail under realistic WBC class-prior shift. Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR), a training-free pseudo-label-balanced feature normalization, improves all evaluated target-prior scenario means and partially improves calibration, although encoder-level exceptions and residual miscalibration remain. Hematology FM benchmarks must therefore jointly audit accuracy, calibration, exposure, and class-prior robustness.

AI.tldr: Frozen hematology foundation-models achieve near-saturated in-domain accuracy but exhibit substantial cross-domain robustness and calibration gaps across scanners, sites, stains, and pipelines; exposure leakage and class-prior shifts complicate benchmarking; a training-free method (CBR) helps but does not fully solve miscalibration.
AI.motivation: To ensure reliable hematology foundation-model deployment, it is essential to evaluate both accuracy and calibration under domain shifts, exposure leakage, and class-prior changes, rather than relying on in-domain performance alone.
AI.method: Evaluate 15 frozen encoders (hematology, pathology, general vision) across four public single-cell acquisition domains. Assess accuracy with in-domain and cross-domain macro-F1, and calibration via ECE. Compare 1-NN retrieval vs source-fitted linear heads. Audit pretraining exposure and identify DinoBloom's internal cohort (MLL23). Test label-free adaptation and margin-entropy-based model selection under balanced/shifted class priors. Apply Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR) as a training-free pseudo-label-balanced feature normalization and evaluate its impact on target-prior performance and calibration.
AI.result: In-domain macro-F1 is saturated (0.98–0.997). Cross-dataset macro-F1 drops 34–72% with ranking shifts (DinoBloom-L drops from in-domain best to 10th on MLL23). Rank transfer varies by probe: 1-NN more stable (median ρ=0.65) than linear head (ρ=0.45) but no probe universally predicts target robustness. Calibration collapses: in-domain source-trained probes have ECE ≈0.004, off-domain ECE ≈0.35; temperature scaling transfers poorly. MLL23 corresponds to DinoBloom’s internal cohort, hindering exposure isolation. Label-free adaptation and entropy-based model selection are safe under balanced priors but fail with realistic class-prior shifts. CBR improves target-prior means across scenarios and partially improves calibration, though encoder-level exceptions and residual miscalibration remain. Overall, hematology FM benchmarks must jointly audit accuracy, calibration, exposure, and class-prior robustness.
AI.conclusion: Hematology foundation-model benchmarks require joint evaluation of accuracy, calibration, exposure, and class-prior robustness. Exposure leakage and dataset shifts can mislead in-domain performance. CBR shows promise as a training-free remediation, but robust evaluation protocols and exposure-aware benchmarking are essential for trustworthy deployment.

title: Same-Player Verification for Account Consistency in Counter-Strike 2
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: In competitive first-person shooter (FPS) games such as Counter-Strike 2 (CS2), account-integrity review often asks whether an account's recent behavior remains consistent with its historical operator. This consistency question arises in cases such as temporary substitution, rank boosting, and high-skill players using lower-ranked accounts, where manual review requires comparing a current match against multiple historical matches. We formulate this review task as same-player verification: we encode the behavioral trajectory of a single player in a match replay (demo) as a demo-player behavioral fingerprint, and train a model to judge whether two behavioral observations come from the same real player. Grounded in CS2 game understanding, the fingerprints cover crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. From 1,330 CS2 demos we extract 13,300 demo-player observations, and sample 663,590 same/different pairs from an 88.4M candidate-pair space for supervised training and evaluation. The final pairwise model reaches an average ROC AUC of 0.931 and achieves 0.722 different-player recall at 95% precision. Feature analysis shows that the strongest identity signals come from low-level operations, especially crosshair control, firing rhythm, and movement-stop-fire coordination, indicating that stable low-level mechanical habits are more informative for this verification task than single-match performance outcomes. In the account-history aggregation evaluation, increasing history depth raises AUC from the K=1 single-pair baseline of 0.931 to 0.986 at K=10. These results show that CS2 demo behavior can support supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling through multi-demo history aggregation.

AI.tldr: Supervised same-player verification for CS2 using demo-level behavioral fingerprints; high accuracy (ROC AUC ~0.93 single-pair, recall 0.722 at 95% precision) with further gains (AUC ~0.986) when aggregating up to 10 demos; strongest signals come from low-level behavioral cues.
AI.motivation: Address account-integrity concerns in competitive FPS by automatically verifying whether two match observations come from the same real player, especially under substitution or rank-boosting scenarios.
AI.method: Encode a player's trajectory in a match replay (demo) as a demo-player fingerprint. Train a pairwise classifier to decide if two observations originate from the same player. Features span crosshair control, movement-stop-fire coordination, economy/buy, combat/engagement, and temporal rhythm. Dataset: 1,330 CS2 demos; 13,300 observations; 663,590 training/evaluation pairs sampled from 88.4M candidate pairs. Evaluation includes account-history aggregation with varying depth K.
AI.result: Final pairwise model achieves ROC AUC of 0.931 for single-pair verification and 0.722 recall for the different-player class at 95% precision. Low-level signals (crosshair, firing rhythm, movement-stop-fire) are the strongest identity cues. History-depth aggregation improves AUC from 0.931 (K=1) to 0.986 (K=10).
AI.conclusion: Demo-based behavioral fingerprints enable supervised same-player verification and account-level identity-consistency modeling via multi-demo history; stable low-level mechanical habits are robust identity indicators, with performance benefiting from aggregating multiple demos.

title: Why and When Neural Networks Improve Local Approximation in Optimization
comment: 30 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material (6 pages) included as an ancillary file. Code and raw results: https://github.com/chengkuobian/neural-surrogates-dfo
summary: Published experience with neural surrogates in derivative-free optimisation is contradictory: the same family of models that cuts the evaluation count of one solver leaves another unchanged, or makes it worse. We show that the contradiction dissolves once three factors are stated, and that these, rather than the fit accuracy a training curve reports, are what delimit when a learned local model pays. Role: a surrogate that proposes candidates the true objective must still approve helps, while one that replaces a gradient the solver depends on hurts. Radius: a model fitted to an optimisation path is reliable only inside a bounded neighbourhood, and its error neither vanishes as that neighbourhood shrinks nor survives its growth. Room: a surrogate can only accelerate progress the base method is still able to make. We formalise radius-aware local generalisation, relate it to the classical fully linear condition, and test each factor with the surrogate class, training pipeline and base method held fixed. Over 117 benchmark instances safeguarded assistance raises the instances solved to high accuracy from 67 to 84 while gradient replacement lowers them to 65; removing the gradient term from the training loss cuts surrogate acceptance from 0.703 to 0.148; and 1000 paired comparisons over ten noise levels show no noise threshold, only a base method that stops early. The same factors bound the gain: a model-based trust-region solver, which leaves little room, drops from 88 to 86 when the identical surrogate is attached, and released interpolation software stays ahead at 103, and on a Monte-Carlo inventory model repairing the acceptance interface is worth 10.40 cost units against 0.00 for the surrogate.

AI.tldr: Three factors govern when neural surrogates help in derivative-free optimization: surrogate role (proposal vs gradient surrogate), radius of locality (bounded neighbourhood), and problem scope (base method's progress). Proper use raises solved instances; gradient-replacing surrogates hurt; benefits are limited by the base method's capacity and by locality; guidance emerges from radius-aware generalisation and relation to fully linear conditions.
AI.motivation: Explain inconsistent empirical findings about neural surrogates in derivative-free optimization by isolating the causal factors that determine when surrogates are beneficial, and provide a formal framework to predict their utility.
AI.method: Develop radius-aware local generalisation formalism and connect it to the classical fully linear condition. Empirically validate by holding surrogate class, training pipeline, and base method fixed, while varying the surrogate role, locality, and problem scope across 117 benchmarks and 1000 paired comparisons across noise levels; perform ablations (gradient term in loss) and test across base solvers (trust-region, interpolation, Monte Carlo).
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Surrogates help when they propose candidate evaluations that the true objective must approve; this raised high-accuracy solved instances from 67 to 84 across 117 benchmarks. (2) Replacing a gradient the solver relies on harms performance, dropping solved instances to 65. (3) Removing the gradient term from training loss dramatically lowers surrogate acceptance from 0.703 to 0.148. (4) Across 1000 comparisons with ten noise levels, no noise threshold exists; the only observable effect is whether the base method stops early. (5) The gain is context-sensitive: a model-based trust-region solver loses lift (88 to 86) with the surrogate attached, interpolation-based methods remain ahead (103), and a Monte-Carlo inventory model shows the cost of repairing the acceptance interface is 10.40 units versus 0.00 for the surrogate.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies radius-aware local generalisation, the surrogate role, and problem scope as the three controlling factors of surrogate usefulness. Surrogates can accelerate progress only within the base method’s capability and within a reliable locality; surrogates that replace gradients or operate beyond the trusted neighborhood can hinder performance. The framework clarifies when surrogates are beneficial and guides practical integration by ensuring the surrogate proposes candidates to be validated, constraining training to the local path, and avoiding gradient-replacement objectives.

title: Longitudinal Robot Learning from Demonstration with Care Providers in a Home Environment
comment: ICRA 2026 Workshop on Bridging the Gap between Robot Learning and Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Learning from demonstration (LfD) methods enable non-expert end users to teach robots novel skills without explicit programming. However most evaluations of the usability of LfD with non-experts has been conducted in controlled laboratory environments with a robotics experimenter present. In this work we identify non-expert end users' key barriers when teaching robots via demonstration without live robotics expert feedback in a home environment. In our human subjects experiment we support the non-expert end users through two forms of demonstrator guidance developed in prior work: pre-training and adaptive feedback. Towards the ecological validity of the evaluation, we conduct this experimentation over multiple visits, with a population of care providers. Finally, we propose to open source the resulting LfD dataset of care providers teaching a robot assistive tasks over multiple visits to a home environment.

AI.tldr: Identifies barriers to teaching robots via demonstration by non-experts in homes; tests pre-training and adaptive feedback; uses multiple home visits with care providers; proposes open-sourcing the LfD dataset.
AI.motivation: Current LfD usability studies are often lab-based and involve a robotics experimenter, limiting ecological validity. There is a need to understand non-expert end-user barriers in real home environments and to provide guidance without live expert feedback.
AI.method: Human-subjects experiment with care providers across multiple home visits. Implement two demonstrator guidance strategies (pre-training and adaptive feedback) from prior work. Data and insights collected aim to support open-sourcing a LfD dataset of in-home teaching tasks.
AI.result: Identified key barriers faced by non-experts when teaching robots via demonstration in home settings without live expert feedback. Demonstrator guidance (pre-training and adaptive feedback) is integrated to support users. Demonstrates feasibility for in-home, multi-visit evaluation and proposes open-sourcing the resulting LfD dataset.
AI.conclusion: Supports ecological validity in LfD usability studies by evaluating non-expert teaching in real homes over multiple visits. The open-source dataset will facilitate replication and broader research in home-assistive robot programming.

title: What Do Audio-Visual Synchronization Metrics Actually Measure?
comment: Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Generative AI for Audio-Visual Content Creation (Gen4AVC), poster presentation; non-archival workshop. 7 pages (4-page main text + references + 2-page appendix), 3 figures, 8 tables. Project page: https://jaishrm07.github.io/avsync-reliability-card/
summary: Automatic AV-sync metrics are widely used to rank and train audio-visual generators, but they are rarely audited as measurement instruments. We jointly audit AV-Align, ImageBind AV-relevance, JavisScore, and Synchformer/DeSync under a common reliability protocol: controlled-distortion monotonicity, preprocessing sensitivity, rank uncertainty, cross-metric agreement, PEAVS-proxy agreement, and learned fusion. The result is an axis split, not a single winner: Synchformer/DeSync is the strongest temporal-offset tracker ($τ=0.84$), ImageBind/JavisScore better match the PEAVS human-aligned proxy ($τ=0.20$) and content-disruption families, and AV-Align is the weakest standalone metric. The metrics mutually disagree (Krippendorff $α=0.066$), and neither linear nor simple $k$-NN fusion improves PEAVS agreement over the best individual metric. We recommend reporting AV-sync as a Reliability Card (metric-family breakdowns with confidence intervals) rather than a single bare synchronization score.

AI.tldr: No single best AV-sync metric across a reliability framework; Synchformer/DeSync excels at temporal-offset tracking, ImageBind/JavisScore aligns with human proxy and disruption content, AV-Align weak as a standalone; fusion does not beat the top metric; report via Reliability Card for transparency.
AI.motivation: To audit AV-sync metrics as measurement instruments under a unified reliability protocol, ensuring robustness, reproducibility, and clear comparability across metric families.
AI.method: Apply a common reliability protocol including controlled-distortion monotonicity, preprocessing sensitivity, rank uncertainty, cross-metric agreement, PEAVS-proxy agreement, and learned fusion; evaluate single metrics and combinations; assess alignment to a human-aligned proxy (PEAVS) and compute inter-metric agreement (e.g., Krippendorff α); quantify temporal-offset tracking performance (τ) per metric; examine content-disruption sensitivity.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals an axis split rather than a single winner. Synchformer/DeSync is the strongest temporal-offset tracker (τ=0.84); ImageBind/JavisScore better match the PEAVS human-aligned proxy (τ=0.20) and content-disruption families; AV-Align is the weakest standalone metric. Inter-metric agreement is low (Krippendorff α=0.066); neither linear nor simple k-NN fusion improves PEAVS agreement over the best individual metric.
AI.conclusion: Recommend reporting AV-sync as a Reliability Card—providing metric-family breakdowns with confidence intervals—instead of a single synchronization score to improve transparency and cross-metric comparability.

title: Semantic Graph Unification for Industrial Digital Threads: Bridging 11 Heterogeneous Manufacturing Systems Through Ontology-Driven Knowledge Graphs
summary: Modern manufacturing enterprises operate heterogeneous systems -- ERP, MES, PLM, SCADA, QMS, SCM -- each with its own data model and API. The resulting silos prevent holistic analysis, delay root-cause investigation, and obstruct Industry 4.0 traceability. Point-to-point integration scales as O(n^2) and accumulates brittle dependencies. This paper presents an open framework for semantic graph unification of industrial digital threads. An ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph unifies data from 11 simulated sources across nine domains through a five-stage ETL pipeline with automated entity resolution spanning 97 owl:sameAs identity links. The ontology encompasses 78 RDFS classes, 108 object properties, and 243 data properties, drawing on ISA-95, OPC UA, eClass, the Asset Administration Shell, RAMI 4.0, and additional standards. An automated discovery engine applies nine strategy categories -- cross-station correlation, alarm coverage, ECN impact, CUSUM/EWMA drift detection -- to surface insights spanning system boundaries. The primary empirical result: blocking 24 cross-system tools reduces recall from 1.00 to 0.31 (F1 from 1.00 to 0.48), showing that 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins. Leave-one-out ablation confirms six of nine strategies contribute unique signals. Verification against a 65-signal manifest (16 positive, 49 null) yields F1 = 1.00 (95% Clopper-Pearson CI [0.79, 1.00]); as the manifest was author-constructed, this constitutes verification not independent validation. The graph is exposed to LLM agents via 287 Model Context Protocol tools as a SPARQL-native semantic layer. Five industry templates (aerospace, CPG, pharma, medical devices, turbine blades) demonstrate schema stability across manufacturing verticals.

AI.tldr: Ontology-driven RDF knowledge graph unifies data from 11 simulated industrial sources using a five-stage ETL pipeline and an automated discovery engine with nine strategies, enabling cross-system insights and SPARQL-based access for LLMs.
AI.motivation: Industrial enterprises suffer data silos across heterogeneous systems (ERP, MES, PLM, SCADA, QMS, SCM), hindering holistic analytics, root-cause investigation, and Industry 4.0 traceability; point-to-point integration scales quadratically and creates brittle dependencies.
AI.method: Developed an open framework with an ontology of 78 RDFS classes, 108 object properties, and 243 data properties. It integrates ISA-95, OPC UA, eClass, Asset Administration Shell, RAMI 4.0, and other standards. A five-stage ETL pipeline performs automated entity resolution via 97 owl:sameAs links. A discovery engine applies nine strategies (e.g., cross-station correlation, alarm coverage, ECN impact, CUSUM/EWMA drift) to surface cross-system insights. The graph is exposed to LLM agents via 287 Model Context Protocol tools as a SPARQL-native semantic layer, and five industry templates demonstrate schema stability across aerospace, CPG, pharma, medical devices, and turbine blades.
AI.result: Empirical findings show significant cross-system dependencies: blocking 24 cross-system tools reduces recall from 1.00 to 0.31 and F1 from 1.00 to 0.48, indicating 69% of discoverable signals require cross-system graph joins. Leave-one-out ablation confirms six of nine strategies contribute unique signals. Validation against a 65-signal manifest yields F1 = 1.00 (CI [0.79, 1.00]); though manifest is author-constructed, hence verification not independent validation. The framework supports SPARQL access and demonstrates schema stability across multiple manufacturing verticals.
AI.conclusion: The work presents an open, ontology-driven semantic graph framework that enables cross-domain industrial insights, improves traceability, and provides a scalable, reusable template across verticals. The integration with LLM tooling through a SPARQL layer and the demonstrated cross-system signals highlight the value of semantic graph unification for Industry 4.0.

title: Physics-Informed Error Field Learning: A Post-Training Optimization Framework for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as an important class of numerical methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, during the late-stage optimization process, further parameter updates often yield diminishing accuracy improvements while increasing computational costs. To address this issue, this paper proposes a Physics-Informed Error Field Learning (PIEFL) framework for PINNs. Unlike conventional approaches that continuously approximate the solution field using a single network, PIEFL introduces an auxiliary error network after the primary network achieves satisfactory accuracy and shifts the learning objective from the solution field to the error field. By deriving error control equations under physical constraints, the error network learns the discrepancy between the current approximation and the exact solution, and the learned error correction is combined with the primary prediction to improve solution accuracy. The proposed framework avoids continuous optimization of the entire solution space and focuses computational resources on correcting existing prediction errors. Moreover, PIEFL requires no modification to the primary network architecture, making it compatible with existing PINN models and applicable as a general post-training optimization strategy. Numerical experiments on representative PDEs demonstrate that PIEFL achieves higher solution accuracy under the same computational budget, validating its effectiveness in improving the performance of PINNs.

AI.tldr: PIEFL adds an auxiliary error network to a trained PINN to learn the residual error between current predictions and the true solution, then combines this learned error with the primary network output. It reframes training from solving the full PDE solution to correcting existing predictions, enabling post-training optimization without changing network architecture, and yielding higher accuracy under the same computational budget.
AI.motivation: In late-stage PINN training, improvements stagnate while costs rise. A targeted error-correction mechanism can leverage remaining resources to reduce residual error more efficiently than further whole-solution optimization.
AI.method: Introduce a secondary error network after the primary PINN has achieved baseline accuracy. Derive physics-informed error control equations to supervise the error network under physical constraints. The error network learns the discrepancy between current approximation and the exact solution, and its output is added to the primary PINN prediction to refine the solution. This approach avoids retraining the entire solution space and acts as a post-training optimization that requires no changes to the primary network architecture.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on representative PDEs show that PIEFL attains higher solution accuracy under the same computational budget compared to standard PINN training.
AI.conclusion: PIEFL is a general post-training optimization strategy for PINNs that improves accuracy by learning and correcting the residual error without altering the primary network, and without additional architectural changes.

title: Development of a Voice-Controlled Tendon-Driven Bionic Hand
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Open-access preprint intended for journal or conference submission
summary: The impairment of the hands can seriously affect the abilities of every individual to perform the every-day activity, so the design of stable and controllable support devices is a significant field of study. This paper is about the design and implementation of an automated bionic hand which is dedicated to the coordinated finger movement through the simplified and efficient actuation mechanism. The method that the proposed system was designed on is the tendon-based method whereby the servo motors generate the movement of the fingers, with assistance of the angular control which is calibrated. An actuation is controlled by a microcontroller that will be programmed by use of an Arduino-based microcontroller to carry out programmed gestures that include open hand, fist, pinch and half flexion. It has an interface that is voice command enabled to make it easy to interact with a Bluetooth based sender receiver architecture which offers an option of executing trained commands which are immediately converted to finger actions. To explore the motions behavior, finger coordination and control response to the input, the behavior of the experiment system is tested. The actuation of the fingers was found to take a total of about 7-8 seconds to achieve full flexion of all fingers in a sequence. The system showed repetitive and constant motion throughout several actuation cycles without loss of any apparent tension or precision of control. There was a stable grasp of objects of different shapes and sizes, which implied consistent coordination between the fingers. These findings indicate that the proposed system offers predictable and steady control behavior and has a simple and efficient mechanical and control architecture.

AI.tldr: A tendon-based prosthetic hand actuated by servo motors and controlled via Arduino with voice and Bluetooth commands; demonstrates stable, repeatable finger movements and reliable grasping, taking 7–8 seconds for full flexion.
AI.motivation: Restore and enhance independence for individuals with hand impairment by providing a stable, controllable, and simple actuation scheme for coordinated finger movement.
AI.method: Tendon-based actuation driven by servos; angular control calibration; Arduino-based microcontroller to execute gestures (open hand, fist, pinch, half flexion); Bluetooth/voice command interface enabling trained commands to map to finger actions; experimental testing of motion behavior, finger coordination, and control response.
AI.result: Actuation time to full finger flexion ~7–8 s; repeated, consistent motion over cycles; stable grasp of objects of varying shapes/sizes; coherent finger coordination; system exhibits predictable, steady control and a simple, efficient architecture.
AI.conclusion: The proposed design provides reliable, coordinated finger actuation with a straightforward mechanical and control framework, indicating viability for practical bionic hand applications, though further validation is likely needed.

title: See More, Detect Less? Taming Information Leakage in Multi-View Anomaly Detection
summary: In multi-view anomaly detection, more cross-view information can actually hurt. When multiple inspection views are naively fused in a reconstruction-based pipeline, normal cues from intact views propagate to the decoder, which faithfully reconstructs anomalous regions, collapsing the reconstruction gap the detector depends on. We call this failure mode \emph{cross-view information leakage} and show that effective multi-view fusion must explicitly restrict the information reaching the decoder. Building on this insight, we present GLAD(Global-Local Attention Driven framework), the first framework combining vision foundation model features with local and global cross-view fusion for multi-view anomaly detection. The Multi-view Merging Attention (MMA) module performs local cross-view fusion at linear complexity with learnable view importance weighting and token-wise gating, letting each view selectively incorporate fine-grained evidence from other views at $\mathcal{O}(N)$ cost. The Object-Guided Attention (OGA) module captures global context by aggregating class tokens from all views into a single object-level representation and broadcasting it back to patch tokens via temperature-scaled sigmoid gating, replacing the original patch representations rather than adding a residual to preserve the reconstruction gap. Experiments on Real-IAD and MANTA-Tiny show that GLAD outperforms state-of-the-art methods across sample-, image-, and pixel-level metrics, confirming that principled information restriction is key to multi-view anomaly reasoning.

AI.tldr: GLAD enables principled multi-view anomaly detection by restricting information flow from multiple views to the decoder using MMA and OGA, achieving linear-time local fusion and global context aggregation, leading to state-of-the-art results on Real-IAD and MANTA-Tiny.
AI.motivation: Naive multi-view fusion in reconstruction-based anomaly detectors can cause cross-view information leakage, where normal cues from intact views mask anomalies. Restricting information to preserve the reconstruction gap is necessary for reliable multi-view reasoning.
AI.method: GLAD combines vision foundation model features with two cross-view modules: (1) Multi-view Merging Attention (MMA) for local cross-view fusion with linear complexity, learnable view weights, and token-wise gating; (2) Object-Guided Attention (OGA) for global context by aggregating class tokens from all views into a single object-level vector and broadcasting back to patch tokens via temperature-scaled sigmoid gating, avoiding naive residual addition.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on Real-IAD and MANTA-Tiny shows GLAD outperforms state-of-the-art methods across sample-, image-, and pixel-level metrics, supporting the claim that restricting information flow improves multi-view anomaly detection.
AI.conclusion: Effective multi-view anomaly reasoning requires explicit information restriction; GLAD demonstrates that fusing vision foundation model features with carefully designed local and global attention modules yields robust cross-view anomaly detection.

title: post-graph-rag: A PostgreSQL-Native Graph RAG Engine
summary:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation connects facts that no single passage states, but current implementations pay for that three times: in infrastructure, requiring a vector store, graph database and document store to be kept consistent; in graph quality, because an extraction pipeline that never refuses output fills the graph with edges that assert nothing; and over time, because a graph that only accumulates treats superseded and current facts alike.
  post-graph-rag is an open-source engine addressing all three. Text chunks with embeddings, a canonical entity graph and community summaries live in one PostgreSQL database, with pgvector for search and edge tables for traversal. Extraction-time invariants run before anything is written: vague predicates, pronominal names and bare quantities are rejected; predicates are normalised onto an optional vocabulary; entities resolve to one vertex per canonical name via model-supplied aliases; and denied relations keep the positive predicate under a negation flag. A temporal layer lets relations carry a validity period from the prose, lets a later document supersede an earlier incompatible assertion from document order alone, and answers as-of queries.
  Against LightRAG on three corpora under identical extraction and embedding models, post-graph-rag builds a denser graph everywhere, up to $2.4\times$ the relations per entity, and a more queryable one: distinct edge labels run at 0.46 to 0.58 per relation, 0.11 under a controlled vocabulary, against 0.77 to 1.33. It answers comparably with lower query latency, and supports temporal evolution the baseline lacks: 13 and 8 relationships superseded on a novel sequence and a decade of filings, against zero. These are engineering measurements, not a benchmark result.
  Code: https://github.com/crajah/post-graph-rag, https://github.com/crajah/post-graph

AI.tldr: Post-graph-RAG is an open-source engine that unifies embeddings, a canonical entity graph, and summaries in a single PostgreSQL store, addressing infrastructure, extraction quality, and temporal evolution issues in retrieval-augmented generation.
AI.motivation: Reduce three pain points of RAG pipelines: separate vector store/graph/doc stores, noisy extraction graphs, and lack of temporal evolution for facts.
AI.method: Single PostgreSQL backend with pgvector; enforce extraction-time invariants; normalise predicates; canonicalize entities; maintain negation for denied relations; add temporal layer with validity periods and as-of queries; compare against LightRAG on three corpora with identical models.
AI.result: Denser and more queryable graphs (up to 2.4x more relations per entity; edge labels 0.46-0.58 per relation overall vs 0.77-1.33; 0.11 with controlled vocab); lower query latency; supports temporal evolution (13 and 8 superseded relations in novel sequence and decade of filings); engineering results, not a benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Post-graph-RAG demonstrates practical gains in graph density, queryability, and temporal reasoning within one store; open-source; results are engineering measurements rather than standardized benchmarks; suitable for RAG systems requiring evolving facts.

title: Resource-Efficient Pruning for Transformer via Low-Rank Importance Estimation
summary: With the rapid development of large-scale pre-trained language models based on Transformer architectures, their high computational and memory costs have become a major obstacle to deployment, especially in resource-constrained environments. Traditional pruning methods typically depend on full gradient-based importance estimation, and they necessitate prior finetuning of the model to achieve satisfactory performance. This process often results in intolerable resource consumption. This paper proposes REP-LIE, a new approach to enable resource-efficient pruning during the process of finetuning. REP-LIE leverages the gradients of LoRA low-rank matrices to estimate the importance of weights without requiring full gradient computation. To address the inherent randomness in importance estimation, a stability score is introduced, serving as the basis for iterative pruning of unimportant model parameters. The pruned model is further finetuned through lightweight updates, eliminating the need for full-parameter optimization in the process of finetuning. Extensive experiments on both medium-scale encoder models and large-scale generative models (LLaMA-7B and Mistral-7B) demonstrate that REP-LIE still achieves competitive performance compared to existing approaches.

AI.tldr: REP-LIE enables resource-efficient pruning during finetuning by using LoRA gradient-based importance estimation and a stability score to guide iterative pruning, followed by lightweight finetuning of the remaining parameters.
AI.motivation: Large Transformer models incur prohibitive computational and memory costs; traditional pruning requires full-gradient estimation and finetuning, resulting in high resource consumption. A method that prunes during finetuning with low overhead is desirable.
AI.method: REP-LIE leverages gradients of LoRA low-rank matrices to estimate weight importance without full gradient computation. It introduces a stability score to mitigate randomness in importance estimation, guiding iterative pruning of unimportant parameters. The pruned model is then fine-tuned via lightweight updates rather than full-parameter optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on medium-scale encoder models and large-scale generative models (LLaMA-7B, Mistral-7B) show REP-LIE achieves competitive performance relative to existing pruning approaches while reducing resource usage.
AI.conclusion: REP-LIE demonstrates that resource-efficient pruning during finetuning is feasible with LoRA-based gradient importance estimation and a stability-driven pruning strategy, enabling competitive results with substantially fewer resources.

title: Generative Action-Chunk Sampling for Adaptive Stiffness Control in Physical Human-Robot Collaboration
summary: Physical human-robot collaboration requires a robot to provide assistance when human intention is clear while remaining compliant when several future motions are plausible. We present an adaptive stiffness framework based on generative action-chunk sampling. Conditioned on an RGB image and external joint-torque estimates, the policy samples multiple future action chunks from an observation-conditioned prior. Variation among the sampled action chunks is used to continuously adapt joint stiffness and damping. Greater variation makes the robot more compliant to facilitate human guidance, whereas lower variation provides firmer assistance. In a real-world collaborative transport task with four possible directions, the proposed method achieved an average success rate of 0.95, compared with 0.83 for a fixed-stiffness ablation and 0.69 for a deterministic baseline. Near direction determination, variation among the sampled action chunks increased and the controller accordingly reduced stiffness. These results suggest that variation among actions sampled by a generative policy can serve as an online control signal for balancing assistance and compliance in physical human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: Adaptive stiffness via generative action-chunk sampling enables online balance of assistance and compliance in human-robot collaboration; shows higher success rate vs baselines.
AI.motivation: Physical HRC requires robots to be supportive when intention is clear but compliant when multiple future motions are plausible; need a mechanism to adjust stiffness dynamically.
AI.method: An observation-conditioned generative policy samples multiple future action chunks from an RGB-and-torque-conditioned prior. Variation among samples informs online adaptation of joint stiffness and damping, increasing compliance with higher variation and firmness with lower variation.
AI.result: In a real-world four-direction transport task, average success rate reached 0.95, compared to 0.83 for a fixed-stiffness ablation and 0.69 for a deterministic baseline. Near direction determination, action-chunk variation increases and stiffness is reduced.
AI.conclusion: Variation among actions from a generative policy can serve as an online signal to balance assistance and compliance in physical HRC, improving performance over fixed or deterministic baselines.

title: Lowering the Barrier to AI-Driven Inspection: A No-Code Workflow for Automated Structural Defect Detection
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to ASME SMASIS 2026 (paper SMASIS2026-190654). Software available at https://github.com/michaelholm6/YOLOEZ
summary:
Structural health monitoring (SHM) is essential in modern engineering, providing data for condition-based maintenance, lifecycle assessment, and predictive decision-making. Traditionally, SHM relied on visual inspection to detect defects such as cracks and deformations. Early computer vision (CV) methods, including thresholding, edge detection, and handcrafted features, aimed to automate this process but were highly sensitive to noise, imaging variations, and multiscale defects, limiting their reliability.
  Recent advances in machine learning, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and You Only Look Once (YOLO), have improved defect detection accuracy and enabled real-time analysis. However, adoption in SHM remains limited due to technical barriers such as data labeling, model training, and deployment, which typically require programming expertise.
  To address this gap, we introduce YOLOEZ, an open-source, GUI-based tool for end-to-end YOLO model application. YOLOEZ integrates data labeling, training, and inference into a single interface, enabling high-performance model development without code while supporting reproducible workflows.
  Evaluation against existing software and classical image processing demonstrates that YOLOEZ not only outperforms traditional methods across most detection metrics, but also lowers adoption barriers present in other modern CV tools. By combining accuracy with accessibility, YOLOEZ facilitates wider use of AI-driven monitoring for predictive maintenance, digital twins, and intelligent structural systems.

AI.tldr: GUI-based end-to-end YOLO workflow for SHM defect detection (YOLOEZ) that integrates labeling, training, and inference to improve accessibility and performance over traditional CV methods.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between advanced CV/YOLO-based SHM and practical deployment by lowering data-labeling and coding barriers, enabling reproducible workflows, and broadening adoption for predictive maintenance and digital twins.
AI.method: An open-source GUI tool that unifies data labeling, model training, and inference for YOLO in SHM, enabling end-to-end pipeline without coding and supporting reproducible configurations.
AI.result: Reportedly outperforms traditional image processing and existing software on detection metrics while reducing adoption barriers and facilitating AI-driven SHM workflows.
AI.conclusion: YOLOEZ potentially democratizes AI-based SHM, combining accuracy with ease of use to promote widespread adoption in predictive maintenance and digital twin contexts.

title: FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion
summary: Scientific agents increasingly analyze data, execute code, and produce research artifacts, yet most benchmarks emphasize final answers, isolated programs, or a single domain. We introduce FrontierChallenge, a cross-domain benchmark comprising 300 end-to-end scientific workflows. In this paper, we release and evaluate 97 of these tasks, spanning quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Each task provides fixed inputs and specifies a bundle of required scientific deliverables. We evaluate twelve frontier models with three agent scaffolds. Pass Rate measures the fraction of tasks satisfying the full-completion criterion, while Avg. Score captures partial progress. Each of the best-performing configurations completed only 20 of the 97 released tasks, yielding a Pass Rate of 20.6%. Partial progress translated especially poorly into complete delivery in analytical chemistry and electrochemistry/environment: Avg. Scores reached 87.6 and 94.9, but the highest Pass Rates were only 4% and 0%. Among non-passing Claude Code trajectories, 75.5% still ended with language claiming completion. These findings show that neither high partial scores nor confident claims of completion reliably indicate that a scientific task has been fully delivered, highlighting the need to evaluate end-to-end workflow execution and the completeness of scientific deliverables together.

AI.tldr: A cross-domain benchmark FrontierChallenge for end-to-end scientific workflows; evaluation of 97 tasks across multiple domains; results show limited pass rate (20.6%) and that high partial scores do not reliably indicate full task delivery, underscoring the need for joint evaluation of end-to-end workflow execution and deliverable completeness.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks emphasize final results, isolated programs, or single domains. There is a need for a cross-domain, end-to-end benchmark that assesses whether agents can manage data, run code, and produce complete scientific deliverables across diverse disciplines.
AI.method: FrontierChallenge comprises 300 end-to-end scientific workflows. The paper releases and evaluates 97 tasks spanning quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Each task has fixed inputs and a bundle of required deliverables. Twelve frontier models are evaluated with three agent scaffolds. Metrics: Pass Rate (fraction of tasks meeting full completion) and Avg. Score (partial progress).
AI.result: Best-performing configurations completed 20 of 97 tasks (Pass Rate 20.6%). Partial progress translated poorly into complete delivery in analytical chemistry (Avg. Score 87.6) and electrochemistry/environment (Avg. Score 94.9), yet Pass Rates were only 4% and 0%, respectively. Among non-passing Claude Code trajectories, 75.5% ended with language claiming completion.
AI.conclusion: The findings show that high partial scores or confident completion claims do not reliably indicate full task delivery. There is a need to evaluate end-to-end workflow execution and the completeness of scientific deliverables together, highlighting limitations of current evaluation practices for scientific AI agents.

title: Clearing the Underbrush: AI-Enhanced RF Interference Suppression
comment: 7 pages, 10 figures, Accepted to the 2026 IEEE Military Communications Conference (MILCOM)
summary: AI-based structured interference rejection has grown more popular because deep learning approaches can outperform traditional methods by jointly considering the signal of interest (SOI) and the signal mixture (SOI plus interference). This work builds on a previous AI-enabled approach utilizing autoregressive transformer-based models by adding a Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) tokenizer layer which aims to improve the interference rejection performance while keeping overall latency to a minimum. Additionally, we experiment with other inference optimization techniques with the goal of speeding up inference without much accuracy loss. We explore this space with an experiment where the SOI is a digitally modulated radio frequency (RF) signal and the structured interference is a digital television signal, an extremely common type of Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM) transmission. Our results achieve low latency and increased interference rejection over traditional techniques and prior work with other AI-enabled methods. We demonstrate the benefits of the AI-enabled approaches via audio metrics such as Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ). Additionally, we explore a variety of applications and detail how our interference rejection algorithm may be used in operationally-relevant scenarios.

AI.tldr: AI-based interference rejection using autoregressive transformers with a Finite Scalar Quantization tokenizer to reduce latency while boosting interference suppression, demonstrated on RF SOI with OFDM interference and evaluated via PESQ.
AI.motivation: Address the need for real-time, high-performance interference rejection in communications by leveraging AI. Build on prior AI-enabled methods with an FSQ tokenizer to improve performance and reduce latency for mixed signal scenarios (SOI+interference).
AI.method: Use autoregressive transformer models augmented with a Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) tokenizer layer; apply inference optimization techniques to speed up processing; experimental setup with a digitally modulated RF SOI and a digital TV OFDM interference; evaluate performance with audio-oriented PESQ metrics.
AI.result: Achieves lower latency and enhanced interference rejection compared to traditional methods and prior AI-based approaches; PESQ-based evaluation indicates improved perceived quality; demonstrates applicability to operational scenarios and potential deployment.
AI.conclusion: AI-enabled interference rejection is promising for real-time systems; FSQ tokenizer contributes to latency reduction and performance gains; further work could extend to additional interference types and deployment considerations.

title: RAEM: Robust Autonomous Exploration for Multi-Floor Environments with a Quadruped Robot
summary: In this paper, we propose RAEM, a robust autonomous exploration framework for quadruped robots operating in multi-floor environments. Most existing ground-robot exploration approaches rely on planar traversability representations, which cannot adequately represent the overlapping structures and cross-floor connectivity of multi-floor buildings. Although tomography-based representations provide effective traversability modeling for multi-floor navigation, maintaining a global tomography map incurs substantial computational overhead for online exploration with frequent replanning. Moreover, sparse and fragmented LiDAR observations in stairwells can degrade local traversability estimation, leading to irregular viewpoint placement and temporary topological disconnections. To address these challenges, RAEM adopts a hybrid local-global traversability representation, in which a local tomography map and an explicitly categorized local 3D grid map are used for online terrain analysis and connectivity evaluation, while an elevation-aware global topological graph is incrementally constructed from these local spatial representations for efficient cross-floor exploration planning. We further introduce a staircase center alignment strategy to reduce abrupt yaw variations during climbing and a dual path searching mechanism to recover guidance paths when the global topology is locally disconnected. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate robust and computationally stable autonomous exploration across multi-floor structures, including continuous exploration of a five-floor stairwell.

AI.tldr: Hybrid local-global traversability framework (RAEM) for multi-floor quadruped exploration, combining local tomography and 3D grid for online analysis with an elevation-aware global topological graph, plus staircase alignment and dual-path recovery; validated in simulation and on five-floor stairwell.
AI.motivation: Planar traversability is inadequate for multi-floor buildings; global tomography incurs high online computation; sparse LiDAR in stairwells degrades local estimates leading to disconnections. A hybrid representation aims to balance accuracy, connectivity, and computational efficiency for robust cross-floor exploration.
AI.method: Maintain a local tomography map and an explicitly categorized local 3D grid map for online terrain analysis and connectivity. Incrementally construct an elevation-aware global topological graph from local representations for cross-floor planning. Introduce a staircase center alignment strategy to stabilize yaw during climbing. Implement dual path searching to recover guidance paths when global topology becomes locally disconnected.
AI.result: Demonstrated robustness and computational stability in both simulation and real-world tests, including continuous exploration of a five-floor stairwell.
AI.conclusion: The RAEM framework effectively blends local-detail representations with a global, elevation-aware topological structure to enable robust, cross-floor autonomous exploration in quadrupeds, mitigating planning overhead and perceptual fragility in stairwells.

title: Lightweight Machine Learning-Driven Monocular Sidewalk Path Extraction for Embedded Micromobility Navigation
summary: Sidewalk-scale path extraction demands perception and planning that run reliably on compact, low-power hardware in cluttered, map-sparse environments. We present a monocular vision pipeline for sidewalk path extraction in micromobility systems that progresses through three design iterations, from a skeleton-graph baseline through distance-transform corridor planning to a lightweight image-space architecture, and provides a systematic comparison of five path-planning methods across both bird's-eye-view (BEV) and image-space domains. A compact SegFormer-B0 student model, trained with a semi-supervised teacher-student framework using OneFormer Swin-L pseudo-labels, achieves a hand-annotated IoU of 0.946 at 11.7 ms per frame, improving over the baseline checkpoint (IoU 0.758, 18.9 ms). In a controlled planner comparison on 32 hand-labeled frames, image-space midpoint planning achieves the lowest lateral center error (14.3 px) at 2.2 ms, a 421x speedup over BEV distance-transform planning (926.8 ms, 65.0 px center error), while maintaining comparable mask-path alignment (98.5% versus 98.6%). A full-video replay across six campus sequences (22,679 frames) confirms that the improved segmentation reduces temporal instability from 1.46% to 0.33% and increases template-path availability from 73.7% to 79.3%. We further show that BEV-only path extraction is fragile in monocular settings: in one profiled run, 99.3% of frames produced no valid BEV path. The final recommended architecture, image-space midpoint primary, image-space distance-transform fallback, and BEV reserved for visualization, runs the full perception-to-path stack in under 50 ms per frame on CPU, making it suitable for embedded pedestrian-speed micromobility systems.

AI.tldr: Efficient monocular sidewalk path extraction for micromobility using an image-space planning pipeline that outperforms BEV-based methods in accuracy and speed, achieving real-time CPU performance with robust temporal stability and higher path availability.
AI.motivation: Enable reliable sidewalk-path perception and planning on compact, low-power hardware in cluttered, map-sparse environments where BEV-based monocular methods are fragile and slower.
AI.method: Progresses through three design iterations (skeleton-graph baseline -> distance-transform corridor planning -> lightweight image-space architecture). Systematically compares five path-planning methods in BEV and image-space. Uses a compact SegFormer-B0 student model trained via semi-supervised teacher-student framework with OneFormer Swin-L pseudo-labels. Evaluations include: IoU improvements (0.758 to 0.946), image-space midpoint planning (14.3 px lateral error, 2.2 ms) vs BEV distance-transform (926.8 ms, 65.0 px), full-video replay across six campus sequences (22,679 frames) showing reduced temporal instability (1.46% to 0.33%) and higher template-path availability (73.7% to 79.3%), and a final architecture: image-space midpoint primary, image-space distance-transform fallback, BEV visualization. Overall runtime under 50 ms per frame on CPU.
AI.result: The image-space pipeline yields higher segmentation IoU and much faster planning in image-space, with comparable mask-path alignment to BEV. BEV-only extraction is highly fragile in monocular settings. The proposed stack achieves sub-50 ms CPU inference, enabling embedded deployment for micromobility at pedestrian speeds. Temporal stability improves and path availability increases at video scale.
AI.conclusion: Image-space planning with a lightweight semantic segmentation backbone provides robust, real-time sidewalk path extraction suitable for embedded micromobility systems, while BEV remains useful only for visualization. The approach demonstrates that monocular image-space methods can outperform BEV-distance-transform planning in terms of speed, stability, and path availability.

title: Solving Robust POMDPs with Omega-regular Objectives via Partially Observable Stochastic Games
summary: Robust POMDPs (RPOMDPs) generalize classical POMDPs to the setting where exact transition probabilities are not known -- rather, they are only known to belong to some uncertainty set of values. In this work, we study the problem of solving RPOMDPs with general omega-regular objectives, which subsume a broad class of objectives such as reachability, safety, and linear temporal logic (LTL) objectives. We show that, for (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, the problem of solving RPOMDPs under omega-regular objectives can be reduced to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) under omega-regular objectives. Moreover, we show for the first time that reductions can be constructed in both directions, establishing the semantic equivalence between (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets and POSGs. This allows us to derive a range of new computational complexity results, including both upper and lower complexity bounds, on solving RPOMDPs with different omega-regular objectives. As a corollary, we also derive new computational complexity results for RMDPs.

AI.tldr: Semantic equivalence between s,a-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty and POSGs for omega-regular objectives, with bidirectional reductions and resulting complexity bounds, including corollaries for RMDPs.
AI.motivation: Understand and characterize the computational complexity of solving robust POMDPs under broad omega-regular objectives by leveraging a reduction to well-studied POSGs, enabling both tractability and hardness results.
AI.method: Proves two-way reductions between RPOMDPs (s,a-rectangular with polytopic uncertainty) and POSGs for omega-regular objectives; shows reductions in both directions; derives upper and lower bounds for solving RPOMDPs; extends corollaries to RMDPs.
AI.result: Establishes semantic equivalence between RPOMDPs and POSGs under the stated conditions; provides reductions in both directions; yields new computational complexity bounds for RPOMDPs with various omega-regular objectives; shows corollaries for RMDPs.
AI.conclusion: Offers a unified framework to analyze RPOMDPs via POSGs, enabling a comprehensive set of complexity results and linking RPOMDPs to RMDPs, thereby broadening the applicability of omega-regular objectives in robust sequential decision making.

title: MSR-IVA: Masked Structural Residual Independent Vector Analysis for State-Aware Fusion of Structural MRI and Dynamic Functional Network Connectivity
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Machine Learning for Signal Processing (MLSP 2026), Atlanta, GA, USA
summary: Multimodal fusion of structural MRI (sMRI) and dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) can reveal how brain structure relates to changing functional states. When the same structural latent representation is coupled with multiple states, applying independent vector analysis (IVA) separately to each state can produce unrelated structural decompositions, while forcing identical decompositions may suppress state-specific relationships. In addition, not every subject expresses every dynamic state. We propose masked structural residual IVA (MSR-IVA), a state-aware framework that combines a shared structural representation with state-specific residual adaptations and masks for incomplete state expression. On an Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, MSR-IVA improved matched source coupling by 6.5% and reduced unmatched dependence by 15.7% relative to the independent pairwise IVA baseline. Among subjects expressing both states, mean absolute cross-state structural source correlation was 0.9177 for MSR-IVA versus 0.2978 for no sharing, demonstrating controlled structural sharing that preserves source correspondence while allowing state-specific adaptation.

AI.tldr: MSR-IVA proposes a state-aware multimodal fusion framework that shares a latent structural representation across dynamic states while allowing state-specific residual adaptations, aided by masks for incomplete state expression. It outperforms independent IVA baselines on ADNI data in coupling accuracy and cross-state consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing IVA approaches either treat states independently, leading to diverging structural decompositions, or force identical decompositions across states, risking loss of state-specific relationships. Additionally, not all subjects express every dynamic state, complicating joint analyses. A method that shares structure but permits state-specific adaptations and can handle missing states is needed for robust multimodal fusion of sMRI and dFNC.
AI.method: MSR-IVA introduces a shared structural latent representation coupled with state-specific residual adaptations and masking mechanisms to handle incomplete state expression. This masks allow parts of the latent structure to be inactive for certain states, enabling both sharing and specialization.
AI.result: On the ADNI cohort, MSR-IVA improved matched source coupling by 6.5% and reduced unmatched dependence by 15.7% relative to independent pairwise IVA. Among subjects expressing both states, mean absolute cross-state structural source correlation was 0.9177 for MSR-IVA versus 0.2978 for no sharing, indicating strong cross-state structural correspondence with preserved state-specific adaptation.
AI.conclusion: MSR-IVA provides controlled structural sharing that preserves source correspondence across dynamic states while enabling state-specific adaptations and accommodating incomplete state expression, leading to improved coupling metrics and higher cross-state correlation on ADNI data.

title: A Taxonomy of Construction Task Activities for Robot Workers
summary: Recent vision-language-action models offer a path toward robots with broader repertoires than conventional task-specific systems. Construction deployment, however, requires a precise inventory of worker activities and the capabilities needed to execute them. We present TARCAT, an occupation-grounded taxonomy derived from 91 O*NET tasks across seven high-employment construction occupations and 30 instructional videos of physical work. TARCAT defines 41 action primitives in 12 groups and three classes and provides a mechanism for composing parameterized primitive sequences into reusable skills. This human-interpretable structure can organize demonstrations, specify robot requirements, and support coding agents that retrieve and extend skill libraries. We also demonstrate selected primitives on a DOBOT CR3 arm with a CRAFT hand. TARCAT thereby provides a common vocabulary for analyzing human work and developing general-purpose construction robots. Annotations are available at https://github.com/AICPS/TARCAT-Taxonomy.

AI.tldr: TARCAT: an occupation-grounded taxonomy of 41 action primitives (12 groups, 3 classes) for construction robotics, derived from 91 O*NET tasks and 30 instructional videos, enabling composable reusable skills and hardware demonstrations; open annotations.
AI.motivation: To enable precise worker-activity inventories and capability specifications for deploying general-purpose construction robots and aligning vision-language-action models with real-world tasks.
AI.method: Derive TARCAT by mapping 91 O*NET tasks across seven high-employment construction occupations and 30 instructional videos to 41 primitives; organize into 12 groups and 3 classes; define a mechanism to compose parameterized primitive sequences into reusable skills; validate with demonstrations on a DOBOT CR3 arm with a CRAFT hand; publish annotations.
AI.result: Defined 41 primitives, 12 groups, 3 classes; established a compositional skill mechanism; performed hardware demonstrations; release annotations at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: TARCAT provides a common, human-interpretable vocabulary for analyzing human work and developing general-purpose construction robots, facilitating demonstrations, robot requirement specification, and skill library extension.

title: What Do Medical Vision-Language Models Learn in Radiology? Transfer, Alignment, and Source-Proxy Leakage Under Distribution Shift
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) can appear reliable in-domain while failing when acquisition domain, paired supervision, or evaluation protocol changes. We study this failure mode as a representation-level blind spot relevant to epistemic intelligence, without claiming a formal estimator of epistemic uncertainty. Using NIH ChestXray14 and CheXpert, we first isolate source-only cross-dataset visual transfer from unsupervised domain-adaptation diagnostics. Using PadChest and OpenI, we then evaluate multimodal alignment under strict pair-index retrieval and quantify metadata-derived source-proxy information retained in frozen embeddings. Self-supervised visual initialization improves NIH-to-CheXpert transfer over supervised ImageNet initialization in matched ResNet-18 comparisons, whereas adversarial adaptation is useful only in a narrow regime and becomes unstable as adversarial pressure increases. Multimodal exact-pair retrieval remains low under external OpenI stress testing, and source-proxy information remains recoverable from learned representations. Qualitative nearest-neighbor and Grad-CAM analyses show clinically plausible cross-dataset structure and thoracic attention patterns in many cases, while device-heavy and false-positive cases remain ambiguous. Auxiliary architecture checks are task-dependent and do not support a universal backbone ranking. Overall, the study shows that apparent competence under a single protocol can conceal transfer, alignment, and shortcut-related failure modes, motivating stress-tested evaluation of medical VLMs under distribution shift.
