AI.tldr: The abstract investigates how medical vision-language models can appear reliable in-domain but fail under distribution shifts, by probing representation-level blind spots and transfer/alignment dynamics across multiple chest X-ray datasets. It shows limited cross-dataset multimodal alignment, persistence of source-proxy information, and mixed benefits from different initializations/adaptation strategies, advocating stress-tested evaluation under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: In-domain success of medical VLMs can conceal transfer and alignment failures due to distribution shift and shortcut cues. The work aims to characterize epistemic blind spots in representations and assess whether current training/evaluation protocols reveal robust generalization.
AI.method: Experiments across NIH ChestXray14, CheXpert, PadChest, and OpenI. Isolate source-only cross-dataset visual transfer from unsupervised domain-adaptation diagnostics; evaluate multimodal alignment under strict pair-index retrieval; quantify metadata-derived source-proxy information in frozen embeddings; compare self-supervised visual initialization to supervised ImageNet initialization in NIH→CheXpert transfers; assess adversarial adaptation; perform qualitative NN retrieval and Grad-CAM analyses; test for universal backbone ranking via auxiliary architecture checks; stress-test under external OpenI conditions.
AI.result: Self-supervised visual initialization improves NIH-to-CheXpert transfer over supervised ImageNet in matched ResNet-18; adversarial adaptation is useful only in a narrow regime and becomes unstable with increased adversarial pressure; multimodal exact-pair retrieval remains low under external OpenI stress; source-proxy information remains recoverable from learned representations; qualitative nearest-neighbor and Grad-CAM show clinically plausible cross-dataset structure and thoracic attention in many cases, but device-heavy and false-positive cases remain ambiguous; architecture checks are task-dependent and do not support a universal backbone ranking.
AI.conclusion: Apparent competence under a single protocol can conceal transfer, alignment, and shortcut-related failure modes. The work motivates stress-tested evaluation of medical VLMs under distribution shift to ensure robust clinical reliability.

title: CVE-SAI: Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing for Risk-Controlled E-commerce Search
summary: Multimodal product models can complete missing e-commerce attributes, yet current methods still optimize attribute-answer accuracy without verifying visual support, conflate transient prediction with persistent index admission, and lack explicit risk control over factually incorrect or visually unsupported values. We address these gaps with Counterfactual Visual Evidence-Guided Selective Attribute Indexing (CVE-SAI), which first infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from the primary image and attribute question without catalog text, and then decides whether that candidate should enter the index. Focus-Zone Distortion (FZD) constructs an attribute-specific visual-dependence proxy through a controlled counterfactual intervention, and Evidence-Guided Attention Redistribution (EGAR) uses the proxy to refine ontology-constrained scoring. The canonical candidate is frozen before evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and candidate-specific catalog-text conflict audits; catalog text can only tighten admission and cannot revise the candidate. Independent family-level calibration selects one policy with a simultaneous one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget. Experiments on five visual attributes derived from Amazon Berkeley Objects show that CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol, and yields the strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems. Separating inference from admission therefore enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination.

AI.tldr: CVE-SAI is a risk-controlled, evidence-guided selective indexing framework for multimodal attribute completion that separates inference from admission and uses counterfactual visual evidence, attention redistribution, and calibration to improve retrieval while limiting unsafe admissions.
AI.motivation: Addresses lack of visual verification and explicit risk control in multimodal attribute inference, which can contaminate persistent indexes with factually unsupported or visually unverified values.
AI.method: CVE-SAI pipeline: (1) CVE infers and freezes an ontology-constrained candidate from the primary image and attribute question without catalog text; then decides admission. FZD builds an attribute-specific visual-dependence proxy via controlled counterfactual intervention. EGAR uses the proxy to refine ontology-constrained scoring. The canonical candidate is frozen before evidence necessity, evidence retention, nuisance-transformation stability, and catalog-text conflict audits; catalog text can only tighten admission and cannot revise the candidate. Independent family-level calibration selects one policy with a one-sided finite-sample bound under a 5% unsafe-admission budget.
AI.result: Experiments on five visual attributes from Amazon Berkeley Objects show CVE-SAI improves attribute inference and evidence localization, achieves the highest certified admission coverage under the shared risk protocol, and yields strongest controlled retrieval performance with the lowest unsafe auto-induced exposure among automatic-admission systems.
AI.conclusion: Separating inference from admission enables visually supported attribute completion to improve retrieval while limiting persistent index contamination.

title: D$^3$-MOPD: Adaptive Dynamic Domain ScheDuling for Efficient Multi-Teacher Distillation
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) distills several domain-expert teachers into a single student by minimizing per-domain reverse-KL divergence on the student's own rollouts. Existing approaches typically fix the per-domain data mixture before training, overlooking the fact that different domains converge at substantially different rates: some plateau early while others continue to improve throughout the training budget. A fixed mixture therefore wastes compute on fast-converging domains and undertrains slower-converging ones. To address this, we propose D$^3$-MOPD (Dynamic Domain ScheDuling for MOPD), a zero-overhead scheduler that repurposes the per-domain reverse-KL signal already produced during training to adapt the domain mixture online. Running asynchronously outside the training process, an off-process watcher periodically tracks each domain's KL trajectory, estimates remaining headroom and current improvement rate, and accordingly adjusts the domain sampling ratios without altering the core training loop. Our D$^3$-MOPD scales naturally to arbitrary numbers of domains, and the expected benefit grows as more domains introduce more diverse convergence patterns for the scheduler to exploit. On a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B student distilled from four domain-expert teachers, D$^3$-MOPD closes 97% of the average student-to-teacher performance gap, compared with 63% for vanilla MOPD, reaches the same peak performance with an approximately 3$\times$ reduction in rollout steps, and surpasses the specialist teachers on three of seven benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Dynamic per-domain scheduling for MOPD (D3-MOPD) uses an off-process watcher to adapt domain mixtures based on KL trajectories, improving sample efficiency and performance across multiple domains; observed gains include near-teacher parity with 3x fewer rollouts and gains over specialist teachers on some benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Fixed domain mixtures ignore varying convergence rates across domains, causing inefficiency; need to adaptively allocate data to slower-converging domains during distillation.
AI.method: Zero-overhead asynchronous scheduler D3-MOPD monitors per-domain KL on-the-fly, estimates remaining headroom and improvement rates, and adjusts sampling ratios without changing training loop. Off-process watcher runs outside training.
AI.result: On a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B student distilled from four domain experts, D3-MOPD closes 97% of the average student-teacher gap vs 63% for vanilla MOPD; achieves peak performance with ~3x fewer rollouts; surpasses specialist teachers on 3/7 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic domain-aware scheduling markedly improves efficiency and effectiveness of multi-teacher on-policy distillation and scales with domain count.

title: LAC: Linear and Angular Compliance for Humanoid Whole-body Control
summary: Real-world humanoid tasks involve physical interaction with objects and humans, yet current controllers either reject external forces as disturbances or restrict compliance to limited body links while ignoring angular effects. We present LAC, a general whole-body controller that simultaneously realizes commanded Linear and Angular Compliance for wrenches applied to the upper body. First, we synthesize whole-body compliant responses into a large-scale augmented dataset. Sampled force and couple events are imposed on contact frames extracted from human interaction data. At each contact link, the external force and a virtual torque from the passively yielding kinematic chain drive a virtual admittance under the commanded stiffness. Subsequently, teacher-student reinforcement learning trains a single policy to track the compliant motions under external wrenches. Finally, extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate whole-body compliant responses to wrenches across the upper body, monotonic modulation over the full range of both stiffness commands, and applicability to teleoperated loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://lac-humanoid.github.io/

AI.tldr: LAC enables simultaneous Linear and Angular Compliance for wrenches on a humanoid's upper body via data-driven RL, unifying whole-body responsiveness to external forces and torques.
AI.motivation: Real-world humanoid manipulation requires comprehensive, angular-aware, full-body compliance; existing controllers reject disturbances or limit compliance.
AI.method: Construct a large augmented dataset by imposing sampled force and torque events on contact frames from human interaction data; use passive kinematic chain to drive virtual admittance under commanded stiffness; train a teacher-student RL policy to track compliant motions under external wrenches; validate in simulation and real-world experiments across upper body and teleoperation tasks.
AI.result: Demonstrates whole-body compliant responses to wrenches across the upper body, monotonic stiffness modulation across the full range, and applicability to teleoperated loco-manipulation.
AI.conclusion: LAC provides a general, data-driven approach for simultaneous linear and angular compliance for upper-body wrenches, enabling robust interaction with objects/humans and improved teleoperation capabilities.

title: OpenCVL: An Open, Diverse, and Large-Scale Dataset for Fine-Grained Cross-View Localization
summary: Fine-grained Cross-View Localization (CVL) estimates the precise position and orientation of a ground-level image by aligning it with geo-referenced aerial imagery, offering a scalable alternative to Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) in challenging urban environments. Existing datasets rely on data collected with high-end sensor suites, which inherently limit image diversity and scalability. While in-the-wild images are abundant, their noisy geo-tags make them unsuitable for reliable evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce OpenCVL, a large-scale, diverse, and open dataset containing 617,388 ground-aerial image pairs spanning 41 cities across four European countries. All images are sourced from permissive platforms, ensuring long-term accessibility and supporting open and reproducible research. The training set combines images captured with high-end sensors with diverse in-the-wild imagery. We further develop a data curation framework that filters and corrects pose annotations to construct reliable in-the-wild evaluation data. In addition, OpenCVL includes dedicated cross-area and snowy test sets to assess generalization and robustness. Experiments with a state-of-the-art CVL model on OpenCVL show that incorporating noisy in-the-wild data consistently improves performance on clean test sets, suggesting a promising direction for scaling CVL with diverse real-world imagery.

AI.tldr: Introduces OpenCVL, a large-scale cross-view localization dataset with 617k ground-aerial image pairs across 41 European cities, plus a data curation framework; demonstrates that noisy in-the-wild data can boost performance on clean test sets.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between limited diversity of high-end sensor CVL datasets and abundant noisy in-the-wild imagery; enable scalable, open evaluation and training for CVL in challenging urban environments.
AI.method: Collects data from permissive platforms to build OpenCVL (617,388 ground-aerial pairs across 41 cities in four European countries). Develops a data curation framework to filter and correct pose annotations for reliable in-the-wild evaluation data. Constructs dedicated cross-area and snowy test sets. Evaluates a state-of-the-art CVL model, showing that incorporating noisy in-the-wild data improves performance on clean test sets.
AI.result: OpenCVL provides a large, diverse, and openly accessible dataset for CVL. The training set benefits from mixing high-end sensor data with in-the-wild imagery, and experimental results indicate that adding noisy in-the-wild data improves performance on clean test sets, supporting scalability and generalization. Cross-area and snowy test sets offer robustness evaluation.
AI.conclusion: OpenCVL is a scalable, diverse, and open dataset that enables reproducible CVL research. Incorporating in-the-wild data is beneficial for model generalization and robustness across different areas and conditions.

title: Retrieve, Match, Escalate: Accurate and Scalable Product Linking with VLM-Distilled Cross-Encoders and Agentic VLMs
summary: Product linking, the entity-resolution task of mapping merchant product records to canonical catalog products, consolidates fragmented listings so downstream search, recommendation, and advertising see one clean entry per product. At marketplace scale, billions of noisy, multi-category records must be resolved against tens of millions of canonical products, where scoring every candidate with a single model is either too weak for the hard cases or too costly for the easy ones. We present a production retrieve-then-match cascade that spends computation in proportion to difficulty: retrieval surfaces plausible matches, a lightweight text cross-encoder auto-resolves the high-confidence majority, and an agentic multimodal vision-language model settles the ambiguous remainder by inspecting product images and issuing web searches for evidence that is in neither record. The cross-encoder is distilled from millions of dual-VLM-consensus labels, retiring human annotation from the training set, and is calibrated to auto-accept links at a 98% precision bar validated against a smaller operator-certified audit. The agent is a self-hosted open-weight model that reaches a closed frontier VLM's precision at a four-point recall cost (88% versus 92%) for roughly one-seventh the per-pair cost, with no fine-tuning. Per-pair cost spans nearly five orders of magnitude from the cheap cross-encoder to the frontier VLM, so escalating only the hard tail to the agent raises end-to-end link coverage from the cheap stage's 68% to 77%.

AI.tldr: A scalable retrieve-then-match cascade for product linking that allocates compute by difficulty: surface plausible candidates, auto-resolve high-confidence links with a lightweight cross-encoder, and resolve remaining ambiguity with a self-hosted multimodal agent that analyzes images and performs targeted web searches. Calibrated to auto-accept at 98% precision; distillation eliminates human labeling; end-to-end coverage improves from 68% to 77% with per-pair cost spanning five orders of magnitude across stages.
AI.motivation: Handle product-linking at marketplace scale where billions of noisy, multi-category records must be mapped to tens of millions of canonical products. A single-model scorer is inefficient: too weak on hard cases or too costly on easy ones. A cascade that allocates computation to harder cases achieves better coverage with lower average cost.
AI.method: A retrieve-then-match cascade: (1) a retrieval step surfaces plausible matches; (2) a lightweight cross-encoder auto-resolves high-confidence links, trained via distillation from millions of dual-VLM-consensus labels and calibrated to auto-accept at ~98% precision; (3) a self-hosted open-weight agent using a multimodal vision-language model analyzes product images and performs web searches for evidence beyond the two records; no fine-tuning required. The agent’s performance is benchmarked against a closed frontier VLM, achieving ~88% precision at a four-point-recall cost with ~1/7 the per-pair cost, enabling end-to-end link coverage to reach 77% (from 68% at the cheap stage).
AI.result: The cascade achieves wide coverage with substantial cost savings: per-pair cost ranges across roughly five orders of magnitude from the cheap cross-encoder to the frontier VLM. The cheap stage covers 68% of links; deferring the hard tail to the agent raises end-to-end coverage to 77%. The cross-encoder auto-accepts links at 98% precision; the agent approaches frontier VLM performance (88% vs 92% in the reported metric) at roughly 1/7 the cost, with no fine-tuning and with self-hosted deployment.
AI.conclusion: A practical, production-grade product-linking system that uses a calibrated, self-bootstrapped cascade to balance accuracy and compute. It eliminates manual labeling in training via distillation, increases coverage by routing only hard cases to heavier models, and demonstrates the viability of a self-hosted agent with web-search evidence to disambiguate challenging records.

title: Rollout-Decoded Reconstruction for Long-Horizon Prediction in Latent World Models
summary: A latent world model trains its decoder on latents anchored to observations, then deploys it on the model's own free-running rollout, hundreds of steps past the last observation. Rollout-Decoded Reconstruction (RDR) closes this gap with a single loss term that free-runs the model during training exactly as evaluation will, decodes every rollout latent, and penalizes reconstruction error against ground truth. The term adds no parameters, costs training-time compute only, and reduces to the standard objective at weight zero, so every comparison in this paper is a one-flag A/B. On the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, RDR raises valid prediction time (the time to first crossing of normalized error 0.5) from $3.87 \pm 0.23$ to $6.97 \pm 0.42$ time units at an identical 193,568 parameters, a $1.80\times$ improvement confirmed on seeds never used in selection and holding in 10 of 10 preregistered configurations at ratios of 1.71-2.50$\times$. The results come from a single system; a sweep in which the advantage grows with latent width is descriptive, and control experiments on two classic tasks are preliminary.

AI.tldr: RDR adds a free-running rollout reconstruction loss during training for latent world models. It decodes every rollout latent and penalizes reconstruction error against ground truth, with no extra parameters. On the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky system it boosts valid prediction time from 3.87 to 6.97 time units (1.8x) at the same parameter count, with robust results across seeds and 10 preregistered configurations; effects grow with latent width. Validation on two classic tasks is preliminary.
AI.motivation: The training objective for latent world models typically anchors decoders to observations, while evaluation uses long free-running rollouts. This mismatch can degrade long-horizon predictions. RDR aims to close the gap by enforcing accurate decoding of rollout latents during training, aligning optimization with evaluation dynamics, and doing so without adding model parameters or extra training weights.
AI.method: During training, for each batch the model is allowed to generate free-running rollouts; every latent in these rollouts is decoded and reconstructed against ground truth, and reconstruction error is added as a loss term. This loss adds no new parameters and reduces to the standard objective when the rollout weight is zero. The approach is evaluated on the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation and by control experiments on two classic tasks, with ablation across seeds and preregistered configurations.
AI.result: In KS, valid prediction time increases from 3.87±0.23 to 6.97±0.42 time units at 193,568 parameters (1.80×). The improvement holds for seeds not used in selection and across all 10 preregistered configurations (1.71–2.50×). The advantage grows with latent width. Control experiments on two classic tasks are preliminary and descriptive.
AI.conclusion: RDR provides a simple, no-parameter loss that makes training-time optimization reflect evaluation-time free-running dynamics, yielding substantial short- to medium-horizon gains in at least one chaotic system. Although promising, broader validation across tasks and systems is needed to assess generality; the approach scales with latent width and can be readily integrated as a safe, one-flag A/B comparison.

title: SUPER ODOMETRY 2.0: Resilient Odometry via Hierarchical Adaptation
summary: Resilient and robust odometry is crucial for autonomous systems operating in complex and dynamic environments. Existing odometry systems often struggle with severe sensory degradations and extreme conditions such as smoke, sandstorms, snow, or low-light conditions, threatening both the safety and functionality of robots. To address these challenges, we present Super Odometry, a sensor fusion framework that dynamically adapts to varying levels of environmental degradation. Super Odometry employs a hierarchical structure to integrate four core modules from lower-level to higher-level adaptability including adaptive feature selection, adaptive state direction selection, adaptive engine selection, and a novel learning- based inertial odometry. The inertial odometry, trained on over 100 hours of heterogeneous robotic platforms, captures comprehensive motion dynamics. Super Odometry elevates the inertial measurement unit (IMU) to equal importance with camera and LiDAR within the sensor fusion framework, providing a reliable fallback when exteroceptive sensors fail. Super Odometry has been validated across 200 kilometers and 800 operational hours on a fleet of aerial, wheeled, and legged robots, under diverse sensor configurations, environmental degradation, and aggressive motion profiles. It marks an important step towards safe and long-term robotic autonomy in all-degraded environments.

AI.tldr: Super Odometry is a hierarchical, adaptive sensor fusion framework that elevates inertial odometry alongside camera and LiDAR, designed to robustly operate under degraded sensing; it uses four adaptive modules and a learning-based IMU, trained over 100+ hours, and validated across 200 km / 800 hours on diverse robots.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems require reliable odometry in environments with smoke, sandstorms, snow, and low-light where exteroceptive sensors fail or degrade; current systems struggle causing safety concerns.
AI.method: A four-module hierarchical adaptation: adaptive feature selection; adaptive state direction selection; adaptive engine selection; learning-based inertial odometry. IMU is treated as equally important to cameras and LiDAR within a fusion framework. Inertial model trained on 100+ hours of heterogeneous robotics data. Validation on 200 km and 800 hours across aerial, wheeled, legged robots under various sensor configurations and environmental degradations.
AI.result: Demonstrates robust odometry with fallback to IMU under exteroceptive failures; validated across multiple platforms and conditions, indicating improved reliability and safety for long-term autonomy in degraded environments.
AI.conclusion: Presents a scalable, resilient odometry approach enabling safe, long-term robotic operation in all-degraded environments; highlights potential for broader adoption and future improvements in sensor fusion adaptability.

title: PointRL: Learning Point-Level Vision-Language Grounding from Verifiable Annotation Evidence
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on point coordinates as a compact and executable interface for visual grounding in GUI interaction, robotic manipulation, and interactive visual systems. However, learning reliable pointing behavior remains difficult because the supervision space is inherently non-unique: many coordinates may be valid within the same target region, while multi-instance instructions require target coverage, count consistency, and duplicate suppression. This work presents PointRL, a verifiable reinforcement learning framework that learns point-level grounding from existing heterogeneous annotation evidence. PointRL converts bounding boxes, masks, and instance labels into pointing instructions, while retaining their target supports, instance membership, and set constraints as hidden verifier evidence, i.e., annotations kept outside the prompt and used by a deterministic checker to score predictions. The proposed reward evaluates parseability, point validity, instance coverage, cardinality consistency, and redundant or missing predictions. On PointArena, PointRL improves the overall accuracy of Qwen3.5-4B from 56.11% to 65.58%. Further evaluations on RoboSpatial, BLINK, and Ref-Adv show same-backbone gains on the evaluated external benchmarks, suggesting that verifiable point-level feedback may benefit spatial grounding in these settings.

AI.tldr: PointRL is a verifiable RL framework for point-level grounding that converts heterogeneous annotation evidence into pointing instructions and uses a deterministic verifier to provide a structured reward, achieving notable gains on multiple vision-language grounding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Point-level grounding in vision-language models suffers from non-unique supervision: many coordinates may satisfy a target region, and multi-instance instructions require coverage, consistent counting, and suppression of duplicates. Existing data provides heterogeneous annotations but lacks verifiable feedback; a verifiable learning signal could improve reliability and generalization.
AI.method: Convert bounding boxes, masks, and instance labels into pointing instructions while preserving their target supports, instance membership, and set constraints as hidden verifier evidence. A deterministic checker uses this evidence to score predictions. The reward comprises parseability, point validity, instance coverage, cardinality consistency, and penalties for redundancy or missing predictions. The model is trained with reinforcement learning (PointRL).
AI.result: On PointArena, Qwen3.5-4B accuracy improves from 56.11% to 65.58%. Additional evaluations on RoboSpatial, BLINK, and Ref-Adv show similar gains with the same backbone, suggesting that verifiable point-level feedback helps spatial grounding across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable point-level feedback via hidden verifier evidence is effective for improving spatial grounding in VLMs and generalizes across diverse datasets, offering a robust supervision signal for point-level grounding.

title: LifePlanner: Evaluating LLM Agents for Geo-spatial Planning with Social Media Data
summary: Geo-spatial planning, like trip design, is a realistic testbed for LLM agents because it requires grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning. Most benchmarks, however, only provide clean geospatial data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals that people use in daily planning. We introduce LifePlanner, a benchmark that enriches map data with large-scale local social media posts and provides access through an MCP toolset. LifePlanner provides an evaluation suite spanning four task categories and three difficulty levels. Experiments show frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval but degrade sharply on complex planning, with the Pass Rate dropping to 40.2%. Results show that failures mainly stem from incomplete evidence acquisition from such a large multimodal database, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length, suggesting that future progress requires effective grounded planning instead of scaling alone.

AI.tldr: LifePlanner is a geospatial planning benchmark that combines enriched map data with local social media posts via an MCP toolset, evaluated across four task categories and three difficulty levels. Frontier LLMs excel at simple retrieval but struggle with complex planning, achieving a Pass Rate of 40.2%. Failures stem from incomplete evidence gathering, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration, not model size or reasoning depth.
AI.motivation: Geospatial planning tasks require grounded tool use, noisy evidence retrieval, and multi-constraint reasoning. Existing benchmarks use clean data and tools, missing the open-ended social signals people use in daily planning.
AI.method: Introduce LifePlanner by enriching map data with large-scale local social media posts and providing access through an MCP toolset. Provide an evaluation suite spanning four task categories and three difficulty levels. Empirically evaluate frontier LLMs to assess performance across retrieval and planning challenges.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs perform well on simple retrieval but degrade on complex planning; Pass Rate drops to 40.2%. Failures mainly due to incomplete evidence acquisition from the multimodal database, imprecise tool use, and weak constraint integration rather than model size or reasoning length.
AI.conclusion: Progress requires effective grounded planning rather than scaling alone; future work should improve evidence acquisition, tool-use accuracy, and constraint integration to enable robust grounded planning.

title: On the Representational Geometry of Dynamic Programs
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures; submitted to NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (Extended Abstract Track)
summary: Standard neural architectures often fail to generalize to longer inputs for dynamic programming (DP) targets. We investigate what makes this hard geometrically. Every finite min-plus DP is a shortest path on a DAG, which is equivalently a tropical polynomial whose extended Newton polyhedron encodes the decision boundary of which path wins. We prove these three descriptions (graph, polynomial, polyhedron) form isomorphic semirings at two levels --- formal polynomials and their computed functions --- connected by operations that characterize all structural redundancies. We then address the length-generalization question geometrically: does the decision boundary at length $T$ decide the boundary at $T+1$? We present two structural negatives. The semiring's two native ways to reduce dimension (setting a variable to each identity) are neither injective nor always closed within the DP. Series and parallel composition fail to construct all DAG topologies from smaller sub-DAGs, and even all terminal-only operations do not capture all DP compositions.

AI.tldr: Min-plus DP equals a shortest path on a DAG, equivalently a tropical polynomial whose extended Newton polyhedron encodes the decision boundary of the winning path. Three representations (graph, polynomial, polyhedron) form isomorphic semirings at two levels (formal polynomials and their computed functions) connected by redundancy-exposing operations.
AI.motivation: Explain why neural architectures struggle to generalize DP targets to longer inputs by providing a geometric/algebraic account of the decision boundaries and their redundancies; unify graph, polynomial, and polyhedron viewpoints.
AI.method: Show isomorphism of three descriptions as semirings at two levels, and identify operations that relate structures and expose redundancies; analyze length-generalization by comparing boundaries at lengths T and T+1; assess dimension-reduction maps and composition operators.
AI.result: Establish the isomorphism among graph/ polynomials/ polyhedra as semirings (formal polynomials and their computed functions) linked by redundancy-exposing operations; demonstrate two structural negatives for length generalization: (1) the semiring’s two natural dimension-reduction methods (setting a variable to an identity) are neither injective nor closed within DP; (2) series and parallel composition fail to generate all DAG topologies from smaller sub-DAGs, and even terminal-only operations do not capture all DP compositions.
AI.conclusion: A geometric/semiring framework explains why DP-based generalization is hard for standard neural nets: structural redundancies and limited compositional expressivity hinder extending decision boundaries from shorter inputs to longer ones.

title: Towards safe and optimal flight: Viability Kernel MPC for Fully Actuated Multirotor
summary: Industrial aerial robotics demands safety guarantees for navigation in unstructured environments while optimizing performance and computational efficiency. This paper presents a method for generating safe pose trajectories for fully actuated multirotors within a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework, leveraging both viability theory and data-driven methods. Obstacle avoidance is enforced through dynamically computed axis-aligned bounding boxes, providing formal safety guarantees without exhaustive offline reachability analysis. Numerical simulations on a fully actuated tilted hexarotor validate the approach, demonstrating successful navigation in cluttered environments with real-time computational performance.

AI.tldr: Safety-guaranteed, MPC-based pose trajectory planning for fully actuated multirotors using viability theory and data-driven methods, with dynamic axis-aligned bounding box obstacle avoidance and no offline reachability; validated in simulations on a tilted hexarotor with real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Industrial aerial robotics demands safety guarantees for navigation in unstructured environments while optimizing performance and computational efficiency; formal safety guarantees are challenging due to complex dynamics and clutter.
AI.method: Integrates Model Predictive Control with viability theory constraints and data-driven components; dynamically computes axis-aligned bounding boxes to bound obstacles within the MPC optimization; avoids exhaustive offline reachability by leveraging viability-based safety bounds; validated on a fully actuated tilted hexarotor in numerical simulations.
AI.result: Demonstrates successful navigation in cluttered environments under real-time computational demands; provides formal safety guarantees via the AABB-based obstacle handling and viability constraints; validates feasibility on a high-degree-of-freedom platform.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MPC-viability/data-driven approach offers a scalable, formally safe navigation framework for industrial aerial robots, avoiding heavy offline reachability computations; suitable for real-time deployment and potentially extendable to other fully actuated platforms and scenarios.

title: WAVE: Reversing the Guidance Hierarchy for Coarse-to-Fine Guided Depth Super-Resolution
summary: Guided depth super-resolution (GDSR) typically extracts RGB guidance features through convolutional hierarchies, inheriting their fine-to-coarse bias. Thus, low-level spatial cues surface in early layers, leaving the deeper layers to suppress those that do not correspond to true depth boundaries, which risks artifacts and blurred edges. The same fine-to-coarse bias persists in semantics-based methods that consume low-level tokens early and global tokens late. We present WAVE, which introduces a multi-level discrete wavelet transform (ML-DWT) as an explicit and interpretable feature-control mechanism, enabling a coarse-to-fine reconstruction by consuming sub-bands and semantic tokens in reverse of their generation order. WAVE further exploits these sub-bands to treat high- and low-frequency content separately, filtering at its source the misleading RGB color and texture cues that often lead to blurred boundaries and artifacts, offering an intuitive alternative to the suppression learned implicitly by an opaque network. WAVE separates structure and detail reconstruction into dedicated modules that: i) model interactions within and across wavelet sub-bands, depth features, and semantic priors, ii) apply semantic gating to the high-frequency bands, and iii) fuse modalities through an invertible coupling mechanism that prevents collapse onto a single modality. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that WAVE matches or outperforms existing methods, with the largest gains at high upsampling factors, where low-resolution depth contains the least structure.

AI.tldr: WAVE introduces a multi-level discrete wavelet transform to guide depth super-resolution, enabling coarse-to-fine reconstruction and semantic gating to separate structure from detail, reducing artifacts and improving edges, especially at high upsampling factors.
AI.motivation: Conventional guided depth super-resolution (GDSR) and semantics-based methods exhibit a fine-to-coarse bias due to early incorporation of low-level spatial cues, leading to blurred edges and artifacts. An interpretable, wavelet-based mechanism can control feature integration and improve depth boundaries.
AI.method: Proposes ML-DWT with sub-bands consumed in reverse of generation order to enable coarse-to-fine reconstruction; separate structure and detail reconstruction; model interactions across wavelet sub-bands, depth features, and semantic priors; apply semantic gating to high-frequency bands; use invertible coupling to fuse modalities and avoid collapse.
AI.result: Empirical results on multiple benchmarks show WAVE matches or surpasses state-of-the-art methods, with the largest improvements at high upsampling factors where low-res depth has less structure.
AI.conclusion: WAVE provides an intuitive alternative to implicit suppression in networks by filtering at the source using wavelet sub-bands, achieving clearer boundaries and reducing artifacts while maintaining modality fusion through invertible coupling.

title: SimVerity: When Does Simulated Agent Success Survive Physical Deployment?
comment: Submitted to the Main Technical Track of AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-27); currently under review
summary: Simulated evaluation is widely used to benchmark AI agents, yet how much evidence a simulated pass provides about physical deployment has not been systematically quantified. We present SimVerity, a verdict-transfer assurance framework: it replays matched scenarios on target smart home deployments and cross-validates agent execution against independently qualified physical witnesses. Our evaluation highlights that deployment success is a real-world process, not a static property in simulation: completion, reported state, observable effect, and settled outcome diverged within the same execution. Although an advanced simulator cleared all 240 light trials, a camera caught 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks. False clearance was predictable: a risk profile learned from measured trials and locked before evaluation predicted failures on a path it never physically measured, beating a property-blind baseline in all eleven held-out sessions across two cohorts. Agent auditability was also measurable: switching one agent loop's model-client/serving configuration raised its scenario-matching share from 52-88% to 100%. Finally, a second qualified simulator added no independent cross-check: it never disagreed on any overlapping case, and only physical measurement exposed their shared blind spots. SimVerity turns verdict transfer into an explicit decision: clear, abstain, or escalate before deployment.

AI.tldr: SimVerity cross-validates simulated AI verdicts with physical witnesses in matched smart-home scenarios, revealing simulation–reality divergence and enabling explicit verdict transfer for deployment decisions.
AI.motivation: Quantify how well simulated evidence about deployment generalizes to real-world physical deployment and to uncover blind spots where simulators may mislead.
AI.method: Replay matched scenarios on target deployments, cross-validate agent execution against qualified physical witnesses, analyze multiple trials (fast/short-time failures), learn a risk profile from measured trials, compare with a second simulator, and measure scenario-matching with configurable agent loops; produce explicit verdicts (clear/abstain/escalate).
AI.result: Real-world deployment outcomes diverged from simulations: completion, reported state, observable effect, and settled outcome can disagree within a single execution. A camera detected 42 sub-second failures invisible to settled-state checks, despite a simulator clearing all 240 light trials. A learned risk profile predicted failures on unmeasured paths, outperforming a property-blind baseline across eleven held-out sessions. Adjusting an agent loop’s model-client/serving configuration raised scenario-matching share from 52–88% to 100%. A second qualified simulator provided no independent cross-check, and only physical measurement revealed shared blind spots between simulators.
AI.conclusion: SimVerity makes verdict transfer explicit and auditable, enabling deployment decisions to be categorized as clear, abstain, or escalate; simulators alone are insufficient—physical witness validation is essential to reveal blind spots and ensure reliable deployment.

title: DeMMO: Longitudinal and Cross-Disease Modelling of Digital Mobility Outcomes via Multi-Task Learning
comment: 24 pages, 5 figures, and 7 tables. Implementation code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/menghui-zhou/DeMMO
summary: Digital mobility outcomes (DMOs) derived from wearable sensors characterise mobility in daily life and offer a promising means of monitoring disease progression. Yet most DMO studies examine one disease at one visit; they do not model how multivariate DMO relationships with multiple clinical outcomes evolve jointly across diseases. Technically, existing temporal multi-task frameworks can model progression within an individual disease, but they do not jointly model multiple prediction outcomes across diseases, particularly when disease cohorts do not share participants. To address these gaps, we propose DeMMO, an interpretable framework for longitudinal, multi-disease, and multi-outcome learning. DeMMO represents each disease-outcome objective by a longitudinal DMO coefficient matrix and combines temporal regularisation with stable and visit-specific feature selection. Its central technical contribution is an automatic cross-disease and cross-outcome relation-learning mechanism that learns signed relations directly from these longitudinal mappings, enabling selective information sharing without paired participants. We evaluate DeMMO on the recently released, large-scale, multicentre Mobilise-D dataset, which provides a new opportunity to study 24 harmonised real-world DMOs over five visits across multiple mobility-limiting conditions. Against nine strong linear, longitudinal, and deep-regression baselines, DeMMO achieves the best overall and outcome-specific prediction performance, with significant improvements over the strongest baselines. Stability selection further identifies reliable longitudinal DMO patterns for subsequent clinical validation and disease monitoring. The implementation code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/menghui-zhou/DeMMO.

AI.tldr: DeMMO is a cross-disease, cross-outcome longitudinal learning framework for digital mobility outcomes (DMOs) that learns signed cross-disease/outcome relations to enable selective information sharing without shared participants, evaluated on Mobilise-D with superior multi-task predictions and stable feature selection.
AI.motivation: Current longitudinal analyses typically model progression within a single disease or outcome and often rely on shared participants. There is a gap in jointly modeling multivariate DMOs across multiple diseases/outcomes, particularly when cohorts do not overlap, hindering insights into disease progression and monitoring.
AI.method: DeMMO represents each disease–outcome objective with a longitudinal DMO coefficient matrix, applies temporal regularisation and stable, visit-specific feature selection, and incorporates an automatic cross-disease and cross-outcome relation-learning mechanism that learns signed relations directly from longitudinal mappings, enabling selective information sharing without requiring paired participants.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on the Mobilise-D dataset with 24 harmonised DMOs over five visits and multiple mobility-limiting conditions showed that DeMMO achieves best overall and outcome-specific prediction performance compared with nine strong baselines (linear, longitudinal, and deep-regression). Stability selection identifies reliable longitudinal DMO patterns for clinical validation and monitoring; code and results are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: DeMMO provides interpretable, cross-disease and cross-outcome sharing for longitudinal DMOs, enabling joint progression modeling across diseases and outcomes even without shared participants, with practical implications for multi-disease monitoring and clinical validation.

title: Transient multimode heat transfer of an industrial automated tape laying process under rapidly changing conditions
summary: This work presents a transient heat-transfer model of an industrial automated tape laying (ATL) process designed to overcome the limitations of conventional thermal models in composite manufacturing. The model solves the heat-conduction equation with coupled advection, conduction, convection, and radiation. A key innovation is the implementation of an analytical view factor approach that accounts for finite emitter and tape widths, thereby correcting systematic overestimations of radiative heat flux inherent in 1.5D simplifications. Furthermore, a local convection assessment incorporates mixed convection effects characterized by the Richardson number, ensuring accuracy across a wide range of process speeds. The ATL system is represented by two interacting subsystems: the moving tape substrate and the infrared heat sources. The tape is discretized using a two-node model that resolves the physical phase shift between the heated and monitored surfaces. Numerical stability under high dynamics is ensured by a monolithic solution strategy using a high-order implicit integration scheme. Model predictions were validated on an industrial ATL line, demonstrating an overall deviation of only 1.08% (NRMSE) under rapid velocity and current modulations. This framework provides a high-fidelity, physics-based foundation for thermal state estimation, supporting consistent in-situ consolidation and improved part quality.

title: MulVec: Fine-Grained Role-Aware Matching for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
summary: Training-free zero-shot composed image retrieval finds a target image in a gallery from a reference image and a text edit without learning from task-specific image triplets. Existing methods typically describe the target as a whole and match this description with a global image representation. This global matching can mix different semantic cues and lose fine- grained details. We propose MULVEC, a role-aware method whose compiler produces a structured query record that is mapped to four retrieval roles: Global describes the full target, Desired states what should appear, Preserve states what should remain, and Forbidden states what should disappear. Frozen encoders map the query to one target description vector and role-specific probe vectors, while each candidate is represented by one global visual vector and a bank of local visual vectors. The retrieval roles then use this shared evidence for their respective purposes, and a fixed weighted sum of their scores ranks the entire gallery in a single retrieval pass. Across CIRCO, CIRR, and FashionIQ and three backbone scales, MULVEC improves CIRCO mAP@5 by up to 23.0% over the strongest compared method and gives the best CIRR and FashionIQ results in our comparison.

AI.tldr: MULVEC is a training-free zero-shot image retrieval method using role-aware structured queries and multi-vector representations to perform a single-pass ranking, achieving strong gains on CIRCO, CIRR, and FashionIQ.
AI.motivation: Global image representations in composed image retrieval blend different semantic cues and can miss fine-grained details; a structured, role-specific query can preserve and constrain target attributes to improve retrieval.
AI.method: Utilizes frozen encoders; a compiler produces a structured query record with four roles (Global, Desired states, Preserve states, Forbidden states). Each candidate is represented by one global visual vector and a bank of local visual vectors. The query maps to one target description vector and role-specific probe vectors. Retrieval uses shared evidence across roles with a fixed weighted sum to rank the gallery in a single pass.
AI.result: Across CIRCO, CIRR, and FashionIQ across three backbone scales, MULVEC yields up to 23.0% mAP@5 improvement on CIRCO over the strongest baselines and achieves the best CIRR and FashionIQ results in the authors’ comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Role-aware, multi-vector, training-free retrieval can outperform global-only descriptions in composed image retrieval across multiple datasets and backbone scales.

title: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World
comment: Presented at the 1st Workshop on Agent Skills (Agent Skills '26), ACM CAIS 2026, San Jose, May 26, 2026
summary: Self-evolving Skill harnesses (AutoSkills, Hermes Agent) generate more advisory orchestration automatically; their reported gains are efficiency, not safety. This misses the actual gap: a Skill describes how an agent should behave; a Policy decides which behavior is allowed to become an action. Today's format covers the first with markdown and scripts; the second is left to the model. Generating more Skills scales the gap, not the safety, especially when a wrong invocation can unlock a door or move money. Two adjacent attacks are documented: malicious skills compromising cloud software, and jailbroken LLM-controlled robots causing physical harm. Their intersection, malicious agent skills causing physical harm, follows directly but has not been reported. We name this class Borrowed Authority: Skills format gives the receiving agent no typed way to reject an inter-agent permission claim, so a malicious or misused Skill can drive actuation by attaching one. We propose Edge Skillguard, a typed authority layer that lives inside the Skill artifact rather than between tools as workflow engines do, with guards over world state and sensor evidence. On a live edge control-plane testbed, the guards reject 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across five attack variants without blocking benign requests, and the result holds at 5x scale and across hosts over a Tailscale mesh. These results suggest that high-risk Skills should co-package typed invocation policy with procedural knowledge, so that physical actions depend on machine-checkable evidence rather than peer-agent claims.

AI.tldr: The abstract argues that current self-evolving skill frameworks increase the number of executable actions without addressing inter-agent policy enforcement, introducing a typed authorization layer (Edge Skillguard) inside Skill artifacts to prevent borrowed-authority misuse; live-edge tests show perfect rejection of such attacks across variants and scale, suggesting safety requires machine-checkable evidence and co-packaged policies with skills.
AI.motivation: To close the safety gap where policies for what actions are allowed are left to model behavior, creating risk that malicious or misused skills can trigger harmful actuation through borrowed authority.
AI.method: Propose Edge Skillguard—an internal, typed invocation policy inside the Skill artifact guarding world state and sensor evidence. Validate on a live edge control-plane testbed by simulating borrowed-authority attacks across five variants; scale tests show 5x expansion across hosts via a Tailscale mesh.
AI.result: The guards rejected 60/60 borrowed-authority requests across the five attack variants without blocking benign requests; results hold under a 5x scale and across mesh-enabled hosts.
AI.conclusion: High-risk skills should co-package typed invocation policy with procedural knowledge so that physical actions depend on machine-checkable evidence rather than inter-agent permission claims.

title: NVExplain: Explaining Time Series Forecasting with Latent Trajectory Analysis and Structure-Preserving Surrogates
summary: Time series forecasting models are widely used in high-stakes settings, yet their predictions remain difficult to interpret because existing post-hoc methods often ignore temporal dependence and fail to provide horizon-specific explanations. We propose a model-agnostic explainability framework that explains forecasting predictions by attributing each forecast horizon to temporally relevant historical lags. The framework models forecasting as a latent trajectory and introduces semantic flow to quantify how information evolves across time in the model's internal representations. By aggregating semantic flow, it constructs a lag-horizon attribution matrix that captures horizon-resolved temporal influence. To improve explainability, we further generate structure-preserving perturbations and fit sparse local surrogate models, producing human-readable and temporally coherent explanations. We evaluate the method using faithfulness and stability diagnostics across multiple benchmark datasets. Results show that the semantic-flow variant achieves competitive or superior faithfulness compared to standard post-hoc baselines, while being substantially more computationally efficient. Stability analysis further demonstrates that the explanations are robust and identifies regimes where interpretation should be applied with caution.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic explainability framework for time-series forecasting that assigns horizon-specific attributions to temporally relevant historical lags via a latent-trajectory and semantic-flow approach, plus structure-preserving perturbations and sparse surrogates; demonstrates competitive faithfulness and higher efficiency, with stability-based guidance.
AI.motivation: Forecasting in high-stakes settings requires horizon-resolved, temporally coherent explanations that respect temporal dependencies; standard post-hoc methods often ignore time structure, reducing interpretability.
AI.method: Model-agnostic explainability framework: explain forecasts by attributing each horizon to temporally relevant historical lags. Model forecasting as a latent trajectory, with semantic flow to quantify information evolution in internal representations. Aggregate into a lag-horizon attribution matrix. Generate structure-preserving perturbations and fit sparse local surrogate models to yield human-readable explanations. Evaluate with faithfulness and stability diagnostics on benchmarks.
AI.result: Semantic-flow variant achieves competitive or superior faithfulness compared to standard post-hoc baselines and is substantially more computationally efficient. Stability analysis shows robust explanations and identifies regimes where interpretation should be used with caution across multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides horizon-resolved, temporally coherent explanations for forecasting, combining efficiency and robustness via semantic flow and surrogate-based explanations, suitable for high-stakes applications.

title: Dynamic Modeling of a Welding Torch Umbilical and Its Impact on Robot Dynamics
summary: Robotic welding is widely used in industrial manufacturing, where the welding torch is often connected to the generator through an external umbilical. With the increasing deployment of lightweight and collaborative robots, the dynamic influence of this umbilical can significantly affect the robot motion and the actuation forces. This paper proposes a constrained multibody dynamic model of a welding umbilical, represented as a serial chain of rigid bodies interconnected by passive joints with elastic and dissipative effects. Prescribed motions at the distal anchor point are introduced through holonomic kinematic constraints. The equations of motion are reduced by projecting the dynamics onto the subspace of admissible velocities, yielding an efficient formulation free of Lagrange multipliers. The reaction wrench exerted by the umbilical on the robot is explicitly recovered. A planar case study illustrates the approach.

AI.tldr: Constrained multibody dynamics model for welding umbilicals yields a multiplier-free, efficient method with explicit reaction wrenches; validated via a planar case study.
AI.motivation: Welding torches connected to generators via external umbilicals influence robot dynamics, especially for lightweight/collaborative robots; accurate, efficient modeling of the umbilical's influence is needed for control and design.
AI.method: Model the umbilical as a serial chain of rigid bodies connected by passive, elastic/dissipative joints; enforce distal anchor prescriptions via holonomic constraints; project equations of motion onto the admissible velocity subspace to eliminate Lagrange multipliers; extract reaction wrenches on the robot.
AI.result: Derives a compact, constraint-consistent dynamic formulation free of Lagrange multipliers and demonstrates the approach on a planar case study; shows explicit computation of the umbilical reaction wrench.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an efficient, explicit way to account for umbilical effects in robotic welding setups; planar validation confirms feasibility, with potential extension to 3D and broader robotic manipulators.

title: V-Link: Recovering Lost Visual Representations in Action DiT for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a scalable path toward generalist robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and continuous action control. However, we reveal a critical limitation of VLA architectures: the action expert has limited access to the 3D geometric and 2D semantic information available in VLM features. This accessibility gap weakens perceptual grounding and limits performance on fine-grained robotic manipulation. To address this issue, we propose V-Link, which explicitly recovers visual representations during the vision-language (VL) to action (A) feature transfer. Specifically, V-Link learns complementary Spatial and Semantic Query representations within the VLM and injects them into Action DiT through asymmetric pathways. Semantic Queries complement the original VLM image tokens, whereas Spatial Queries provide dedicated geometric conditioning for spatially grounded action generation. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, our V-Link improves the average success rate over base model GR00T N1.6 by +1.9%, +31.2%, and +18.8%, respectively. On the AGIBOT A3 Ultra, V-Link further achieves gains of +20% and +24% on two real-world humanoid tasks.

AI.tldr: V-Link closes the action access gap by introducing Spatial and Semantic Queries that recover visual representations during VL-to-action transfer, yielding consistent performance gains across multiple sim-to-real robotic platforms.
AI.motivation: To address the limited access of the action module to 3D geometry and 2D semantics embedded in VLM features, which hampers perceptual grounding and fine-grained manipulation.
AI.method: Introduce Spatial Queries (for geometric conditioning) and Semantic Queries (augmented tokens) within the VLM and inject them via asymmetric pathways into the Action DiT. Train end-to-end across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world AGIBOT A3 Ultra tasks.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in success rate: +1.9%, +31.2%, +18.8% over LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0 respectively; +20% and +24% gains on two real-world humanoid tasks on AGIBOT A3 Ultra.
AI.conclusion: V-Link effectively recovers and fuses visual representations to enhance perception-grounded action generation; explicit geometric and semantic conditioning in VL-to-action transfer yields robust gains across simulated and real-world robotic manipulation, suggesting wide applicability and avenues for further ablations and efficiency considerations.

title: PhysElite: How Far Are LLMs from Solving Olympiad-Level Physics Problems?
summary: Understanding how (multimodal) large language models perform on physics problems requires benchmarks that reflect the difficulty and breadth of expert-level physical reasoning. Existing physics benchmarks remain limited in the following two important ways: (1) short of high-difficulty datasets, and (2) lack of comprehensive coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and step-by-step solution processes. As a result, model performance on current datasets may not be fully representative of their ability to solve complex physics problems. To address these issues, we present PhysElite, a large-scale bilingual multimodal benchmark for Olympiad-level physics reasoning. PhysElite contains 11,586 Olympiad-tier problems. For each problem, we provide corresponding visual diagrams, step-by-step bilingual Chinese-English solution derivations, and the final answer. We benchmark 18 open-source and closed-source MLLMs, and find that even the strongest model reaches only 33.7% answer accuracy. We additionally conduct step-level process evaluation to diagnose where models fail in the reasoning chain. Our datasets are released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/physelite/PhysElite.

AI.tldr: PhysElite is a large bilingual multimodal benchmark (11,586 Olympiad-level physics problems) with diagrams, bilingual step-by-step solutions, and finals answers; evaluated 18 MLLMs, strongest at 33.7% accuracy; includes step-level diagnosis; dataset released on HuggingFace.
AI.motivation: Fill gaps in existing physics benchmarks by increasing difficulty and expanding coverage of visual forms, knowledge points, and explicit solution processes, enabling robust evaluation of multimodal physics reasoning.
AI.method: Assembled 11,586 problems with corresponding visual diagrams and bilingual (Chinese-English) step-by-step derivations and final answers; benchmarked 18 open/closed-source MLLMs; performed step-level process analysis to identify misconception points; released dataset on HuggingFace.
AI.result: Final-answer accuracy for the best model: 33.7%; step-level analysis pinpointed chaining failures; dataset and evaluation protocol released publicly.
AI.conclusion: PhysElite provides a rigorous, multilingual, multimodal testbed for Olympiad-level physics reasoning, highlighting current model gaps and guiding future improvements in multimodal reasoning, cross-lingual understanding, and complex problem-solving.

title: The Frame Kernel Method for Multiscale Operator Learning
summary: We present a natively multiscale operator learning method for the surrogate modeling of (numerical solvers for) multiscale partial differential equations (PDEs). The primary novelty of our method lies in a novel multiscale kernel frame function approximation technique. Leveraging this new kernel frame technique, we cast the operator learning problem as one of learning frame coefficients of output functions as a function of frame coefficients of input functions. The generalization step then automatically allows for a multiscale decomposition of the output functions. Our method is applicable to both tensor-product grids and point clouds. We present interpolation proofs, error estimates, and numerical convergence rates for our frame approximation. We the demonstrate the applicability of our method for the surrogate modeling of inherently multiscale PDEs. The new multiscale frame kernel method is significantly more accurate than popular neural operators on challenging problems from the literature, while simultaneously admitting an a posteriori multiscale decomposition upon generalization.

AI.tldr: A multiscale operator learning framework using a novel multiscale kernel frame function approximation to learn frame coefficients; results include interpolation proofs, error estimates, and convergence rates; claims superior accuracy to neural operators on multiscale PDE surrogate modeling; enables a posteriori multiscale decomposition.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of existing neural operators in multiscale PDE surrogate modeling; enable native multiscale decomposition and accurate surrogate modeling on both tensor-product grids and point clouds.
AI.method: Introduce multiscale kernel frame function approximation; formulate operator learning as learning frame coefficients; derive interpolation proofs, error estimates, convergence rates; applicable to grids and point clouds.
AI.result: Frame method more accurate than popular neural operators on challenging problems; provides a posteriori multiscale decomposition upon generalization.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a scalable, accurate, and theoretically grounded surrogate modeling approach for multiscale PDEs with broad applicability and interpretable multiscale decompositions.

title: A Tendon-Driven Five-Fingered Hand with Distributed Tactile Perception for Dexterous Manipulation
comment: Accepted by International Conference on Service Robotics (ICoSR) 2026
summary: To apply the techniques of embodied artificial intelligence to human-oid robots for complex manipulations, dexterous robotic hands are indispensable, which are restricted by the dexterity and tactile perception capability. In this work, we proposed a novel design of tendon-driven five-fingered hand with dis-tributed tactile perception. With a soft-rigid-hybrid structure employed, both compliance and operational force are endowed to the hand. Dual-modality tactile sensing elements are distributed on the distal and middle phalanges of all five fingers, enabling the simultaneous detection of static contact and dynamic force variations. Manipulation experiments, including counting gestures, finger-to-thumb pinching, object grasping, and bottle-grasp tactile recording, demonstrate the feasibility of the integrated actuation-perception system.

AI.tldr: A tendon-driven, five-finger robotic hand with a soft-rigid-hybrid structure and distributed dual-modality tactile sensors on distal and middle phalanges enables simultaneous static contact and dynamic force sensing for dexterous manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Advance embodied artificial intelligence for human-oid robots by enhancing dexterity and tactile perception through integrated actuation and perception in a tendon-driven hand.
AI.method: Design and fabricate a tendon-driven five-finger hand with a soft-rigid-hybrid construction; integrate dual-modality tactile sensors on distal and middle phalanges of all fingers to capture static contact and dynamic force changes; validate with manipulation experiments (counting gestures, finger-to-thumb pinching, object grasping, bottle-grasp tactile recording).
AI.result: Demonstrated feasibility of an integrated actuation-perception system; tactile sensors successfully capture static contact and dynamic force variations during diverse manipulation tasks; the hand achieves basic dexterous actions.
AI.conclusion: The integrated tendon-driven, soft-rigid-hybrid hand with distributed tactile sensing constitutes a viable approach to dexterous manipulation for human-oid robots; future work could explore sensor fusion, advanced control strategies, and more complex manipulations.

title: Not All Attention Heads Contribute to Critical Visual Token Selection: Head-Aware Pruning Matters More
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have exhibited impressive performance across diverse visual scenarios. However, this success comes at the cost of explosive growth in visual tokens, which imposes substantial memory and computational overhead during inference, ultimately increasing latency. To improve VLM inference efficiency, a typical class of visual token pruning methods estimates token importance by aggregating attention scores across all heads in the pruning layer of the Large Language Model (LLM) backbone and prunes tokens based on aggregated scores. However, in this paper, we reveal a compelling phenomenon: the capability to pinpoint critical visual tokens is concentrated within a small fraction of heads. Aggregation exclusively on these heads can improve task performance. Inspired by this observation, we propose ProViP, a training-free progressive visual token pruning framework. ProViP first removes redundant visual tokens based on the embedding similarity of input tokens before reasoning of the LLM backbone, and then further prunes tokens during reasoning via head-aware pruning. Experiments demonstrate that ProViP delivers outstanding task performance and inference efficiency. For instance, when applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B, ProViP retains 95.9% of the original performance and achieves 1.62x inference speedup under an 88.9% pruning ratio.

AI.tldr: ProViP is a training-free progressive visual token pruning framework for VLMs that prunes tokens in two stages—embedding-based pre-pruning and head-aware pruning during reasoning—achieving substantial speedups with minimal accuracy loss (e.g., 1.62x speedup at 88.9% pruning on LLaVA-1.5-7B and 95.9% of original performance retained).
AI.motivation: To address the memory and compute bottleneck from growing visual tokens in VLMs and limitations of aggregating attention across all heads; reveal that critical tokens are concentrated in a small subset of heads.
AI.method: 1) Pre-reasoning pruning by embedding-similarity across input tokens to remove redundancy; 2) During LLM reasoning, head-aware pruning to selectively prune tokens using the most informative heads.
AI.result: Empirical results show strong task performance and inference efficiency; on LLaVA-1.5-7B, preserves 95.9% accuracy with 1.62x speedup at 88.9% pruning.
AI.conclusion: ProViP offers a training-free, efficient token pruning paradigm that exploits head-sparsity to maintain performance while significantly reducing tokens and computation.

title: Towards Reliable, Generalizable, and Specific In-Context Knowledge Editing via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
comment: Our work proposes a multi-objective reinforcement learning algorithm that optimizes prompt construction for reliable, generalizable, and specific in-context knowledge-editing
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful but limited by static parametric knowledge that becomes outdated once pretraining ends. Knowledge editing addresses this problem by updating model behavior on target facts without full retraining. In particular, in-context knowledge editing has gained attention because it is training-free and readily applicable to black-box LLMs. Recent reinforcement learning (RL)-based approaches improve over fixed retrieval strategies by adapting prompt construction to the quantity-quality trade-off. Despite initial success, they fail to model the prompt as a structured entity under the distinct and often competing objectives of reliability, generality, and specificity. Previous methods largely optimize a single objective and make decisions over only part of the prompt construction process, thereby overlooking both the balance of different objectives and the global organization of demonstrations. We propose Multi-Objective In-context Knowledge Editing (MO-IKE), a multi-objective RL algorithm that formulates prompt construction for in-context knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process. MO-IKE trains a dynamic retriever to optimize competing objectives in knowledge editing, enabling more balanced and globally coherent prompt construction. On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, while increasing retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.

AI.tldr: MO-IKE proposes a multi-objective RL approach with a constrained MDP for in-context knowledge editing, enabling balanced, globally coherent prompt construction and yielding measurable gains in reliability, generality, and specificity on Llama-3.2.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from static, outdated parametric knowledge post-pretraining. In-context editing is attractive because it is training-free and applicable to black-box LLMs, but existing RL-based methods optimize a single objective and modify only parts of the prompt, neglecting the global organization and trade-offs among reliability, generality, and specificity.
AI.method: Formulates in-context knowledge editing as a Constrained Markov Decision Process and trains a dynamic retriever to optimize multiple competing objectives (reliability, generality, specificity) for prompt construction, achieving more balanced and globally coherent prompts.
AI.result: On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE raises edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%; paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%; retention rate (specificity) increases by 23.0% relative to prior RL-based methods.
AI.conclusion: A multi-objective, constrained-RL approach that models the prompt as a structured, globally optimized artifact yields improved knowledge editing performance, suggesting broader applicability of constraint-based RL for in-context editing.

title: The Von-Neumann State-Space Transformer for neural decoding
summary: Cortical computation is strikingly low-dimensional: a handful of latent variables, carried in a neural population's activity, steer the higher-dimensional responses of individual neurons. Our aim is sample efficiency-models that decode well from limited data and at small parameter budgets. In a standard Transformer layer, the feed-forward block applies the same operator to every token. We suggest a von-Neumann inspired hypothesis of efficient computation as an alternative for neural decoding: a controller decodes an instruction and then executes a token-specific operator; the usual realization-a soft mixture of experts-only blends their outputs, not operators. We introduce a von-Neumann State-Space Transformer (VN-SST), a memory-augmented Transformer whose feed-forward block is a low-rank instruction bank: a shared base operator plus a small set of learned low-rank instructions, from which a per-token code synthesizes the weight matrix actually used at that token. The code is read from a low- dimensional projection of a carried state-space memory, so a slow latent trajectory acts as an instruction pointer-mirroring how low-dimensional dynamics may route cortical computation. On three motor-cortex neural-decoding benchmarks, VN-SST is far more data-efficient than a modern Transformer, each jointly predicting spikes and decoding behavior. This model wins by a wide margin on the scarcest benchmark, leads on the other two, and turns longer context into rising rather than falling accuracy. We evaluated that the network compresses a large instruction bank to a few bits per token, so program capacity acts as a control channel, not an accuracy lever. The same model is also more parameter-efficient on two small text benchmarks used for language modeling (LLMs), suggesting a generic mechanism.

AI.tldr: Introducing VN-SST, a memory-augmented Transformer with a von Neumann-inspired, low-rank instruction bank that generates per-token weight matrices from a compact code, enabling strong data efficiency in neural decoding and competitive parameter efficiency in NLP tasks.
AI.motivation: Cortical computation appears low-dimensional and samples neural decoding from limited data; there is a need for architectures that are highly data-efficient and parameter-efficient while maintaining performance across domains.
AI.method: Propose a von-Neumann State-Space Transformer (VN-SST) where the feed-forward block uses a shared base operator plus a small set of learned low-rank instructions. A per-token code synthesizes the weight matrix from a low-dimensional projection of a carried state-space memory, effectively routing computation via a slow latent trajectory. The instruction bank is compressed to a few bits per token, acting as a control channel.
AI.result: VN-SST achieves superior data efficiency on three motor-cortex neural-decoding benchmarks, jointly predicting spikes and decoding behavior, and outperforms a modern Transformer especially in scarce-data regimes. It scales better with longer context. The model also achieves improved parameter efficiency on two small text benchmarks, suggesting a generic mechanism for cross-domain efficiency.
AI.conclusion: A memory-augmented, von Neumann-inspired decoding mechanism can route token-specific operators through a compact instruction code, enabling data- and parameter-efficient neural decoding. The approach hints at a generic principle for efficient computation that could generalize beyond neuroscience to NLP and other domains.

title: ConfAL-WM: Confidence-Guided Active Learning for Action-Conditioned World Models
summary: Action-conditioned world models have become an important foundation for embodied prediction, planning, and synthetic data generation, but their errors under new task and scene distributions are often concentrated in localized spatiotemporal regions such as robot arms, manipulated objects, contact areas, and occluded objects. This paper presents ConfAL-WM, a confidence-guided active learning framework for post-training embodied world models. Built upon EVAC, we attach a lightweight confidence probe to UNet decoder features and predict dense confidence maps in the latent space. These maps are aggregated into task-, frame-, and patch-level scores, enabling both efficient data selection and localized training enhancement. Our pipeline first retrains the confidence probe and warms up EVAC with a small subset of target-domain data, then performs task-level prescreening to allocate sampling budgets, and finally applies selected-data retraining with optional frame or patch weighted data enhancement. Experiments on RoboTwin2.0 show that confidence-guided selection improves post-training efficiency, while dense frame and patch weighting further enhances prediction quality and embodied trajectory consistency compared with scalar reward, progress, and judge-based scoring baselines. A quick visual overview of this work is available at https://ConfAL-WM.github.io.
