AI.tldr: ConfAL-WM: confidence-guided active learning for post-training embodied world models that attaches a confidence probe to EVAC/UNet features to generate dense latent-space confidence maps for task/frame/patch-aware data selection and training weightings, improving efficiency and trajectory quality on RoboTwin2.0.
AI.motivation: Embodied world models often exhibit localized errors on new task/scene distributions (arms, objects, contact zones, occlusions). A lightweight, task-aware mechanism is needed to identify and focus training data to these failure regions after initial training.
AI.method: Attach a lightweight confidence probe to UNet decoder features to predict dense confidence maps in latent space. Aggregate into task-, frame-, and patch-level scores for data selection and localized retraining. The pipeline: (1) retrain the confidence probe and warm up EVAC with a small target-domain subset; (2) task-level prescreening to allocate sampling budgets; (3) selected-data retraining with optional frame/patch weighted data enhancement.
AI.result: On RoboTwin2.0, confidence-guided selection improves post-training efficiency. Dense frame/patch weighting further enhances prediction quality and embodied trajectory consistency compared with scalar reward, progress, and judge-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: ConfAL-WM provides an effective post-training, data-efficient framework for improving embodied world model accuracy and consistency in target domains via confidence-guided data selection and localized retraining.

title: GraftSR: Grafting Authentic Textures for Real-World Image Super-Resolution via Identical-Instance Guidance
summary: Diffusion-based real-world image super-resolution (SR) achieves impressive perceptual quality but inherently suffers from severe texture hallucination. To overcome this limitation, we propose GraftSR, a texture-reference-guided generative SR framework that leverages reference images of the identical instance to anchor the restoration of authentic textures. However, severe spatial misalignment between low-quality inputs and their references poses significant challenges, often leading to ambiguous transfer targets and background feature leakage. To address these issues, GraftSR employs a novel dual-mask reference guidance mechanism that systematically decouples the cross-view texture injection process. By explicitly isolating what authentic textures to extract from the reference and precisely localizing where to apply them within the target, GraftSR achieves robust texture transfer without relying on brittle spatial alignment. Furthermore, to bridge the critical gap in appropriate training data, we construct TexRefSR-141K, the first large-scale dataset providing high-quality reference tuples equipped with complementary spatial masks. Extensive experiments on our newly established benchmark, TexRefSR-Eval, demonstrate that GraftSR sets a new state-of-the-art. Notably, it reduces LPIPS by 20.2\% over top-performing baselines, achieving superior reference-faithful restoration.

AI.tldr: Proposes GraftSR, a dual-mask, texture-reference-guided SR framework to reduce texture hallucination in diffusion-based real-world SR; introduces TexRefSR-141K dataset and TexRefSR-Eval benchmark; achieves state-of-the-art with 20.2% LPIPS improvement.
AI.motivation: Address severe texture hallucination in diffusion-based real-world SR and misalignment between inputs and references; provide robust, localization-guided texture transfer without brittle alignment; and supply high-quality reference data for training/testing.
AI.method: Dual-mask reference guidance: decouples which textures to extract from reference and where to apply them in target; uses identical-instance reference images; constructs TexRefSR-141K with spatial masks; evaluation on TexRefSR-Eval showing improvement.
AI.result: LPIPS reduced by 20.2% vs top baselines; achieves state-of-the-art on TexRefSR-Eval; demonstrates robust texture transfer with reduced leakage.
AI.conclusion: GraftSR advances texture-faithful SR via reference-guided, alignment-insensitive transfer and provides a new benchmark dataset to catalyze future research.

title: FuzzingBrain-Bench V1: Evaluating Open-Ended Bug Discovery by LLMs
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables. Ze Sheng and Aleksandar Kezic contributed equally. Benchmark corpus and harnesses: https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench Counts verified against the built PDF and sources: 21 pages, 12 figure environments, 7 tables
summary:
Evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to discover software bugs is increasingly important. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate this capability by asking the model to generate a proof-of-concept input that triggers a predefined target vulnerability. However, this setup may overlook valid crashes discovered by the model when they do not match the predefined target. As a result, the evaluation may not reflect the model's real capability.
  We present FuzzingBrain-Bench, a benchmark for assessing AI models' ability to discover bugs in open-source software. Models are given an open-source project and a sanitizer-instrumented harness in a self-contained Docker image. Their goal is to generate inputs that trigger as many distinct crashes as possible through the harness. A model's performance on each challenge is scored based on the number of distinct crash signatures it produces, capped at a predefined maximum and weighted by a difficulty coefficient.
  FuzzingBrain-Bench V1 consists of 77 challenges drawn from 43 open-source projects, with 36 C, 32 C++, and 9 Java/JVM challenges. We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Claude Opus 4.8 on the full benchmark. Claude Opus 4.8 performs best, triggering crashes in 60 of 77 challenges and achieving a score of 196 out of 579. None of the three models triggers a crash in 13 challenges. The FuzzingBrain-Bench corpus and harnesses are publicly available at https://github.com/fuzzingbrain/FuzzingBrain-Bench.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (FuzzingBrain-Bench) evaluates LLMs on open-ended bug discovery by generating inputs that trigger crashes in sanitizer-instrumented harnesses across 77 challenges from 43 open-source projects (C, C++, Java). Claude family shows varying performance, with Opus 4.8 best (60 crashes; 196/579).
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focusing on predefined vulnerabilities may miss valid crashes; need an open-ended evaluation of models' bug-finding ability in real software.
AI.method: Provide open-source project + sanitizer-instrumented harness inside a Docker image; models produce inputs to trigger crashes; score is based on distinct crash signatures, capped, and weighted by challenge difficulty.
AI.result: Opus 4.8 achieved the best performance, triggering crashes in 60 of 77 challenges and scoring 196/579; 13 challenges yielded no crashes; full benchmark with dataset and harnesses is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark enables assessment of LLMs' broad bug-discovery capabilities and provides public resources; results suggest gaps in current models and the value of open-ended fuzzing-style evaluation.

title: Understanding the Energy Scaling of Large Language Model Inference Across Context Lengths and Attention Architectures
summary: The growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) has raised increasing concerns about the energy consumption and environmental impact of inference. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of decode-phase energy consumption across representative open-source LLMs employing Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Grouped Query Attention (GQA), and Grouped Query Attention with Sliding Window Attention (SWA) to characterize how attention architecture influences decode-phase energy consumption under varying inference workloads. We evaluate four models across different context lengths, batch sizes, and generation workloads while measuring GPU energy using NVIDIA hardware counters. We examine the effects of context length, attention mechanism, Key-Value (KV) cache growth, and batching on decode-phase energy consumption. Results show that attention mechanism is the primary factor governing how decode energy scales with context length. MHA models exhibit substantially steeper energy growth than GQA models, whereas GQA with SWA maintains nearly constant energy consumption. We further show that model size primarily determines absolute energy consumption, while batching reduces both energy per generated token and request latency by up to 87%. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting energy-efficient LLM architectures and inference configurations.

AI.tldr: Systematic empirical study of decode-phase energy in LLMs, comparing MHA, GQA, and SWA attention. Key finding: attention type governs energy scaling with context; MHA scales steeply, GQA moderate, SWA nearly constant. Model size sets absolute energy; batching reduces energy per token and latency up to 87%. Provides guidance for energy-efficient architecture/configuration.
AI.motivation: Address rising concerns about energy use in LLM inference by understanding how attention architectures and workloads affect decode-phase energy, to inform architecture choices and deployment strategies.
AI.method: Empirical measurements on four open-source LLMs using MHA, GQA, and SWA under varying context lengths, batch sizes, and generation workloads. GPU energy quantified via NVIDIA hardware counters. Analyzed effects of context length, attention mode, KV cache growth, and batching on decode-phase energy.
AI.result: MHA models show steep energy growth with increasing context length; GQA reduces scaling; GQA with SWA maintains nearly constant energy across contexts. Model size dictates absolute energy; batching reduces energy per generated token and reduces latency (up to 87%).
AI.conclusion: Energy-efficient deployment favors attention architectures like GQA/SWA and appropriate batching; design choices in context length and model size critically affect decode-phase energy performance.

title: RA-VLA: Retrieval-Augmented VLA for Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide a versatile foundation for general robotic manipulation, yet they exhibit significant brittleness when confronted with novel task distributions. While In-Context Imitation Learning (ICIL) offers a training-free alternative, existing frameworks suffer from an adaptation bottleneck that hinders the effective translation of expert context to executable actions. This failure originates from superficial retrieval mechanisms and an inherent behavioral inertia that anchors the policy to its pre-trained priors. To address these limitations, we present RA-VLA, a retrieval-augmented VLA framework that integrates behavior-aligned context retrieval with a grounded execution pipeline. By enforcing faithful adherence to functional cues within a scalable architecture, RA-VLA facilitates seamless task adaptation while preserving inference efficiency. Our empirical evaluations across the LIBERO benchmark and a real-world UR5e environment demonstrate that RA-VLA achieves superior success rates and computational efficiency, establishing a robust framework for training-free robotic adaptation.

AI.tldr: RA-VLA is a retrieval-augmented Vision-Language-Action framework that aligns behaviorally relevant retrieved context with a grounded execution pipeline to enable training-free robotic adaptation, achieving superior success and efficiency on LIBERO and UR5e.
AI.motivation: Overcome brittleness of VLA-based robotic manipulation under novel task distributions and fix the adaptation bottleneck in In-Context Imitation Learning by moving beyond superficial retrieval and priors.
AI.method: Introduce RA-VLA: a retrieval-augmented VLA framework with behavior-aligned context retrieval and a grounded execution pipeline. Enforces faithful adherence to functional cues within a scalable architecture to enable seamless task adaptation with efficient inference.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on the LIBERO benchmark and real UR5e setup shows higher success rates and improved computational efficiency, demonstrating effective training-free adaptation for robotic manipulation.
AI.conclusion: RA-VLA provides a robust, scalable approach to training-free robotic adaptation by tightly coupling behavior-aligned retrieval with grounded execution, improving generalization and efficiency.

title: CoRE: Weakly Supervised Coarse-to-Fine Risk Evidence Learning in Driving Videos
summary: Perceived risk in driving evolves over time and may be supported by specific scene entities, yet supervision is typically limited to coarse video-level judgments. Learning \emph{when} supporting evidence emerges and \emph{which entities} support a risk predictor would ordinarily require costly temporal- and entity-level annotations. We introduce \textbf{CoRE}, a weakly supervised coarse-to-fine framework that learns fine-grained prediction support from coarse video supervision. CoRE first trains a video-level predictor and then freezes it. Structured interventions over candidate temporal regions or entity tracks measure how each candidate changes the coarse prediction, producing graded prediction-effect targets. These targets are distilled into a student that directly predicts temporal and entity support from the original video, without requiring interventions at inference. We evaluate this learning principle across three complementary settings: RISEE tests perceived-risk support from subjective clip-level judgments without temporal or entity-level risk annotations; DoTA provides independent temporal event annotations for evaluating weakly supervised traffic-anomaly localization; and UCF-Crime tests whether the same coarse-to-fine mechanism extends to a standard non-driving anomaly-detection benchmark. Across these settings, CoRE learns informative fine-grained support from coarse supervision, with strong temporal localization on DoTA and competitive performance on UCF-Crime. These results show that coarse video predictions can provide useful supervision for recovering the fine-grained evidence supporting them, without requiring corresponding fine-grained labels.

AI.tldr: CoRE is a weakly supervised coarse-to-fine framework that learns fine-grained temporal and entity-level evidence for risk prediction from coarse video-level labels; it trains a video-level predictor, freezes it, applies structured interventions to generate prediction-effect targets, and distills these into a student that directly predicts support from the video without fine-grained labels; evaluated on three datasets with strong temporal localization and competitive anomaly detection performance.
AI.motivation: Perceived driving risk evolves over time and is tied to specific scene entities, but fine-grained (temporal/entity) annotations are costly. A method that learns such evidence from coarse video-level supervision would be valuable.
AI.method: Train a video-level risk predictor, freeze it, perform structured interventions over candidate temporal regions and entity tracks to assess changes in the coarse prediction, generate graded prediction-effect targets, and distill these into a student that predicts temporal and entity support directly from the video at inference without requiring interventions.
AI.result: CoRE enables learning informative fine-grained support from coarse supervision across three settings (RISEE, DoTA, UCF-Crime). It yields strong temporal localization on DoTA and competitive performance on UCF-Crime, demonstrating that coarse predictions can supervise the recovery of fine-grained evidence without explicit fine-grained labels.
AI.conclusion: CoRE demonstrates the viability of coarse-to-fine learning to recover fine-grained evidence (temporal and entity support) from only coarse video supervision, enabling efficient and scalable weakly supervised risk explanation and anomaly detection.

title: Tunable Tool-Call Rates in LLM Agents via Representation Steering
summary: Deciding whether to call a tool is a core competence of an LLM agent, and a costly one to get wrong: needless calls add latency, accrue cost, and may trigger irreversible side effects, while missing calls leave the model confidently wrong on questions it could only answer through tool-calls. Models manage this balance poorly, both over-using and under-using tools. Existing methods such as post-training and prompt engineering are expensive and difficult to modify at inference time. We show that whether an instruction-tuned model calls a tool can be controlled by a single linear direction in its residual stream, extracted without any training from the model's own tool-use preference signal and turned into an inference-time intervention with no prompt change. Adding the direction with strength $α$ moves the call rate monotonically from near $0\% $ to over $90\%$ while keeping calls well-formed. The steering works in both directions: dialing it down suppresses calls, and dialing it up induces new calls that land precisely on the questions the model cannot answer from its own knowledge. We also show that the direction generalizes to unseen tools with strength comparable to each tool's own direction and without favoring any specific tool choice. With live tool execution, a single sweep of the steering traces a cost/accuracy Pareto frontier and nearly doubles open-domain QA accuracy ($0.29 \! \rightarrow \! 0.56$); the same recipe transfers across a diverse range of models spanning dense, MoE, and multimodal architectures, without any training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/YuqiChen4188/Steering-Tool-Use-Propensity.

AI.tldr: A training-free, inference-time method to steer tool-use propensity in instruction-tuned LLMs via a single residual-stream direction; enables precise control of tool calls, improves QA accuracy, and generalizes across tools and architectures.
AI.motivation: Deciding when to call external tools is critical and costly; existing calibration methods require retraining or prompt engineering and are hard to adapt at inference. A lightweight, train-free control would reduce latency, cost, and risk of wrong tool use.
AI.method: Identify a single linear direction in the model's residual stream encoding tool-use preference. extract from the model's own signals without training. At inference, add this direction with strength α to steer tool-use: increasing α raises call rate from ~0% toward >90%, decreasing α suppresses calls. Works for both directions; generalizes to unseen tools; no prompt changes; can be applied across architectures without training.
AI.result: With live tool execution, tool-use steering achieves a cost/accuracy Pareto frontier and nearly doubles open-domain QA accuracy (0.29 to 0.56). Direction generalizes to unseen tools with comparable strength. Transfers across dense, MoE, and multimodal models; code released.
AI.conclusion: A simple, training-free mechanism to calibrate tool-use propensity in LLMs by injecting a residual-direction; robust, broadly applicable, and actionable for runtime trade-offs between accuracy and tool usage.

title: Flower Hub: A Reproducible Benchmarking Platform for Federated Learning in Simulation and Deployment
summary: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a key approach for training models across decentralized data, yet benchmarking in FL remains difficult to reproduce, compare, and extend. Existing evaluations are often tied to custom infrastructure, released as incomplete research code, and conducted primarily in simulation, which limits portability and practical relevance. We present Flower Hub, a platform for publishing, discovering, and executing decentralized and federated applications. We show how it enables reproducible benchmarking by packaging benchmarks as executable, versioned applications with standardized metadata, pinned dependencies, and explicit evaluation workflows. We instantiate this approach with a multi-domain benchmark suite spanning cross-silo and cross-device settings, and including tasks in medical imaging, financial tabular learning, legal instruction tuning, phishing URL detection, and audio tagging. We further demonstrate that the same benchmarking application can run across both simulation and deployment runtimes without changing the application code, enabling unified evaluation across varying learning environments. Beyond model quality, our benchmark design supports system-aware reporting, including runtime and communication metrics. This work advances benchmarking in FL settings from ad hoc code artifacts towards portable, executable, and reusable benchmark applications.

AI.tldr: Flower Hub provides a platform to publish, discover, and execute federated learning benchmarks as executable, versioned apps, enabling reproducible, cross-domain benchmarking that works across simulation and deployment runtimes with system-aware metrics.
AI.motivation: Benchmarking in federated learning is hard to reproduce, compare, and extend due to custom infrastructure, incomplete code, and simulation-only evaluation.
AI.method: Introduce Flower Hub and a multi-domain benchmark suite covering cross-silo and cross-device FL tasks (medical imaging, financial tabular data, legal instruction tuning, phishing URL detection, audio tagging). Benchmarks are packaged as executable, versioned applications with standardized metadata, pinned dependencies, and explicit evaluation workflows; same application code runs in both simulation and deployment runtimes.
AI.result: Demonstrate cross-runtime portability of benchmarking apps (sim→deploy) without code changes; support system-aware reporting (runtime and communication metrics); enable portable, reusable benchmark applications for FL.
AI.conclusion: This work shifts FL benchmarking from ad hoc code to portable, executable benchmark applications, enabling reproducibility, portability, and broader cross-domain evaluation.

title: Advantage-Driven Explicit Memory for Social Navigation
summary: Robot policies are predominantly learned with classical parametric variants of imitation learning or RL, where training stores the agent's behavior exclusively in the policy's network parameters, putting a heavy burden on the representation learning algorithm. We propose a new navigation agent equipped with non-parametric memory which explicitly indexes prior steps leading to critical events. The advantages are twofold: first, it allows the policy to outsource some of its behavior into an explicit memory; second, it encourages a form of continual learning by allowing an agent to collect data from its testing episodes during deployment and therefore to better generalize to OOD situations. In the context of social navigation, we show that this improves the agent's capability to retain sparse, high-cost failures, such as human collisions. If the policy is trained in simulation, this also naturally addresses the sim-to-real gap, partially, by basing some of the decision making on real data. We integrate the explicit memory into a recurrent PPO architecture and use hidden states for memory retrieval to capture continuous spatiotemporal dynamics. The goal of exploiting rare, high-impact events is achieved by leveraging the RL agent's advantage signals. We train our agent in simulation with a combination of photorealistic rendering and non-visual crowd simulation and show that the agent is robust with respect to OOD social behavior.

AI.tldr: A non-parametric memory-augmented navigation agent uses explicit memory to index prior steps leading to critical events, enabling continual learning, improved generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, and robust handling of high-cost failures, integrated into a recurrent PPO with memory retrieval; trained in photorealistic simulation with non-visual crowd models, showing partial sim-to-real benefits.
AI.motivation: Parametric policy learning (imitation/RL) places all behavior in network parameters, making it hard to retain rare, high-cost events and perform continual learning. An explicit memory can offload behavior, improve safety in social navigation, and help generalize to new environments, including after deployment.
AI.method: Introduce a non-parametric memory that indexes prior steps leading to critical events; integrate memory with a recurrent PPO architecture and retrieve memory via hidden states to capture spatiotemporal dynamics; leverage RL advantage signals to focus on rare events; train in simulation using photorealistic rendering and non-visual crowd simulation; memory enables data collection during deployment to support continual learning.
AI.result: The agent demonstrates improved retention of sparse, high-cost failures (e.g., human collisions) and better robustness to OOD social behavior; partial mitigation of the sim-to-real gap through reliance on real data for decision-making during deployment.
AI.conclusion: Non-parametric memory enables the policy to outsource aspects of behavior, supports continual learning, and improves safety and generalization in social navigation by leveraging explicit memory and deployment-time data, with practical benefits in simulation-to-real transfer.

title: Where to Look Matters: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Long-Video Understanding
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have made substantial progress in long-video understanding, with standard backbone models typically answering questions from frames sampled across the full video. However, as videos become longer, the full-video context inevitably contains more question-irrelevant temporal content, which can distract the model from the evidence needed to answer a specific question. We empirically find that focusing the visual input on short annotated clue intervals containing question-relevant evidence consistently improves prediction accuracy across model scales compared with using the corresponding full videos, while requiring fewer input frames. Based on this finding, we introduce Clue-OPSD, a clue-privileged on-policy self-distillation framework for long-video understanding. During training, a full-video student learns from a self-teacher conditioned on the corresponding clue interval by aligning their next-token distributions along student-generated trajectories. Clue-OPSD thus uses clue intervals as privileged supervision without relying on ground-truth answer labels, while requiring no clue annotations or additional modules at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple long-video understanding benchmarks and Qwen3.5 model scales demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding backbone models and strong performance against supervised post-training baselines.

AI.tldr: Clue-OPSD is a clue-privileged on-policy self-distillation framework that improves long-video understanding by training a full-video student using a clue-conditioned self-teacher, achieving higher accuracy with fewer frames and without requiring inference-time clue annotations.
AI.motivation: Long videos introduce substantial irrelevant temporal content that distracts models; focusing on short, evidence-rich clue intervals can improve prediction accuracy while reducing input needs. The method aims to leverage clue-derived supervision without extra labeling or inference-time modules.
AI.method: During training, a full-video student learns from a self-teacher conditioned on the corresponding clue interval by aligning their next-token distributions along student-generated trajectories. Clue-OPSD uses clue intervals as privileged supervision without relying on ground-truth answers and requires no clue annotations or extra modules at inference time.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple long-video benchmarks and Qwen3.5 model scales demonstrate consistent improvements over backbone models and competitive performance against supervised post-training baselines.
AI.conclusion: Clue-OPSD effectively leverages clue-interval supervision to guide long-video reasoning, yielding consistent gains without ground-truth labels or inference-time changes.

title: Federation Is Nearly Free, Reasoning Is Not: Tradeoffs for AI Co-Scientists in Protein Characterization Workflows
comment: 24 Pages, 4 main figures, 5 main tables, 2 supplementary figures
summary: Natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows involve a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and reasoning at the expense of determinism, reproducibility, and observability. Such agents increasingly must communicate across institutional boundaries, where federation topology can shape latency and cost. We systematically evaluated these tradeoffs using a controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science. We use a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, we ask an agent to confidently characterize its function by routing across common tools. We compare federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model, and prompt expertise. We also stratify results by protein novelty. We find that the choice of LLM dominated prediction quality far more than topology or prompting (Opus ~92%-94% vs o4-mini ~40%-50%). The PPO policy was nearly as accurate as the best LLM (88%) at zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency, but yields no reasoning trace. Expert prompted LLMs reached the highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent; prompt dependence was largest when the task was hardest. Federation imposed a negligible penalty on performance. These results offer actionable guidance for deploying agents for scientific workflows: for routine, verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery.

AI.tldr: LLM choice dominates performance; a cheap deterministic PPO policy offers near-frontier accuracy with full reproducibility; federation topology has negligible impact; reserve flexible LLM reasoning for open-ended discovery.
AI.motivation: Investigate the fundamental trade-offs in natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows between flexibility/reasoning and determinism/reproducibility/observability, and how federation topology affects latency and cost. Systematically evaluate these trade-offs on a production agentic platform using a verifiable protein-function task, comparing topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, various language models and prompts, and stratifying by protein novelty.
AI.method: Controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science. Verifiable task: given a protein sequence, an agent characterizes its function by routing across common tools. Compare federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, multiple language models, and prompt expertise. Stratify results by protein novelty. Measure accuracy, cost, latency, consistency, and reasoning trace.
AI.result: LLMs dominated prediction quality by far more than topology or prompting (e.g., Opus ~92–94% accuracy vs smaller models ~40–50%). The PPO policy achieved nearly as high accuracy as the best LLM (≈88%) at zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency, but provided no reasoning trace. Expert-prompted LLMs reached the highest accuracy but incurred high cost and were less consistent; prompt dependence grew with task hardness. Federation imposed a negligible penalty on performance.
AI.conclusion: For routine, verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy delivers near-frontier accuracy with reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery; federation topology has little impact on performance and can be leveraged to manage latency/cost without sacrificing results.

title: GRAPE: Gradient Refinement and Progress-Aware Exploitation for Query-Efficient High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization
summary: Optimizing expensive, high-dimensional black-box functions remains a central challenge in modern machine learning and scientific discovery. While local Bayesian optimization mitigates the curse of dimensionality, existing techniques often prioritize the probability of descent over the magnitude of progress. This leads to overly conservative steps that yield negligible improvement, wasting queries on directions that are nearly certain to descend but offer little decrease. We introduce Gradient Refinement and Progress-Aware Exploitation (GRAPE), a two-stage framework that first sharpens the local gradient posterior via a closed-form acquisition function, then selects update directions by maximizing the expected decrease conditional on descent. Theoretical analysis proves that this gradient refinement stage monotonically minimizes local uncertainty and that the progress-aware direction converges to true steepest descent as the posterior sharpens. Empirically, GRAPE demonstrates superior query efficiency across high-dimensional tasks: in black-box adversarial attacks, it achieves an average 5.4$\times$ speedup over baselines, and on large language model prompt optimization tasks, it outperforms the second best method by a reduction of 3.8 log-units in the final average regret.

AI.tldr: GRAPE is a two-stage local Bayesian optimization framework that sharpens the gradient posterior and selects descent directions by expected decrease, achieving faster optimization with provable guarantees and strong empirical gains in high-dimensional black-box tasks.
AI.motivation: To overcome overly conservative progress in local BO by focusing on descent probability rather than magnitude; improve query efficiency in high-dimensional, expensive-to-evaluate functions.
AI.method: Stage 1: gradient refinement via a closed-form acquisition function to sharpen the local gradient posterior. Stage 2: choose update directions by maximizing the expected decrease conditioned on descent. Theoretical results: monotone reduction of local uncertainty; convergence of the chosen direction to true steepest descent as posterior sharpens.
AI.result: Empirically, 5.4x speedup over baselines in black-box adversarial attacks; 3.8 log-unit improvement in final average regret on LLM prompt optimization tasks.
AI.conclusion: GRAPE yields improved query efficiency in high-dimensional black-box optimization, with both theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance.

title: Leveraging Inter-object Affordances for Efficient Planning in Contact-rich Tasks
summary: Traditional task-and-motion planning (TAMP) approaches primarily focus on defining sequences of actions along with the necessary geometric and kinematic constraints to execute long-horizon tasks. However, their applicability in real-world settings is limited, as they typically assume simplified object models that overlook key physical properties critical for the successful execution of contact-rich tasks. Moreover, they often use sub-symbolic reasoning during motion planning, which drastically increases planning time and decreases overall success rates. We propose a method that leverages a TAMP approach, defining object-centric abstractions of execution constraints, called Unified TAMP (U-TAMP), to execute robotic tasks involving interactions among objects with heterogeneous shapes, sizes, and materials. Using a Vision-Language Model (VLM), we generate abstractions of inter-object affordances for characterizing physical interaction constraints between objects in contact-rich tasks, such as grasp and support constraints. These constraints are used to enrich the U-TAMP planning domain to deal with objects with variable physical properties. We perform experiments in simulated kitchen table organization scenarios and compare our results with those of the original U-TAMP, as well as a state-of-the-art VLM-based planner that leverages common sense knowledge of objects' affordances for plan generation. Our approach achieves significantly higher planning success rates and improves planning times by one to two orders of magnitude compared to other methods.

AI.tldr: Introducing Unified TAMP (U-TAMP) augmented with Vision-Language Model (VLM) affordances yields faster, more reliable planning for contact-rich object interactions across heterogeneous objects, outperforming original U-TAMP and other VLM-based planners.
AI.motivation: Traditional TAMP struggles with real-world contact-rich tasks due to oversimplified object models and sub-symbolic motion planning, leading to long planning times and low success rates. There is a need to incorporate inter-object physical properties and affordances to improve planning efficiency and success.
AI.method: Define object-centric execution constraints within U-TAMP and use a Vision-Language Model to extract inter-object affordances (e.g., grasp, support) as planning constraints; enrich the planning domain with these affordances; evaluate in simulated kitchen-table organization scenarios; compare against the original U-TAMP and a state-of-the-art VLM-based planner.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves significantly higher planning success rates and reduces planning time by one to two orders of magnitude compared to the baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating VLM-derived affordances into U-TAMP effectively handles heterogeneous object properties in contact-rich manipulation tasks, yielding robust and efficient planning.

title: FlashNormal: Detailed Surface Normal Estimation from Flash and No-Flash Images
comment: (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: High-quality surface normal estimation is preferred for detailed surface shape recovery and image editing. Existing single image-based methods, though being a practical setup, often struggle to recover fine surface details and are sensitive to inherent shape-reflectance ambiguity. While photometric stereo achieves high-fidelity surface normal estimation from images under varying lights, its applicability is strictly limited by requiring a multi-illumination capture setup. To this end, we propose FlashNormal, a diffusion-based surface normal estimator from flash/no-flash image pairs. While retaining high practicability on modern smartphones, our proposal takes advantage of flash-induced shading variations, and leverages curvature-guided detail enhancement strategy, improving surface detail recovery and mitigating shape-reflectance ambiguity effectively. To evaluate our proposed method, we further present EvalFlash, the first real-world flash/no-flash evaluation dataset containing 20 objects aligned with ground-truth surface normals for quantitative benchmarking. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FlashNormal over state-of-the-art single image-based methods and show a significant out-performance over flash/no-flash-based normal estimation method on EvalFlash.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based surface normal estimator, FlashNormal, uses flash/no-flash image pairs and curvature-guided enhancement to recover fine geometry, addressing shape-reflectance ambiguity in single-image methods. It is evaluated on EvalFlash, a real-world dataset with 20 objects and ground-truth normals, showing superiority over state-of-the-art single-image methods and existing flash/no-flash baselines.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of single-image normal estimation (loss of fine details, shape-reflectance ambiguity) and the practicality gap of photometric stereo (requires multi-illumination). Leverage flash-induced shading variations in a mobile-friendly setup to improve surface normal estimation.
AI.method: A diffusion-based normal estimator conditioned on flash/no-flash pairs, with a curvature-guided detail enhancement strategy. A real-world EvalFlash dataset with 20 aligned objects and ground-truth normals is introduced for benchmarking.
AI.result: FlashNormal outperforms state-of-the-art single-image normal estimation methods and significantly surpasses existing flash/no-flash-based normal estimation methods on EvalFlash according to extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: FlashNormal provides a practical, high-fidelity surface normal estimation solution for real-world smartphone capture, and EvalFlash offers a real-world benchmark for flash/no-flash normal estimation.

title: LLM-Driven, Datasheet-Aware Automated Hardware Compatibility Verification for Early-Stage, Pre-Schematic Embedded System Design
summary: We present an LLM-driven, datasheet-aware framework for early-stage hardware compatibility verification that identifies documentation-level interface incompatibilities based on hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions. It does not require, and can therefore be used, before detailed schematic simulation and implementation. We view trustworthy LLM-assisted design automation not as directly generating answers from documents, but as transforming engineering information through traceable verification stages. Given hardware datasheets and high-level component connectivity descriptions, the framework constructs a design graph that captures device connectivity and shared interaction domains, retrieves only the engineering properties required by explicit, domain-oriented verification criteria , and generates deterministic scripts for compatibility evaluation. By decomposing compatibility analysis into modular stages and preserving intermediate results, the framework reduces context overhead, improves transparency and tractability, enables scaling, and avoids reliance on LLMs for numerical computation. Evaluated on seven embedded-system designs comprising 34 datasheets, our framework achieves 97.5% compatibility-verification accuracy and an 8.6 times reduction in input context size compared with ``upload-and-query'' workflows. These results demonstrate the feasibility of LLM-assisted, specification-based hardware compatibility verification at an early design stage, as well as the need for, and substantial benefits of, modular task decomposition, formalized verification criteria, and task-aware compact context construction.

AI.tldr: LLM-assisted, datasheet-aware framework for early-stage hardware compatibility verification using modular verification stages; achieves high accuracy and substantial context reduction.
AI.motivation: Reduce context overload and increase transparency in LLM-driven design automation; enable trustworthy, specification-based verification at an early design stage before detailed schematics; emphasize traceability and modular decomposition.
AI.method: Constructs a design graph from datasheets and high-level connectivity descriptions; retrieves only engineering properties required by explicit domain-oriented verification criteria; generates deterministic scripts for compatibility evaluation; decomposes analysis into modular stages with preserved intermediate results; avoids relying on LLMs for numerical computation.
AI.result: Evaluated on seven embedded-system designs comprising 34 datasheets; 97.5% compatibility-verification accuracy; 8.6× reduction in input context size versus upload-and-query workflows.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of LLM-assisted, specification-based hardware compatibility verification at early design stages; highlights benefits of modular task decomposition, formal verification criteria, and task-aware compact context construction; suggests need for broader validation and exploration of scalability and generalizability.

title: Toward Machine Learning with the Unit as a Primitive: Learning from Unit-Linked Events
summary: Machine learning is usually formalized through samples, while the persistent individual to which multiple observed or possible events refer often remains implicit. We propose the \emph{unit} as an explicit primitive at the level of task semantics. A learning task first declares a population of persistent referents and a sameness criterion; the realized value $u$ denotes the selected referent. Supervised learning is the main formal specialization. Its semantic object is a family of unit-conditioned response laws. Homogeneity is the special case in which those laws coincide; a sample-only conditional is silent as to whether the world is homogeneous or the observed law is only the marginal of a heterogeneous family. What is learned from data is a pair $(T_φ,R_θ)$: a tokenizer that produces a contextual unit token and one shared response-law form that reads it. The structured class takes that form to be a simple relation in the token; a linear predictor is the running instance. The token is the learner-side representation through which the task-side unit affects prediction, while a learner specification that omits unit information is unit-insensitive; homogeneity remains a property of the world-side response family. When identity is unresolved, the world-side law mixes unit-conditioned targets, while the learner composes its shared form with a token. A trusted resolver may fix the unit and supply a lookup token; otherwise \emph{unit abduction} forms a token of the same type from factual evidence. Unlinked single-row observations can fail to distinguish a heterogeneous unit world from a homogeneous pooled world; trusted same-unit pairs separate a restricted witness. The formal results concern this supervised specialization.

AI.tldr: Introduces a unit-based semantic primitive for ML tasks, formalizing how persistent referents and sameness constraints shape learning; introduces tokenizer and shared response-law form (T_φ, R_θ) and mechanisms like unit abduction and trusted resolvers; analyzes identifiability and homogeneity vs heterogeneity in supervised settings.
AI.motivation: Address the implicit treatment of persistent individuals in ML and to separate world-side heterogeneity from learner-side interpretations. Provide a semantic foundation for unit-aware learning beyond sample-centric formalisms.
AI.method: Define a unit as a persistent referent within a population, with sameness criteria and realized value u selecting a referent. Supervised learning is specialized to a family of unit-conditioned response laws. Learn a pair (T_φ, R_θ): a tokenizer that outputs a contextual unit token and a single shared response-law form; a structured class uses this form as a relation in the token; a linear predictor is the instance. Include unit-sensitive vs unit-insensitive learners, unit abduction to generate tokens, trusted resolvers to fix units, and separation of world-side law from learner-side encoding.
AI.result: Formal results pertain to this supervised specialization, clarifying how unit information (or its absence) affects identifiability between homogeneous and heterogeneous worlds, and how tokenization and abduction influence learning dynamics.
AI.conclusion: A principled framework tying unit-level semantics to supervised learning, highlighting when unit information matters, and introducing mechanisms (abduction, trusted resolvers) to resolve identity and mixture issues between world and learner.

title: EgoNav: Bridging Learned Waypoints and Geometry-Aware Local Control for Robust Indoor Navigation
summary: Image-goal navigation using lightweight topological maps is a practical paradigm for indoor robot deployment: the map requires only geotagged images, and localization relies on visual matching rather than precise pose estimation. However, learned waypoint predictors can produce targets that violate geometric constraints or deviate from the global path. Executing these waypoints safely further requires a local planner capable of collision avoidance, yet existing systems either lack one or rely on fixed parameters that cannot adapt to confined spaces. To address these limitations while retaining the navigational intuition of the learned predictor, we present EgoNav, a hierarchical system that implements this idea by generating candidates from semantically segmented traversable regions and scoring them alongside the learned waypoint for geometric safety, directional coherence, and fidelity to the learned prior. An adaptive local path planner then executes the refined waypoint with parameters modulated based on the refinement outcome. Experiments in Habitat-sim and on a physical humanoid robot show that EgoNav consistently outperforms contemporary baselines in both success rate and path efficiency.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical EgoNav system combines learned image-goal predictors with semantically segmented traversable regions to propose safe, geometry-consistent waypoints and an adaptive local planner that improves success rate and efficiency in indoor navigation.
AI.motivation: Learned waypoint predictors can violate geometric constraints and lack reliable collision avoidance, especially in confined spaces. A system that preserves intuitive perception-based navigation while enforcing safety and adaptability is desirable.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) generate waypoint candidates from semantically segmented traversable regions; (2) score these candidates against the learned waypoint for geometric safety, directional coherence, and fidelity; an adaptive local planner executes the refined waypoint with parameters modulated based on refinement outcome.
AI.result: In Habitat-sim and on a physical humanoid robot, EgoNav outperforms contemporary baselines in both success rate and path efficiency.
AI.conclusion: A hierarchical integration of semantic topological cues with learned priors yields safer, more efficient image-goal navigation with an adaptable control loop.

title: RSFusionDet: Underwater RGB-Sonar Multimodal Object Detection
summary: Underwater unimodal object detection faces many challenges in sensor imaging, such as optical images limited by underwater noise and visible distance, and sonar images limited by less object structural information. While, optical images have rich object structural information, and sonar images are less affected by underwater noise and have a longer visible distance. Optical (RGB modality) and sonar (Sonar modality) images have complementary information underwater. In this paper, we create an RGB-Sonar multimodal object detection dataset, \textbf{R}GB-\textbf{S}onar \textbf{Fusion} (RSFusion) and propose evaluation metrics for the benchmark. And we propose the \textbf{R}GB-\textbf{S}onar \textbf{Fusion} \textbf{Det}ector (RSFusionDet) with a new RGB-Sonar multimodal object detection result expression for RGB-Sonar multimodal object detection. We analyze the features of RGB and Sonar modal information, and design a Cross-Attention Fusion (CAFusion) module to fuse RGB-Sonar spatial misalignment features and Object Matching Head (OMHead) with Loss (OMLoss) to match identical objects in RGB-Sonar modalities. Our RSFusionDet achieves 76.4/48.6 AP (RGB/Sonar) for object detection and 83.4 \(\text{F1-Score}_{match}\) for object matching, on RSFusion, which outperforms other object detection models. Compared with the DINO baseline, our method improves by 0.7/1.4 AP (RGB/Sonar) while simultaneously providing reliable cross-modal object matching. The code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/LEFTeyex/RSFusionDet.

AI.tldr: We propose RSFusionDet, a RGB-Sonar multimodal object detector, along with the RSFusion dataset and new evaluation metrics. It uses Cross-Attention Fusion (CAFusion) to fuse spatially misaligned RGB and Sonar features and an Object Matching Head (OMHead) with OM Loss (OMLoss) to match corresponding objects across modalities. It achieves 76.4 AP (RGB) and 48.6 AP (Sonar), with 83.4 F1-match on RSFusion, outperforming baselines by 0.7–1.4 AP (RGB/Sonar).
AI.motivation: Underwater object detection is hampered by modality-specific limitations: optical RGB images suffer from underwater noise and limited range, while sonar images provide longer range but sparse structural information. RGB and sonar are complementary; exploiting both should improve detection and cross-modal object correspondence.
AI.method: Introduce RSFusion dataset and RSFusionDet detector. Key components include Cross-Attention Fusion (CAFusion) to align/fuse RGB and Sonar features despite spatial misalignment, and an Object Matching Head (OMHead) with Loss (OMLoss) to associate identical objects across modalities. Also establish evaluation metrics and a benchmark for RGB-Sonar fusion.
AI.result: RSFusionDet achieves 76.4 AP (RGB) and 48.6 AP (Sonar), and 83.4 in F1-match on the RSFusion benchmark. Relative to DINO, it improves by 0.7 AP (RGB) and 1.4 AP (Sonar) while offering reliable cross-modal object matching.
AI.conclusion: RSFusionDet demonstrates effective cross-modal fusion of RGB and Sonar data for robust underwater object detection and cross-modal object matching. The RSFusion dataset and metrics support benchmarking and further research, with code available publicly.

title: FLARE: Verifying MILP Reformulations with LLM-Based Theorem Proving
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental tool for combinatorial optimization with extensive real-world applications. A central challenge is designing computationally efficient MILP formulations. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to automate the modeling process, from deriving formulations to strengthening them. Reliable automation requires robust methods for verifying that proposed formulations preserve the underlying optimization problem. However, existing approaches evaluate formulations numerically and fail to reason about general problem instances. We resolve this limitation by introducing a constructive definition of MILP reformulation that can be formalized in Lean and machine-checked. We develop FLARE (Formulation-Level Automated Reformulation Evaluation), a method that uses an LLM-based agent and the Lean proof assistant to verify proposed reformulations against a reference formulation. To evaluate our approach, we introduce FormulationBench, a challenging dataset of 20 problems and 109 formulations. FLARE outperforms existing methods, with 100% accuracy on the NP-hard subset of FormulationBench. Furthermore, FLARE produces a machine-checkable certificate for every reformulation it accepts. For cases where formal guarantees are not necessary, we introduce FLARE-NL, a fast and cheap LLM proxy that matches FLARE's accuracy but produces no certificate. These methods enable reliable verification in automated optimization modeling.

AI.tldr: Introduces FLARE for formal verification of MILP reformulations using LLMs and Lean; introduces FormulationBench; achieves 100% accuracy on NP-hard subset; FLARE-NL provides fast, certificate-free accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current verification of MILP reformulations relies on numerical tests and local checks that do not guarantee correctness across problem instances. A formal, machine-checkable definition of reformulations is needed to ensure faithfulness to the original problem and enable automated verification.
AI.method: Define a constructive MILP reformulation notion that can be formalized in Lean. Use an LLM-based agent to propose reformulations and Lean as the verifier to check equivalence to a reference formulation, including feasibility and objective equivalence, with a machine-checkable certificate. Evaluate on FormulationBench (20 problems, 109 formulations).
AI.result: FLARE outperforms existing methods, achieving 100% accuracy on the NP-hard subset of FormulationBench. It provides machine-checkable certificates for accepted reformulations. FLARE-NL, a faster LLM proxy, matches FLARE’s accuracy but does not provide certificates.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables reliable verification in automated optimization modeling by combining LLM-driven reformulation generation with formal proof-based verification. FormulationBench provides a challenging benchmark, and FLARE–NL offers a cheaper alternative when formal guarantees are unnecessary.

title: Multimodal Injury Risk Prediction in Tennis
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Published in the 2025 IEEE 5th International Conference on Human-Machine Systems (ICHMS)
summary: Machine learning has had a significant positive impact on the prediction of athlete performance and injury risk. Most works in this field rely on subjective observations and expert assessments, which restrict their effectiveness. In sports like soccer, basketball, and wrestling, some studies attempt to address this challenge by integrating data from alternative sources, such as readings from wearable devices, alongside traditional subjective observations and expert assessments to enhance accuracy. However, similar research in tennis remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose a multimodal Predictive Athlete Readiness framework for Tennis (PART) to assess both performance and injury risk in tennis players. By leveraging machine learning and deep learning techniques, PART processes multiple sources of data collected from nine collegiate tennis players, including physiological metrics, training and match data, sleep data from wearable devices, self-reported information via daily questionnaires, jump assessments, and motion analysis from match play videos. PART captures four characteristics of tennis players: overall wellness, injury risk, physical capability, and playing style. By integrating these four characteristics by supervised learning, it is capable of providing a holistic assessment of the tennis athlete's condition, along with advanced forecasts of specific body areas at risk such as the upper body (e.g., elbows) or lower body (e.g., knees). Our evaluation, conducted with data from nine collegiate tennis players, shows that PART achieves strong performance in predicting both overall wellness and injury risk. Additionally, our framework also shows promise for recreational tennis players, who often suffer from injuries due to incorrect playing techniques.

AI.tldr: A multimodal ML framework (PART) for tennis readiness that predicts performance and injury risk using diverse data from nine collegiate players; shows strong wellness and injury-risk prediction and suggests applicability to recreational players.
AI.motivation: To reduce reliance on subjective assessments by integrating physiological, training, sleep, self-reported, jumping, and video data to produce holistic readiness metrics and area-specific injury forecasts in tennis.
AI.method: Collect multi-source data from nine collegiate players (physiological metrics, training/match data, wearable sleep data, daily questionnaires, jump tests, and match-video motion analysis). Define four readiness facets (overall wellness, injury risk, physical capability, playing style). Use supervised learning to fuse modalities and forecast both holistic readiness and joint-specific risks (e.g., elbows, knees).
AI.result: PART demonstrates strong predictive performance for overall wellness and injury risk; demonstrates potential to forecast upper- and lower-body injury risks. Indicates promise for extending to recreational players.
AI.conclusion: A promising first step toward data-driven, holistic athlete readiness in tennis; limitations include small sample size and scope. Requires larger-scale validation, ablation studies, and external validation; future work could improve interpretability, generalizability, and real-time deployment.

title: GaussianDream++: Efficient 3D Gaussian World Modeling for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have advanced language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet action-imitation objectives provide only weak supervision for metric 3D structure and short-horizon physical evolution. Geometry-enhanced policies mainly improve current-scene grounding, whereas predictive policies often model future dynamics in RGB or latent spaces and may incur substantial deployment cost. GaussianDream demonstrates that training-time current Gaussian reconstruction and future Gaussian prediction provide effective 3D supervision, but its dense VGGT/TGE-based prefix jointly carries state, dynamics, and action-conditioning information. We present \textbf{\methodname}, a compact, policy-native extension that inserts \textbf{World State Tokens} and \textbf{World Prediction Tokens} directly into the VLA backbone. A training-only \textbf{World Representation Head} decodes these tokens into a Current World and coupled Future Prediction over shared Gaussian primitives, while static--dynamic factorization preserves persistent structure and focuses residual motion on interaction-relevant regions. At inference, the head, renderer, auxiliary objectives, and VGGT/TGE pathway are removed, leaving only 20 world tokens without online Gaussian decoding or rollout. \method achieves \textbf{98.6\%} on LIBERO and \textbf{87.8\%} on LIBERO-Plus, with clear gains under Camera and Layout shifts. Real-robot experiments further improve average success from 29.2\% to 52.5\% over reproduced $π_{0.5}$ while maintaining efficient closed-loop control.

AI.tldr: A compact, policy-native World State Tokens and World Prediction Tokens framework for Vision-Language-Action policies enables training-time 3D supervision via Gaussian primitives, while inference uses only 20 world tokens after removing heavy components; achieves strong LIBERO metrics and improved real-robot success.
AI.motivation: Action-imitation objectives provide weak supervision for 3D structure; existing geometry- and predictive-based approaches have deployment costs or limited grounding. A compact, train-time world-representation module could provide 3D supervision and robust generalization with minimal online overhead.
AI.method: Insert World State Tokens and World Prediction Tokens into the VLA backbone. A training-only World Representation Head decodes tokens into a Current World and coupled Future Prediction over shared Gaussian primitives, with static-dynamic factorization to separate persistent structure from residual motion. At inference, the head, renderer, auxiliary objectives, and VGGT/TGE pathway are removed, leaving 20 world tokens and no online Gaussian decoding or rollout.
AI.result: Achieves 98.6% on LIBERO and 87.8% on LIBERO-Plus, with improved robustness under Camera and Layout shifts. Real-robot experiments show average success rising from 29.2% to 52.5% over reproduced π0.5, while maintaining efficient closed-loop control.
AI.conclusion: World Tokens provide a compact, training-time-supervised 3D representation within VLA policies, enabling strong performance and robustness with minimal online computation. The approach improves upon GaussianDream by decoupling training-time supervision from online decoding and introducing a lightweight, token-based world representation.

title: Capacity Overflow: A Blind Spot for Backdoor Attacks in Vision MoE
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become a prevalent paradigm for scaling Vision Transformers efficiently. To ensure computational scalability and prevent expert overload, Vision MoE architectures employ a capacity-bounded token dispatch mechanism, where each expert's processing budget depends on the inference batch size. This work identifies this batch-dependent behavior as an overlooked attack surface, and proposes a stealthy supply-chain backdoor attack that exploits this property through a three-phase framework. First, we inject a backdoor into an early MoE layer. Second, we train a neutralizer in a deeper MoE layer that suppresses the backdoor under normal capacity. Third, we configure a batch-adaptive capacity factor that preserves high capacity for small batches while reducing it for large batches, naturally disabling the neutralizer via token overflow at deployment-scale batch sizes. The attack remains in dormant mode during small-batch security audits and enters activation mode during large-batch deployment. Experiments on V-MoE and Swin-MoE across ImageNet-100 and GTSRB demonstrate activation-mode attack success rates of 76-87% with dormant-mode ASR below 9%, while evading Neural Cleanse, STRIP, Fine-Pruning, and Activation Clustering. Our findings reveal a fundamental security risk arising from batch-dependent execution in scalable Vision MoE architectures.

AI.tldr: A stealthy supply-chain backdoor in Vision MoEs exploits batch-dependent capacity via a three-phase framework (inject backdoor, train a neutralizer, and batch-adaptive capacity) to activate at large deployment batch sizes while remaining dormant during audits.
AI.motivation: Identify and assess an overlooked attack surface in scalable Vision MoEs: batch-dependent capacity that governs token dispatch and processing budgets.
AI.method: Three-phase framework: (1) inject backdoor into an early MoE layer; (2) train a neutralizer in a deeper MoE layer to suppress the backdoor under normal capacity; (3) implement a batch-adaptive capacity factor that preserves high capacity for small batches but reduces it for large batches, disabling the neutralizer via token overflow at deployment-scale batch sizes.
AI.result: Empirical results show activation-mode success rates of 76–87% on V-MoE and Swin-MoE across ImageNet-100 and GTSRB, with dormant-mode ASR below 9%; the attack evades Neural Cleanse, STRIP, Fine-Pruning, and Activation Clustering defenses.
AI.conclusion: Batch-dependent execution in scalable Vision MoEs poses a fundamental security risk; requires defense strategies addressing capacity-control mechanisms and supply-chain integrity to prevent stealth backdoors.

title: Hierarchical MoE for Multi-Modal ILD Diagnosis
summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine specialized predictors under learned routing, offering a principled mechanism for leveraging heterogeneity in medical data. We present a hierarchical multimodal MoE for interstitial lung disease (ILD) classification that integrates a frozen, pre-trained imaging expert with structured electronic health records (EHR) via two-stage gating. A modality-level gate assigns patient-specific weights to imaging and EHR predictions, while a sub-gating module decomposes the EHR branch into clinically defined feature groups with learned, group-specific contributions. This design preserves stable imaging representations while enabling input-dependent clinical weighting and explicit EHR specialization. Under strict patient-level cross-validation, the model achieved the highest mean AUC among the evaluated methods (0.8750 +- 0.0443), compared with 0.8646 for imaging-only REN and 0.7685 for SwinUNETR. The framework extends interpretability across anatomical regions, imaging--EHR utilization, and clinically defined EHR feature groups.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical multimodal MoE for ILD classification combining a frozen imaging expert with structured EHR via two-stage gating, enabling input-dependent weighting and EHR specialization; achieves state-of-the-art mean AUC on patient-level CV.
AI.motivation: Leverage heterogeneity in medical data and improve ILD classification by integrating imaging and EHR while preserving stable imaging representations and increasing interpretability.
AI.method: Two-stage gating MoE: modality-level gate assigns weights to imaging vs EHR; EHR branch decomposed into clinically defined feature groups with group-specific contributions; uses a frozen pre-trained imaging expert; interpretability across anatomical regions and EHR groups.
AI.result: Mean AUC 0.8750 ± 0.0443 on patient-level cross-validation, higher than imaging-only REN (0.8646) and SwinUNETR (0.7685).
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical multimodal MoE improves performance and interpretability in ILD classification by effectively combining stable imaging features with structured EHR signals and explicit feature-group specialization.

title: When Does Context Routing Help? A Systematic Study of Multi-Modal Fusion in Time Series Forecasting
summary:
Multi-modal time series forecasting methods integrate auxiliary context into temporal predictions through increasingly sophisticated fusion mechanisms. A growing body of work reports substantial gains, yet it is often unclear whether they reflect genuine use of the context or incidental architectural effects. We ask a narrower, checkable question: when can auxiliary context help a forecaster at all?
  We identify two dataset-level conditions that must both hold: (1) the target is not dominated by a last-value shortcut (low autocorrelation rho_h), and (2) the context carries information about the target beyond history (non-zero conditional mutual information delta; when delta=0 no predictor can benefit---a distribution-free result). Through controlled experiments on MoME (a 14.3B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, 6 datasets, 10 seeds) and four additional fusion mechanisms implemented within a single-backbone testbed (5 datasets), we find that when both conditions hold, text-conditioned expert modulation contributes a sizeable MSE reduction; when either fails, the contribution collapses to the capacity floor of the modulation pathway and carries no context-attributable signal.
  We establish causality through two interventions: adding a shortcut to MoME suppresses routing contribution by 77-93% across 3 datasets; progressively corrupting context quality drives the context-specific benefit from +44% to negative. We validate the autocorrelation component of our diagnostic on 27 Monash Archive datasets. We provide a calibrated pre-training diagnostic that, on the datasets we test, yields no false positives in well-powered settings. We are explicit about the asymmetry of our evidence: the negative arm is broadly reliable, while the large positive magnitudes come from a single model family (MoME) and are corroborated only in direction by the testbed.

AI.tldr: Two dataset-level conditions must hold for auxiliary context to help forecasters: (i) low target autocorrelation (rho_h), i.e., the target is not dominated by last-value shortcuts; (ii) non-zero conditional mutual information between context and target beyond history (delta>0). When both hold, text-conditioned expert modulation yields sizeable MSE reductions; if either fails, gains collapse to the modulation pathway capacity floor and contain no context-attributable signal.
AI.motivation: Clarify when auxiliary context in multi-modal time-series forecasting provides genuine predictive benefit versus architectural artefacts, and provide a checkable diagnostic to assess context usefulness.
AI.method: Controlled experiments using MoME (14.3B parameters, 6 datasets, 10 seeds) and four additional fusion mechanisms in a single-backbone testbed (5 datasets). Define rho_h (autocorrelation) and delta (conditional mutual information). Evaluate context usefulness via MSE reductions. Conduct causal interventions: add a shortcut to suppress routing; corrupt context quality to modulate context benefit. Validate autocorrelation component on 27 Monash Archive datasets. Provide calibrated pre-training diagnostic to avoid false positives in well-powered settings.
AI.result: When both conditions hold, text-conditioned expert modulation yields a sizeable reduction in MSE. If either condition fails, the context contribution collapses to the capacity floor of the modulation pathway with no context-attributable signal. Interventions show routing contribution drops by 77–93% across 3 datasets; degrading context quality shifts context-specific benefit from +44% to negative. Autocorrelation component validated on 27 Monash Archive datasets; calibrated pre-training diagnostic has no false positives in well-powered settings.
AI.conclusion: The evidence is asymmetric: negative results are broadly reliable across settings, but large positive gains are primarily observed for the MoME family and are only directionally supported by the testbed. Practically, use the two-condition diagnostic to decide when auxiliary context is likely to help; further validation across architectures beyond MoME is needed to generalize the positive findings.

title: PRISM: Projection-Integrated Sampling-Based MPC with Bayesian Cost Tuning for Bimanual Manipulation
summary:
Bimanual manipulation in cluttered, contact-rich environments remains challenging because it requires coordinated motion generation, interaction-aware planning, and reliable execution under tight kinematic constraints. We present PRISM, a projection-integrated sampling-based Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that uses a GPU-accelerated physics simulator as an online world model for complex dual-arm manipulation.
  The main algorithmic contribution is a QP-guided control sampling strategy that decouples trajectory exploration from kinematic feasibility. At each MPC step, sampled joint-velocity trajectories are projected onto the set of motions satisfying joint position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk bounds, together with an initial-velocity boundary condition, before rollout evaluation. This enables broad yet feasible exploration of coordinated bimanual behaviors. To support efficient online execution, we derive a custom ADMM/Bregman-splitting QP solver that exploits joint-wise separability and reusable matrix factorizations. We further use Bayesian optimization to tune task-cost weights offline, reducing manual parameter selection.
  We evaluate PRISM on challenging variants of PerAct$^{2}$ tasks, including obstacle-constrained ball transport, tray transport, cube handover, and box lifting. Experiments show improved robustness and task success relative to representative sampling-based baselines, while maintaining real-time or near-real-time execution. We also demonstrate successful sim-to-real transfer on dual UR5e manipulators, highlighting the practical potential of physics-based online planning for contact-rich bimanual manipulation. Project details, including code and supplementary videos, are available at \href{https://sites.google.com/view/prismbimanual}{\texttt{https://sites.google.com/view/prismbimanual}}.

AI.tldr: PRISM is a projection-integrated MPC for bimanual manipulation using a GPU-based online world model; it decouples exploration from kinematic feasibility through a QP-guided control sampling strategy; includes an ADMM/Bregman-splitting QP solver and Bayesian optimization for task costs; demonstrates sim-to-real on dual UR5e with improved robustness.
AI.motivation: To enable robust, real-time capable bimanual manipulation in cluttered, contact-rich environments by ensuring sampled trajectories satisfy complex kinematic constraints and are compatible with an online physics-based world model.
AI.method: PRISM combines sampling-based MPC with projection of joint-velocity samples onto a feasible set defined by joint position/velocity/acceleration/jerk bounds and an initial-velocity boundary. It employs a GPU-accelerated physics simulator as an online world model, and introduces a custom ADMM/Bregman-splitting QP solver that exploits joint-wise separability and reusable matrix factorizations. Bayesian optimization tunes task-cost weights offline to reduce manual parameter selection.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on PerAct2-like tasks (obstacle-constrained ball transport, tray transport, cube handover, box lifting) shows higher robustness and task success than representative baselines, with real-time or near-real-time execution. Successful sim-to-real transfer on dual UR5e manipulators demonstrates practical viability of physics-based online planning for contact-rich bimanual manipulation.
AI.conclusion: PRISM enables broad yet feasible exploration for coordinated bimanual tasks by integrating projection-based feasibility with sampling-based MPC, supported by a fast QP solver and offline-tuned costs. This yields robust real-time performance and credible sim-to-real transfer, highlighting its potential for complex manipulation in cluttered environments.

title: Efficient Training with Foresight: Multi-Token Auxiliary Supervision for Autoregressive Image Generation
summary: Autoregressive (AR) image generation has shown strong potential for scalable high-fidelity synthesis by modeling images as discrete token sequences. However, traditional next token prediction (NTP) continues to suffer from sparse and myopic supervision, insufficiently discriminative representations, and high training cost caused by dense computation over the full token sequence. To address these issues, we propose multi-token autoregressive (MTAR), a unified training framework that improves autoregressive image generation from three aspects: prediction objectives, representation regularization, and training efficiency. Specifically, MTAR introduces multi-token prediction (MTP) to alleviate the sparsity and myopia of traditional NTP by imposing joint supervision on multiple future tokens; employs token-level contrastive regularization (TCR) to explicitly enhance the separability of sampled token representations and thereby improve representation discriminability; and incorporates semantic dropping (SD) as a semantics-aware training acceleration strategy to reduce redundant computation on low-information tokens while preserving informative learning signals. All three components are applied only during training and introduce no additional overhead during autoregressive inference. On ImageNet, MTAR achieves a better balance between generation quality and training efficiency. Compared with LlamaGen, MTAR achieves up to 0.95 lower FID and 39\% faster training. Moreover, even with only 1/3 of the training iterations, it still attains performance comparable to or better than the baseline, substantially reducing training time.

AI.tldr: MTAR introduces a unified training framework for autoregressive image generation with multi-token prediction (MTP), token-level contrastive regularization (TCR), and semantic dropping (SD). These training-only components improve representation discriminability, reduce sparsity, and accelerate training without increasing inference cost, achieving better ImageNet results and faster training than LlamaGen, even with fewer iterations.
AI.motivation: Overcome the limitations of traditional next-token prediction (sparse, myopic supervision; weak discriminative representations) and high training cost in AR image generation.
AI.method: Combine three training-time strategies: (1) Multi-token prediction (MTP) imposes joint supervision on multiple future tokens; (2) Token-level contrastive regularization (TCR) enhances separability of token representations; (3) Semantic dropping (SD) reduces computation on low-information tokens. All components are applied only during training and add no inference overhead.
AI.result: On ImageNet, MTAR achieves a better quality-efficiency trade-off than baselines, e.g., up to 0.95 lower FID and 39% faster training than LlamaGen; with only one-third of training iterations, MTAR attains comparable or better performance than the baseline.
AI.conclusion: MTAR provides a cohesive training framework that improves AR image generation by addressing sparsity, representation discriminability, and training efficiency, with demonstrated gains on ImageNet and no at-inference overhead.

title: PhaseShift: Topology-Aware Data Harmonization and Model Consolidation Across Signalized Intersections
summary: Learned traffic-behavior models are commonly trained separately for each intersection, creating model portfolios that cannot share evidence across sites.
