We present PhaseShift, a topology-aware framework that harmonizes heterogeneous roadside trajectories into a shared actor-centric representation and trains one reusable backbone. Ego-relative coordinates, trajectory-induced movement paths, normalized signal context, and variable-cardinality interaction tokens remove site conventions while preserving behaviorally relevant topology. The backbone supports pooled operation, zero-shot at a held-out intersection, and low-data adaptation. We evaluate five intersections in two Florida regions on balanced field data, 100k training windows and equal-sized test sets per site under a replay-conditioned, best-of-sampled-trajectory protocol. At 10s, one pooled model lowers both minADE and minFDE relative to trained local models at all five sites, with median reductions of 36.8% and 22.0%. Leave-one-intersection-out deployment, including one cross-region fold, beats local training on both 10-s metrics at four of five sites, although short-horizon performance is less uniform. Fine-tuning with 1,000 target update windows improves on zero-shot at three sites and is the strongest regime at one. At site 7, every cross-site mixture sharply lowers long-horizon error under a fixed 100k-window budget; test-likelihood gains argue against a best-of-sample dispersion-only explanation. Local models fall behind calibrated IDM at the two highest-flow sites after long autoregressive rollouts; pretrained-backbone regimes do not. Within this five-site evaluation, PhaseShift demonstrates consolidation across heterogeneous physical control settings while identifying sites that still require adaptation. The protocol measures conditional single-vehicle generation under replayed context, not closed-loop traffic simulation.

AI.tldr: PhaseShift provides a reusable, topology-aware backbone to harmonize heterogeneous roadside trajectories across multiple intersections, enabling zero-shot transfer and data-efficient adaptation, with substantial gains over locally trained models at the 10 s horizon and robust cross-site improvements, though some sites still require adaptation; evaluation uses replayed context rather than closed-loop simulation.
AI.motivation: To overcome per-intersection models that cannot share evidence, addressing cross-site heterogeneity in control settings and topology by learning a unified actor-centric representation.
AI.method: Introduce PhaseShift: ego-relative coordinates; trajectory-induced movement paths; normalized signal context; variable-cardinality interaction tokens; shared backbone with pooled operation; zero-shot transfer to held-out intersections; low-data adaptation; cross-site and cross-region evaluation; replay-conditioned evaluation protocol; dataset: five Florida intersections, 100k training windows per site, balanced test sets.
AI.result: 10 s horizon: pooled model reduces minADE/minFDE vs local models; median reductions 36.8%/22.0%. Leave-one-intersection-out beats local training on 10 s metrics at 4/5 sites; cross-region fold; 1 k-window fine-tuning improves zero-shot at 3 sites; at site 7 cross-site mixture lowers long-horizon error; test-likelihood gains argue beyond dispersion-only explanation; local models behind IDM at two high-flow sites after long rollouts; pretrained backbones do not help; overall consolidation across diverse control settings; protocol uses conditional single-vehicle generation under replayed context, not closed-loop.
AI.conclusion: PhaseShift demonstrates that a topology-aware, reusable backbone can consolidate heterogeneous intersection data, enabling cross-site generalization and efficient adaptation, while identifying sites requiring targeted fine-tuning; enables pooling-based learning without simulating closed-loop traffic.

title: Rethinking the Transferable Adversarial Attacks and Robust Defense in Federated Learning
summary: The development of federated learning (FL) techniques has helped improve the privacy preservation of users' data and extended the applications of machine learning models. However, the involvement of a large number of users in FL also creates open opportunities for different adversaries, such as poisoning attacks, Byzantine attacks, and adversarial example attacks. Yet, recent research has disclosed that existing poisoning attacks and Byzantine attacks can not achieve satisfactory penetration in realistic FL scenarios caused by strong assumptions, \textit{e.g.,} client selection rate, and the ratio of malicious attackers. In this paper, the transferability of adversarial examples among different client models is analyzed to understand the relation between adversarial examples and clients' data distribution. Moreover, to mitigate the attacks of transferable adversarial examples, we design a defense mechanism stemming from the transferability of model robustness by adversarial training. As a result, through theoretical analysis of transferability, we gain insights into adversarial examples and the vulnerability of federated learning systems. Our proposed adversarial attack and defense methods are evaluated via real-life datasets in various settings to show their performance over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the transferability of adversarial examples in federated learning and proposes a transferability-informed defense using adversarial training, backed by theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation.
AI.motivation: Federated learning faces poisoning, Byzantine, and adversarial attacks; existing attacks under realistic assumptions may fail. The paper explores how adversarial examples transfer across client models and how to defend using transferability principles.
AI.method: The authors analyze cross-client transferability of adversarial inputs, derive theoretical insights into robustness transfer, and design a defense based on adversarial training to improve FL resilience. They validate with real-world datasets under various settings and compare with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.result: The defense improves robustness against transferable adversarial examples and demonstrates insights into FL vulnerability; empirical results show performance gains over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: The work provides theoretical and empirical understanding of adversarial transfer in FL and offers a practical defense, highlighting remaining challenges in secure FL under realistic constraints.

title: Opportunities of Self Supervised Learning for GNSS: Evaluation of a Deep Learning-Enhanced PVT Algorithm
summary: This work proposes a Deep Learning Enhanced PVT algorithm to mitigate multipath interference in dense urban areas. A supervised objective jointly predicts range corrections and uncertainty, while a JEPA-based self-supervised pretraining stage improves representation quality. The algorithm is evaluated over diverse driving scenarios, substantially improving PVT accuracy, particularly for unseen harsh urban conditions. These results highlight the potential of unlabelled GNSS data to improve generalization performance.

AI.tldr: A Deep Learning Enhanced PVT framework uses joint supervised corrections and JEPA-based self-supervised pretraining to mitigate urban multipath, improving PVT accuracy and generalization, especially under unseen harsh urban conditions.
AI.motivation: Urban GNSS signals suffer from multipath and NLOS effects in dense environments; there is a need to leverage unlabeled data to improve generalization of PVT systems.
AI.method: A DL-enhanced PVT algorithm with a supervised objective predicting range corrections and uncertainty, combined with JEPA-based self-supervised pretraining to improve representation quality; evaluated on diverse driving scenarios.
AI.result: Substantial improvements in PVT accuracy, notably for unseen harsh urban conditions; demonstrates effective generalization and the utility of unlabeled GNSS data for performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Integrating supervised range correction with self-supervised representation learning can robustly mitigate urban multipath effects and enhance PVT generalization using unlabeled data.

title: PIVOT: A Multi-Trajectory Dataset and Testbed for Pose, Intrinsics, and Novel Viewpoint Evaluation in Real-World 3D Reconstruction
summary:
Neural radiance fields (NeRFs), 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), and related novel-view synthesis methods are commonly evaluated under capture and reconstruction conditions cleaner than those encountered by robots, drones, and autonomous systems. Benchmarks often rely on reconstruction-friendly trajectories, optimized camera poses and intrinsics, and held-out views sampled from trajectories represented during training. These assumptions can obscure performance with measured poses, reusable camera calibration, and structurally different camera paths.
  We introduce PIVOT (Pose, Intrinsics and Viewpoint Oriented Testbed), a multi-trajectory dataset, processing pipeline, and evaluation framework for independently studying these factors. PIVOT captures each scene using diverse camera trajectories and retains, where available, both sensor-derived measured poses and COLMAP-optimized poses, together with calibrated and optimized camera intrinsics. It defines three benchmark families: (1) seen versus unseen trajectory novel-view generalization, (2) measured versus optimized pose sensitivity, and (3) calibrated versus optimized intrinsics sensitivity. We also introduce a directed pose-space Chamfer distance to quantify how well training poses cover an evaluation trajectory.
  PIVOT v1 contains five real-world scenes captured with a DJI Mini 4 Pro and provides an open processing and Nerfstudio-based evaluation toolchain. Benchmark results show a consistent quality gap between held-out views on represented trajectories and unseen trajectories, as well as substantial sensitivity to pose source and camera intrinsics.

AI.tldr: A new dataset and evaluation framework (PIVOT) to study the impact of pose, intrinsics, and viewpoint in neural rendering, featuring multiple trajectories, measured and COLMAP poses, calibrated and optimized intrinsics, and a Chamfer-based pose coverage metric; v1 with five real-world scenes and an open Nerfstudio-based toolchain.
AI.motivation: To expose how neural rendering methods perform under real-world capture conditions with measured poses and varying intrinsics/trajectories, which are often simplified in benchmarks.
AI.method: Capture real scenes with diverse camera trajectories using a consumer drone; store measured and COLMAP poses; provide both calibrated and optimized intrinsics; define three benchmark families (seen vs unseen trajectory generalization, pose sensitivity, intrinsics sensitivity); introduce a directed pose-space Chamfer distance; open processing/toolchain.
AI.result: PIVOT v1 includes five scenes; benchmarks reveal a quality gap between held-out views on represented trajectories versus unseen trajectories; and show substantial sensitivity to pose source and camera intrinsics.
AI.conclusion: PIVOT enables systematic study of pose, intrinsics, and viewpoint effects on novel-view synthesis in realistic capture settings; provides open tooling and dataset to benchmark strategies like NeRF and 3DGS under non-ideal conditions.

title: BixBench3: Benchmarking AI agents on research-study-scale computational biology tasks
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to accelerate biological research by automating computational analyses. Yet the ability of AI agents to carry out computational biology at the scale of complete research studies has not been systematically evaluated. Here we introduce BixBench3, a benchmark that measures the capacity of AI agents to process raw biological data through to scientific results. We designed BixBench3 tasks to mirror the delegation of work from a scientist to an agent: the scientist chooses the research question and high-level methods, then delegates implementation of all analyses to the agent. In each task, an agent receives a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data derived from a published scientific study, and must execute a sequence of analyses to achieve the research objective. The data artifacts resulting from these analyses - such as peak call matrices or differential expression tables - are programmatically graded against the corresponding artifacts generated and reported in the original study. Across 20 BixBench3 tasks encompassing the generation of 138 unique artifacts, we find that 13 frontier models achieve scores ranging from 0.00 for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to 0.48 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Agents perform worse on tasks with larger raw datasets (0.36 on tasks with <100 GB versus 0.10 on tasks with >100 GB) and on analyses requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). On average, agents use 6.8 hours, 102 million tokens, and $43 to complete each task, with the longest attempts consuming 24 hours, 1.07 billion tokens, and $525. Notably, the highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper than less performant options. These results reveal that LLMs vary substantially in their ability to (1) execute multiple sequential analysis steps coherently, (2) manage large quantities of raw data, and (3) work across scientific domains.

AI.tldr: Introduces BixBench3, an end-to-end benchmark for AI agents to convert raw biological data into publishable results; across 20 tasks, frontier models show limited, variable capability (0–0.48), with performance dropping on larger datasets and multi-step analyses; cost and time metrics indicate efficiency correlates with score.
AI.motivation: Assess whether AI agents can perform complete computational biology studies at scale, beyond single-step analyses.
AI.method: 20 tasks, 138 artifacts; agent receives objective, methodological guidance, and raw data; executes sequence of analyses; artifacts graded against original study; 13 frontier models evaluated; data sizes, steps tracked; costs/time tokens measured.
AI.result: Scores range 0.00–0.48; data size and step count negatively impact performance; averages: 6.8 hours, 102M tokens, $43 per task; longest 24h, 1.07B tokens, $525; top agents used fewer tokens and cheaper.
AI.conclusion: LLMs vary in executing sequential analyses, handling large raw data, and cross-domain work; current capabilities limited; benchmark reveals room for improvement and provides quantitative guidance.

title: Drift Variation Autoencoder: Unifying Generation and Representation Learning through Conditional Posterior Flow Matching
summary: Stochastic masking, cropping, or modality removal makes deterministic reconstruction an incomplete target: one observation can admit many clean completions. This work takes the corresponding posterior $P(X\mid C)$ as the common statistical object for conditional generation and generatively sufficient representation learning. Drift Variation autoencoder trains a masked encoder $Z=E(C)$ and a conditional flow decoder with one clean-prediction Flow Matching loss. The analysis first decomposes the ideal conditional KL into generator approximation and the representation deficiency $I(X;C\mid Z)$. It then derives orthogonal risk decompositions for conditional Flow Matching. For an affine Gaussian path, the clean-prediction representation gap is zero if and only if $P(X\mid Z)=P(X\mid C)$. Thus the encoder-dependent excess clean-prediction risk induced by Flow Matching and the profiled ideal conditional KL have the same posterior-sufficient zero set, without being numerically equal objectives. An exact conditional field with a zero-noise endpoint then generates $P(X\mid Z)$ and hence $P(X\mid C)$ at a joint ideal optimum. The result extends to continuous multimodal product spaces when the complete modality tuple remains the Flow target for every observation mask. On CrossGeom-4, an 18-run controlled benchmark, observable factors have linear-probe $R^2$ of $0.9990$-$0.9992$, shuffling the joint model's encoder condition increases conditional error by $13.5\times$-$15.7\times$, and joint target attention reduces disagreement on an unobserved factor shared by two outputs by $90.1$-$92.8\%$ relative to independent target decoders. Visible modalities are also generated and reconstructed, directly validating the full-tuple objective. Unconditional mode balance remains imperfect, delimiting the empirical claim to a controlled multimodal proof of concept.

AI.tldr: Drift Variation Autoencoder (DVA) anchors conditional generation and representation learning to the posterior P(X|C) under partial observability, via a masked encoder Z and a conditional flow decoder trained with Flow Matching; theory links conditional KL to representation deficiency and provides an exact zero-noise-optimum scenario; empirical validation on CrossGeom-4 shows strong conditional control and coherent multimodal generation, though unconditional mode balance remains imperfect.
AI.motivation: Stochastic masking of modalities yields many plausible completions; the posterior P(X|C) is the natural target for conditional generation and representation learning, and Flow Matching can be analyzed in terms of the encoder-induced representation deficiency.
AI.method: Propose Drift Variation Autoencoder (DVA): encoder Z = E(C); conditional flow decoder; Flow Matching loss; theoretical decomposition of the ideal conditional KL into generator approximation and I(X;C|Z); orthogonal risk decompositions for conditional Flow Matching; for an affine Gaussian path, the clean-prediction gap vanishes iff P(X|Z)=P(X|C); extend to continuous multimodal product spaces where the full modality tuple remains the Flow target; empirical evaluation on CrossGeom-4 with controlled masking and joint-target attention.
AI.result: For affine Gaussian paths, the clean-prediction gap is zero iff P(X|Z)=P(X|C); encoder-dependent excess risk and the posterior-sufficient zero-set coincide; an exact zero-noise conditional field can recover P(X|Z) and thus P(X|C); CrossGeom-4 results: observable factors achieve R^2 ~ 0.9990–0.9992; shuffling encoder conditioning increases conditional error by ~13.5–15.7x; joint-target attention reduces disagreement on a common unobserved factor by 90.1–92.8%; visible modalities can be generated/reconstructed; unconditional mode balance remains imperfect (proof-of-concept scope).
AI.conclusion: The work provides a principled link between Flow Matching and posterior sufficiency for conditional generation under partial observability, delivering a controlled multimodal proof-of-concept with strong conditional control and coherent full-tuple objectives, while highlighting remaining gaps in unconditional balance and scalability.

title: LM-X: Explainable Action Modeling with Progress, Event, and Uncertainty Prediction for Generalist Robot Manipulation
summary: Generalist vision--language--action (VLA) policies learn long-horizon behavior mainly through short-horizon action prediction and reveal little beyond sampled commands. This creates two coupled bottlenecks: a single action target must implicitly absorb task progress, intermediate intent, and local reliability, while these control states remain hidden during execution. Inspired by functional principles of biological sensorimotor control, we introduce LM-X , which organizes prediction across task, event, and motor scales without claiming anatomical correspondence. Three explicitly supervised signals are emitted online and directly condition action generation: return-to-go (RTG) measures visible task progress, event-to-go (ETG) identifies the next semantic transition, and heteroscedastic action flow estimates local reliability through propagated variance. Explanation is therefore intrinsic to control rather than generated post hoc. Before a costly 20-day pretraining run on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs, a controlled five-task pretraining gate verifies the design: the complete model improves success by 16.0 points over the action-only backbone and by 10.8 points over the strongest single-head variant. We then train LM-X on more than 20,000 hours of real-robot trajectories, including over 1,000 hours of failed policy rollouts. LM-X achieves 74.1\% across 50 randomized-hard RoboTwin2.0 tasks versus 55.4\% for GR00T N1.7, and 68.6\% versus 50.7\% across seven real-robot tasks. RTG tracks semantic progress and visible regression, while variance rises during hesitation and oscillatory control. These results show that explicit multi-timescale predictive state can strengthen control while exposing interpretable internal estimates.

AI.tldr: LM-X introduces explicit, multi-timescale supervision for generalist VLA policies using three online signals—return-to-go (RTG), event-to-go (ETG), and heteroscedastic action flow for local reliability—to strengthen control and expose interpretable internal estimates, validated on RoboTwin2.0 and real-robot tasks with significant gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: Address bottlenecks in vision--language--action policies where a single action target must implicitly carry task progress, intermediate intent, and local reliability, while crucial state information remains hidden during execution.
AI.method: LM-X organizes prediction across task-, event-, and motor-scales with three online, explicitly supervised signals (RTG, ETG, variance). The signals directly condition action generation, making explanation intrinsic to control. A five-task pretraining gate precedes large-scale pretraining on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs. The model is trained on >20k hours of real-robot trajectories (including >1k hours of failed rollouts).
AI.result: Quantitative gains include 16.0-point improvement over an action-only backbone and 10.8-point improvement over a strong single-head variant in a controlled study. On RoboTwin2.0, LM-X achieves 74.1% across 50 randomized-hard tasks vs 55.4% for GR00T N1.7; on seven real-robot tasks, 68.6% vs 50.7%. RTG tracks semantic progress and regression; variance rises during hesitation and oscillation, indicating meaningful internal estimates.
AI.conclusion: Explicit multi-timescale predictive state enhances control fidelity while providing interpretable internal signals (RTG, ETG, and variance). The approach yields robust performance gains in both simulated-hard tasks and real-robot settings, suggesting that intrinsic explanation via online supervision can strengthen policy control.

title: AdaptiveEmbed: Sample-Adaptive Multi-Vector Representation for Multimodal Retrieval
summary: Multi-vector representations have emerged as an effective paradigm for multimodal retrieval, representing each sample with multiple complementary embeddings to capture fine-grained cross-modal information. However, existing approaches typically employ a fixed representation capacity, assigning the same number of vectors to all samples regardless of their individual retrieval demands. Such a fixed-capacity formulation overlooks the fact that different samples may require different amounts of representation capacity for effective retrieval. In this work, we introduce \emph{Sample-Adaptive Multi-Vector Representation} (SAMVR), a new problem setting for multimodal retrieval that studies how multi-vector representation capacity can be allocated at the sample level. Under SAMVR, each sample is represented by a \emph{content-adaptive embedding set} (CAES), whose capacity is determined according to the sample-specific retrieval utility of additional representation vectors. To instantiate SAMVR, we propose \emph{AdaptiveEmbed}, a unified framework for learning sample-adaptive multi-vector representations. AdaptiveEmbed learns structured multi-vector representations through \emph{Multi-Group Contrastive Learning} (MGCL) with the symmetric \emph{set-to-set similarity} (SetSim), and further employs \emph{Utility Policy Optimization} (UPO) to determine sample-specific representation capacity via \emph{Marginal Utility Allocation} (MUA). Experiments across multimodal retrieval benchmarks involving image, text, video, and audio show that sample-adaptive capacity allocation achieves overall better retrieval performance than fixed-capacity multi-vector representations, validating the effectiveness of SAMVR for multimodal retrieval. These results establish SAMVR as a viable formulation for adaptive capacity allocation in multi-vector multimodal retrieval.

AI.tldr: SAMVR enables sample-adaptive multi-vector representations for multimodal retrieval by allocating capacity per sample based on marginal utility, using AdaptiveEmbed with MGCL and SetSim, plus UPO/MUA, yielding better retrieval than fixed-capacity methods.
AI.motivation: Fixed-capacity multi-vector representations waste model capacity by allocating the same number of vectors to all samples regardless of their retrieval utility; adaptivity could improve efficiency and performance.
AI.method: AdaptiveEmbed framework: learns content-adaptive embedding sets (CAES) through Multi-Group Contrastive Learning (MGCL) with symmetric set-to-set similarity (SetSim); uses Utility Policy Optimization (UPO) to decide per-sample capacity via Marginal Utility Allocation (MUA).
AI.result: Empirical results on image, text, video, and audio multimodal retrieval show that sample-adaptive capacity allocation yields better retrieval performance than fixed-capacity multi-vector representations.
AI.conclusion: SAMVR demonstrates the viability of adaptive capacity allocation for multi-vector multimodal retrieval and provides a concrete framework (AdaptiveEmbed) and mechanisms (MGCL, SetSim, UPO, MUA) to realize it.

title: FinRiskAtlas: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Large Language Models for Financial Risk Review
summary: Deploying large language models for professional financial review requires more than measuring general financial competence: models must perform the specific review operation required by a workflow and determine whether available evidence is sufficient for a defensible decision. Existing financial benchmarks cover knowledge, reasoning, compliance, and professional tasks, but their evaluation units are often organized around datasets or task formulations rather than the decisions that deployed systems support. We introduce FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark that evaluates financial LLMs along two complementary dimensions: operation execution under fixed evidence states and evidence-state control under evolving review conditions. The static benchmark contains 9,742 instances across 53 task families, including 42 Domain Knowledge families and eleven downstream review operations defined by explicit evaluation contracts. FinRisk-Ask extends this framework through offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified professional trajectories, withholding future evidence during inference and using it only to construct expert-verified evidence targets. Across 33 model configurations, operation-level evaluation yields non-redundant rankings (mean pairwise Spearman correlation 0.42 across downstream operations), and knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual operations. FinRisk-Ask further shows that entering the Ask branch more frequently does not necessarily improve request targeting or end-to-end evidence acquisition. These results show that broad financial capability scores do not fully capture where models are reliable in professional workflows, motivating evaluation units aligned with the decisions and evidence states that deployed systems must support.

AI.tldr: Introduces FinRiskAtlas, a Chinese-language benchmark for evaluating financial LLMs along two axes: operation execution given fixed evidence and evidence-state control under evolving review conditions. Includes a static set (9,742 instances, 53 task families) and FinRisk-Ask (offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 professional trajectories). Evaluated across 33 model configurations; results show non-redundant operation rankings (mean Spearman 0.42) and potential regret from knowledge-based shortlisting (up to 18.01 points). Finds that more frequent “Ask” does not always improve evidence acquisition, arguing for evaluation units tied to decisions and evidence states in professional workflows.
AI.motivation: Benchmarking financial LLMs often targets general competence or isolated tasks, but deployed systems require reliable decision-making within real workflows and varying evidence states. There is a need for evaluation units that reflect the actual decisions and the evidence available to support them.
AI.method: Two-dimensional evaluation: (1) operation execution under fixed evidence states (static benchmark with 9,742 instances across 53 task families, including 42 Domain Knowledge families and 11 downstream review operations via explicit evaluation contracts); (2) evidence-state control under evolving review conditions (FinRisk-Ask) using offline replay of 680 pre-action states from 104 de-identified professional trajectories, withholding future evidence during inference and using it to construct expert-verified evidence targets. Evaluation across 33 model configurations.
AI.result: Operation-level evaluation yields non-redundant rankings (mean pairwise Spearman 0.42). Knowledge-based shortlisting can incur up to 18.01 points of regret on individual operations. Entering the Ask branch more frequently does not reliably improve request targeting or end-to-end evidence acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Broad financial capability scores do not fully capture reliability in professional workflows. Evaluation units should align with the decisions and evidence states that deployed systems must support.

title: SNAP-KG: Streaming Node Assignment via Projection for Knowledge Graph Entity Integration
comment: Accepted at the 25th International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC 2026)
summary: Knowledge graph (KG) construction pipelines must continuously integrate newly arriving entities into a growing graph. Unlike inserting triples between existing nodes, a newly arriving entity has no graph connectivity: it emerges from the acquisition phase as a raw feature vector and must be assigned to a semantic community before entity resolution and link prediction can operate over a tractable candidate set. Existing multi-view graph clustering methods exploit multiple relation types as structural views, but are transductive: they assume a fixed graph and cannot assign unseen entities without retraining. We propose SNAP-KG (Streaming Node Assignment via Projection for Knowledge Graph Entity Integration), a framework supporting graph-structural multi-view relational clustering and inductive inference for streaming entities. SNAP-KG trains a projector to map a new entity directly to the learned embedding space using only raw features, enabling immediate cluster assignment without graph access or model retraining. Experiments on five benchmark multi-view graph datasets and a production-scale KG of 2.4 million nodes demonstrate multiple orders-of-magnitude inference speedups over retraining-based approaches and competitive clustering quality. As a candidate scoping mechanism for downstream tasks, SNAP-KG achieves 62-75% candidate search reduction on the five benchmark datasets and 97% on OGB-WikiKG2 for entity resolution and link prediction.

AI.tldr: SNAP-KG enables inductive streaming integration of new KG entities by learning a projector that maps raw features into the embedding space for immediate cluster assignment without graph access or retraining, delivering large speedups with competitive clustering quality and substantial downstream task reductions.
AI.motivation: New entities in knowledge graphs arrive without graph connectivity, requiring rapid, inductive assignment to semantic communities for downstream entity resolution and link prediction; existing multi-view clustering is transductive and retraining-heavy, hindering streaming scenarios.
AI.method: Train a projection-based mapper that embeds raw features of a new entity into the learned embedding space, enabling immediate cluster assignment for streaming entities without graph access or retraining; supports graph-structural multi-view relational clustering in an inductive setting.
AI.result: Orders-of-magnitude inference speedups versus retraining-based approaches; competitive clustering quality on five benchmark multi-view graph datasets and a 2.4M-node production KG; candidate search reductions of 62–75% on five benchmarks and 97% on OGB-WikiKG2 for downstream tasks (entity resolution and link prediction).
AI.conclusion: SNAP-KG provides an effective inductive, streaming-friendly framework for KG entity integration that yields substantial speedups and maintains strong clustering performance, with meaningful reductions in downstream candidate search space.

title: TacForcing: Streaming Action Generation with Execution-Time Tactile Feedback
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires adapting to contact states that can evolve substantially within an action horizon. However, chunk-based vision-language-action models predict complete action chunks from observations collected before execution, leaving tactile conditioning stale during execution. Existing tactile-reactive approaches typically rely on separate high-frequency controllers, which increase both architectural and training complexity. In this paper, we introduce TacForcing, a streaming action-generation framework that effectively incorporates execution-time tactile feedback. Instead of employing a separate reactive controller, TacForcing replaces the standard action expert with a streaming action expert to generate actions conditioned on the evolving tactile observations acquired during execution. TacForcing also introduces Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA), which restricts tactile conditioning to actions nearing execution, thereby reducing the temporal mismatch between tactile acquisition and action execution. Across six simulated UniVTAC tasks and three real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, TacForcing achieves average success rates of 65% and 69%, respectively, outperforming strong baselines in both settings.

AI.tldr: TacForcing is a streaming action-generation framework that integrates execution-time tactile feedback into action generation for contact-rich manipulation, using a streaming action expert and Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA) to align tactile conditioning with near-term actions, achieving higher success rates than baselines on UniVTAC and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between pre-collected action chunks and evolving tactile states during execution in contact-rich manipulation. Chunk-based models may become stale; separate high-frequency tactile controllers add complexity. A streaming, tactile-conditioned predictor can adapt actions in real-time.
AI.method: Introduce TacForcing: replace the traditional action expert with a streaming action expert conditioned on continuous tactile observations during execution. Propose Execution-Aware Tactile Attention (EATA) to limit tactile conditioning to actions near execution, reducing temporal mismatch. Evaluate on six UniVTAC tasks (simulated) and three real-world tasks, comparing to strong baselines.
AI.result: TacForcing achieves average success rates of 65% on six UniVTAC tasks and 69% on three real-world tasks, outperforming strong baselines in both simulated and real settings.
AI.conclusion: A streaming action-generation approach with execution-time tactile conditioning and EATA improves performance in contact-rich manipulation, offering a simpler architecture without a separate reactive controller and effectively leveraging tactile feedback during execution.

title: Bootstrapping a 4D LiDAR Annotation Tool from Video Foundation Models
summary: Progress in 4D LiDAR segmentation is bottlenecked by data. Assigning temporally consistent labels across sparse point cloud sequences is costly and hard to scale, and every new task or domain tends to demand fresh dense annotation. This motivates a simple question of whether high-quality LiDAR training data can be produced automatically, without any human labeling. To this end, we introduce LiDAR-SAM2, a framework that turns a 2D video foundation model, SAM2, into a scalable source of supervision for the 4D LiDAR domain. On the data side, it automatically generates temporally coherent LiDAR-level labels from SAM2 video masks through multi-view projection and spatio-temporal aggregation. On the modeling side, a tailored modality interface and a two-stage learning objective adapt SAM2's video segmentation kernel to spatio-temporal LiDAR structure, so that a single click per object yields a consistent mask track across the sequence. Trained with no human LiDAR annotation, LiDAR-SAM2 produces semantic and panoptic labels on SemanticKITTI that approach the quality of full human annotation from only a few points, and models trained on these labels approach the performance of full ground-truth supervision. This positions LiDAR-SAM2 as a scalable labeling tool that substantially reduces the annotation burden for 3D and 4D scene understanding.

AI.tldr: LiDAR-SAM2 enables automatic, temporally coherent LiDAR labeling for 4D data using a 2D video foundation model (SAM2) with multi-view projection and spatio-temporal aggregation; a tailored learning objective adapts SAM2 to LiDAR, enabling per-object clicks to yield consistent masks across sequences; training without LiDAR annotations approaches human-labeled quality, reducing annotation burden.
AI.motivation: The 4D LiDAR segmentation data bottleneck: temporally consistent labeling across sparse point clouds is costly, and new tasks/domains require fresh dense annotations. A zero- or low-label approach could dramatically scale 3D/4D scene understanding.
AI.method: Data side: generate temporally coherent LiDAR-level labels from SAM2 video masks via multi-view projection and spatio-temporal aggregation. Modeling side: design a tailored modality interface and a two-stage learning objective to adapt SAM2's video segmentation kernel to spatio-temporal LiDAR structure, enabling a single click per object to produce a consistent mask track across the sequence.
AI.result: Trained with no human LiDAR annotation, LiDAR-SAM2 yields semantic and panoptic labels on SemanticKITTI that approach full human annotation quality from only a few points; models trained on these labels approach performance of full ground-truth supervision.
AI.conclusion: LiDAR-SAM2 functions as a scalable labeling tool that substantially reduces the annotation burden for 3D and 4D scene understanding, with strong potential to generalize across domains and tasks.

title: Learning What to Share and What to Personalize: Hierarchical Strategy Co-Evolution for Agent Memory
summary: Memory-augmented agents maintain compact user profiles throughout extended conversations, enabling personalized and consistent responses without the need to process the entire dialogue history. The quality of these user profiles relies on the underlying memory management strategy: at each step, the agent must determine what to retain, compress, or discard. However, existing methods typically employ a static, one-size-fits-all strategy established before training. In practice, the optimal memory decision is inherently user-specific and dynamically evolves alongside policy optimization. To address this, we propose \textbf{HiPS} (\textbf{Hi}erarchical \textbf{P}ersonalized \textbf{S}trategy), a framework that decouples memory management into a globally shared foundation and a user-specific adaptive tier. Specifically, HiPS employs \textbf{Universal Strategy} to extract shared principles from cross-persona trajectories, alongside \textbf{Persona Delta Distillation} to generate tailored rules for users whose behaviors diverge from general patterns. \textbf{Cross-Level Rule Flow} dynamically calibrates their boundary by promoting broadly validated personal rules and demoting contradicted global ones. The architecture establishes a co-evolution loop where a mechanism guarantees that all strategy refinements are anchored to task outcomes. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over memory-augmented baselines.

AI.tldr: HiPS decouples memory management into a global shared foundation and a user-specific adaptive tier, via universal strategy, persona delta distillation, and cross-level rule flow, enabling dynamic, personalized memory decisions that co-evolve with task outcomes, yielding improvements over memory-augmented baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-augmented agents rely on static, pre-trained memory strategies, failing to adapt to individual users and evolving policies; there is a need for dynamically personalized memory control aligned with task performance.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework HiPS: (1) Universal Strategy to learn shared memory principles from cross-persona trajectories; (2) Persona Delta Distillation to craft tailored rules for users deviating from general patterns; (3) Cross-Level Rule Flow to calibrate rule boundaries by promoting validated personal rules and demoting contradicted global ones; (4) a co-evolution loop ensuring strategy refinements are anchored to task outcomes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistent improvements over memory-augmented baselines.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, personalized memory management can be effectively achieved by a hierarchical decomposition of strategy and a co-evolution mechanism, leading to improved performance over static memory strategies.

title: Bayesian Flow Networks for Offline Trajectory Planning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) leverages static datasets to learn decision policies without real-time environment interaction. While recent sequence-modeling approaches rely on continuous diffusion models for trajectory synthesis, applying these methods to discrete planning tasks requires a categorical formulation rather than the standard Gaussian construction. We present BFN-RL, a unified generative modeling framework for offline RL based on Bayesian Flow Networks (BFNs). By iteratively evolving distribution parameters rather than noisy data instances, BFN-RL natively models both discrete and continuous trajectory spaces within a single probabilistic formulation. The categorical planner generates future state sequences, and a learned inverse-dynamics model converts consecutive generated states into actions. Evaluations in discrete planning and continuous control show that BFN-RL can generate effective trajectories across both categorical and continuous state spaces. Our results establish BFNs as a versatile generative foundation for offline trajectory planning across data modalities.

AI.tldr: BFN-RL introduces a unified offline RL framework using Bayesian Flow Networks to handle both discrete and continuous trajectory spaces by evolving distribution parameters instead of data samples, enabling a categorical planner to generate future states and an inverse dynamics model to derive actions.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in offline RL where discrete planning tasks require a categorical formulation and existing diffusion-based trajectory generation is not directly suitable for discrete spaces.
AI.method: BFN-RL employs Bayesian Flow Networks to iteratively evolve distribution parameters, enabling a single probabilistic formulation for discrete and continuous trajectories. A categorical planner generates future state sequences, and a learned inverse-dynamics model converts consecutive states into actions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations in discrete planning and continuous control show that BFN-RL can generate effective trajectories across both categorical and continuous state spaces.
AI.conclusion: BFNs provide a versatile generative foundation for offline trajectory planning across data modalities, unifying discrete and continuous planning under a single probabilistic framework.

title: AGRO-Nav: Autonomous Graph-based Orchard Navigation
summary: Orchards form semi-structured environments in which parallel tree rows create natural driving corridors, yet narrow inter-row clearance and dense foliage lead geometry-agnostic grid planners to drift off the row center and risk trunk or canopy contact. We present AGRO-Nav, an automated framework for static graph-based global planning in orchards. From tree-row lines fitted to trunk clusters in a SLAM point cloud, it builds, without any manual waypoints, a sparse topological graph of intra- and inter-row connectivity; a global route is then found by Dijkstra search on this graph, connected to the start and goal by any-angle Theta* segments, and smoothed with a cubic B-spline. In real-orchard trials, AGRO-Nav follows the row center with a mean error of about 0.08 m, far below the A* (0.31 m) and Theta* (0.43 m) shortest-path baselines, while planning roughly four to five times faster. In Isaac Sim, it attains the lowest error among A*, Theta*, and a reproduced RANSAC midline baseline and remains stable as tree density drops to 70%, where the RANSAC baseline degrades. The resulting trajectories---straight row-centered segments joined by controlled turns---suit differential-drive and four-wheel-steering platforms.

AI.tldr: AGRO-Nav: a graph-based global planner for orchards that builds a sparse topological graph from SLAM-based tree-row fits, enabling robust, faster, and accurate row-centered navigation.
AI.motivation: In orchards with tight inter-row clearance and dense foliage, geometry-agnostic grid planners drift off rows, risking trunk/canopy contact; need a topology-aware global planner that preserves row center and is efficient across varying densities.
AI.method: Fit tree-row lines to trunk clusters in SLAM point clouds; construct a sparse intra-/inter-row topological graph; compute global route with Dijkstra on the graph; connect start/goal with any-angle Theta* segments; smooth trajectory with a cubic B-spline.
AI.result: Real-world tests show mean row-centering error ~0.08 m, substantially better than A* (0.31 m) and Theta* (0.43 m); planning speed 4–5× faster than baselines. In Isaac Sim, achieves lowest error among A*, Theta*, and a reproduced RANSAC midline baseline and remains stable as density drops to 70%. Generated trajectories are straight row-centered segments with controlled turns, suitable for differential-drive and four-wheel-steering platforms.
AI.conclusion: AGRO-Nav delivers robust, efficient topology-based global planning for orchard navigation, maintaining centerline trajectories with resilience to density changes and compatibility with common mobile robot architectures.

title: Saliency-Depth Conditioning for Zero-Shot Segmentation of Communication-Tower Components in Cluttered UAV Imagery
summary: Fine-grained segmentation of communication-tower components in UAV imagery is essential for automated inspection, yet task-specific models are hard to develop due to limited instance-level annotations. Zero-shot segmentation models offer a promising alternative, but in cluttered scenes, visually similar background structures interfere with component localization, causing missed instances and false positives. We propose a model-agnostic saliency-depth foreground-conditioning strategy combining appearance-based saliency with monocular relative depth to construct a coarse tower prior and suppress irrelevant content. We integrate this module with Grounded-SAM and SAM 3, yielding SD-Grounded-SAM and SD-SAM 3. SD-Grounded-SAM further applies geometric and depth-aware box refinement before mask generation, while SD-SAM 3 relies on SAM 3's internal setup. On TOW-300, a dataset of 340 communication-tower UAV images, our strategy improves both baselines: SD-SAM 3 achieves the strongest instance-segmentation performance, while SD-Grounded-SAM produces fewer false positives. Ablations confirm complementary gains from saliency, depth, and box refinement, improving robustness in cluttered scenes.

AI.tldr: Proposes a model-agnostic saliency-depth foreground-conditioning strategy to boost zero-shot segmentation of UAV-tower components; integrates with Grounded-SAM and SAM 3 to form SD-Grounded-SAM and SD-SAM 3; achieves fewer false positives and stronger instance segmentation on TOW-300; ablations show gains from saliency, depth, and box refinement.
AI.motivation: In cluttered UAV imagery with limited instance-level annotations, zero-shot segmentation struggles due to interference from visually similar background structures; a coarse foreground prior is needed to better localize tower components and suppress irrelevant content.
AI.method: Combine appearance-based saliency with monocular relative depth to create a coarse tower prior, then integrate this conditioning with Grounded-SAM and SAM 3. SD-Grounded-SAM adds geometric and depth-aware box refinement before mask generation, while SD-SAM 3 relies on SAM 3's internal setup.
AI.result: On the TOW-300 dataset (340 UAV images), the proposed strategy improves baseline methods: SD-SAM 3 yields the strongest instance-segmentation performance; SD-Grounded-SAM produces fewer false positives. Ablations show complementary gains from saliency, depth, and box refinement, enhancing robustness in cluttered scenes.
AI.conclusion: The saliency-depth foreground-conditioning strategy provides an effective, model-agnostic foreground prior that enhances zero-shot segmentation of tower components in cluttered UAV imagery, yielding improved instance segmentation with reduced false positives; benefits are transferable across SAM configurations and supported by ablation evidence.

title: Where vs What: Decomposing Structural and Content Failures in LLM-Generated Structured Outputs
summary: Structured outputs such as JSON and tables are central to modern LLM-based systems, yet generation failures are evaluated monolithically, conflating two distinct error modes: placement errors (correct values at wrong positions) and value errors (wrong values at intended positions). We introduce Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD), a framework that independently measures structural fidelity and content accuracy. Applying SCD to nested JSON and table tasks across six models (7B to frontier), we uncover a consistent phenomenon: structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy as complexity increases. At the highest complexity, even DeepSeek-V4-Flash (with reasoning) misplaces 35% of recalled values, while Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. Controlled ablations suggest that this pattern is associated with reliance on semantic shortcuts rather than topological understanding of output structure. Based on these findings, we propose SA-RLVR, converting SCD metrics into verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning via GRPO. SA-RLVR successfully optimizes structural addressing across distinct topologies: it lifts JSON Value Placement Accuracy (VPA) from 26% to 63% while generalizing to held-out schemas; moreover, it consistently drives VPA improvements in the table domain, demonstrating that structure-aware rewards can directly enhance multi-domain structural positioning.

AI.tldr: Introduces Structure-Content Decomposition (SCD) to separately evaluate structure vs. content in structured outputs; finds structure degrades earlier than content as task complexity grows; proposes SA-RLVR using GRPO to optimize structure with significant gains in JSON and table outputs.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of structured outputs (e.g., JSON, tables) is monolithic, conflating placement errors (wrong values in correct spots) with value errors (wrong values in wrong spots). There is a need to disentangle these error modes to diagnose and improve systems.
AI.method: Define SCD to decompose outputs into structural fidelity and content accuracy. Apply SCD to nested JSON and table tasks across six models (7B to frontier). Quantify placement vs value errors; perform ablations to analyze causes (semantic shortcuts vs topological understanding). Propose SA-RLVR—convert SCD metrics into verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning via GRPO—and optimize structure-aware rewards.
AI.result: Structural fidelity degrades earlier and more sharply than content accuracy as complexity increases. At peak complexity, DeepSeek-V4-Flash misplaces 35% of recalled values; Qwen2.5-7B misplaces 74%. SA-RLVR lifts JSON Value Placement Accuracy (VPA) from 26% to 63% and generalizes to held-out schemas; also yields consistent improvements in table domain, demonstrating cross-domain effectiveness of structure-aware rewards.
AI.conclusion: Separating structure and content in evaluation reveals distinct error dynamics and shows that structure-aware reinforcement learning (SA-RLVR via GRPO) can substantially improve correct placement of values in both JSON and tables across models and schemas.

title: Simultaneous inference of environmental and interaction forces in collective dynamics
summary: Collective dynamics arise in a wide range of physical, biological, and engineering applications. Examples include cell migration, swarm robotics, social dynamics, and animal behavior. A defining characteristic of these systems is the emergence of large-scale coordination from local interactions among agents; a fundamental question is thus to understand the local interactions that give rise to the observed emergent dynamics. We are interested in methods for learning interactions generally, which can describe a wide class of physical systems exhibiting collective dynamics defined by an interaction kernel, without a priori assumptions on the analytical form of this kernel (i.e. it is nonparametric). The advantage of this kernel-based approach is that it incorporates the underlying physics of the model (i.e. collective dynamics), which more general equation-learning approaches may ignore, potentially limiting their effectiveness for model accuracy and predictions. In this work, we extend existing variational learning approaches to collective systems with both interaction kernels and environmental/intra-agent forces. The proposed framework simultaneously infers the interaction kernel non-parametrically while learning the environmental force using either semi-parametric or fully nonparametric representations. The methodology is validated on several benchmark models exhibiting synchronization, alignment, attraction-repulsion, and external environmental forces. We also introduce a model-selection procedure based on our nonparametric learning framework to identify models that optimally explain a given set of trajectory observations. By exploiting the feature-identification capability of the learned models, the proposed procedure can distinguish among different collective dynamics frameworks and recover mechanistic interaction mechanisms directly from trajectory data.

AI.tldr: Nonparametric kernel learning for collective dynamics with environmental forces; jointly infers interaction kernels and forces; includes model selection to identify governing interaction mechanisms from trajectory data; validated on benchmarks (synchronization, alignment, attraction-repulsion, environmental forces).
AI.motivation: Understand how local agent interactions drive emergent large-scale coordination in diverse systems and learn these interactions without assuming a fixed analytic form, leveraging physics-informed, nonparametric learning to improve accuracy and interpretability.
AI.method: Extend variational learning to collective systems by nonparametrically inferring the interaction kernel and representing environmental/intra-agent forces semi-parametrically or fully nonparametrically. Incorporate a model-selection procedure using the learned nonparametric representations to distinguish among different collective-dynamics frameworks. Validate on trajectory data from models exhibiting synchronization, alignment, attraction-repulsion, and external forces.
AI.result: The approach accurately recovers interaction kernels and forces across benchmark dynamics, enables model selection to identify the governing framework, and recovers mechanistic interaction mechanisms directly from trajectory observations.
AI.conclusion: A flexible, physics-informed, nonparametric framework for learning and comparing interaction rules in collective dynamics, capable of recovering mechanistic insights from trajectory data and distinguishing among competing models.

title: Anytime Global Tensor Motion Planning
summary: Global Tensor Motion Planning (GTMP) solves motion planning with batched tensor operations over a layered multipartite graph. We generalize GTMP so that adjacent-layer edges are realized by any black-box local planner (e.g., linear interpolation, splines, sampling-based planning, trajectory optimization, or generative sampling). We provide two anytime policies on top of this generalization: Anytime GTMP with random restarts at a fixed budget, which covers every homotopy class almost surely, and AO-GTMP with informed expansion with growing budgets, which converges to the optimal cost. We prove that a single sampled graph covers every endpoint-fixed homotopy class admitting a \(δ\)-clear representative of bounded length. We also prove that additional samples per layer reduce the per-layer miss probability exponentially, whereas stronger local planners reduce the required layer count only sublinearly. On manipulation benchmarks the method matches state-of-the-art performance, and on 2D navigation it returns batches of topologically diverse solutions, while the informed baselines concentrate on one or two classes.

AI.tldr: Generalized GTMP framework enabling batched tensor planning over layered graphs with black-box local planners per layer; introduces two anytime policies (random-restart and informed expansion) providing homotopy class coverage and convergence to optimal cost; analyzes sampling effects and layer complexity; empirically competitive, offering topologically diverse solutions.
AI.motivation: Extend Global Tensor Motion Planning (GTMP) to allow arbitrary, possibly black-box, local planners for inter-layer edges, while maintaining theoretical guarantees and enabling anytime performance and topological diversity.
AI.method: Represent motion planning as a layered multipartite graph with tensor-based batched operations. Replace fixed inter-layer planners with black-box local planners. Propose two anytime policies: (1) Anytime GTMP with random restarts at a fixed budget to cover all homotopy classes almost surely; (2) AO-GTMP with informed expansion and growing budgets to converge to the optimal cost. Theoretical results: a single sampled graph covers endpoint-fixed δ-clear homotopy classes of bounded length; adding samples per layer reduces per-layer miss probability exponentially; stronger local planners reduce required layer count sublinearly. Empirical evaluation on manipulation benchmarks (state-of-the-art performance) and 2D navigation (topologically diverse solution batches).
AI.result: The framework delivers theoretical guarantees of homotopy class coverage and asymptotic optimality under the two policies; it achieves competitive performance on manipulation tasks and promotes topological diversity in 2D navigation.
AI.conclusion: Generalized GTMP with black-box local planners and two anytime policies achieves coverage of homotopy classes and convergence to optimal cost, with favorable empirical performance and enhanced topological diversity.

title: VGA-BenchV2: An Expanded Unified Benchmark and Multi-Model Framework for Evaluating Video Aesthetics and Generation Quality
summary: We introduce VGA-BenchV2, an extended human-aligned benchmark and optimization framework for jointly evaluating and improving video generation quality and aesthetic value. Built upon VGA-Bench, VGA-BenchV2 preserves the original fine-grained taxonomy with two primary dimensions-Aesthetic and Generation-and 52 sub-dimensions. Guided by this taxonomy, we curate 1,016 diverse prompts and collect over 60,000 videos generated by 12 mainstream video generation models. More importantly, VGA-BenchV2 substantially expands human-labeled supervision by adding 36,000 task-level annotations, including 16,200 for aesthetic quality, 13,200 for aesthetic tagging, and 6,600 for generation quality, corresponding to 13.46x, 11.15x, and 1.55x scale-ups over VGA-Bench, respectively. Leveraging this enlarged annotation corpus, we develop a hybrid evaluator architecture consisting of VAQA-Net for continuous aesthetic scoring and two Qwen-based Large Vision-Language Model evaluators, VTag-Net and VGQA-Net, for aesthetic tagging and generation quality assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong alignment with human judgments across diverse generation models. Beyond evaluation, VGA-BenchV2 further introduces an evaluation-to-optimization pipeline, where the learned aesthetic evaluator serves as a reward model for reinforcement learning-based generator fine-tuning. This closes the loop from benchmark construction and human supervision to automated evaluation and model optimization, enabling video generators to improve not only in realism but also in aesthetic quality and human preference alignment. Resources are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/BestiVictoryLab/VGA-Bench.

AI.tldr: An expanded, taxonomy-driven video-generation benchmark with large-scale annotations and a hybrid evaluator, enabling RL-based optimization of aesthetic quality and human-preference alignment.
AI.motivation: To better evaluate and optimize video generation by jointly considering aesthetics and generation quality, addressing the limited granularity and limited validation of prior benchmarks.
AI.method: Extend the VGA-Bench taxonomy (Aesthetic and Generation with 52 sub-dimensions); curate 1,016 prompts and collect >60k videos from 12 models; add 36k task-level annotations (16.2k aesthetic quality, 13.2k aesthetic tagging, 6.6k generation quality); develop a hybrid evaluative framework: VAQA-Net for continuous aesthetic scoring; VTag-Net and VGQA-Net (Qwen-based LVLMs) for tagging and generation quality; validate alignment with human judgments; introduce an evaluation-to-optimization pipeline using the aesthetic evaluator as a reward for RL-based generator fine-tuning.
AI.result: Demonstrates strong alignment with human judgments across diverse generation models; provides a large, richly annotated benchmark and a usable evaluation-to-optimization pipeline; resources available at HuggingFace dataset hub.
AI.conclusion: VGA-BenchV2 enables end-to-end evaluation and optimization of video generators for both realism and aesthetic value, promoting human-preference-aligned improvements and scalable automatic evaluation.

title: Can your AI agent be cheaper? Investigating the effects of task specifications on token spend in agentic coding tasks
summary: Agentic coding workflows are now widely deployed in real-world systems. With long-horizon reasoning and tool use, token usage has become an important consideration for both cost and efficiency. Two engineers using AI will solve the same problem differently. How the specification of a task shapes an agent's token spend, and whether that spend can be predicted in advance, are open questions. Here, we study the effects of different task specifications on agentic token spend with the Kimi K3 model at three thinking efforts. Across $2,700$ runs, we show that reducing a full task specification to a bare user story raises token spend by $29.7\%$, while run-to-run variance remains unaffected by any prompt changes. We show that prompt-sensitivity is task-dependent, running from $13\%$ to $115\%$. We fit a simple predictor that can price a full distribution of task specifications and thinking effort configurations from a single cheap probe on an unseen task within $36\%$, improving over prior work in predicting token spend. Our work provides initial results quantifying the effects of task specification on agentic token spend and introduces a method that can be used to systematically evaluate the cost of AI coding workflows.

AI.tldr: Task specification materially affects token expenditure in agentic coding workflows; a cheap probe can predict spend distributions with notable accuracy.
AI.motivation: Quantify how task framing influences token usage and forecast costs to improve efficiency in long-horizon AI reasoning within coding workflows.
AI.method: Empirical study using the Kimi K3 model across three thinking-effort levels and 2,700 runs, comparing full task specifications to bare user stories; measured token spend; developed a predictive model to price distributions of task specs and thinking-effort configurations from a cheap probe on unseen tasks.
AI.result: Reducing to a bare user story increases token spend by 29.7%; run-to-run variance is unaffected by prompt changes; prompt-sensitivity ranges from 13% to 115%; a simple predictor prices the full distribution from a cheap probe within 36%, outperforming prior work.
AI.conclusion: Task specification materially impacts token expenditure; provides a framework to evaluate and manage costs in AI coding workflows.

title: Transforms for LLM Quantization: The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design
summary: Most competitive 4-bit LLM research pipelines now open the same way: apply a linear, function-preserving transform (rotation, scaling, permutation, non-orthogonal affine) so the outlier mass sits more favorably against the group scales, and only then round. Yet we are aware of no survey dedicated to this transform stage, and its literature is quietly re-deriving an older theory. We identify and formalize the principle that organizes it, the Great Inversion: allocation-flexible coding rewards energy concentration, whereas the grouped shared-scale quantization a deployed matrix instruction performs rewards within-group flattening. Classical transform coding (1963: decorrelate, allocate bits, quantize) spends different bits per coordinate at a fixed total rate; for a Gaussian source at high rate the Karhunen-Loeve transform's concentration minimizes distortion. A deployed operand tile instead carries one absolute-maximum scale per group and equal bits everywhere, with no allocation; on a uniform grid that objective rewards flattening, approached by Hadamard incoherence. We prove that opposition under within-group majorization: the prescriptions point in opposite directions, each backed by a proof against its own objective, and for a generic spectrum no optimality guarantee transfers. A second axis is the number format: the non-uniform FP4 grid makes flattening buy less, MXFP4's power-of-two block scale still rewards a rotation confined to that block, and NVFP4's mantissa-carrying scale largely removes that pull, so the target pole depends jointly on allocation regime and format. We survey 200 works to a June 2026 cutoff; classify 43 transform methods by structure, data-awareness, searched-versus-constructed, and runtime cost; record, where reported, how they compose with GPTQ rounding; distill a first-choice guide by deployment regime; and close with the open problems it exposes.

AI.tldr: Formalizes the Great Inversion in LLM transform/quantization, contrasting allocation-flexible coding (energy concentration) with grouped shared-scale quantization (within-group flattening). Analyzes impact of numeric formats (FP4 variants) and Hadamard incoherence, finds no universal optimality; surveys literature and offers deployment-guided guidance and open problems.
AI.motivation: Address the absence of a dedicated survey of the transform stage in competitive 4-bit LLM pipelines and formalize the organizing principle behind transform-based quantization, including how data format and allocation regime interact with performance.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis and formal proofs; comparison to classical transform coding; analysis of within-group majorization; exploration of Hadamard incoherence; examination of 3 FP4-style formats (FP4, MXFP4, NVFP4); empirical survey of 200 works up to June 2026; classification of 43 transform methods by structure, data-awareness, searched-vs-constructed, and runtime cost; evaluation of composition with GPTQ rounding; synthesis into deployment-guided recommendations and open problems.
AI.result: Introduces and formalizes the Great Inversion principle: allocation-flexible coding concentrates energy vs grouped shared-scale quantization promotes within-group flattening. Demonstrates that the two prescriptions are opposites under within-group majorization and do not yield a universal optimality guarantee for generic spectra. Shows that target behavior depends jointly on allocation regime and numeric format (FP4 variants, Hadamard-like flattening effects, and mantissa-carrying scales). Provides a comprehensive survey of 200 works and 43 transform methods, classifies them, records their interaction with GPTQ rounding, and distills a first-choice deployment guide with a set of open problems.
AI.conclusion: The transform stage in 4-bit LLM quantization remains theoretically nuanced with regime-dependent optima; no single best transform exists across spectra or formats. The work delivers a structured taxonomy, deployment-oriented guidance, and a roadmap of open problems for future research.

title: MA-VLA: Multi-Arm Vision-Language-Action Model for Collaboration and Compositional Generalization
summary: Multi-arm collaboration is becoming a core capability in embodied manipulation. Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate perception, language, and control, but most represent language as a single global instruction and do not provide an explicit mechanism for assigning and composing arm-specific behaviors. This design limits transfer to collaboration patterns that differ from those observed during training. We present MA-VLA, a unified framework for multi-arm collaboration via atomic action assignment. MA-VLA decomposes cooperative behavior into mid-level atomic prompts and allocates them to individual arms, enabling explicit subgoal specification and compositional reuse across tasks. To reduce reliance on fixed execution roles, we introduce Arm Shuffle, a training-time permutation of the observation, state, and assigned atomic prompts for each arm. This permutation enforces role-agnostic instruction following and supports recomposition into unseen coordination patterns, which we term multi-arm compositional generalization. We also construct a benchmark in which test-time collaboration patterns are absent in training set. Across simulation and real-world evaluations, prior state-of-the-art VLAs largely fail under these unseen collaborations, while MA-VLA consistently succeeds. These results indicate that structured, per-arm atomic action assignment offers a practical route to scalable generalization in multi-arm embodied systems. Code, models, and data are available at https://github.com/zhangzaibin/future-robots

AI.tldr: MA-VLA enables explicit per-arm action assignment with atomic prompts and Arm Shuffle to achieve multi-arm compositional generalization, outperforming prior VLA models on unseen collaboration tasks in both simulation and real-world settings.
AI.motivation: To overcome limited transfer of vision-language-action models to new multi-arm collaboration patterns by moving from a single global instruction to per-arm atomic prompts and a role-agnostic training regime.
AI.method: Introduce MA-VLA, which decomposes cooperative behavior into mid-level atomic prompts and assigns them to individual arms. Incorporate Arm Shuffle to permute observations, states, and prompts during training to enforce role-agnostic instruction following and enable recomposition into unseen coordination patterns.
AI.result: MA-VLA consistently succeeds on unseen collaboration patterns across simulation and real-world evaluations, while prior SOTA VLAs fail. A benchmark with test-time collaborations absent from training was constructed, and code/models/data are released.
AI.conclusion: Structured per-arm atomic action assignment with Arm Shuffle is a practical approach to scalable generalization in multi-arm embodied systems and enables transfer to unseen coordination patterns.

title: Automatic weld seam segmentation for industrial quality control: a comparison of RGB and polarimetric imaging with CNN and transformer architectures
summary: Visual inspection of welded assemblies remains one of the least automated stages in many industrial production processes, still depending largely on the experience of human operators and thus subject to inter-operator variability; the manufacturing of special-purpose machinery cabins, the setting of this study, is one representative case. This work evaluates the feasibility of automatic weld seam segmentation from RGB and polarimetric imagery, comparing controlled laboratory acquisitions with images captured under real, uncontrolled conditions. Convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures and transformer-based architectures are benchmarked under a unified, threshold-independent protocol, training each CNN with three random seeds to separate genuine effects from seed noise. In controlled RGB conditions, CNN models reach a mean mask mAP50 of up to 0.87, but drop to 0.22-0.48 under uncontrolled acquisition, showing that the acquisition setup is a first-order component of the inspection system. Polarimetric imaging with alignment-preserving geometric augmentation localizes previously unseen welds with a mean mask mAP50 up to 0.93: on par with, rather than ahead of, the best controlled-RGB result, but reaching that accuracy on uncontrolled RGB without requiring acquisition control. The clearest architectural finding concerns viewpoint robustness. In-distribution, transformers and CNNs are broadly comparable; but under a test-time viewpoint shift, the transformer models, and RF-DETR in particular, retain high accuracy while every CNN collapses. The gap holds across three seeds and a resolution-matched control, pointing to architecture rather than training resolution. Within the CNN family, capacity brings no reliable in-distribution gain once seed variance is accounted for: small CNNs suffice for fixed viewpoints, transformers for variable ones.

AI.tldr: A study benchmarks CNNs and transformers for automatic weld-seam segmentation using RGB and polarimetric images under controlled and uncontrolled conditions. Key findings: acquisition/setup and viewpoint shifts greatly affect performance; transformers show robustness to viewpoint changes, especially RF-DETR, while CNNs fail under shifts. Polarimetric imagery with geometry-preserving augmentation matches top RGB performance under challenging conditions. Among CNNs, increasing capacity yields limited gains; transformers handle variable viewpoints with more reliability.
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on human experts for weld inspection, which is highly variable across operators and conditions. The work investigates how different architectures and imaging modalities perform under realistic, uncontrolled acquisition settings to guide robust deployment in industrial welding inspection.
AI.method: A unified benchmarking protocol evaluating CNN and transformer architectures on weld-seam segmentation using RGB and polarimetric imagery. Models trained with three random seeds. Experiments compare controlled RGB, uncontrolled RGB, and polarimetric, with alignment-preserving geometric augmentation for polarimetric data. Evaluation via threshold-independent mAP50; analysis of viewpoint robustness via test-time shifts; comparison across seeds and network capacities.
AI.result: Controlled RGB achieves mean mAP50 up to 0.87; uncontrolled RGB drops to 0.22–0.48. Polarimetric imaging with alignment-preserving augmentation localizes unseen welds with mean mAP50 up to 0.93, comparable to best controlled RGB and effective under uncontrolled RGB without acquisition control. Under viewpoint shifts, transformers (RF-DETR) maintain high accuracy while CNNs collapse. Across seeds and resolutions, CNN capacity yields no reliable in-distribution gains; small CNNs suffice for fixed viewpoints, transformers for variable viewpoints.
AI.conclusion: Architectural choice dominates robustness to viewpoint variation; transformer-based models (notably RF-DETR) are preferred for variable viewpoints, while CNNs are adequate only in fixed-view scenarios. Polarimetric data with geometry-aware augmentation can match or exceed RGB performance under adverse acquisition, underscoring the importance of imaging modality and data handling in automated weld-seam inspection.

title: Paint What You See: Benchmarking Dexterous Visual Tool Use in Multimodal Agents
summary: Evaluation is shifting from static QA toward agentic settings where models act through external tools. We identify a critical yet underexplored capability within this space - dexterous visual tool use: fine-grained, closed-loop parameterized visual action in which models infer tool parameters from visual evidence, and those parameters directly govern the final result. Existing benchmarks cover web navigation, GUI operation, and software engineering, but rarely target this coupling between visual evidence and execution precision. We propose EASEL, a benchmark evaluating a controlled instance of dexterous visual tool use that adopts reference-guided visual reconstruction as its primary proxy task: the agent incrementally paints a canvas to match a reference image. EASEL additionally includes semantic tasks spanning region annotation, handwriting, and path planning. We further provide EASEL-Data, a 440k-sample two-stage curriculum dataset for trajectory supervision, and EASEL-9B to investigate its effect on this capability. Evaluation of 25 models reveals that current multimodal agents systematically struggle on EASEL. Reconstruction similarity bottlenecks at low levels (0.40-0.54), while trajectory diagnostics expose severe closed-loop instability - models typically saturate early or degrade post-peak. Semantic tasks reveal sharp capability boundaries in precision annotation and path planning. EASEL-9B, trained on EASEL-Data, surpasses the base model by a relative 6.3%, ranking third among all evaluated models.

AI.tldr: EASEL introduces a benchmark for dexterous visual tool use, focusing on reference-guided visual reconstruction and related semantic tasks, with data and model evaluations showing current models struggle, but EASEL-9B yields moderate gains.
AI.motivation: To study fine-grained, closed-loop visual-to-action coupling in agentic models, addressing a gap where visual evidence must drive precise tool-executed outcomes.
AI.method: Propose EASEL benchmark with a primary proxy task of incremental painting to match a reference image; include semantic tasks (region annotation, handwriting, path planning); provide EASEL-Data (440k samples two-stage curriculum) and EASEL-9B; evaluate 25 models.
AI.result: Models show weak performance: reconstruction similarity 0.40-0.54; severe closed-loop instability; semantic task boundaries; EASEL-9B trained on EASEL-Data improves base by 6.3% relative, ranking third.
AI.conclusion: EASEL reveals the current limits of dexterous visual tool use and the potential of staged data to improve capabilities; underscores need for improved closed-loop control in multimodal systems.

title: What Should a Large Language Model See? Physical Invariants as a Data Representation for PDE Discovery
summary: Understanding how molecular interactions govern macroscopic behaviour is a central challenge in molecular sciences.
