However, conventional theory building cannot keep pace with the vast datasets modern experimentation routinely produces. Large language models offer a promising route to automating theory construction, but a spatiotemporal field cannot be directly placed in a prompt. Existing models generally learn about the data only through a score measuring how well each proposal fits it. Here we introduce data interpretation, a stage that measures the field into the quantities a theorist would consult and supplies them to the model as a direct input. On a benchmark of simulated fields, interpretation nearly triples the accuracy of recovered equations relative to showing the raw data, at negligible computational cost and without any training. By allowing a language model to read field data as a theorist does, data interpretation offers a practical route to automated field theory construction that can coevolve with experimentation.

AI.tldr: A data interpretation stage converts spatiotemporal field data into interpretable, theorist-ready quantities for LLM-based theory construction, achieving ~3x higher equation-recovery accuracy on simulated fields without training.
AI.motivation: Big datasets outpace conventional theory-building; LLMs need interpretable inputs rather than raw fields to discover governing equations.
AI.method: Introduce a data interpretation module that extracts field-derived quantities (e.g., local invariants, gradients, correlations, differential operators, conserved quantities) and feeds them to a language model as direct inputs; evaluate on simulated-field benchmarks in a zero-shot setting without model training; compare to prompts that show raw data.
AI.result: Interpretation substantially improves equation-recovery accuracy (about triple) over raw-field prompts, with negligible computational cost and no training required.
AI.conclusion: Reading field data in a theorist-like manner enables practical automated field theory construction; the data interpretation stage can coevolve with experimentation to accelerate discovery.

title: VISTA: Visually Inferred Spatial ConTact Attention for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires precise interaction feedback. While vision-centric imitation learning is prevalent, external visual observations provide indirect and ambiguous cues about contact states, particularly under occlusion or subtle object--gripper interactions; dedicated tactile or force sensors can provide rich contact information but introduce additional hardware complexity, calibration requirements, and deployment costs. To bridge this gap, we propose VISTA-Policy, an imitation learning paradigm that utilizes the Visual Deformation Field (VDF), a 3D displacement representation of a compliant gripper, as high-dimensional visuo-physical feedback. The framework integrates: 1) a Physics-Aware Encoding Engine for real-time VDF decoding; 2) an Energy Aggregation Denoising Mechanism to isolate true interaction signals; and 3) a Deformation-Augmented Policy Network with incremental gripper actions for precise closed-loop correction. Extensive evaluations on Cross-Scale Object Grasping, Cap Unscrewing, and Calligraphy Writing demonstrate that VISTA-Policy outperforms the strong pure-vision baseline 3D Diffusion Policy and the tactile baseline. VISTA-Policy further demonstrates substantial out-of-distribution generalization to unseen object scales and robustness against dynamic disturbances, offering a durable and cost-effective route toward general-purpose fine-grained manipulation in unstructured environments. Project videos and supplementary materials are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/vista-policy.

AI.tldr: VISTA-Policy integrates a Visual Deformation Field (VDF) from a compliant gripper with a physics-aware encoder, denoising, and a deformation-augmented policy to enable precise closed-loop manipulation using visuo-physical feedback, outperforming vision-only and tactile baselines and generalizing across scales and disturbances.
AI.motivation: Vision-based imitation learning struggles to infer fine contact states due to occlusion or subtle interactions; tactile sensors add hardware, calibration, and deployment costs. A cost-effective approach that fuses visuo-physical feedback is desirable for robust contact-rich manipulation.
AI.method: 1) Physics-Aware Encoding Engine decodes the Visual Deformation Field (VDF) in real time. 2) Energy Aggregation Denoising Mechanism isolates true interaction signals from noise. 3) Deformation-Augmented Policy Network uses incremental gripper actions to apply precise closed-loop corrections.
AI.result: Experiments on Cross-Scale Object Grasping, Cap Unscrewing, and Calligraphy Writing show VISTA-Policy outperforms a strong pure-vision baseline (3D Diffusion Policy) and a tactile baseline, with strong out-of-distribution generalization to unseen scales and robustness to dynamic disturbances.
AI.conclusion: VISTA-Policy provides a durable, cost-effective route to general-purpose fine-grained manipulation in unstructured environments by effectively fusing visual and deformation-based feedback for precise control.

title: PAGS: Autofocusing Photoacoustic Tomography via Speed-of-Sound-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting
summary: Photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) combines optical absorption contrast with acoustic detection for high-resolution deep-tissue imaging. A persistent challenge is that unknown speed-of-sound (SoS) heterogeneity changes acoustic time-of-flight, causing defocusing artifacts when reconstruction assumes a uniform SoS. Existing SoS-adaptive methods either rely on calibrated acoustic priors or optimize dense physical medium models, which becomes expensive and difficult to scale in 3D. We propose PAGS, a differentiable framework for blind autofocusing PACT via speed-of-sound-adaptive Gaussian splatting. PAGS represents the initial pressure field with sparse Gaussian photoacoustic (PA) sources and replaces explicit medium recovery with a compact anisotropic path-averaged SoS (ASoS) field parameterized by spherical harmonic probes. This latent propagation field directly controls source-to-transducer arrival-time alignment, while an analytic Gaussian acoustic projection maps the source representation to transducer signals efficiently. The resulting closed-loop signal-domain optimization jointly updates the Gaussian PA source parameters and the ASoS field from measured data, without calibrated SoS priors. Experiments on simulated and physical phantom data demonstrate improved reconstruction sharpness under heterogeneous acoustic media, robustness to sparse-view sampling, and computational benefits from the analytic Gaussian projection.

AI.tldr: PAGS enables blind autofocusing in photoacoustic computed tomography by jointly optimizing sparse Gaussian PA sources and a speed-of-sound field, using a latent anisotropic path-averaged SoS and an analytic Gaussian projection to improve reconstruction in heterogeneous media without calibrated priors.
AI.motivation: Unknown acoustic speed-of-sound heterogeneity defocuses reconstructions in PACT; existing SoS-adaptive methods rely on calibrated priors or dense medium models, which are costly and hard to scale to 3D.
AI.method: Represent initial pressure with sparse Gaussian PA sources. Use a latent ASoS field parameterized by spherical harmonic probes to capture path-averaged SoS. Apply an analytic Gaussian acoustic projection to map the source representation to transducer signals. Perform closed-loop, signal-domain optimization that jointly updates Gaussian PA source parameters and the ASoS field using measured data, without calibrated SoS priors.
AI.result: Simulations and physical phantom experiments show sharper reconstructions in heterogeneous media, robustness to sparse-view sampling, and computational efficiency due to the analytic projection.
AI.conclusion: PAGS offers a differentiable, blind autofocusing framework for PACT that avoids explicit medium recovery priors, scales better to 3D, and improves image quality under SoS heterogeneity.

title: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
summary: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

AI.tldr: Proposes Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor of update robustness for neural unlearning, showing update structure (forget-critical vs retain-critical) matters more than global weight-distance; introduces Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) to enforce selective updates and improve relearning robustness.
AI.motivation: Unlearning robustness is not well captured by global weight-space distance: small fine-tuning can reintroduce forgotten information. A predictor that assesses how an update aligns with forget-critical and retain-critical weights, without retraining, could better explain and improve robustness.
AI.method: Define FRAG as a training-free metric that quantifies forget-retain alignment of a proposed update. Compare selective (forgetting) versus dense updates. Develop FRP to prune updates to be forget-selective and retain-sparing. Evaluate robustness of relearning attacks and compare FRAG/FRP against distance-based predictors. Code released.
AI.result: FRAG more reliably distinguishes selective vs dense updates than global distance. FRP improves relearning robustness by promoting update selectivity. Empirical results suggest weight selectivity explains robustness better than distance alone.
AI.conclusion: Update structure—which weights are altered for forgetting vs retaining—drives relearning robustness. FRAG provides a practical, training-free predictor, and FRP demonstrates that structure-aware pruning can enhance unlearning reliability beyond what distance metrics capture.

title: Hyperbolic Latent Geometry for Tree-Structured Prototype Networks: A Local-vs-Global Trade-off
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures, 1 table (including appendix). Code, sweep CSVs, and figure-generation scripts: https://github.com/pgrindehollevik-harvard/hyperbolic
summary: We study a tree-structured regularizer over class-prototype layouts in a hierarchical-classification model and ask whether the choice of latent manifold for the prototypes (Euclidean R^d vs. the Poincare ball B^d_c) affects how well that regularizer can be satisfied without distorting the data likelihood. The two manifolds differ only in their volume growth: hyperbolic space grows exponentially with radius and embeds trees with provably lower distortion than R^d of matched dimension, so the structured regularizer should be cheaper to satisfy on B^d_c. Across 150 seed-replicated regularized maximum-likelihood fits spanning embedding dimension, curvature, and regularizer strength on WikiArt (27 styles, 81,446 paintings, frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 features), we find a single robust effect: Poincare prototypes preserve the topology of the nearest-neighbor graph in latent space substantially better than matched Euclidean prototypes (sibling recall@5 +8.7 pp, cousin recall +15.2 pp; paired-t p < 10^-4, sign agreement 0.94), and the gap holds across three reference-tree definitions (hand-built lineage, CLIP-derived, and DINOv2-derived). On classification, Euclidean prototypes are tied with logistic regression on raw encoder features, indicating no detectable contribution from the latent geometry; only the hyperbolic fit improves on a k-NN encoder baseline for local retrieval. Global tree-fidelity comparisons are unstable across reference trees and we do not claim a winner. The results give an empirical separation, on a real hierarchical-classification problem, between two natural latent geometries for a class-structured regularizer.

AI.tldr: Hyperbolic (Poincaré ball) prototypes more faithfully preserve the topology of the nearest-neighbor graph in latent space than Euclidean prototypes in a tree-structured regularizer for hierarchical classification; the gain is robust across multiple reference trees and datasets, while classification gains are limited to local retrieval improvements from hyperbolic geometry; no clear global winner for tree fidelity.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether latent geometry (Euclidean vs hyperbolic) affects the ability of a tree-structured regularizer to be satisfied without distorting data likelihood, leveraging hyperbolic space’s exponential volume growth to embed trees with lower distortion.
AI.method: Aggregate 150 seed-replicated regularized maximum-likelihood fits across embedding dimension, curvature, and regularizer strength on WikiArt (27 styles, 81,446 paintings) using frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 features. Compare class prototypes on Euclidean R^d versus Poincaré ball B^d_c. Evaluate topology preservation via nearest-neighbor graphs under three reference-tree definitions (hand-built lineage, CLIP-derived, DINOv2-derived). Assess classification performance against baselines (logistic regression on raw features, k-NN on encoder features).
AI.result: Poincaré prototypes substantially outperform Euclidean prototypes in preserving nearest-neighbor topology: sibling recall@5 improves by 8.7 percentage points; cousin recall improves by 15.2 points (paired t-test p < 1e-4; sign agreement 0.94). The improvement is robust across all three reference-tree definitions. In classification, Euclidean prototypes do not outperform logistic regression on raw encoder features; hyperbolic prototypes only improve local retrieval over a k-NN encoder baseline. Global tree-fidelity comparisons are unstable across reference trees, so no overall winner is claimed.
AI.conclusion: Empirically, a hyperbolic latent geometry provides a meaningful separation from Euclidean geometry for a class-structured regularizer in hierarchical classification on real data, with clear gains in topology preservation, while global tree fidelity remains inconclusive; geometry choice matters for regularizer satisfaction without distorting likelihood.

title: Low-Resolution Perception for Robotic Packing
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to IFAC World Congress 2026
summary: This work tackles the problem of scalable perception for robotic packing with low-cost, low-resolution depth sensing. We propose a framework where reconstruction cues drive next-view selection and grasp evidence updates a per-object stability estimate, jointly deciding what to acquire next and when to grasp. During the reconstruction, a low-resolution Next Best View (NBV) strategy explicitly avoids redundant views while preserving task-relevant geometry. We validate the approach in two steps: (i) an ablation study of the utility function under very low resolution, and (ii) a full end-to-end evaluation across policies, showing how low-resolution perception is a practical, scalable option for robotic packing.

AI.tldr: A scalable perception framework for robotic packing using low-resolution depth with NBV-driven reconstruction and per-object grasp evidence to decide next view and grasp.
AI.motivation: Address scalability and cost in robotic packing perception by leveraging affordable, low-resolution depth sensors and jointly optimizing sensing and manipulation.
AI.method: Compute Next Best View to minimize redundant views while preserving key geometry; update per-object stability based on grasp evidence; fuse reconstruction cues to drive both sensing (what to acquire next) and action (when to grasp); conduct ablation study of the utility function under low resolution; perform end-to-end evaluations across policies.
AI.result: Validation in two steps: (i) ablation study of the utility function under very low resolution, and (ii) full end-to-end evaluation across policies; demonstrates that low-resolution perception is a practical, scalable option for robotic packing and that NBV reduces view redundancy while preserving task-relevant geometry.
AI.conclusion: Low-resolution depth sensing is a viable option for scalable robotic packing. The NBV-guided reconstruction and grasp-evidence stability update enable an efficient perception-action loop, supporting deployment with affordable sensors and suggesting broader applicability to related manipulation tasks.

title: 4DStreamCtrl: Interactive Video Generation with Online 4D Control
summary: Generative video models now synthesize footage nearly indistinguishable from reality. Their promise as interactive tools hinges on fine-grained control of how objects and the camera move over time, yet each existing approach captures only part of this: camera-parameter methods steer the viewpoint but cannot move objects, 2D-trajectory methods act in the image plane and ignore depth and occlusion, and recent 3D methods add geometry but run only offline at a fixed length. In particular, none combines 3D-consistent control of both camera and objects with real-time, streaming generation. Here we show that camera motion, object trajectories, and depth can be unified into a single 3D point-track representation, from which one model performs joint camera and object control, depth editing, and motion transfer in a single forward pass. To learn this interface at scale, we mine in-the-wild video for 3D motion supervision, yielding OpenVidHD-Motion3D, and encode it with a lightweight Geometric Motion Head that plugs into a pretrained video diffusion model. Because this encoder is temporally separable, we distill the model into a causal streaming student that generates arbitrarily long video in four denoising steps at memory independent of length. This unified design surpasses prior camera-only, 2D, and offline-3D methods in motion-control precision while covering modalities they address only in isolation. 4DStreamCtrl runs at 20 FPS on a single high-end GPU for 480p video and stays temporally coherent over hundreds of frames, enabling, to our knowledge, interactive 4D-controllable streaming generation for the first time. More broadly, grounding generation in explicit 3D geometry with efficient causal inference points toward interactive world models with closed-loop spatiotemporal control, from controllable simulators to real-time visual imagination for embodied agents.

AI.tldr: Unified 3D point-track approach enabling real-time, 4D-controllable video generation; combines camera motion, object trajectories, and depth; introduces OpenVidHD-Motion3D supervision and Geometric Motion Head; streaming causal model 4DStreamCtrl achieving 20 FPS at 480p; claims to outperform prior methods in motion control and coherence.
AI.motivation: Enable interactive, controllable video synthesis that jointly handles camera and object motion with depth, enabling real-time, long-horizon generation.
AI.method: 3D point-track representation; OpenVidHD-Motion3D supervision from in-the-wild video; Geometric Motion Head plugged into pretrained diffusion model; temporally separable encoder; distillation to a causal streaming student; four denoising steps; streaming memory independent of length.
AI.result: Surpasses camera-only, 2D, offline-3D methods in motion-control precision; 20 FPS 480p, temporally coherent for hundreds of frames; first demonstration of interactive 4D-controllable streaming generation.
AI.conclusion: Grounding generation in explicit 3D geometry with efficient causal inference enables interactive world models and real-time embodied agent imagery; potential for controllable simulators and real-time visual imagination.

title: Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning
comment: 82 pages, 15 figures. Code, prompts, and evaluation data are available at https://github.com/paulrosu11/training-auditing-agents-public
summary: Alignment auditing of frontier models increasingly relies on LLM auditors to surface undesirable behaviors at scale, but current automated auditors can struggle with coherent investigation and audit realism. In this work, we improve LLM auditors with reinforcement learning. In our best training environment, the policy investigates target models that potentially possess hidden behaviors planted via their system prompt. An LLM judge, which knows whether the target has a hidden behavior, holistically compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation to determine the reward. With systematic ablations, we find that pairwise rewards yield more robust training compared to pointwise rewards, and that adding targets without planted behaviors helps maintain a low false positive rate. Training improves investigation quality against targets with planted behaviors, the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in unmodified production models, and audit realism, while false-positive rates stay below 1%. Furthermore, auditing capabilities generalize across scaffolds: performance on AuditBench's adversarially fine-tuned targets substantially improves [Sheshadri et al., 2026].

AI.tldr: RL-enhanced LLM auditors yield robust, realistic investigations with low false positives; pairwise rewards outperform pointwise, and incorporating non-planted targets improves calibration and generalization.
AI.motivation: To address scalability and realism gaps in automated auditors for frontier models; current methods struggle with coherent investigation and believable audits.
AI.method: Train an LLM-based policy to investigate target models that may harbor hidden behaviors; deploy an LLM judge that knows whether the target has a hidden behavior and compares the policy's investigation to a reference investigation to assign a reward; perform systematic ablations showing pairwise rewards are more robust; include targets without planted behaviors to reduce false positives; evaluate against targets with planted behaviors and production models; test cross-scaffold generalization with AuditBench and adversarially fine-tuned targets.
AI.result: Training improves the quality of investigations, increases the rate of concerning behaviors surfaced in planted targets and unmodified production models, and enhances audit realism; false-positive rate remains below 1%; results generalize across scaffolds, notably improving on AuditBench adversarial targets.
AI.conclusion: RL-based auditing with pairwise reward signals yields robust, realistic, and generalizable auditors for frontier models, with calibration benefits from including non-planted targets.

title: Learning Mixtures of Plackett-Luce Models for Multi-Objective Alignment
summary: We consider the problem of learning a mixture of $k$ Plackett-Luce models given multi-way ranking responses from annotators that may represent heterogeneous underlying preferences. This problem has many applications in AI alignment and preference optimization. Prior work has studied mixtures of Bradley-Terry models from pairwise comparisons. However, uncovering mixture models is theoretically unidentifiable when $k$ exceeds $m/2$, where $m$ is the length of a ranking. We propose an efficient implementation to address this limitation, which involves first augmenting the rankings to a larger size by generating new responses from a base language model, followed by a gradient-based estimation to reduce inference cost in the input embedding space. Based on this procedure, we then design an expectation-maximization algorithm with these two steps to fit a mixture of Plackett-Luce models, called MoPLEx. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify this approach. First, we show that the gradient-based approximation estimates true probabilities with less than 5% error on models with up to 34 billion parameters. Second, we show that MoPLEx improves clustering and ranking accuracy by an average of 43.7% and 15.2% over baselines using single ranking and mixtures of Bradley-Terry models, on preference optimization datasets. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MoPLEx for tackling multi-way rankings from heterogeneous preferences through measuring alignment between gradients.

AI.tldr: MoPLEx: an EM-based method to learn mixtures of Plackett-Luce models from multi-way rankings by augmenting data with synthetic responses from a base language model and using gradient-based estimation to reduce cost; shows high accuracy and substantial improvements over baselines in clustering and ranking on preference datasets.
AI.motivation: Address heterogeneity in preferences by modeling mixtures of Plackett-Luce rankings, while overcoming theoretical identifiability limits that occur when the number of components k exceeds m/2 for ranking length m; enable scalable learning from multi-way rankings.
AI.method: Augment rankings to larger size via synthetic responses generated by a base language model; apply an EM algorithm with two steps: gradient-based probability estimation in embedding space to reduce inference cost, followed by standard EM updates for mixture PL parameters, yielding MoPLEx.
AI.result: The gradient-based approximation estimates true probabilities with <5% error for models up to 34B parameters. MoPLEx achieves average improvements of 43.7% in clustering accuracy and 15.2% in ranking accuracy over baselines (single-ranking methods and mixtures of Bradley-Terry models) on preference optimization datasets.
AI.conclusion: MoPLEx provides an effective and scalable pipeline for learning mixtures of Plackett-Luce models from heterogeneous, multi-way rankings, combining data augmentation with gradient-based inference to overcome identifiability constraints and achieve substantial performance gains.

title: A Statistical Audit of Physical AI Benchmark Redundancy
summary: Physical AI models are evaluated on suites of benchmarks that differ across model reports, leaving the model-by-benchmark matrix sparse and the relationship between benchmarks unmeasured. We construct a matrix of 51 models on 12 physical AI benchmarks, selected from a registry of 51 benchmarks and 152 models by reporting density, combining scores from model cards and benchmark papers with our own evaluation runs under each benchmark's official protocol. We measure how much information the benchmarks share and show quantitative evidence of Redundancy. Redundancy affects reported rankings: collapsing the two substitute pairs into single columns moves 22 of 51 models by three or more places under an equally weighted average. We then select benchmarks greedily under a utility combining score dispersion with variance not explained by the already-selected set, and obtain a four-benchmark subset retaining 78.5\% of the utility of all 12, on which we fit a Bradley--Terry ranking. The procedure requires only benchmark-level scores with sufficient overlap and is not specific to physical AI.

AI.tldr: A 51x12 matrix of physical AI model-benchmark performance reveals benchmark redundancy; collapsing substitute pairs shifts rankings; a four-benchmark subset retains 78.5% of overall utility; rankings on this subset via Bradley-Terry, method generalizable beyond physical AI.
AI.motivation: Benchmark suites are uneven and overlapping, leaving sparse model-by-benchmark matrices and unclear inter-benchmark relationships. Quantify redundancy, streamline benchmarking, and produce robust rankings.
AI.method: Assemble matrix from 51 benchmarks and 152 models; integrate scores from model cards, benchmark papers, and new evaluations under official protocols; quantify information overlap among benchmarks; demonstrate ranking sensitivity to benchmark redundancy; greedily select a minimal benchmark subset by a utility function (score dispersion plus unexplained variance); apply Bradley-Terry to rank models on the subset.
AI.result: Found measurable redundancy; collapsing two substitute columns changes 22/51 models by ≥3 positions; four-benchmark subset retains 78.5% of full utility; provides stable Bradley-Terry ranking on the subset.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields a benchmark-level, data-driven method for evaluating models that is not tied to physical AI and can generalize to other domains; enables more efficient and robust benchmarking.

title: DeCO: Discriminative Evidence Composition for Fine-Grained Dataset Distillation
summary: Dataset distillation compresses a large training set into a compact synthetic set while preserving its downstream utility. However, existing methods primarily preserve global image statistics and may overlook the localized evidence essential for fine-grained visual classification (FGVC), such as object parts, subtle textures, and region-specific structures. We formulate fine-grained dataset distillation as budgeted discriminative-evidence preservation and propose Discriminative Evidence Composition (DeCO). DeCO uses attention rollout from a pretrained TransFG teacher to identify informative patches, applies spatial diversification to reduce redundant coverage, and organizes the resulting regions into class-wise evidence banks. Multiple same-class regions are then packed into compact grid-composed images. The teacher is used only for dataset construction, whereas downstream students are trained with standard hard-label supervision without teacher logits. Experiments on CUB-200-2011, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars show that DeCO consistently outperforms representative coreset and dataset-distillation baselines under different IPC budgets.

AI.tldr: DeCO is a dataset distillation method for fine-grained visual classification that selects discriminative patches via attention rollout from a TransFG teacher, diversifies spatial coverage, and bundles regions into class-wise grid images; trained with hard labels, it outperforms baselines under various IPC budgets.
AI.motivation: FGVC heavily relies on localized evidence (parts, textures, regions). Existing distillation methods prioritize global statistics and may miss critical discriminative cues, necessitating a budgeted approach that preserves local evidence.
AI.method: Uses a pretrained TransFG teacher to perform attention rollout and identify informative patches. Applies spatial diversification to reduce redundancy, organizes regions into class-wise evidence banks, and packs multiple same-class patches into grid-composed images. The teacher is used solely for dataset construction; downstream students are trained with standard hard-label supervision.
AI.result: Across CUB-200-2011, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars, DeCO consistently outperforms representative coreset and dataset-distillation baselines under different IPC budgets.
AI.conclusion: DeCO effectively preserves discriminative evidence for FGVC in distilled datasets, enabling improved downstream performance without relying on teacher logits.

title: PonsRAG: A Pons-Inspired RAG Bridging Cognitive Islands for Coordinated Long Narrative Reasoning
summary: Long Narrative Reasoning is an essential capability for processing and reasoning over complex narratives. While retrieval-augmented generation provides a promising framework, existing methods still face two critical challenges: cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection. To address these issues, we propose PonsRAG, a coordinated RAG framework inspired by the biological pons. PonsRAG consists of two key components: Triple-Layer Indexing, which organizes documents into a connected knowledge structure to bridge cognitive islands, and Coordinated Reasoning, which retrieves evidence across distinct layers and integrates cross-layer information into a unified context. We evaluate PonsRAG on four long-context narrative benchmarks, and experimental results show that it outperforms the strongest baseline, achieving a 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.

AI.tldr: PonsRAG introduces a coordinated RAG framework with Triple-Layer Indexing and Coordinated Reasoning to bridge cognitive islands and integrate cross-layer evidence in long-context narratives, achieving 11.56% relative improvement on four multi-choice benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To overcome cognitive islanding and cross-layer evidence disconnection that hinder retrieval-augmented generation for long narratives.
AI.method: Propose PonsRAG, consisting of Triple-Layer Indexing to connect documents into a cohesive knowledge structure and Coordinated Reasoning to fetch and fuse evidence across multiple layers into a unified context.
AI.result: PonsRAG outperforms the strongest baseline on four long-context narrative benchmarks, achieving a 11.56% relative improvement in average accuracy on multi-choice tasks.
AI.conclusion: Coordinated cross-layer evidence retrieval and a connected indexing structure effectively mitigate cognitive fragmentation in long-context narrative reasoning, enhancing retrieval-augmented generation performance.

title: LibriBrain100: One Hundred Hours of Broad and Deep MEG Data for Neural Speech Decoding at Scale
comment: 10 content pages + 22 pages for references and appendices (in total: 32 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables)
summary: We introduce LibriBrain100, a large-scale MEG dataset for speech decoding designed from the ground up for reproducible, standardised evaluation. LibriBrain100 more than doubles the size of the original LibriBrain release, resulting in over 100 hours of high-quality MEG acquired while subjects listened to naturalistic continuous speech. With $\sim$80 hours from a single subject, LibriBrain100 sets a new record for deep, within-subject neural data (8$\times$ more than the next comparable dataset and roughly 80$\times$ more than other datasets). To demonstrate the payoff of this depth-first design, we evaluate on a word-classification benchmark---an increasingly well-established stepping stone towards the open challenge of noninvasive brain-to-text decoding. Using an existing decoding model, we achieve state-of-the-art performance---validating both the quality of the recordings and the value of within-subject data at scale. Because collecting 80 hours of data per user is impractical for real-world applications, we also collected $\sim$40 minutes of additional data from each of 32 subjects. Using the same word-classification benchmark, we demonstrate the value of broad multi-subject data: supervised finetuning of a pre-trained model can substantially compensate for limited per-subject data. We provide standard train, validation, and test splits, all reproducible through an open-sourced Python library that supports easy downloading, optional preprocessing, and data loading for common deep learning frameworks. In addition, the dataset and evaluation infrastructure are being released alongside an open machine-learning competition with a public leaderboard for standardised benchmarking. Ultimately, our hope is that LibriBrain100 will accelerate progress towards practical non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, capable of restoring communication to people living with severe paralysis.

AI.tldr: LibriBrain100 scales MEG-based speech decoding to 100+ hours, enabling reproducible benchmarking; achieves state-of-the-art word-classification; demonstrates benefits of fine-tuning with multi-subject data; released with open library and leaderboard; aims to advance noninvasive brain-computer interface communication.
AI.motivation: The field lacks large, standardized MEG datasets for reproducible benchmarking in speech decoding and brain-to-text efforts; existing datasets are shallow per-subject and hinder scalable evaluation.
AI.method: Constructed LibriBrain100 with ~100 hours MEG from naturalistic speech; ~80 hours from one subject; ~40 minutes from 32 subjects; provides train/val/test splits, open Python data-loading library, preprocessing; uses an existing decoding model for evaluation on a word-classification task; includes an open ML competition with a public leaderboard.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on word-classification in within-subject data; demonstrates that broad multi-subject data and supervised fine-tuning can compensate for limited per-subject data; dataset design supports reproducible benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: LibriBrain100 enables scalable, reproducible evaluation for noninvasive brain-computer interfaces and has potential to accelerate progress toward practical brain-to-text decoding; released with open infrastructure and leaderboard to standardize benchmarking.

title: DESCENT: Directed Edge Scene Encoding for Airport Surface Movement Prediction
summary: Advanced automation is a key technology for enhancing the safety of ground operations amidst the increasing density of commercial air traffic. While motion forecasting is a well-studied task in autonomous driving, its application to airport surface movements remains underexplored. To enable efficient and accurate prediction in this domain, we propose DESCENT, a transformer-based architecture designed to handle heterogeneous dynamics and strict topological constraints. Our approach features a Potential Reachable Set (PRS) context sampling mechanism that adaptively collects airfield environment context across diverse operational phases. Combined with a detection transformer-based decoder, DESCENT generates accurate trajectory forecasts. Extensive evaluations on the Amelia-10 benchmark demonstrate significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. These gains are especially pronounced in safety-critical scenarios, where our domain-aware sampling provides critical long-horizon context necessary for safe navigation.

AI.tldr: DESCENT is a transformer-based airport surface trajectory forecaster using a Potential Reachable Set (PRS) context sampling with a detection-transformer decoder, achieving state-of-the-art results on the Amelia-10 benchmark, especially in long-horizon safety-critical scenarios.
AI.motivation: Ground operations face dense airfield traffic and strict topological constraints; current autonomous-driving motion forecasting methods do not directly address airport-specific dynamics, necessitating domain-aware context collection and long-horizon safe predictions.
AI.method: DESCENT employs a transformer-based architecture with a PRS context sampling mechanism that adaptively gathers airfield context across operational phases, coupled with a detection-transformer-based decoder to forecast trajectories under heterogeneous dynamics and topological constraints.
AI.result: On Amelia-10, DESCENT achieves significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with pronounced gains in safety-critical scenarios due to the domain-aware long-horizon context.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that domain-specific context sampling (PRS) and a detection-transformer decoder can substantially improve accurate, safe trajectory forecasting for airport surface movements, validated by strong Amelia-10 results.

title: Gaussian Splatting Underwater: A Controlled Cross-Regime Study
summary: The underwater environment is challenging for 3D reconstruction, because particles suspended in the water scatter and diffuse light, turbidity varies, absorption depends on wavelength, and illumination is rarely uniform. Methods based on Gaussian splatting have generally been developed for conditions that allow good image quality, and have primarily been tested on relatively shallow water. This paper examines how well Gaussian splatting performs across publicly available underwater datasets representing different degrees of turbidity, loss of illumination, and colour attenuation, together with an industrial survey. Five systems with public code are run under one protocol, with shared poses, initialisation, budget, and evaluator, to establish their relative advantages, disadvantages, and limitations. What these methods can do turns out to depend more on the setup than on the architecture. Water clarity binds upstream of rendering, since structure-from-motion registers 99.5 \% of frames in clear water and 0.0 \% at 12 NTU. Illumination geometry decides whether a medium model helps at all: under an artificial light that moves with the camera, medium-blind splatting beats both medium-aware systems. On the survey the benchmark's photometric leader comes last, beaten on geometry by a restoration pre-pass in front of vanilla 3DGS---and none of it is visible in the scores the field reports. Scene builds, per-run configurations, and evaluation code are released at https://github.com/olayasturias/uw3dgs

AI.tldr: Gaussian splatting for underwater 3D reconstruction is highly setup-dependent; dataset turbidity and illumination dominate performance; medium models help only under certain lighting, and a moving-cam light can negate their benefit; broad cross-dataset benchmarking reveals limited visible gains in real-field scores. Code and data are released.
AI.motivation: Underwater imaging suffers from scattering, turbidity, wavelength-dependent absorption, and nonuniform illumination. Gaussian splatting methods usually assume good image quality and shallow water; there is a need for systematic evaluation across diverse underwater conditions to understand their limits and guide method design.
AI.method: Five publicly available Gaussian-splatting pipelines (with public code) were run under a unified protocol across multiple underwater datasets representing different turbidity and illumination conditions, plus an industrial survey. Shared poses, initialization, budget, and evaluator enable fair comparison. The study analyzes the influence of water clarity (structure-from-motion performance) and illumination geometry on the effectiveness of medium models, and compares a medium-aware approach to a medium-blind baseline, including a restoration pre-pass against vanilla 3DGS. The authors release scene builds, per-run configurations, and evaluation code.
AI.result: Water clarity governs upstream reconstruction success: SfM registered 99.5% of frames in clear water but 0% at 12 NTU. Illumination geometry dictates the utility of medium models: with a camera-linked moving light, a medium-blind splatting outperforms both medium-aware variants. On the survey, the photometric leader loses to a geometry-focused restoration pre-pass ahead of vanilla 3DGS, and none of the methods are visible in field scores.
AI.conclusion: The performance of Gaussian splatting under water is driven more by acquisition/setup conditions than network or representation architecture. Key factors are water clarity before rendering and the illumination scheme. The results highlight the need for standardized, diverse benchmarks and suggest that medium-aware models offer limited gains unless illumination is favorable. The code and configurations are publicly released to support reproducibility.

title: CaSKG: Counterfactual-Causal Skill Graphs for Scalable Agent Skill Retrieval
summary: Reusable skill libraries allow large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedural knowledge across tasks, but they also turn memory access into a challenging retrieval problem. Full-library prompting preserves coverage at high context cost, vector retrieval returns compact neighborhoods but treats skills as independent text, and graph-based retrieval can recover workflow context only when the edges that carry relevance are reliable. We propose CaSKG, a counterfactual-causal skill graph framework that calibrates procedural relations before retrieval. CaSKG first builds a high-recall directed candidate graph from semantic, lexical, input/output, and structural evidence, with repair evidence and an optional LLM judge further refining candidate scores. It then applies direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes that remove, substitute, and reorder skill pairs, aggregates the evidence with Bayesian smoothing, and publishes a state-filtered weighted graph for task-conditioned expansion. The graph is constructed offline and used without changing the downstream agent policy or task interface. Across six LLM backbones on ALFWorld ID-140 and ScienceWorld U211, CaSKG achieves the highest task score in all twelve combinations of model and benchmark. Relative to Graph-of-Skills (GoS), it improves the six-model macro-average ScienceWorld score from 72.62 to 80.50 and ALFWorld success from 80.01\% to 86.79\%, while reducing mean environment steps on both benchmarks. Qualitative and ablation analyses further show that calibrated edges help retrieval preserve prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and final completion steps. These results position edge-confidence calibration as an effective route to compact and executable skill retrieval at scale\footnote{Code is available at: https://github.com/ZhiyuanLi218/Caskg }.

AI.tldr: CaSKG calibrates procedural edges in a skill graph via counterfactual probes to improve retrieval and task performance across multiple LLM backbones and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reusable skill libraries for LLM agents face retrieval challenges: preserving coverage vs efficiency; edges between skills may be unreliable; need a calibrated, compact, executable retrieval mechanism.
AI.method: Construct a high-recall directed candidate graph from semantic, lexical, input/output, and structural cues; optionally refine with an LLM judge; apply direction-conditioned textual counterfactual probes to remove, substitute, and reorder skill pairs; aggregate evidence with Bayesian smoothing; publish a state-filtered weighted graph for task-conditioned expansion; offline construction without changing downstream policies or interfaces.
AI.result: CaSKG achieves the highest task score in all twelve combinations of six LLM backbones and two benchmarks (ALFWorld ID-140, ScienceWorld U211); ScienceWorld macro-average improves from 72.62 to 80.50; ALFWorld success improves from 80.01% to 86.79%; mean environment steps reduced on both benchmarks; qualitative and ablation analyses indicate calibrated edges preserve prerequisites, state-changing actions, verification routines, and final completion steps; code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Edge-confidence calibration is an effective strategy for compact, executable skill retrieval at scale.

title: Representing MAX functions using two-hidden-layer ReLU networks
summary:
We study exact representations of $\mathrm{MAX}_N(x)=\max{x_1,\ldots,x_N}$ using two-hidden-layer ReLU neural networks. This problem has been studied in recent years in an attempt to characterize the exact number of hidden layers required to represent continuous piecewise linear functions. The best lower bound is 2, while the current upper bound is logarithmic in $N$. It remains completely open if the right answer is a constant number of hidden layers (possibly even 2!) or not. In fact, a recent breakthrough was the representation of $\mathrm{MAX}_5$ as a two-hidden-layer ReLU function obtained in [Bakaev et al., 2026], and the case of $\mathrm{MAX}_N$ was stated as open for $N\geq 6$ in that paper.
  Using a careful computer assisted search, we obtain two-hidden-layer ReLU representations of $\mathrm{MAX}_5, \mathrm{MAX}_6, \mathrm{MAX}_7$, and $\mathrm{MAX}_8$. We obtain these by considering rational linear combinations of terms of the form $\max\{\sum_{r=1}^{s}\max(x_{a_r},x_{b_r}),\sum_{r=1}^{s}\max(x_{c_r},x_{d_r})\}$, where $a_r,b_r,c_r,d_r\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Each inner maximum of two coordinates can be computed in a first hidden layer, and the outer maximum of the two side-sums can be computed in a second hidden layer. Consequently, every finite linear combination of these terms has a two-hidden-layer ReLU realization. An identity for $\mathrm{MAX}_N$ in this form therefore gives an exact two-hidden-layer ReLU representation of $\mathrm{MAX}_N$.
  Very recently, two-hidden-layer representations of $\mathrm{MAX}_N$ of the above form were obtained for all $N\leq 10$ in [Ruess et al., 2026]. Our representations are different and were developed independently. While our techniques share most of the high-level ideas presented in [Ruess et al., 2026], there are also some minor differences which may be of interest for future research on this problem.

AI.tldr: Two-hidden-layer ReLU representations of MAX_N for N=5..8 via a constructive approach using inner max terms, aligned with recent independent results.
AI.motivation: Assess the depth needed to exactly represent MAX_N with ReLU networks and advance the open question of whether two hidden layers suffice for all N; provide explicit small-N constructions.
AI.method: Represent MAX_N as a rational linear combination of terms of the form max{ sum_r max(x_{a_r}, x_{b_r}), sum_r max(x_{c_r}, x_{d_r}) }. Compute each inner max in the first layer and the outer max in the second layer; use computer-assisted search to find coefficients and index selections that yield MAX_N exactly for N=5..8; compare with and differ from recent independent formulations.
AI.result: Explicit two-hidden-layer representations for MAX_5, MAX_6, MAX_7, MAX_8 are obtained; these are independent from, yet related to, Ruess et al. (2026), which gives two-hidden-layer representations for all N≤10.
AI.conclusion: Provides concrete evidence that two-hidden-layer realizations exist for small N; supports the broader aim of a constant-depth representation for MAX_N and informs future work on general N and alternative constructions, including potential unification with independently discovered methods.

title: Phantom Navigator: Stealthy and Precise Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Redirection with Real-Time Tracking and GPS Spoofing
summary: Redirecting unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) from their intended mission trajectories has been an active area of research. However, existing UAV redirection attacks lack reliability, precision, and covertness for a targeted diversion. They primarily rely on physical capture, communication hijacking, or sensor spoofing. Yet, physical interception is costly, offers only a single opportunity for success, and poses a high risk of collateral damage; network-based attacks demand deep technical expertise and access to encrypted communication channels; and sensor spoofing techniques typically fall short in achieving the accuracy and robustness required to steer a UAV toward a specified target. Consequently, we propose Phantom Navigator, a UAV redirection attack to mislead drones to a designated spoofing target, covertly and precisely. Our approach combines offline pre-redirection reachability analysis, which provides high-fidelity estimates of achievable redirect ranges, with an online closed-loop, stealthy execution layer that ensures successful redirection in practice. Based on this approach, we build a physical attack platform equipped with a LiDAR--camera detection, tracking, and spoofing stack that performs real-time identification, pose estimation, and computation of targeted spoofing signals to covertly and accurately redirect victim UAVs to a designated location. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our redirection methodology and the attack implementation in real-world case studies.

AI.tldr: A covert, precise UAV redirection attack (Phantom Navigator) that combines offline reachability analysis with an online stealthy control layer and a LiDAR-camera spoofing stack to redirect victim drones to a designated spoofing target; demonstrated in real-world cases.
AI.motivation: Limitations of existing UAV redirection methods (physical interception, network hijacking, sensor spoofing) motivate a reliable, precise, covert alternative.
AI.method: Offline pre-redirection reachability analysis to estimate achievable redirect ranges; online closed-loop stealthy execution; a physical platform with LiDAR-camera detection, tracking, spoofing; real-time identification, pose estimation, and computation of spoofing signals; real-time feedback to guide the UAV.
AI.result: Real-world demonstrations show covert and accurate redirection toward a designated location, validating the approach.
AI.conclusion: Phantom Navigator advances UAV redirection by combining precomputed reachability with stealthy control; highlights security risks and the need for countermeasures against such covert attacks.

title: Semi-Supervised Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Image Classification
summary: Vision-language models like CLIP have shown sig- nificant potential in handling natural images, yet their perfor- mance is often limited by the distinct characteristics of satellite imagery. While parameter-efficient adaptation techniques exist, their efficacy is frequently limited by the scarcity of annotated samples. In this letter, we propose Self-Evolutionary CLIP (SE- CLIP), a semi-supervised framework designed for recursive label mining in scene classification. The approach follows a dual-phase pipeline, where an initial warm-up on a few annotated seeds is followed by a recursive discovery phase that iteratively identifies high-confidence samples from unlabeled pools. To maintain the integrity of the evolving support set, we employ a class-balanced selection strategy that prevents the model from being dominated by easily learned categories. Results on the UCM and NWPU benchmarks indicate that SE-CLIP significantly outperforms existing semi-supervised approaches. The framework provides a viable solution for adapting VLMs to the remote sensing domain with minimal human intervention.

AI.tldr: SE-CLIP is a semi-supervised framework for satellite image scene classification that iteratively mines labels from unlabeled data after a seed-based warm-up, using class-balanced selection to avoid easy-category dominance, and achieves state-of-the-art results on UCM and NWPU with minimal supervision.
AI.motivation: CLIP-like vision-language models struggle on satellite imagery due to domain shift and scarce labeled data; existing parameter-efficient adaptations are data-hungry. A semi-supervised, self-evolving approach can leverage unlabeled data to adapt VLMs to remote sensing with limited annotation.
AI.method: A dual-phase pipeline: (1) warm-up with a small annotated seed set to establish an initial model; (2) recursive discovery phase that mines high-confidence samples from an unlabeled pool. A class-balanced selection strategy maintains a diverse, robust support set to prevent dominance by easily learned categories.
AI.result: On the UCM and NWPU remote-sensing benchmarks, SE-CLIP significantly outperforms existing semi-supervised methods.
AI.conclusion: SE-CLIP provides a viable, low-human-intervention pathway for adapting vision-language models to the remote sensing domain, improving scene classification with minimal labeled data.

title: Agentic Game Development as a Verifiable Trajectory Data Engine for Scaling World Models
summary: A common strategy for scaling world models is to train on more crawled video with more compute. We argue that this strategy is inefficient: scaling world models also requires a recursive data engine that offers grounded reward signals. The success of code agents illustrates why this matters. As code is executable, compilers and runtimes can provide high-quality rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training of LLMs. By contrast, spatial generation still relies largely on fuzzy proxies such as CLIP scores. These signals are fuzzy and biased, making them hard to support RL post-training. Compared with these, game development provides a missing reward environment for spatial world models. A scene encoded by a game engine is an executable world specification: the engine can efficiently check collision, physics, navigability and bounded playability, while the developer provides the global verification signal by judging whether the scene should be accepted. Game development also provides real-world long-horizon trajectory data for RL post-training. We therefore propose Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV), a post-training paradigm that combines dense engine signals with implicit human acceptance feedback from the development process.

AI.tldr: Proposes RLHEV, a post-training paradigm using executable game-engine environments and human verification signals to supply grounded, long-horizon rewards for spatial world models, addressing inefficiencies in scaling with crawled video and compute.
AI.motivation: Current spatial generation relies on fuzzy proxies (e.g., CLIP) and lacks grounded, long-horizon reward signals. Code agents demonstrate the value of executable reward pipelines via compilers/runtimes. Game development provides executable world specifications and real-world trajectory data, enabling more reliable post-training signals.
AI.method: Introduce Reinforcement Learning with Human-Engine Verification (RLHEV) as a post-training paradigm that combines dense engine signals (collision, physics, navigability, bounded playability) with implicit human acceptance feedback from the development process, leveraging game engines as both world specification and data source.
AI.result: Conceptual framework and design proposal. No empirical results are presented; claims potential improvements in data efficiency, alignment, and robustness through executable signals and human-in-the-loop verification.
AI.conclusion: RLHEV offers a path to more data-efficient post-training of spatial world models by using game-engine executable environments and human-in-the-loop acceptance signals, addressing shortcomings of fuzzy proxies and the limitations of purely passive data collection.

title: Trust the Mass: Forced Weights in KV-Cache Eviction
summary: Every deployed sparse-attention or KV-cache-eviction rule keeps a subset of the keys, discards the rest, and renormalizes the attention weights over the kept set. Enumerating the exact best subset under that constraint on $168{,}192$ attention rows from five models shows that keeping the largest weights is already near-optimal, since the best subset closes only a median $2$ to $5\%$ of the remaining gap to full attention. If selection closes this little, published margins between eviction methods must come from elsewhere, so we measure the bytes each method holds. In the shared evaluation pipeline, the strongest query-agnostic methods hold the full cache because their per-head selections are stored as masks, and only ragged per-head storage frees that memory. Enforcing a nominal budget on one fixed selection costs $14$ to $62$ benchmark points. We trace an $87.6$-point retrieval margin to rankings computed while the question is visible. ContourKV, a training-free allocator built from the dropped-mass statistic, wins $93$ of $160$ paired comparisons against that state of the art and loses $22$ at the byte count of the budget-enforcing baselines, and it ties the strongest of them.

AI.tldr: Sparse attention with key/selection: keeping the largest weights is near-optimal; margins among eviction methods mainly come from storage costs rather than selection quality. ContourKV, a training-free allocator based on dropped mass, achieves strong performance across pairwise comparisons, indicating allocation strategy can dominate when budgets are enforced.
AI.motivation: Assess what truly drives performance in sparse-attention and KV-cache eviction: the quality of the selected key subset vs. the storage/encoding costs of that selection.
AI.method: Exact enumeration over 168,192 attention rows from five models to identify the best subset under eviction constraints; compare per-head masks (binary storage) vs. ragged and full caches; measure impact of enforcing fixed-budget selections on retrieval accuracy; perform paired comparisons against state-of-the-art eviction methods.
AI.result: The best subset criterion (largest weights) closes a median of 2–5% of the remaining gap to full attention, suggesting near-optimality of simple weight-based subset selection. Differences between eviction methods largely vanish once storage costs are accounted for; strongest query-agnostic methods keep full caches via masks, while per-head selection storage dominates memory usage. Enforcing a budget costs 14–62 benchmark points. An 87.6-point retrieval margin is traced to rankings when the question is visible. ContourKV wins 93 of 160 paired comparisons against the state of the art and loses 22 at the byte-count of budget-enforcing baselines, tying the strongest ahí.
AI.conclusion: Selection quality (keeping the largest weights) provides near-optimal performance; actual margins across eviction methods are driven by how storage/masking is implemented. ContourKV, built from the dropped-mass statistic and training-free, offers competitive performance, often outperforming competing eviction schemes while respecting budget constraints. Overall, allocation strategy and storage efficiency are the primary levers for sparse-attention performance.

title: When Obstacles Bend: Modeling Vegetation Deformation in the context of Field Robotics
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Autonomous robots operating in natural environments must often interact with vegetation rather than simply avoid it. In this context, traversability is typically defined from the robot's perspective, by measuring how a specific platform responds when moving through the environment. While practical, this viewpoint entangles the assessment of the environment with the robot's own dynamics, making the resulting characterization difficult to transfer across different platforms. More importantly, it does not directly reflect the properties of the vegetation itself, which are the true source of interaction and potential damage in applications such as agriculture and environmental monitoring. To address this limitation, we propose to characterize vegetation through its intrinsic mechanical properties, independently of any specific robot. By combining deformation measurements with contact force data, we estimate the underlying mechanical parameters and reconstruct the vegetation's response to interaction. This enables vegetation-aware navigation based on intrinsic environmental properties rather than platform-dependent metrics.

AI.tldr: Characterize vegetation via intrinsic mechanical properties using deformation and contact-force data to enable platform-independent, vegetation-aware navigation.
AI.motivation: Current traversability metrics tie environment assessment to the robot's dynamics, hindering transferability and failing to capture vegetation properties that drive interaction and damage; a robot-agnostic vegetation model is needed.
AI.method: Integrate deformation measurements with contact force data to infer vegetation mechanical parameters and reconstruct its response to interaction, yielding a plant-vehicle interaction model independent of the robot platform.
AI.result: Ability to estimate intrinsic vegetation parameters and predict response, enabling navigation decisions based on vegetation properties rather than robot-specific performance.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling environment properties from robot dynamics improves transferability of vegetation interactions for tasks like agriculture and environmental monitoring.

title: SMART: MLLM-guided Temporal Alignment for Unifying Sign Language Recognition and Spotting
summary: Continuous sign language recognition (CSLR) aims to recognize gloss sequences from unsegmented sign videos under weak sequence-level supervision. However, existing methods rely on sentence-level gloss annotations, providing limited temporal and semantic guidance for fine-grained representation learning. Conventional video-text alignment also requires large batch sizes, making it inefficient for memory-intensive sign language video training. In this work, we propose SMART, an MLLM-guided temporal alignment framework for joint sign recognition and spotting. SMART uses MLLMgenerated motion descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues and performs stable videotext alignment under small-batch training. To improve temporal representation learning, we introduce a Multi-Scale Temporal Adapter that models temporal interactions during transformer encoding. For dense temporal localization, SMART incorporates CSFormer, a CSLR-guided spotting module that injects recognition-derived gloss evidence into a boundary-aware spotting network. This unified framework enables CSLR features to benefit spotting, while spotting supervision complements weak CTC-based recognition. Experiments on four sign language benchmarks, including PHOENIX14-T, CSL-Daily, Large-scale KSL, and Disaster and Safety KSL datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of SMART across both recognition and spotting tasks.

AI.tldr: A unified CSLR and spotting framework (SMART) guided by multimodal LLMs, enabling stable small-batch video-text alignment and enhanced temporal modeling via a Multi-Scale Temporal Adapter and a CSLR-guided spotting module, achieving strong recognition and localization across multiple sign language benchmarks.
AI.motivation: CSLR suffers from weak supervision (relying on sentence-level gloss annotations) and inefficient large-batch video-text alignment. There is a need for data-efficient, temporally precise models that can jointly address recognition and dense temporal localization in sign languages.
AI.method: SMART utilizes MLLM-generated motion descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues for stable video-text alignment with small batches. It introduces a Multi-Scale Temporal Adapter to capture temporal interactions during transformer encoding. For dense localization, CSFormer injects recognition-derived gloss evidence into a boundary-aware spotting network, enabling a unified framework where recognition helps spotting and spotting supervision complements CTC-based recognition.
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmark datasets (PHOENIX14-T, CSL-Daily, Large-scale KSL, Disaster and Safety KSL) demonstrate improved performance for both CSLR recognition and dense spotting tasks, validating the effectiveness of SMART across both objectives.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging MLLM-guided semantics and novel temporal modeling, SMART offers a data-efficient, unified approach to CSLR and spotting that improves temporal representation learning and dense localization in sign-language video analysis.

title: Using profiles of cognitive capability to assess AI suitability for workplace tasks
summary: Organisations deploying AI face a scoping problem: which tasks can be automated, which should remain with humans, and which are best shared between the two. Aggregate benchmark scores provide little insight into where systems will succeed or fail in practice, while human judgements of model capabilities quickly become outdated. We introduce a pipeline that profiles agents and tasks using a shared set of core cognitive capabilities. Cognitive capability profiling infers an agent's capabilities from performance on a benchmark battery annotated for the cognitive demands of each item. Task requirements weighting elicits from domain experts the relative importance of these same capabilities for their work. As both use a common set of cognitive dimensions, they can be updated independently as models and roles change, and combined to estimate AI suitability at the level of a domain, organisation, role, or individual duty. We validate capability recovery on synthetic agents, profile six AI systems, and elicit task requirements from 410 employees across six occupational domains. AI systems differed more across cognitive dimensions than across model families, while workplace activities converged on a shared cognitive core. The resulting scores provide a comparative scoping tool for identifying promising candidates for piloting and areas where current systems are unlikely to be well suited. We discuss extending the framework to profile human workers alongside AI systems, moving from AI suitability towards human-machine task allocation.

AI.tldr: A framework couples cognitive capability profiling of agents with task requirements weighting to predict AI suitability for work, enabling independent updates to model capabilities and task demands and enabling domain-level scoping and human–machine task allocation.
AI.motivation: Aggregate benchmark scores poorly predict real-world performance and human judgments quickly become outdated; there is a need for a scalable, updateable method to match AI capabilities to job tasks.
AI.method: Develop a pipeline that (1) profiles agents with a benchmark battery annotated for cognitive demands to obtain cognitive capability scores, (2) elicits task requirements from domain experts for the same cognitive dimensions, (3) combines both on a common cognitive-dimension space to estimate AI suitability at domain/role/individual levels; (4) validate capability recovery on synthetic agents, profile six AI systems, and collect task requirements from 410 employees across six domains.
AI.result: AI systems vary more across cognitive dimensions than by model family; workplace activities converge on a shared cognitive core; the produced scores serve as a scoping tool to identify promising pilots and gaps; framework can be extended to profile human workers alongside AI for human–machine task allocation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed cognitive capability profiling framework enables independent, updateable assessment of AI suitability for tasks and supports move toward human–machine collaboration, with validated recovery, cross-domain applicability, and potential extension to include human workers.

title: Output Dilution: Redundant but Fragile Representations in MoE Models
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Code and outputs at https://github.com/deepsteer/deepsteer
summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models appear to encode moral content as robustly as dense models, yet prove far more fragile in their encoding. In OLMoE-1B-7B, linear probes recover moral valence from nearly every expert-layer combination, with mean peak-layer accuracy above 90%. But these representations collapse under levels of activation noise that a dense model of matched size easily tolerates, with a 4.2-fold difference in robustness.
  We trace this to output dilution. Because the MoE block averages across active experts before contributing to the residual stream, the feedforward signal reaching downstream layers is nearly two orders of magnitude smaller than in a dense MLP. Moral information, our interest, survives aggregation intact but at a scale trivially overwhelmed by perturbation. Routing itself remains stable under noise while the vulnerability originates entirely in the diluted aggregate.
  Checkpoint trajectories confirm this is architectural, not learned. Experts never specialize and accuracy saturates within the first few thousand steps. In sparse architectures, redundant encoding does not imply robust encoding.

AI.tldr: Mixture-of-Experts encode moral content like dense models but are fragile to activation noise due to strong output dilution; no evidence that sparse routing affords robustness—experts do not specialize and the architectural design reduces downstream signal to a scale easily perturbed.
AI.motivation: Understand how MoE architectures encode moral content, and why their representations may be fragile compared to dense models; assess whether sparsity offers robustness.
AI.method: Probe linear classifiers of moral valence across multiple expert-layer combinations in OLMoE-1B-7B, test robustness to activation noise, analyze aggregation effect (averaging across active experts) on downstream signal, examine training trajectories for specialization, compare with dense MLP.
AI.result: Moral valence is recoverable across many expert-layer combinations with peak accuracy >90%, but robustness under activation noise collapses, showing a 4.2x disadvantage versus dense models. The MF (feedforward) signal reaching downstream layers is diluted by nearly two orders of magnitude due to aggregation across experts; moral information survives but at a greatly reduced scale that is vulnerable to perturbation. Routing remains stable; the vulnerability originates in the diluted aggregate, not the routing. Checkpoint trajectories indicate architectural origin (not learned): experts never specialize and accuracy saturates early; redundant sparse encoding does not imply robust encoding.
AI.conclusion: The fragility of moral representations in MoE is an architectural consequence of output dilution from expert aggregation. Sparse routing alone does not guarantee robust encoding; addressing signal dilution or maintaining signal scale is necessary for robust moral content encoding in MoE architectures.

title: $R^3$: Training Robots to Reason in Natural Language via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reasoning in language allows foundation models to spend more test-time compute on hard problems, such as those requiring decomposition, constraint tracking, and prediction of future consequences. Whether this mechanism can improve robotic manipulation remains unclear, where long-horizon tasks require tracking partial progress, reasoning about object relations, recovering from mistakes, and steering noisy low-level policies. In this paper, we study whether VLMs can be trained to reason directly in natural language to guide low-level manipulation policies. We introduce $R^3$, a simple post-training recipe that turns off-the-shelf VLMs into robotic reasoners: it first mid-trains a VLM on expert-generated reasoning traces to initialize the desired reasoning style, then improves the reasoner with single-step rubric-based RL from offline action data. Unlike prior robotic reasoning methods that mostly use structured traces as auxiliary supervision, $R^3$ trains free-form language reasoning to produce test-time guidance for action. We instantiate $R^3$ on Language Table and simulated bimanual grocery packing, two controlled testbeds for studying robotic reasoning and long-horizon manipulation. $R^3$ improves exploration and generalization across unseen tasks and significantly outperforms instruction-only imitation learning baselines on both benchmarks. Our analyses suggest that free-form language reasoning can function as a test-time compute mechanism for steering low-level policies. Our project page is available at https://robotic-reasoner.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Post-training recipe R^3 turns off-the-shelf vision-language models into robotic reasoners by training on expert reasoning traces and applying single-step rubric-based RL, enabling free-form language guidance for low-level manipulation; demonstrates improved exploration and generalization in language-table tasks and simulated grocery packing.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks require maintaining progress, reasoning about object relations, and recovering from mistakes. Prior robotic reasoning often uses structured traces; question remains whether free-form natural language reasoning can guide low-level policies in practice.
AI.method: R^3 trains a VLM to reason in text: (1) mid-train on expert-generated reasoning traces to instantiate the desired reasoning style; (2) apply single-step rubric-based RL from offline action data to refine the reasoner; at test-time, use free-form language reasoning to guide action selection. Evaluation uses Language Table and simulated bimanual grocery packing.
AI.result: R^3 improves exploration and generalization to unseen tasks and significantly outperforms instruction-only imitation baselines on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Free-form language reasoning can function as a test-time compute mechanism to steer low-level robotic policies; R^3 provides a simple post-training recipe to convert VLMs into robotic reasoners.

title: Pose-Anchored Optical Flow for Low-Latency Human Action Anticipation in Human-Robot Teaming
comment: Presented at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026) in Kitakyushu, Japan
summary: Human-robot interaction (HRI) requires robots to interpret human actions early in their execution in order to respond safely, efficiently, and naturally. However, many existing approaches to human action recognition rely either on sparse skeletal representations, which lack fine-grained motion cues, or dense optical flow, which can be computationally expensive for low-latency perception pipelines. In this paper, we propose PoseOFF, a pose-anchored optical flow representation that captures local motion information around human joints to support earlier human intent understanding. By conditioning motion feature extraction on human pose, PoseOFF encodes localised motion dynamics at semantically meaningful body locations, forming a structured motion representation that is explicitly aligned with human kinematics. We evaluate PoseOFF across multiple benchmark datasets and backbone architectures for action anticipation, demonstrating consistent improvements in recognition accuracy, particularly at early observation ratios. Our results show that PoseOFF enables models to achieve comparable or improved performance while observing less of the action sequence, highlighting its effectiveness for early prediction. Importantly, these gains are achieved without requiring full-frame motion processing, making the approach practical for real-time and resource-constrained settings. These findings suggest that pose-centred motion representations such as PoseOFF can enhance the ability of interactive robot systems to infer human actions earlier, supporting more responsive and anticipatory behaviour in human-robot interaction scenarios.

AI.tldr: PoseOFF introduces a pose-anchored optical flow representation to capture local joint-centered motion for early action anticipation in human-robot interaction, enabling better performance with less action observed and lower computation.
AI.motivation: Existing action recognition methods rely on sparse skeletal data or dense optical flow, which either miss fine-grained cues or incur high latency. There is a need for a pose-conditioned, localized motion representation that aligns with human kinematics for early intent understanding in HRI.
AI.method: Propose PoseOFF: a pose-anchored optical flow representation that conditions motion feature extraction on human pose. It encodes localized motion dynamics around joints into a structured representation aligned with body kinematics, evaluated with multiple datasets and backbones for action anticipation.
AI.result: PoseOFF yields consistent accuracy gains, especially at early observation ratios, achieving comparable or improved performance while requiring less full-frame motion processing, enabling real-time applicability in resource-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: Pose-centered motion representations enhance early action inference in HRI, enabling more responsive and anticipatory robot behavior without full-frame motion processing.

title: Narcissus: Program Synthesis Using Context-Aware LLM Approximations
