AI.result: PDC consistently improves the initial sample, outperforms independent generations under a constrained computation setting, and shows robustness to unmasking strategies and hyperparameters.
AI.conclusion: Prefix-conditioned regeneration is an effective DLM-specific primitive for test-time verification, enabling reliable improvement of diffusion language model outputs through a simple, prefix-aware consistency signal.

title: Beyond Pairwise Feedback: Listwise Vision-Language Supervision for Preference-Based Reward Learning
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures. Srivalli Katkuri and Maxwell Kawada contributed equally to this work
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a powerful source of supervision for reinforcement learning, enabling agents to leverage rich semantic knowledge during training. Inspired by the success of preference-based reward learning (PbRL) in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), vision-language model generated image-based preferences provide an effective source for learning reward functions. This can be done by visually comparing two outcomes through the Bradley-Terry (BT) model. However, this pairwise formulation utilizes only two observations at a time, despite VLMs being capable of ranking multiple candidates. The Plackett-Luce (PL) formulation can shape a reward model with listwise rankings as opposed to pairwise preferences, allowing for a more suited use of a VLM based ranking. In this work, to our knowledge, we introduce the first framework that combines VLM-generated preferences with the Plackett-Luce model for reward learning. We evaluate our approach on Meta-World manipulation tasks and show that Plackett-Luce (PL) reward models can train robotic policies from VLM-generated rankings as effectively as pairwise Bradley-Terry, $K$-wise Bradley-Terry, and RL-VLM-F baselines. Across all environments, at least one PL ranking size ($K \in \{3,4,5\}$) consistently performs with or outperforms other methods in mean success rate. Unlike pairwise methods, which are restricted to $K=2$, PL supports different ranking sizes and can therefore be adapted to the environment and desired feedback format. Our best PL configuration achieves an 86% mean final success rate and matches the Oracle baseline on Drawer Open. Overall, these results demonstrate that listwise VLM preference supervision is a competitive and flexible approach to reward learning for reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: Introduces a Plackett-Luce (PL) listwise ranking framework for reward learning from Vision-Language Model (VLM) generated preferences, showing strong, flexible performance on Meta-World tasks and matching or exceeding pairwise BT baselines.
AI.motivation: To exploit VLMs' ranking capabilities with listwise PL methods, addressing limitations of pairwise Bradley–Terry (BT) approaches and enabling flexible ranking sizes beyond K=2 for reward learning in RL.
AI.method: Generate image-based preferences with a VLM; model rewards using Plackett-Luce for listwise rankings across K candidates; evaluate across multiple PL ranking sizes (K=3,4,5) on Meta-World manipulation tasks; compare against BT, K-BT, and RL-VLM-F baselines using mean final success rate and Oracle as reference.
AI.result: PL-based reward models with K in {3,4,5} consistently perform at least as well as (often better than) pairwise BT, K-BT, and RL-VLM-F baselines; at least one PL configuration matches or surpasses all baselines across environments; best PL achieves 86% mean final success rate and matches Oracle on Drawer Open.
AI.conclusion: Listwise VLM-based preference supervision is a competitive and flexible approach for reward learning in RL, enabling adaptable feedback sizes and achieving strong performance comparable to or better than established baselines.

title: MLLMCLIP: Feature-Level Distillation of MLLM for Robust Vision-Language Representations
summary: Pretrained vision-language models such as CLIP excel at zero-shot recognition but often fail at compositionality, particularly attribute-object and relational structures. Recent studies mitigate this issue by augmenting training with synthetic hard negatives generated by a cascade of large language models and text-to-image models, which incurs substantial pipeline overhead. We instead propose MLLMCLIP, a heterogeneous distillation framework that transfers multimodal knowledge directly from a generative Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) teacher into a discriminative CLIP student, bypassing synthetic data entirely. To bridge the architectural mismatch between the two paradigms, we introduce an attention-based per-layer token selection and a CKA-based distillation loss. Compared to prior CLIP-enhancement methods, MLLMCLIP achieves state-of-the-art compositional accuracy while delivering consistent gains on standard zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval, showing that feature-level distillation strengthens both compositional and general vision-language representation capability.

AI.tldr: MLLMCLIP distills multimodal knowledge from a generative Multimodal LLM (MLLM) teacher into a discriminative CLIP student to boost compositionality without synthetic data, using attention-based per-layer token selection and a CKA distillation loss, achieving state-of-the-art compositionality and strong zero-shot and retrieval gains.
AI.motivation: CLIP shows strong zero-shot recognition but fails on compositionality (attribute-object and relational structures). Prior methods rely on synthetic hard negatives from a cascade of LLMs and text-to-image models, incurring heavy pipeline overhead; a data-free, architecture-bridging distillation could improve representations efficiently.
AI.method: Heterogeneous distillation from a generative MLLM teacher to a discriminative CLIP student. Introduces per-layer attention-based token selection to bridge architectural gaps and a CKA-based distillation loss to align representations, with no synthetic data usage.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art compositional accuracy and provides consistent gains on zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval compared to prior CLIP-enhancement methods.
AI.conclusion: Feature-level distillation from an MLLM to a CLIP student strengthens both compositional and general vision-language representations, offering an efficient, data-free route to improved multimodal understanding.

title: Candidate supply and answer selection shape the value of LLM judging in multi-agent systems
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) sometimes already have the potential to answer correctly, but still report a wrong answer. Explaining this outcome is difficult because generation, communication and final answer-selection rules usually change simultaneously. We conceptualize multi-agent reasoning as an evolutionary pipeline of candidate generation, peer communication and terminal selection, wherein consensus without quality control can exhibit patterns of memetic drift. We study two questions: (1) when an LLM judge provides effective selection pressure by supplying a signal of answer correctness for candidates generated in a multi-agent system, and (2) when using that signal improves the reported answer. To map judge reliability, we analysed 15,336 questions from MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MedXpertQA and MuSR, with Humanity's Last Exam analysed separately. To test these rules, we replayed 81,390 fixed candidate pools drawn from 16,278 questions across five benchmarks. We report three findings. (1) A correct answer is often already present among the generated candidates, but the system can still converge on and report a wrong answer. (2) Judge reliability is not a fixed trait of the model, but varies with the task, the generator and how rare the correct answer is. (3) Combining answer frequency with the judge's evaluation changed only the final answer-selection rule and raised accuracy from 63.82% to 70.82-70.95%, primarily by rescuing correct answers that were outnumbered by popular errors. In the systems studied here, the value of generating more candidates depends on whether those extra samples make correct answers present, frequent or recognisable. By isolating generation, recognition and selection, these findings establish a diagnostic basis for designing multi-agent architectures that protect generated correct answers from being lost.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how an LLM judge acts as a selection pressure in multi-agent reasoning and when it improves final answers. It finds judge reliability varies by task and generator; adding judge signals raises accuracy from 63.82% to about 71% by rescuing correct answers overwhelmed by errors, and the benefit of generating more candidates depends on whether they reveal correct, frequent, or recognizable answers.
AI.motivation: To understand why multi-agent systems sometimes produce correct candidates but report wrong answers (memetic drift) and to determine when a judge-based signal can improve final answers by guiding selection.
AI.method: Empirical analysis across large question banks: (i) map judge reliability using 15,336 questions from MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MedXpertQA, MuSR (with Humanity's Last Exam analyzed separately); (ii) test rules by replaying 81,390 fixed candidate pools drawn from 16,278 questions on five benchmarks; isolate generation, recognition (judge signal), and selection.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) Correct answers often exist among candidates, yet the system can converge on a wrong answer; (2) Judge reliability is task/generator/rarity dependent, not fixed; (3) Combining answer frequency with judge evaluation changes only the final selection rule and raises accuracy from 63.82% to 70.82–70.95%, mainly by rescuing correct answers outnumbered by popular errors.
AI.conclusion: Isolating the stages of generation, recognition, and selection yields a diagnostic basis for designing multi-agent architectures that protect correct answers from being lost; judge signals can improve final answers, but their effectiveness hinges on task context and the distribution of candidate quality.

title: Activation-Space Order-Swap Geometry: A Site-Asymmetry Audit
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures. Under review at the NeurReps Proceedings Track
summary: Order-dependent activation statistics are often interpreted as evidence of interaction, but that interpretation can be confounded by where interventions enter the network. We introduce a no-fit site-asymmetry audit. For a twice-differentiable readout, the open-path order-swap decomposes into a canonical additive response measured by single interventions and an antisymmetrized second difference free of first-order and pure self-curvature terms to second order. Across six open-weight language-model families, the single-intervention baseline explains 84.3-97.7 percent of the bracket norm (mean 93.7 percent), while the no-interaction self-curvature term is 1.8-5.2 times larger than the corrected residual in the two families with the plus/minus injection split. The corrected residual clears a generic-interaction null in three of six families under a confound-free prompt split and two of six after configuration robustness. A known-positive surrogate recovers planted mixed interaction, while a matched site-separation test changes the baseline share and a random architecture reproduces the first-order regime. The same estimator transfers to released non-language references: trained residual fractions fall below a fixed Gaussian-direction null in 11/12 contrasts (5/6 ViT-B/16, 6/6 ResNet-50), a portability check rather than pooled evidence. The contribution is a reusable measurement criterion: run the single-intervention baseline before reading an order-swap vector as interaction or geometric structure; if it explains the vector, form the second difference instead. All claims are scoped to activation-space interventions at distinct sites; we do not claim that representation geometry is globally Abelian.

AI.tldr: A no-fit site-asymmetry audit to distinguish interaction from geometry in order-dependent activation statistics; baseline single interventions account for most of the order-swap; apply antisymmetrized second difference only when not explained; validated across six open-weight LMs and transfer to vision models; provides a reusable criterion.
AI.motivation: Interventions enter the network at different sites, which can confound inference that order-dependent statistics reveal interaction. The paper seeks a robust audit that separates genuine interaction from geometry-related artifacts.
AI.method: Twice-differentiable readout; open-path order-swap decomposed into a canonical additive response to single interventions and an antisymmetrized second difference free of first-order/self-curvature terms to second order. Compute a single-intervention baseline; compare to full vector; if the baseline explains the vector, form the second difference (to isolate interaction). Evaluate across six open-weight language-model families, with plus/minus injection splits, confound-free prompt splits, configuration robustness tests; extend to non-language references via residual analyses and portability checks.
AI.result: Single-intervention baseline explains 84.3–97.7% of bracket norm (mean 93.7%). The no-interaction self-curvature term is 1.8–5.2× larger than the corrected residual in the two plus/minus injection split families. Corrected residual clears a generic-interaction null in 3/6 families under confound-free prompts and in 2/6 after configuration robustness. A known-positive surrogate recovers planted mixed interaction; matched site-separation tests shift baseline shares; random architectures reproduce the first-order regime. On released non-language references, trained residual fractions fall below a fixed Gaussian-direction null in 11/12 contrasts (5/6 ViT-B/16, 6/6 ResNet-50). This suggests portability (not pooled evidence).
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a reusable measurement criterion: run the single-intervention baseline before reading an order-swap vector; if it explains the vector, form the second difference instead. All claims are scoped to activation-space interventions at distinct sites; no claim about global Abelian geometry.

title: V-Rubrics: Visual Faithfulness via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Vision-language models can produce fluent answers that are insufficiently grounded in the visual evidence: a single unsupported object, chart value, or intermediate inference can undermine an otherwise plausible response. We argue that this is a credit-assignment failure in multimodal post-training. Scalar outcome rewards indicate whether an answer is acceptable, but do not identify which visual facts are grounded, which reasoning steps are valid, or which instruction constraints are missed. We introduce Visual Rubrics-Based Reinforcement Learning, which decomposes reference responses into atomic propositions and scores generated answers along Visual Faithfulness (VF), Reasoning Consistency (RC), and Instruction Following (IF). The resulting rubric items provide structured partial credit and localize rubric credit when supporting evidence spans are available. We first obtain an SFT checkpoint by fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on the public OpenMMReasoner-SFT-874K corpus, adapting OpenMMReasoner's cold-start data recipe. We construct V-Rubrics 50K, a 50,248-example training set from 17 visually grounded sources, by applying rule-based filters before deriving example difficulty from rejection-sampling scores and then annotating every example with Gemini-3-Pro under the same structured prompt and protocol. We train our model based on the same SFT checkpoint using component-wise, prefix-localized rubric credit. Experiments show that our rubricbased GRPO improves over both the shared SFT baseline and answer-only GRPO, with the largest gains on knowledge-oriented and visually grounded reasoning benchmarks. The results show rubrics as a useful reward abstraction for visual post-training.

AI.tldr: Visual Rubrics-Based Reinforcement Learning (VR-RL) decomposes visual-language model outputs into atomic propositions and scores across Visual Faithfulness, Reasoning Consistency, and Instruction Following. It builds a 50k-example dataset (V-Rubrics 50K) and fine-tunes an SFT checkpoint (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct) with component-wise rubric credit, achieving improvements over baselines, especially on knowledge-grounded tasks.
AI.motivation: To address credit-assignment failure in multimodal post-training where scalar rewards cannot identify which visual facts or reasoning steps are grounded or which constraints are missed.
AI.method: Decompose responses into atomic propositions; score outputs along Visual Faithfulness (VF), Reasoning Consistency (RC), and Instruction Following (IF). Build V-Rubrics 50K dataset from 17 visually grounded sources using rule-based filters, estimate example difficulty via rejection-sampling, and annotate with Gemini-3-Pro under a unified prompt. Fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on OpenMMReasoner-SFT-874K to obtain an SFT checkpoint, then train with component-wise, prefix-localized rubric credit (rubric-based GRPO).
AI.result: Rubric-based GRPO outperforms the shared SFT baseline and an answer-only GRPO, with the largest gains on knowledge-oriented and visually grounded reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Rubrics provide a useful reward abstraction for visual post-training and help localize credit to grounded evidence and reasoning steps.

title: LivingRAG: Augmenting Graph RAG with Experience
summary: Graph-based RAG improves multi-hop question answering by organizing evidence as a knowledge graph. However, most existing RAG systems process each query in isolation and discard useful reasoning from the LLM's response after inference. As a result, later related queries need to retrieve evidence and reason from scratch. We propose LivingRAG, a Graph RAG framework with writable and reusable reasoning experience. LivingRAG adds a writable experience store to a graph-based retrieval backbone, enabling verified experiences to be reused during inference in two ways. Stored graph signals help retrieval find entities and passages that were useful in earlier related queries. Stored summaries provide a reference reasoning pattern for answer generation. We analyze online QA streams and find reusable signals from shared entities, graph neighborhoods, and question templates. Experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks show that LivingRAG improves accuracy over strong RAG baselines and reduces completion-token use when relevant prior experience is reused.

AI.tldr: LivingRAG adds a writable, reusable reasoning experience store to a graph-based RAG, enabling reuse of prior experiences to improve multi-hop QA and reduce token usage.
AI.motivation: Conventional RAG often treats queries in isolation and discards reasoning from the LLM, causing inefficiency for related queries.
AI.method: Introduce a writable experience store on a graph-based retrieval backbone; store verified experiences (graph signals and summaries); reuse during inference for retrieval guidance and pattern-based answer generation; analyze online QA streams to identify reusable signals.
AI.result: On multi-hop QA benchmarks, LivingRAG improves accuracy over strong RAG baselines and reduces completion-token usage by reusing relevant prior experience.
AI.conclusion: Reusable, writable reasoning experiences in a graph-based RAG framework enhance QA performance and efficiency, validating the approach.

title: Two Dimensions Govern Agnostic Multiclass Transductive Learning
summary: In transductive classification, an adversary fixes a labeled population, one label is hidden uniformly, and the learner sees all remaining labels. For binary classes, agnostic transductive and PAC learning have the same minimax rate. Whether this extends to multiclass learning was open, especially for unbounded label spaces where uniform convergence can fail. We resolve the question up to logarithmic factors. For every multiclass class $\mathcal H$ with DS dimension $d_{DS}$ and Natarajan dimension $d_{\mathrm N}$, the optimal agnostic transductive excess error satisfies $\widetildeΘ\left(\frac{d_{DS}}{n}+\sqrt{\frac{d_{\mathrm N}}{n}}\right).$ The result holds for arbitrary label spaces. The two terms are both necessary. A DS pseudo-cube gives the realizable $d_{DS}/n$ obstruction, while a Natarajan cube with repeated points and fair labels gives the agnostic $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm N}/n}$ obstruction. The upper bound uses a random-reservation principle. The learner deliberately ignores a constant fraction of the visible labels, which makes the true test point uniform in a large unseen block. We combine realizable compression, a label-space reduction, and inside-menu agnostic compression across this finite-population split. A new without-replacement multiplicative-weights lemma preserves the fast $d_{DS}/n$ term. Consequently, agnostic multiclass PAC and transductive learning obey the same two-dimension law up to logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: A tight two-term minimax rate for agnostic multiclass transductive learning: tilde Theta(d_DS/n + sqrt(d_N/n)) for any label space.
AI.motivation: Extend binary transductive/PAC equivalence to multiclass with unbounded label spaces and characterize minimax excess error under adversarial label hiding.
AI.method: Introduce random-reservation principle; realizable compression; label-space reduction; inside-menu agnostic compression; finite-population split; new without-replacement multiplicative-weights lemma; construct DS pseudo-cubes and Natarajan cubes to show lower bounds.
AI.result: Optimal agnostic transductive excess error is tilde Theta(d_DS/n + sqrt(d_N/n)) where d_DS is the DS-dimension and d_N is the Natarajan dimension. Valid for arbitrary label spaces; both terms necessary. PAC and transductive bounds coincide up to log factors.
AI.conclusion: Agnostic multiclass PAC and transductive learning obey the same two-dimension law up to logarithmic factors, resolving the multiclass extension question (up to log factors).

title: A Dual-Transformer for Multi-Camera View Recommendation
summary:
Multi-camera systems are foundational to modern media production, and multi-camera editing is a critical task. This involves the proper selection of the appropriate camera view at each moment. In this paper, we propose a novel Dual-Transformer architecture with Cross-Attention that heavily outperformed the current SOTA models over the TVMCE dataset (TV Shows Multicamera Editing dataset). Our model decouples these tasks: (1) a dedicated temporal encoder first processes the sequence of past frames to build a rich memory of the recent history, and (2) the candidate camera views then act as queries to this memory via a cross-attention module, allowing each candidate to independently interrogate the historical context and find the most relevant information for its own evaluation.
  Our approach achieved 56.60% Precision@0.5, representing a substantial improvement over the prior best result of 37.16%. We further conducted an ablation study exploring the use of lightweight backbone architectures, where the SwinV2 backbone yielded the best performance, achieving 69.65% Precision@0.5.
  Using this best-performing configuration, we then investigated the feasibility of adapting the model to replicate the editing style of a specific human editor. To this end, we fine-tuned the model using varying proportions of the initial segment of a target video. Our results demonstrate that even with only 20% of the video used for fine-tuning, the model exhibited measurable improvements in Precision@0.5, indicating strong potential for data-efficient personalization of editing style adapted to each individual TV show or producer.

AI.tldr: A Dual-Transformer with cross-attention for multicamera editing; builds a past-frame memory via a temporal encoder; candidate views query memory; achieves state-of-the-art Precision@0.5 on TVMCE; backbone ablation favors SwinV2; shows data-efficient personalization via partial fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Improve camera-view selection in multi-camera editing by leveraging temporal context and cross-attentive querying of candidate views, surpassing heuristic baselines and enabling personalized editing styles.
AI.method: Proposed architecture: separate temporal encoder to encode past frames into memory; cross-attention where each candidate camera view acts as a query to the memory, enabling independent evaluation; experiments include ablations with lightweight backbones (SwinV2); dataset TVMCE; fine-tuning with partial video for style replication.
AI.result: Main: 56.60% Precision@0.5 (vs 37.16% SOTA). SwinV2 backbone: 69.65% Precision@0.5. Personalization: with 20% of video for fine-tuning, measurable improvements in Precision@0.5.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled temporal memory and cross-attention for camera-view selection yields substantial gains; SwinV2 is effective; data-efficient personalization is viable for adapting editing style.

title: Quantitative Analysis of $ω$-Regular Robust MDPs
summary:
Robust Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) generalize classical MDPs by allowing uncertainty in transition probabilities and optimizing against their worst-case realization. We consider $(s,a)$-rectangular RMDPs with \emph{linearly defined} uncertainty sets and study parity objectives, which are a canonical representation of $ω$-regular objectives. An uncertainty set is linearly defined if it is described by linear inequalities over the transition distribution together with auxiliary variables, which capture the standard $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ balls as well as general polytopic uncertainty sets.
  The quantitative value is the supremum, over all agent policies, of the satisfaction probability guaranteed against the adversarial environment. Previous work studied the qualitative analysis, namely the almost-sure (resp. positive) problem that asks whether a single agent policy guarantees satisfaction with probability one (resp. positive probability) against every environment policy. In this work, we solve the exact quantitative problem.
  Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that both the agent and the environment admit pure memoryless optimal policies. Second, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for quantitative parity on linearly defined robust Markov chains and use it as a subroutine in a policy-iteration algorithm for RMDPs. The algorithm combines quantitative one-step improvements with qualitative almost-sure improvements. Finally, we report experiments comparing our approach with the explicit reduction to stochastic games.

AI.tldr: Linearly defined uncertainty in (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs with parity objectives; both agent and environment have pure memoryless optimal policies; a polynomial-time algorithm solves quantitative parity on linearly defined robust Markov chains, used within a policy-iteration framework for RMDPs; experiments compare to explicit stochastic-game reductions.
AI.motivation: Provide exact quantitative guarantees for parity objectives under model uncertainty in robust MDPs, generalizing L1/L∞ balls to polytopic sets, and moving beyond qualitative analysis to optimization of worst-case satisfaction probability.
AI.method: Prove that optimal policies for both agent and environment can be pure memoryless. Develop a polynomial-time algorithm for quantitative parity on linearly defined robust Markov chains. Integrate into a policy-iteration algorithm for RMDPs by combining quantitative one-step improvements with qualitative almost-sure improvements. Validate by experiments contrasting with explicit reductions to stochastic games.
AI.result: Polynomial-time algorithm for linearly defined robust parity on Markov chains; a policy-iteration framework for RMDPs achieving exact quantitative solutions; empirical results showing competitiveness with reductions to stochastic games.
AI.conclusion: Bridges qualitative analysis to exact quantitative analysis in linearly defined RMDPs with parity objectives, offering efficient algorithms and practical evaluation.

title: Neither Precision Nor Architecture Alone: Controlled Tests of Failure Remedies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables; appendix with full proofs included
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) frequently fail on stiff or advection-dominated PDEs, and two recent accounts offer competing remedies: switching from FP32 to FP64 to repair an L-BFGS stopping artifact, or replacing the MLP with a state-space-model (SSM) backbone plus sub-sequence alignment to counter architectural simplicity bias. We test both under matched, seed-paired controls in a pre-registered 144-run study spanning convection, reaction, and wave, plus an independent 85-run convection/wave study; success is relative $\ell_2$ error below $0.05$. The two remedies act on disjoint regime-and-seed slices: neither substitutes for the other. On hard convection ($β{=}50$), alignment recovers 2/5 seeds in FP32 and 3/5 in FP64, where the unaligned SSM succeeds on 0/5 seeds at either precision and the vanilla MLP moves only from 0/5 to 1/5 across the precision switch---the recoveries trace to the alignment objective, not the backbone. On reaction the backbone alone already succeeds on 3/5--4/5 seeds, so each remedy covers a regime the other does not. Responses are also seed-specific: the same precision switch flips individual seeds in opposite directions and, on wave, lowers median error with no statistically significant success gain. Tightening the inner L-BFGS tolerance in an independent repeated-step runner likewise lowers median error at a large runtime cost, with success counts unchanged. Precision, stopping, backbone, and alignment must therefore be evaluated jointly and reported per seed.

AI.tldr: PINNs on stiff/advection-dominated PDEs benefit from two regime-specific remedies: FP32→FP64 for L-BFGS stopping artifact, and a state-space-model backbone with subsequence alignment; results are seed- and regime-dependent; no single remedy works for all seeds/tasks.
AI.motivation: To understand failure modes of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) on stiff/advection-dominated PDEs and to compare two proposed remedies under controlled, matched seeds.
AI.method: Pre-registered multi-run study: 144 runs across convection, reaction, and wave; seed-paired controls; independent 85-run convection/wave study; compare FP32 vs FP64, MLP vs SSM backbone with alignment; evaluate via success defined as relative L2 error < 0.05; analyze per-seed outcomes; also test inner L-BFGS tolerance.
AI.result: Remedies act on disjoint regime/seed slices; neither substitutes for the other. On hard convection (beta=50), alignment recovers 2/5 seeds in FP32 and 3/5 in FP64; unaligned SSM fails (0/5) at either precision; vanilla MLP improves slightly from 0/5 to 1/5 with precision switch. On reaction, backbone alone achieves 3/5–4/5 seeds; each remedy covers regimes the other does not. On wave, precision switch lowers median error but without significant success gains; tightening inner L-BFGS tolerance reduces median error but does not change success counts; seed-specific effects: the same precision switch can help or hurt seeds. Overall, precision, stopping, backbone, and alignment must be evaluated jointly and reported per seed.
AI.conclusion: There is no universal remedy for PINN failures on stiff/advection-dominated PDEs; the effects are seed- and regime-specific. Reporting should be per seed, jointly considering precision, stopping criteria, backbone choice, and alignment objective; matching controls and pre-registration are essential for robust conclusions.

title: VBVR-Pro: A Scalable and Verifiable Suite for Native Visual Reasoning
summary: Native visual reasoning treats visual generation as the medium of reasoning itself: visual states (i.e. images and videos) are not merely inputs to be understood or outputs to be rendered, but first-class substrates for problem solving beyond language. Yet progress remains bottlenecked by the lack of scalable training tasks, reliable feedback, and controlled comparisons across generative substrates. In this work, we introduce VBVR-Pro, a closed-loop testbed that makes native visual reasoning through generation trainable, verifiable, optimizable, and experimentally controllable. 1) Task scaling. VBVR-Pro turns visual reasoning into a controlled task space of 300 procedurally generated tasks. Models trained on VBVR-Pro show strong transfer beyond the proposed suite across seven external visual reasoning benchmarks such as RISE-Video, MME-CoF-Pro, and BabyVision. 2) Verifiable rewards. VBVR-Pro provides verifiable reward scorers for task-grounded evaluation. Through a systematic study of leading MLLMs as judges, we identify recurring failure modes of the prevalent VLM-as-a-judge paradigm. In contrast, the proposed scorers are grounded in deterministic, task-specific rules, achieve fine-grained alignment with human judgments. Importantly, they serve as reliable reward signals for large-scale multi-task reinforcement learning and demonstrate stronger post-RL performance across visual reasoning tasks. 3) Mechanism study. VBVR-Pro enables controlled modality studies across more than 30 image, video, and interleaved generators. Our analysis shows that video generation remains strongest for tasks requiring persistent spatiotemporal state tracking, while interleaved generation provides a compute-efficient alternative. Critically, ablations and probing suggest the presence of vision-native trajectories that are crucial to visual reasoning. We release all data, models, scorers, and code.

AI.tldr: VBVR-Pro provides a scalable, verifiable, and controllable testbed for native visual reasoning via generation, featuring 300 procedurally generated tasks, deterministic reward scorers, and extensive modality analyses, enabling RL-based learning and cross-benchmark transfer.
AI.motivation: Address bottlenecks in scalable training tasks, reliable feedback, and controlled comparisons for visual reasoning through generation. Emphasizes verifiable, task-grounded rewards and principled modality studies to uncover vision-native trajectories.
AI.method: Construct a closed-loop platform (VBVR-Pro) with 300 procedurally generated tasks; develop deterministic, verifiable reward scorers; compare against LLM-based judges; conduct mechanism studies across 30 image/video/interleaved generators; perform ablations and probing; release data, models, scorers, and code.
AI.result: Models trained on VBVR-Pro transfer to seven external visual reasoning benchmarks (e.g., RISE-Video, MME-CoF-Pro, BabyVision). Verifiable scorers align with human judgments and provide reliable rewards for multi-task RL, outperforming LLM-as-judge baselines. Video generation best supports persistent spatiotemporal state tracking; interleaved generation offers compute efficiency. Ablations/probing reveal vision-native trajectories crucial to reasoning.
AI.conclusion: VBVR-Pro establishes a scalable, verifiable, and controllable platform for native visual reasoning through generation, enabling robust multi-task RL, cross-modality insights, and reproducible research; resources (data, models, scorers, code) are released to the community.

title: When Should a Network Emit Geometry, and When Should It Detect It? Readout, Reconciliation, and Representation in Floorplan Vectorization
summary: A network trained to recover the walls, openings, and rooms of a rasterized floorplan can produce its output in two ways: by emitting the geometry as an autoregressive coordinate sequence, or by detecting it on dense junction and centerline heatmaps and assembling a graph. We compare the two readouts on the same trained network. On real scans (CubiCasa5K) detection is better on every wall measure (+2.7 wall F1 at tolerance 0.05, +5.1 at 0.015; paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero), and reading an opening heatmap the decoder never used raises opening F1 by 2.6x without retraining. Within real scans the readout's advantage grows with plan size and reverses on small plans; on clean vector renders sequence decoding is better by 5 to 8 points where its training covered the render style, while under full domain shift the readout, given calibrated thresholds, stays ahead; neither ink density nor plan size explains the reversal. With matched data and recipe, a room-centric system with a reconciliation step and a wall-first sequence model reach comparable wall quality, so the output representation matters less than is usually assumed. A prior from the other family helps at the output but not at the input: deterministic fusion of the two outputs raises wall F1 by 7 points, whereas conditioning one model on the other's output gives no gain in three forms, including two ground-truth-content controls. We also provide an edit-cost metric that scores a draft by the human work needed to correct it, corrected CubiCasa5K annotations, and ResPlan-FP, a CC BY 4.0 benchmark of 16,998 plans with frozen splits and three baseline tracks. Code, the benchmark, and the corrected annotations are available at https://github.com/Cyprinus12138/fpvec-lab

AI.tldr: Two readouts for floorplan recovery—autoregressive coordinate sequences vs dense heatmap-based graphs—are competitive: heatmaps excel on real scans for walls; sequence decoding can win on clean vector renders; domain shift and plan size affect results; combining readouts and using prior information at the output aids performance; inputs benefit less from cross-family priors.
AI.motivation: Assess how the representation of recovered geometry (sequence vs heatmap/graph) affects accuracy, generalization, and computational trade-offs in floorplan reconstruction, and whether fusion or cross-prior information can improve results.
AI.method: Train a single network to recover walls, openings, and rooms. Compare two readouts on the same model: (1) autoregressive sequence of coordinates; (2) dense heatmaps (junction/centerline) with graph assembly. Evaluate on real scans (CubiCasa5K) using wall F1 at various tolerances; test effect of using an opening heatmap not seen by the decoder; analyze plan-size effects and domain shift. Compare to a room-centric system with reconciliation; explore fusion strategies: deterministic fusion of outputs vs conditioning one model on the other; introduce an edit-cost metric and benchmark (ResPlan-FP) with corrected CubiCasa5K annotations. Code and data are provided in the linked repository.
AI.result: On CubiCasa5K real scans, the heatmap/detection readout outperforms the sequence readout on all wall measures (e.g., +2.7 F1 at 0.05 tolerance, +5.1 at 0.015; bootstrap intervals exclude zero). Reading an unused opening heatmap raises opening F1 by 2.6x. Readout advantages grow with plan size and reverse on small plans; sequence excels on clean vector renders when trained for the render style, but with full domain shift the readout remains ahead when thresholds are calibrated. A room-centric system with reconciliation and a wall-first sequence model can achieve comparable wall quality. Deterministic fusion of the two outputs raises wall F1 by about 7 points; conditioning one model on the other yields no gain across three evaluations. An output-centric prior helps at the output but not input. An edit-cost metric and ResPlan-FP benchmark (16,998 plans) are provided, along with code and corrected annotations.
AI.conclusion: Output representation matters, but with matched data and recipe, both readouts can reach comparable wall quality; leveraging priors across representations helps at the output level. Fusion strategies can yield larger gains than conditioning; the chosen readout should align with data characteristics and domain shifts. The work provides practical tools (edit-cost metric, corrected annotations, benchmark) for evaluation.

title: SciMIF: Understanding Multimodal Instruction Following in Scientific Domains
summary: Understanding instruction-following capabilities in scientific domains is essential for effectively leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to advance the development of scientific fields. In this work, we introduce SciMIF, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the capability of MLLMs in following complex scientific instructions. Specifically, based on an extensive analysis of 22 distinct tasks across 5 representative scientific disciplines, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy comprising 10 constraint groups that captures both general functional requirements and discipline-specific characteristics. Guided by this taxonomy, we develop a high-fidelity instruction injection pipeline to systematically augment existing scientific datasets. We conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple state-of-the-art closed-source and open-source MLLMs. Our findings reveal significant performance disparities across different scientific disciplines, with chemistry posing greater challenges for current MLLMs. Furthermore, we observe that increasing the model scale does not yield corresponding improvements in constraint adherence, and current models still struggle severely with fine-grained constraints and instructions requiring the deep application of disciplinary knowledge. SciMIF fills the current void in evaluating multimodal instruction adherence within scientific domains, laying a crucial foundation for future enhancements of MLLMs in rigorous scientific applications. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/shenye7436/SciMIF .

AI.tldr: SciMIF introduces a benchmark to evaluate instruction-following in multimodal LLMs within scientific domains. It defines a 10-group constraint taxonomy over 22 tasks across 5 disciplines, builds an instruction-injection pipeline to augment datasets, and evaluates state-of-the-art MLLMs, revealing discipline gaps (chemistry hardest), scale-growth does not guarantee better constraint adherence, and persisting challenges with fine-grained and domain-knowledge-intensive instructions.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of standardized evaluation of multimodal instruction adherence in scientific contexts, enabling systematic benchmarking and targeted improvement of MLLMs for rigorous scientific applications.
AI.method: Develop a taxonomy of 10 constraint groups guided by 22 tasks across 5 disciplines; construct a high-fidelity instruction-injection pipeline to augment existing scientific datasets; evaluate multiple closed-source and open-source MLLMs; release data and code for reproducibility.
AI.result: Notable performance disparities across disciplines with chemistry posing greater challenges; increasing model scale does not consistently improve constraint adherence; current models struggle with fine-grained constraints and deep disciplinary knowledge.
AI.conclusion: SciMIF provides a foundational benchmark for evaluating multimodal instruction adherence in science, guiding future enhancements of MLLMs for rigorous scientific use; data and code will be released to foster reproducibility and community advancement.

title: On the Separation of Human and AI-Generated Images in CLIP Embedding Space
summary:
We identify a previously unreported phenomenon in CLIP representations: human and AI-generated paintings spontaneously separate along the dominant principal directions of their joint embedding distribution, without any supervised objective designed to distinguish the two classes. Rather than exploiting this phenomenon for detection, our objective is to interpret it: we seek to identify the visual information underlying the separation and to trace it back from the embedding space to the image domain. We pursue this objective through a progressive investigation combining interpretable image representations with gradient-based inversion, used systematically as an experimental probe of the relationships identified in feature space. Robustness experiments and increasingly expressive statistical descriptors progressively rule out several intuitive explanations based on global image properties and simple local statistics, and point instead to distributed multiscale image structure. Multiscale scattering provides the most informative interpretable representation considered, but offers only a partial account of the phenomenon.
  Direct inversion provides a complementary and striking observation: substantial displacements along the dominant CLIP directions can be induced by image perturbations that remain nearly imperceptible to human observers, showing that the directions involved in the separation are highly sensitive to image variations with very low perceptual salience for humans. Taken together, these results reveal a significant difference between the visual evidence reflected in CLIP representations and that readily accessible to human perception, raising broader questions about the relationship between artificial and human vision and, ultimately, between artificial and human aesthetic judgment.

AI.tldr: CLIP embeddings reveal a spontaneous separation between human- and AI-generated paintings along the dominant joint principal directions, without supervised guidance. The work aims to interpret this separation by tracing information from embedding space back to the image domain using interpretable representations and gradient-based inversion, not for detection.
AI.motivation: To understand what visual information in images drives the observed separation in CLIP space and how this information relates to human perceptual and aesthetic judgments, rather than building a classifier.
AI.method: Progressively combine interpretable image representations with gradient-based inversion as an experimental probe. Use robustness tests and descriptive statistics to rule out simple global/local explanations, highlighting distributed multiscale image structure. Employ multiscale scattering as a primary interpretable representation and perform direct image perturbation (inversion) to assess sensitivity of CLIP directions.
AI.result: The embedding-space separation arises in the absence of supervised objectives and is linked to distributed multiscale image structure. Multiscale scattering provides substantial explanatory power but does not fully account for the phenomenon. Direct inversions show that large CLIP-direction displacements can be produced by imperceptible image perturbations, indicating high sensitivity of these directions to low-salience image changes. This reveals a notable gap between CLIP's visual evidence and human perception.
AI.conclusion: There is a significant difference between the information CLIP encoding captures and what humans perceive, prompting broader questions about artificial vs. human vision and aesthetic judgment, and suggesting that interpretability requires accounting for multiscale, distributed image structure and perceptually subtle perturbations.

title: Multi-Granularity Context-Enhanced RAG over Multimodal Knowledge Graphs
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used to mitigate hallucination issues in large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In particular, knowledge graph (KG)-based RAG leverages structured knowledge to provide (M)LLMs with high-quality external information. Building on these works, recent studies have explored multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) as knowledge bases for GraphRAG. This enables Graph RAG to integrate knowledge across multiple modalities, thereby further enhancing its performance. However, existing MMKG-based RAG methods generally follow a common pipeline in which different modalities are largely processed independently before being fusion. As a result, textual context is only used to a limited extent during visual information extraction and subsequent multimodal knowledge fusion. This brings a semantic gap between images and text which limits the multimodal GraphRAG performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for constructing a Context-Enhanced MMKG (CEMMKG) to better support multimodal GraphRAG. The proposed CEMMKG enriches each image with complementary textual context at both local and global scopes. Local context goes beyond the surrounding text by incorporating sentences that are semantically related to the image, while global context provides a summary of the entire passage. We further introduce a multi-granularity design for the local context, allowing it to capture semantically relevant information at different levels of detail. Extensive experiments on the selected vision-centric dataset validate that CEMMKG is effective in leveraging contextual information to improve MMKG-based RAG performance. Moreover, its effectiveness across different MMKG-based RAG methods demonstrates its broad applicability.

AI.tldr: Introduces Context-Enhanced MMKG (CEMMKG) to reduce cross-modal semantic gaps in MMKG-based GraphRAG by enriching images with local and global textual context and a multi-granular local-context design; improves multimodal knowledge fusion and RAG performance on vision-centric data.
AI.motivation: Address the semantic gap between visual and textual modalities in MMKG-based GraphRAG pipelines where modalities are processed independently, limiting information fusion and performance.
AI.method: Construct a Context-Enhanced MMKG (CEMMKG) that augments each image with textual context at local and global scopes. Local context includes semantically related sentences; multiple granularity levels capture varying detail. Global context provides a passage-level summary. Integrate these contexts into MMKG to enhance multimodal graph reasoning for RAG.
AI.result: Experiments on a vision-centric dataset show that CEMMKG improves MMKG-based RAG performance by leveraging contextual information; effectiveness is demonstrated across different MMKG-based RAG methods, indicating broad applicability.
AI.conclusion: Contextual enrichment across local and global textual contexts, with a multi-granularity local design, can bridge the text–image semantic gap and enhance GraphRAG performance, suggesting strong potential for generalization across MMKG-based RAG pipelines.

title: Escaping Low-Dimensional Overlap: Multi-Task Model Merging via High-Dimensional Sparse Disentanglement
summary: Model merging provides an efficient way to construct multi-task generalist models without additional training, but its performance often degrades under severe task interference. Task interference in model merging primarily stems from \textit{superposition}, where task-specific features become entangled within the parameter space. This entanglement renders conventional decomposition methods insufficient for effectively isolating useful task directions from interfering components. In this paper, we propose a sparse-representation-based merging framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to project task vectors into a high-dimensional sparse feature space, enabling feature-level disentanglement before fusion. To reduce computational overhead, we further introduce a lightweight Group-Ranked Zeroth-Order Optimizer (GR-ZOO) to identify task-critical layers for selective merging. Experiments on both Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms representative baselines, including Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merge, DARE, Fisher-Merge,and several recent training-free merging methods, across mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction following, and general knowledge tasks. In a highly conflicting four-task setting on Qwen2.5-1.5B, our method further achieves a 2.78\% improvement over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: Sparse-representation merging framework using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to project task vectors into a high-dimensional sparse feature space for feature-level disentanglement before fusion, plus a lightweight Group-Ranked Zeroth-Order Optimizer (GR-ZOO) for selective merging of task-critical layers. Demonstrates consistent improvements over baselines across math reasoning, code generation, instruction following, and knowledge tasks on Qwen models; achieves 2.78% gain in a highly conflicting four-task setting.
AI.motivation: Model merging suffers from severe task interference due to superposition, causing entangled task-specific features in parameter space and degraded performance. Existing decomposition methods fail to isolate useful task directions. A disentangled, sparse representation and efficient layer selection could alleviate interference and enable effective training-free merging.
AI.method: 1) Use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to map task vectors into a high-dimensional sparse feature space, enabling feature-level disentanglement prior to fusion. 2) Introduce Group-Ranked Zeroth-Order Optimizer (GR-ZOO) to identify task-critical layers for selective merging, reducing computational overhead. 3) Evaluate on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B across multiple tasks (math reasoning, code generation, instruction following, general knowledge).
AI.result: The proposed method consistently outperforms representative baselines (Task Arithmetic, TIES-Merge, DARE, Fisher-Merge, etc.) and other training-free merging approaches across the assessed tasks; in a highly conflicting four-task setting on Qwen2.5-1.5B, it achieves a 2.78% improvement over the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Sparse representation with SAEs plus GR-ZOO enables more robust, training-free multi-task merging by disentangling task directions at the feature level and efficiently selecting task-critical layers. The approach demonstrates strong cross-task and cross-model-size performance improvements, suggesting practical viability and scalability.

title: Plans You Can Check: Verifier-Grounded Learning of an Open-Weight Planner for Executable Video-Editing
comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP '26
summary: Practical video editing is not only pixel generation: an editor must turn a brief, a clip pool, music metadata, and hard constraints into an executable timeline. We study this decision layer as \emph{executable video-editing planning} and introduce RefineCut, which, unlike workflow systems that wrap a prompted frontier model, trains a compact open-weight planner for it. The planner edits a typed timeline through structured patches covering clip selection, trimming, ordering, transitions, and duration and music alignment; a deterministic verifier applies each patch and checks it against an explicit constraint ledger. Because editing has no single ground-truth repair, we do not imitate teachers directly: RefineCut replays every multi-teacher branch through the verifier and keeps verifier-best repairs as supervision. A second stage, RefineCut-Evo, lets the student score its own repairs with the verifier and a task rubric and trains on high-margin preference pairs, so the final $8$B planner runs in a closed verifier loop with no teacher calls at inference. On RefineCut-Bench ($3{,}578$ tasks, $7{,}971$ captioned clips, $499$ music tracks, explicit ledgers), verifier-replayed distillation lifts the planner from $0.620$ to $0.858$ on the protocol-specific Video-Editing Score and RefineCut-Evo reaches $0.924$; the gain transfers to Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B, and in the same closed loop the $8$B planner matches or exceeds its frontier teachers. Code and RefineCut-Bench are publicly released; see the Data Availability statement.

AI.tldr: RefineCut provides an executable video-editing planner trained with a verifier-based self-imitation loop, achieving state-of-the-art scores on RefineCut-Bench and transferring to larger models, with no teacher calls at inference.
AI.motivation: Video editing requires a concrete, executable plan that maps brief assets to a constraint-satisfying timeline; existing workflow systems rely on prompts and do not provide enforceable guarantees for edits.
AI.method: A typed timeline planner applies structured patches (clip selection, trimming, ordering, transitions, duration/music alignment). A deterministic verifier enforces a constraint ledger on each patch. Training uses verifier-replayed, multi-teacher branches with verifier-best repairs. RefineCut-Evo trains the student on high-margin preference pairs using the verifier and rubric in a closed loop, enabling an 8B planner to function without teacher calls at inference.
AI.result: On RefineCut-Bench (3,578 tasks; 7,971 captioned clips; 499 music tracks; explicit ledgers), verifier-replayed distillation boosts Video-Editing Score from 0.620 to 0.858; RefineCut-Evo reaches 0.924. Gains transfer to Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B; the 8B planner matches or exceeds frontier teachers in the same loop.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-based, self-improving planning enables high-quality, constraint-consistent executable video editing with open-weight models and demonstrates effective transfer to larger LLMs; code and benchmark are publicly released.

title: ProgRouter: Online Progress-Guided Orchestration for Multi-Agent LLM Workflows under Quality-Cost Tradeoffs
comment: Accepted in Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026. Index Terms: Collaborative agentic workflows, LLM agent orchestration, Quality-cost trade-off, Task progress prediction, Online decision-making
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflows have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex, open-ended tasks through collaborative reasoning among specialized LLM agents, but they incur substantial operating costs due to repeated LLM invocations and long-horizon context accumulation. Existing cascade routing methods make one-shot, query-level decisions and cannot adapt to the dynamic, state-dependent nature of multi-step workflows, in which the right LLM at each step depends on evolving task progress, remaining task difficulty, and cost-efficiency requirements. We present ProgRouter, an online progress-guided routing framework that adaptively selects LLM agents across workflow steps to preserve task-solving quality while adhering to time and cost budgets. ProgRouter introduces a multi-view task progress scorer that combines coarse workflow outcome regimes with fine-grained signals on subtask completion, progress trends, and workflow state quality. Then, a dual-path task progress predictor and an adaptive meta-gating mechanism estimate the progress gain for each candidate routed LLM. ProgRouter makes online step-wise routing decisions that balance progress gain, task time budgets, and long-term operating cost efficiency. Experiments on HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500, and ASQA, spanning agentic code generation, mathematical reasoning, and retrieval-augmented long-form question answering, demonstrate that ProgRouter reduces the operating cost relative to key baselines while maintaining strong task-solving performance.

AI.tldr: ProgRouter is an online, progress-guided routing framework for multi-agent LLM workflows that adaptively selects agents at each step to optimize task-solving quality under time and cost budgets. It introduces (1) a multi-view task progress scorer, (2) a dual-path progress predictor, and (3) an adaptive meta-gating mechanism for stepwise routing, and shows cost reductions with preserved performance across diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Operating costs in multi-agent LLM workflows are high due to repeated LLM invocations and growing context; one-shot cascade routing cannot adapt to evolving progress and state.
AI.method: Develop an online framework that (i) scores progress using coarse workflow regimes and fine-grained subtask/trajectory signals; (ii) predicts progress gain via dual-path modeling; (iii) employs an adaptive gate to select the most beneficial LLM at each step; (iv) makes stepwise routing decisions under time and cost constraints; (v) evaluates on code generation, math reasoning, and retrieval-augmented QA benchmarks.
AI.result: ProgRouter reduces operational cost relative to key baselines while maintaining strong task-solving performance across HumanEval Plus, MBPP, MATH-500, and ASQA.
AI.conclusion: Online, progress-guided routing balances progress gain, time budgets, and long-term cost efficiency in multi-agent LLM workflows, demonstrating practical gains across diverse tasks.

title: PaSta: Noisy Node Classification with Partial Label Learning
summary: Noisy node classification problem is a fundamental yet challenging task for real-world graph-related web services, where node labels are often corrupted or unreliable due to weak supervision or automatic annotation. However, existing methods typically train models based on one-hot labels, which not only makes models susceptible to overfitting on noisy labels, but also leads to error accumulation after pseudo-label-guided enhancement. In this paper, we propose a novel Partial label-based Self-training framework (PaSta for short) that leverages partial label learning technique to overcome the limitations of existing methods. Specifically, PaSta first trains multiple annotators to comprehensively capture the class distribution of nodes and aggregates their predictions to construct high-quality partial labels. Subsequently, we design a partial label-based classification model with two well-crafted loss functions to guide the model learning at both label and representation spaces. To further enhance the robustness against noisy labels, we introduce a self-training strategy where the labels refined by partial label learning are then used to further optimize the annotators in a closed-loop iterative manner. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that, compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, PaSta achieves an average improvement of 1.1% in classification performance under various noise settings.

AI.tldr: A partial-label learning framework PaSta for noisy node classification uses multiple annotators to produce high-quality partial labels, a two-loss classifier operating on label and representation spaces, and a closed-loop self-training loop to iteratively refine annotators, achieving 1.1% average improvement over SOTA on five datasets.
AI.motivation: Noisy labels in graph node classification (due to weak supervision or automatic annotation) cause overfitting with one-hot labels and error accumulation with pseudo-labels. There is a need for robust learning under label noise.
AI.method: 1) Train multiple annotators to estimate the class distribution of nodes and aggregate their predictions into partial labels. 2) Develop a partial-label-based classifier with two loss functions guiding learning in label space and representation space. 3) Implement a self-training loop where partial-label-refined labels are used to further update the annotators (closed-loop) to enhance robustness against noise.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on five datasets shows PaSta achieves an average improvement of 1.1% in classification performance over state-of-the-art methods under various noise settings.
AI.conclusion: PaSta demonstrates that combining partial-label learning with a self-training loop effectively mitigates label-noise issues in graph node classification and yields consistent performance gains over existing methods.

title: SeVeR: Selective Visual Exposure and Retrieval for 3D Medical Image Question Answering
summary: Volumetric medical VQA requires reasoning over long and redundant 3D visual token sequences, especially in multi-sequence MRI where complementary modalities provide diverse diagnostic cues but expose the decoder to many repeated anatomical regions. To investigate reasoning under multi-sequence visual redundancy, we first introduce BreMRIs-VQA, a clinically curated breast MRI benchmark with 1.19M QA pairs from 71.0K sequences and 12.9K patients, covering both free-text and multiple-choice questions. We further propose SeVeR, a selective visual exposure framework that compresses dense volumes into modality-wise prototypes and retrieves complementary multi-level evidence with change-aware gated attention during decoding, trained with a marginal-utility self-consistency objective that suppresses unhelpful retrieval. Experiments on BreMRIs-VQA and public benchmarks show that SeVeR improves both discriminative and generative performance while exposing substantially fewer visual tokens.

AI.tldr: Introduces BreMRIs-VQA benchmark and SeVeR framework for multi-sequence volumetric MRI VQA; prototype-based compression and selective evidence retrieval with change-aware gated attention yield better QA with fewer visual tokens.
AI.motivation: Volumetric VQA for medical imaging must reason over long, redundant 3D sequences; multi-sequence MRI adds complementary cues but increases redundancy, hindering efficient decoding.
AI.method: Develop BreMRIs-VQA: a large breast MRI QA dataset (1.19M QA pairs, 71.0K sequences, 12.9K patients) with free-text and multiple-choice questions. Propose SeVeR: selective visual exposure that compresses dense volumes into modality-wise prototypes and retrieves multi-level evidence via change-aware gated attention during decoding; trained with marginal-utility self-consistency objective to suppress unhelpful retrieval.
AI.result: SeVeR yields improved discriminative and generative QA performance on BreMRIs-VQA and public benchmarks, while using substantially fewer visual tokens.
AI.conclusion: Selective exposure and prototype compression effectively reduce visual redundancy in multi-sequence volumetric VQA, enabling accurate QA with fewer tokens, demonstrating practical utility for clinical imaging analysis.

title: AsymSpec: Context-Asymmetric Speculative Decoding for Agentic LLMs
summary: Agentic LLM pipelines face escalating inference costs as context accumulates across retrieval, tool use, and multi-turn interactions. To control latency, deployments routinely compress inputs, but this degrades task accuracy. Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates generation losslessly, yet it assumes the drafter and verifier share an identical context, preventing SD from resolving the accuracy-overhead trade-off. We propose AsymSpec, an asymmetric speculative decoding framework that breaks this symmetry: a lightweight drafter reads the full input while the large verifier operates on the compressed view. The drafter steers the verifier via a contrastive $δ$-fusion of logits, modulated by a divergence-aware acceptance gate that preserves verification stability and high draft acceptance rates. Evaluated across four agentic capabilities and two end-to-end agent benchmarks, AsymSpec reaches $\approx 90\%$ of full-context accuracy on average, delivering $1.3$--$1.7\times$ throughput speedups at $0.2$--$0.3\times$ the compute cost on isolated text capabilities. These results show that asymmetric context access yields substantial gains precisely when compression discards critical reasoning signals.

AI.tldr: AsymSpec enables asymmetric speculative decoding: a small drafter reads the full input while a large verifier operates on a compressed view, achieving near full-context accuracy with notable throughput gains.
AI.motivation: To reduce latency and compute costs in agentic LLM pipelines where context accumulation from retrieval, tools, and long interactions degrades efficiency, and to overcome the limitation of standard speculative decoding which requires identical contexts.
AI.method: Introduce a contrastive delta-fusion (δ-fusion) of logits from the drafter and verifier, modulated by a divergence-aware acceptance gate to maintain verification stability; deploy an asymmetric setup where the drafter processes the full input and the verifier uses a compressed view.
AI.result: Across four agentic capabilities and two end-to-end benchmarks, AsymSpec reaches about 90% of full-context accuracy on average, with 1.3–1.7× throughput and 0.2–0.3× compute cost for isolated text capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric context access yields substantial gains by preserving critical reasoning signals during compression, enabling faster inference with minimal accuracy loss.

title: Refusal geometry reflects refusal training: diverse refusal prefixes can raise stable rank and weaken refusal vector ablation attacks
summary: Refusal training protects AI models from jailbreaks by training models to decline unsafe queries, reducing the risk of misuse. Recent work finds that refusal behavior in aligned language models can be mediated by a single activation direction or a low-dimensional refusal subspace shared across harmful prompts: ablating those directions suppresses refusals while largely preserves other model capabilities. Yet it remains unclear why safety-critical features in a wide range of models emerge and concentrated, low-dimensional structure. In a case study of OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct we find that the refusal geometry reflects refusal training: activation updates resulting from refusal-completion first-token losses explain the resulting refusal direction and refusal subspace. We study refusal directions through the training dynamics across refusal datasets and reveal that their brittleness is associated with repetitive refusal starts, which in turn is linked to concentration of gradients and refusal features in a low-dimensional subspace. Across frozen-model analyses and controlled synthetic fine-tuning, we find evidence of a hardening lever: diverse refusal starts can raise stable ranks of gradients and activation changes, making refusals harder to remove with a vector ablation attack.

AI.tldr: Refusal training induces a low-dimensional, robust subspace for safe responses; ablations of this subspace can suppress refusals while preserving other abilities, and the brittleness of refusals tracks training dynamics and gradient concentration across datasets and starts.
AI.motivation: To understand why safety-critical refusals emerge as a concentrated, low-dimensional structure across models and training regimes, and how this structure can be made more or less brittle.
AI.method: Case study on OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct; analyze refusal-related activation directions and first-token losses; examine training dynamics across refusal datasets; perform frozen-model analyses and controlled synthetic fine-tuning; apply vector ablations to study impact on refusals and other capabilities; assess gradient ranks and subspace concentration.
AI.result: Refusal geometry mirrors refusal training; activation updates from refusal-completion losses determine the refusal direction and subspace. Brittleness correlates with repetitive refusal starts and gradient concentration in a low-dimensional subspace. Across experiments, ablations suppress refusals while largely preserving other abilities; diverse refusal starts can raise stable gradient ranks, hardening refusals against vector ablation attacks.
AI.conclusion: Safety-critical refusal features appear as a concentrated, hard-to-remove low-dimensional subspace shaped by training dynamics. The findings reveal a lever (refusal start diversity) that can harden refusals, and provide a framework for diagnosing and potentially mitigating brittleness in safety mechanisms.

title: MAMA-FLUX.2: Image-to-Image Synthesis of Post-Contrast Breast DCE-MRI for the MAMA-SYNTH Challenge
summary: Dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI is central to cancer diagnosis and monitoring, but requires gadolinium-based contrast agents. In this work, we address pre-to-post contrast breast MRI synthesis for the MAMA-SYNTH challenge. We propose MAMA-FLUX.2, a conditional latent flow-matching approach based on FLUX.2-Klein-4B. The pre-contrast image is encoded as spatial conditioning, while the model predicts the flow field associated with the post-contrast target latent. To adapt the pretrained model efficiently, we use LoRA fine-tuning and introduce a regional training objective combining global flow matching, tumor-region supervision, and stable foreground regularization. We further investigate LoRA rank, intensity windowing, and regional loss weights on axial slices, prioritizing clinically relevant tumor-focused metrics. Our ablation study shows that moderate tumor and stable-foreground weighting improves the trade-off between image fidelity and tumor-region accuracy. The final model achieves the best overall balance with LoRA rank/$α=64/64$, $\mathrm{MHA}_{\max}=25$, $λ_{\mathrm{tumor}}=0.25$, and $λ_{\mathrm{stable}}=0.1$. These results demonstrate that compact pretrained rectified-flow transformers can be adapted for contrast-enhanced MRI synthesis using parameter-efficient fine-tuning and task-aware regional losses.

AI.tldr: Proposes MAMA-FLUX.2, a conditional latent flow-matching method for pre-to-post contrast breast MRI synthesis, achieving efficient adaptation via LoRA fine-tuning and region-aware losses with improved tumor-focused fidelity.
AI.motivation: Address the need for accurate post-contrast image synthesis while reducing gadolinium use, by leveraging pretrained rectified-flow transformers and parameter-efficient fine-tuning for tumor-focused MRI synthesis.
AI.method: Conditional latent flow-matching using FLUX.2-Klein-4B. Pre-contrast image serves as spatial conditioning; model predicts the post-contrast latent flow. Fine-tuning uses LoRA; employs a regional objective combining global flow matching, tumor-region supervision, and stable foreground regularization. Explores LoRA rank, intensity windowing, and regional loss weights on axial slices.
AI.result: Ablation shows moderate tumor and stable-foreground weighting improve the trade-off between image fidelity and tumor-region accuracy. Final settings: LoRA rank/α=64/64, MHA_max=25, λ_tumor=0.25, λ_stable=0.1; achieves best overall balance.
AI.conclusion: Compact pretrained rectified-flow transformers can be adapted for contrast-enhanced MRI synthesis via parameter-efficient fine-tuning and task-aware regional losses, enabling effective pre-to-post contrast synthesis with tumor-focused fidelity.

title: Imitation Learning for Connection-Tableau Construction
summary: An automated theorem prover builds a proof step by step, choosing at each point what to add and what to remove. We cast this construction as a policy acting in a transition system induced by a formal calculus, which fixes which steps are sound: for clausal connection tableaux, leanCoP-style search and plCoP/rlCoP-style planning then become stateful policies over one interface, and policy-learning methods apply directly. We equip such policies with a graph neural network that scores proof edits from structure that transfers across problems, train it by imitation learning from found proofs, and measure how performance holds as we remove search scaffolding, from full symbolic backtracking to a policy the network drives alone. Within a fixed step budget on M2k, MPTP2078-bushy, and TPTP v9.2.1, learned policies solve up to 46% more problems than leanCoP, and reach proofs in an order of magnitude fewer steps.

AI.tldr: Policy-based automated theorem proving using GNN-guided proof edits improves efficiency and problem-solving rate over leanCoP on standard benchmarks, achieving up to 46% more solved with fewer steps.
AI.motivation: To unify different theorem-proving strategies under a single policy interface and enable transfer of learning across problems by leveraging structural graph representations; and to reduce reliance on backtracking by learning effective proof-edit policies.
AI.method: Cast proof search as a policy in a transition system for clausal connection tableaux; employ a graph neural network to score proof edits derived from the problem structure; train the network via imitation learning from found proofs; evaluate under a fixed step budget across M2k, MPTP2078-bushy, and TPTP v9.2.1 and compare to leanCoP; analyze performance as search scaffolding is removed.
AI.result: Learned policies solve up to 46% more problems than leanCoP within the same step budget and reach proofs in an order of magnitude fewer steps; performance tracks as scaffolding is reduced.
AI.conclusion: Policy-guided, structure-aware proof search with imitation-trained GNN scoring yields significant gains and demonstrates transferability across benchmarks, approaching standalone policy performance with reduced backtracking.

title: Joint Initialization of Flux Networks and Effective Multiplication Factor for Physics-Informed Neural Networks Solving Neutron Diffusion Problems
summary: Efficient determination of the effective multiplication factor (keff) is an important computational task in reactor core neutronics analysis. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) incorporate neutron diffusion equations and boundary conditions into network training to efficiently determine the neutron flux distribution and keff. To further improve the efficiency of keff calculations using PINNs, a Joint Initialization Physics-Informed Neural Network (JI-PINN) is proposed in this work. In this method, a low-resolution approximate solution to the K-eigenvalue problem is used to construct a joint initial state for the flux network parameters and keff, and both are then jointly optimized under physical constraints. The proposed method was validated on a two-dimensional two-group two-material case, the IAEA 2D benchmark, a two-dimensional two-group four-material case, and a three-dimensional single-group case. For these test cases, the total computational time was reduced by 25.4%, 38.2%, 49.4%, and 28.9%, respectively, while comparable solution accuracy was maintained. The occurrence of anomalous results associated with marked deviations of keff from the reference value was also reduced. The proposed method provides a more efficient and robust initialization strategy for solving neutron diffusion K-eigenvalue problem with PINNs.

AI.tldr: JI-PINN uses a low-res K-eigenvalue approximation to jointly initialize flux network parameters and keff, yielding faster and more robust PINN-based keff solutions across multiple benchmarks with maintained accuracy.
AI.motivation: Improve speed and robustness of keff determination with PINNs by mitigating poor initialization and convergence issues through a joint initialization strategy.
AI.method: Compute a low-resolution approximate solution to the K-eigenvalue problem to form a joint initial state for the neural network parameters (flux) and keff, then jointly optimize the PINN under physics constraints for neutron diffusion with K-eigenvalue. Validate on 2D two-group two-material (IAEA 2D), 2D two-group four-material, and 3D single-group benchmarks.
AI.result: Total computational time reduced by 25.4%, 38.2%, 49.4%, and 28.9% across the four test cases, with comparable accuracy and fewer anomalous keff deviations.
AI.conclusion: JI-PINN provides a more efficient and robust initialization strategy for solving neutron diffusion K-eigenvalue problems with PINNs, improving convergence reliability and reducing computational cost.

title: Diffusion Transformers for Roof Graph Synthesis and Reconstruction
comment: Pre-review manuscript. Accepted at the ICPR 2026 Workshop on Pattern Recognition in Remote Sensing (PRRS)
summary: We present RoofDiT, a generative framework for 2D roof graph synthesis and reconstruction. Roofs are compactly described as planar graphs of junctions and structural edges, but existing methods often rely on fixed geometric rules or direct reconstruction objectives. RoofDiT instead models roof structures directly as vertex-edge graphs and learns a conditional generative prior over their geometry and connectivity. Our framework follows a two-stage design: a diffusion transformer generates roof vertices, and an edge prediction module infers the corresponding graph topology.
