To improve geometric fidelity, RoofDiT combines relative geometry-aware attention with footprint and aerial-image conditioning, while using an alignment regularizer to encourage common horizontal, vertical, and diagonal roof patterns. The same model supports unconditional generation, footprint-conditioned synthesis, and image-guided reconstruction by changing the conditioning signal. Experiments show improved graph generation quality over a diffusion baseline, favorable performance against a straight-skeleton prior in the footprint-conditioned setting, and the highest edge F1 among compared methods for image-guided reconstruction.

AI.tldr: RoofDiT presents a two-stage generative framework that models roofs as vertex-edge graphs. A diffusion transformer first generates roof vertices, then an edge predictor infers topology, guided by footprint/images and aided by a geometry-aware attention and an alignment regularizer. It achieves strong performance in pure graph generation, footprint-conditioned synthesis, and image-guided reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Current roof modeling often relies on fixed geometric rules or direct reconstruction objectives, limiting variability and fidelity. A graph-based, generative approach with conditioning on realistic cues (footprints, aerial images) can better capture diverse roof layouts and common architectural patterns.
AI.method: A two-stage model: (1) diffusion transformer to generate roof vertices (nodes), and (2) an edge prediction module to infer the graph topology. Enhancements include relative geometry-aware attention, conditioning on footprint and aerial images, and an alignment regularizer encouraging axis-aligned patterns (horizontal/vertical/diagonal). The framework supports unconditional generation, footprint-conditioned synthesis, and image-guided reconstruction by changing conditioning signals.
AI.result: Compared to a diffusion baseline, RoofDiT yields higher-quality graph generation. In footprint-conditioned settings, it outperforms a straight-skeleton prior. For image-guided reconstruction, it achieves the highest edge F1 among evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: RoofDiT demonstrates that modeling roofs as vertex-edge graphs with a conditional generative prior and geometry-aware conditioning yields robust, versatile roof synthesis and reconstruction across unconditional, footprint-conditioned, and image-guided tasks.

title: Trace Integrity for LLM Data Agents: A Vision for Auditable Structured Reasoning in Real-World Systems
summary: Answer accuracy is an insufficient reliability signal for LLM data agents. In structured-data tasks, a benchmark-correct answer can be produced by an invalid trace. This paper introduces Trace Integrity, a deployment reliability criterion for evaluating whether the computation recorded behind an answer is explicit, executable, schema-valid, operator-faithful, replayable, answer-consistent, and auditable. We identify the Structure Gap as the deployment failure mode that makes Trace Integrity necessary: natural-language reasoning and free-form rationales do not reliably specify the operator-level programs required by real-world systems. We operationalize Trace Integrity with execution contracts, structured artifacts that bind user intent to schema elements, operator plans, assumptions, executable queries, verification status, and final-answer linkage. We also introduce CAIT (Correct Answer / Invalid Trace) Rate, which measures how often answer-only evaluation counts computationally unsupported outputs as successes. In an empirical demonstration on BIRD Mini-Dev, Direct SQL, Operation Summary + SQL, and Contract-First SQL achieve answer accuracies of 20%, 22%, and 24%, while their Trace Integrity Pass Rates are 39%, 43%, and 40% and their CAIT Rates remain high at 55%, 59.1%, and 45.8%, showing that answer accuracy, trace validity, and silent-failure risk are distinct evaluation signals. Real-world LLM data agents should, therefore, be evaluated not only by whether their outputs match a reference answer, but by whether those outputs are backed by auditable computation.

AI.tldr: Trace Integrity framework defines a deployment reliability criterion for LLM data agents, using execution contracts and CAIT rate to ensure auditable, executable traces beyond plain answer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Answer accuracy alone is unreliable as a signal; a Structure Gap exists between natural-language reasoning and operator-level programs, risking silent failures in real-world systems.
AI.method: Define Trace Integrity criteria (explicit, executable, schema-valid, operator-faithful, replayable, answer-consistent, auditable); implement execution contracts binding user intent to schema elements, operator plans, assumptions, executable queries, verification status, and final-answer linkage; propose CAIT (Correct Answer / Invalid Trace) Rate; evaluate on BIRD Mini-Dev, Direct SQL, Operation Summary + SQL, and Contract-First SQL.
AI.result: Across setups—BIRD Mini-Dev (20% accuracy, TI Pass 39%), Direct SQL (22% accuracy, TI Pass 43%), Operation Summary + SQL (24% accuracy, TI Pass 40%) with CAIT rates of 55%, 59.1%, and 45.8% respectively—the Trace Integrity framework and CAIT rate reveal that answer accuracy, trace validity, and silent-failure risk are distinct signals.
AI.conclusion: Real-world evaluation of LLM data agents should include trace-backed auditable computation, not solely reference-answer matching.

title: Resolving Multi-Modal Regression by Difference-Quotient-Based Clustering:Fast Coarse Conditional-Label Assignment
summary: Multimodal regression suffers from the mean-collapse pathology: under squared loss, an unconstrained regressor converges to the conditional mean, which for K > 1 lies away from all modes. We attribute this failure to pairwise contradictions--samples with nearly identical inputs but distant outputs--and propose Difference-Quotient Clustering (DQC), which partitions data to minimize intra-cluster output-vs-input discrepancy. Each sample is assigned to the cluster that minimizes its maximum contradiction ratio; a logits generator and a conditional network are then trained on the resulting labels. Since the generating modality is unknown at test time, we evaluate via minimum squared error (minMSE) against all K true outputs. On synthetic benchmarks (K=5, 10), DQC achieves test minMSE 0.19 (K=5, nx=500), versus 0.09 for an oracle, 1.08 for random labels, and 1.33 for mean collapse. We observe two empirical regularities: larger intra-cluster contradictions require deeper networks, and oracle labels generalize from fewer samples than cluster-derived equivalents. The clustering is a hard, parallelizable O(n^2/2) front-end for coarse conditional assignment, reducing the burden of downstream generative refinement. A second-stage re-clustering on residual errors is outlined as future work.

AI.tldr: Proposes Difference-Quotient Clustering (DQC) to mitigate mean-collapse in multimodal regression by hard clustering samples to minimize maximum input-output contradiction, then train a logits generator and a conditional network on cluster labels; evaluated via minMSE against all K true outputs, showing improvement on synthetic benchmarks but still below an oracle, and outlining a path for future work with residual re-clustering.
AI.motivation: Mean-collapse under squared loss causes regressors to converge to the conditional mean in multimodal regression. The paper aims to restore multimodal fidelity by partitioning data into coherent modes before learning conditional mappings.
AI.method: Hard, parallelizable clustering that minimizes intra-cluster output-vs-input discrepancy via the maximum contradiction ratio per sample. Assign each sample to the cluster minimizing this ratio. Train a logits generator and a conditional network on the resulting cluster labels. At test time, evaluate using minMSE across all K true outputs since the generating modality is unknown.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmarks with K=5 and K=10, DQC achieves minMSE of 0.19 (vs oracle 0.09, random labels 1.08, mean collapse 1.33). Observed regularities: larger intra-cluster contradictions require deeper networks; oracle labels generalize from fewer samples than cluster-derived labels. Clustering acts as a coarse front-end (O(n^2)) for conditional assignment; potential second-stage re-clustering on residuals is proposed.
AI.conclusion: DQC provides a practical front-end to reduce mean-collapse in multimodal regression by separating modalities via clustering before learning, with promising results on synthetic data and clear directions for improving accuracy and integrating residual refinement.

title: Towards Purified Multi-Label Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has been widely explored in single-label recognition, effectively mitigating distribution shifts, especially when combined with vision-language models. However, real-world images often contain multiple objects, while the more practical multi-label test-time adaptation (MLTTA) has received little attention so far. Recent cache-based TTA methods have shown promising efficiency and effectiveness, yet directly extending them to multi-label scenarios suffers from a one-to-many mapping problem: a shared global representation entangling co-occurring objects is stored as class-wise cache prototypes, inducing dominant-label bias and compromised cache calibration. While introducing region-level cues helps isolate class-specific evidence, such regional evidence can also be unreliable under distribution shifts, making its identification and utilization non-trivial. To address these issues, we introduce PuRF, a novel PuRiFication-driven cache-based method for multi-label test-time adaptation of vision-language models. Specifically, PuRF first performs region purification to identify reliable regions, providing comprehensive regional cues for multi-label recognition and enabling fine-grained alignment. Based on these purified regions, PuRF conducts cache purification to enhance cache representation and adaptability, where episodic purification builds a discriminative region-based cache, and temporal refreshing further promotes long-term cache adaptability. Experiments demonstrate that PuRF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a notable 4.05% mAP improvement on ViT-B/32 across five datasets.

AI.tldr: PuRF introduces region purification and cache purification to address one-to-many mapping in multi-label test-time adaptation (MLTTA) for vision–language models, improving alignment between region-level cues and class prototypes.
AI.motivation: MLTTA suffers from co-occurring objects being entangled in a shared global cache, leading to dominant-label bias and poor cache calibration; region-level cues can help but may be unreliable under distribution shifts.
AI.method: PuRF identifies reliable regions via region purification, then builds a region-based cache. Episodic purification creates a discriminative region cache; temporal refreshing maintains long-term cache adaptability.
AI.result: PuRF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods, achieving 4.05% mAP improvement on ViT-B/32 across five datasets.
AI.conclusion: Region-purification-driven cache purification effectively enables fine-grained alignment for MLTTA in vision–language models, yielding robust performance under distribution shifts.

title: SwarmWorld: Stigmergic technological evolution in societies of language-model agents
summary: Collective intelligence can emerge when individuals coordinate through a shared environment, allowing local actions to accumulate into durable social organization. Language-model agents offer a new substrate for this process, yet most multi-agent systems rely on direct conversation, predefined roles, or centralized workflows. It remains unclear whether decentralized agents can build functional technologies and outperform independent search. Here, initially homogeneous LLM agents in SwarmWorld self-organize without assigned roles or recipes into evolving technological societies. Agents explore a spatial environment, process resources, test materials, construct persistent artifacts, and write executable controllers evaluated by a deterministic simulator under unseen disturbances after the agents are removed. SwarmWorld splits cognition from consequence: agents propose architectures and controllers within fixed action and material schemas, while the simulated world determines function. Shared societies develop broader, more resilient technological portfolios than a strong best-of-N isolated-search baseline, although isolated search remains competitive for the strongest artifact. Agents differentiate into exploration, construction, maintenance, and coordination behaviors, transitioning as the world matures. Technologies accumulate through collaborative construction, executable inheritance, and persistent agent-artifact networks, with most reuse beginning through physical observation rather than communication. Explicit cultural mechanisms amplify collaboration and organization, but functional benefits depend on outcome and timescale. Physical stigmergy alone supports capable societies, while interaction drives persistent technological ecologies rather than universally superior individual inventions.

AI.tldr: Decentralized LLM agents in SwarmWorld self-organize into enduring technocultural ecologies; they outperform isolated search in portfolio breadth and resilience, though not universally superior for the top artifact.
AI.motivation: Examine whether decentralized, role-free LLM agent collectives can generate functional technologies and how environmental interactions and culture influence collective intelligence.
AI.method: Homogeneous LLM agents in a fixed action/material world explore resources, test materials, construct artifacts, and generate executable controllers; a deterministic simulator assesses function under disturbances after removal; artifacts are persistent; reuse via observation; cultural mechanisms influence collaboration; stigmergy links actions and outcomes.
AI.result: Shared societies yield broader, more resilient technology portfolios compared to best-of-N isolated search; strongest artifact remains competitive with isolation; agents differentiate into exploration, construction, maintenance, coordination; technology accumulation through collaborative construction and inheritance; most reuse driven by physical observation; explicit culture amplifies collaboration; physical stigmergy suffices to support capable societies; interaction drives persistent techno-ecologies rather than universal superiority of individuals.
AI.conclusion: Decentralized, stigmergy-enabled LLM agent systems can cultivate durable, distributed technologies and ecologies, with benefits dependent on timescale and contextual factors.

title: A Storage-Retrieval Gap in Parametric Knowledge Graph Memory
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables, accepted at SKGi 2026
summary: Graph retrieval-augmented generation places retrieved subgraphs into the model's context window at query time, paying a recurring token cost and exposing source data on every call. We study an alternative: compiling a knowledge graph offline into a bank of LoRA adapters, one per entity, that serve as a parametric knowledge layer queried by injecting weights rather than text, at zero query-time context cost. On the MetaQA dataset, we find that subgraph-trained adapters encode context-free factual knowledge that generalizes to unseen questions: on single-valued relations the adapter gains $+0.243$ exact-match score over a base model that is nearly blind closed-book ($0.007$), and only the correct adapter recovers this knowledge (an oracle gap of $+0.283$ over the base model). However, the stored knowledge is not recoverable by similarity: given a query with no subgraph, embedding-based and weight-space geometry retrieval both perform at chance, because a semantically neighbouring entity's adapter does not contain the answer - knowledge is stored locally and does not transfer. Weight geometry correlates with subgraph semantics ($ρ= +0.329$) but not with functional retrievability. We quantify the byte and context-token costs against graph retrieval-augmented generation and discuss deployment implications. Our results establish that parametric knowledge graph memory is feasible for storing knowledge, and identify selecting and composing the right adapters by a mechanism other than semantic similarity as the central open problem - motivating a learned, query-conditioned composition mechanism.

AI.tldr: Offline parametric knowledge storage using per-entity LoRA adapters enables zero-cost query-time knowledge retrieval, but knowledge is local and not transferable via similarity; requires a non-semantic-similarity adapter-composition mechanism.
AI.motivation: Reduce query-time token cost and data exposure of retrieved graphs by storing knowledge in model parameters; evaluate feasibility and limitations of parametric memory vs graph retrieval.
AI.method: Compile a knowledge graph offline into a bank of LoRA adapters (one per entity) and query by injecting weights instead of text; evaluate on MetaQA; compare against subgraph retrieval approaches; analyze transferability, retrieval methods, and costs.
AI.result: Adapters improve exact-match on single-valued relations (+0.243 EM vs base model 0.007); only the correct adapter recovers knowledge (oracle gap +0.283). Stored knowledge is not recoverable by similarity: retrieval by embedding-based or weight-space methods fails when no subgraph is present. Weight-space geometry correlates with subgraph semantics (ρ = +0.329) but not with retrievability. quantifies byte and context-token costs; parametric memory is feasible; the central open problem is how to select/compose adapters without relying on semantic similarity.
AI.conclusion: Parametric knowledge graph memory is feasible, but effective adapter selection and composition require a mechanism beyond semantic similarity; this motivates learning a query-conditioned composition strategy.

title: Deep Learning Segmentation of Diffusion-Weighted MRI Acute Ischaemic Stroke: A Pragmatic Evaluation Across Three Datasets
summary:
Objective: Diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI-MRI) is the gold standard for visualizing and quantifying acute ischaemic stroke (AIS). Although deep learning methods can accurately segment AIS lesions, the optimal image inputs and model architecture remain uncertain. We evaluated whether accurate AIS lesion segmentation can be achieved using a pragmatic deep learning approach with minimal preprocessing and clinically feasible inference times.
  Materials and Methods: Self-configured nnU-Net models were trained on 1,744 DWI cases from local, national, and open-access datasets and tested on 436 cases. Four experimental conditions were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation: with or without brain extraction and using either DWI alone or DWI plus apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images as inputs. Two architectures were compared: the baseline nnU-Net (base) and a residual encoder nnU-Net (ResEnc). Performance was benchmarked against the DeepISLES ensemble model from the 2022 ISLES challenge.
  Results: In the test set (n=436), the base model achieved a median (IQR) Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.84 (0.19). For the base model, only two of six pairwise comparisons between input configurations showed significant differences. ResEnc produced small but significant improvements in DSC compared with the base model for DWI, DWI+brain extraction, and DWI+ADC inputs (all p<0.02), but not for DWI+ADC+brain extraction (p>0.50). The base model significantly outperformed DeepISLES, particularly in patients with smaller infarct volumes (signed-rank test, p<0.01).
  Conclusions: A baseline nnU-Net trained on DWI alone, without preprocessing, enabled fast and accurate AIS lesion segmentation. This streamlined approach may facilitate clinical research and support acute stroke imaging workflows

AI.tldr: A practical DWI-based AIS lesion segmentation using a baseline nnU-Net (DWI only, no preprocessing) achieves high accuracy (median DSC ~0.84) with fast inference; adding residual encoder offers limited gains; base model outperforms DeepISLES, especially for small infarcts, enabling streamlined clinical workflows.
AI.motivation: Determine whether accurate AIS lesion segmentation can be achieved with minimal preprocessing and clinically feasible inference times, by identifying effective input configurations and architectures.
AI.method: Train self-configured nnU-Net models on 1,744 DWI cases from local, national, and open-access datasets; test on 436 cases. Evaluate four input conditions (with/without brain extraction; DWI vs DWI+ADC) using five-fold cross-validation. Compare baseline nnU-Net (base) to residual encoder nnU-Net (ResEnc). Benchmark against DeepISLES ensemble from the 2022 ISLES challenge.
AI.result: In the test set (n=436), base model achieved median DSC 0.84 (IQR 0.19). Among input configurations, only two of six pairwise comparisons were significant for the base model. ResEnc produced small but significant DSC improvements over the base for DWI, DWI+brain extraction, and DWI+ADC inputs (p<0.02), but not for DWI+ADC+brain extraction (p>0.50). The base model significantly outperformed DeepISLES, particularly in patients with smaller infarct volumes (p<0.01).
AI.conclusion: A baseline nnU-Net trained on DWI alone, without preprocessing, enables fast and accurate AIS lesion segmentation, supporting clinical research and acute stroke imaging workflows.

title: Planetary Prediction Engine: Autonomous Geospatial Prediction via Intelligent Data Selection and Foundation Model Embeddings
summary: Addressing critical global challenges, from food security and disaster risk to disease outbreaks and socio-economic vulnerability, demands high-fidelity geospatial modeling. However, building predictive planetary models remains bottlenecked by a fragmented data ecosystem, requiring manual data retrieval, multimodal data curation and fusion along with iterative model selection. We present the Planetary Prediction Engine (PPE), an autonomous AI system that executes this end-to-end workflow directly from natural-language queries. PPE synthesizes multimodal datasets on the fly, retrieving spatiotemporally relevant covariates across open-web and Earth observation platforms (Data Commons, Google Earth Engine) and fusing them with geospatial foundation model embeddings (PDFM, AlphaEarth). Simultaneously, it searches over task-tailored model architecture families with automated overfitting guards. Across diverse tasks, geographies, and scientific domains, PPE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art or manually tuned expert baselines. For US spatial regression, PPE improves mean $R^2$ across 21 CDC health indicators (76.8% vs. 60.0%), FEMA national risk indices (64.9% vs. 60.0%), and the Social Vulnerability Index (66.2% vs. 58.6%). For spatial downscaling in data-scarce settings, PPE integrates localized proxies to double baseline accuracy in Nigerian food security indicators ($R^2$ of 66.1% vs. 31.5%). For epidemiological nowcasting of the 2026 DRC Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, PPE achieves a Recall@10 of 83.3% (identifying 15 of 18 newly invaded health zones across five weekly forecasts), a +10.3 percentage-point improvement over the public state-of-the-art modeling (~73%). By combining autonomous multimodal planetary data discovery with targeted model optimization, PPE lowers the technical barrier to planetary-scale analytics, enabling rapid, customized, expert-level deployment.

AI.tldr: Autonomous PPE system for end-to-end planetary prediction using multimodal data fusion and model search; achieves state-of-the-art improvements across health, disaster risk, and food security tasks.
AI.motivation: Fragmented, manual data collection and model tuning impede scalable, high-fidelity geospatial predictions; an autonomous system could streamline data discovery, integration, and model selection from natural language prompts.
AI.method: Retrieves spatiotemporal covariates from open web and EO platforms (Data Commons, GEE), fuses with geospatial foundation model embeddings (PDFM, AlphaEarth), and performs automated architecture search with overfitting guards; operates from NL queries to deliver end-to-end predictions.
AI.result: Consistent performance gains: US spatial regression metrics improved (CDC indicators R^2: 76.8% vs 60.0%; FEMA: 64.9% vs 60.0%; SVI: 66.2% vs 58.6%). Nigerian food security R^2 66.1% vs 31.5%. Ebola nowcasting Recall@10 83.3% (15/18) vs ~73%.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous multimodal data discovery coupled with targeted model optimization lowers barriers to planetary-scale analytics, enabling rapid, expert-level deployments across domains.

title: FedQoS: Federated QoS-Risk Learning for Heterogeneous Indoor-Outdoor Access Selection
comment: Accepted at the IEEE PIMRC 2026 Workshop on Intelligent Aerial and Spaceborne Systems for 6G (6G-SAGA): AI Native SAGIN for Indoor, Personal, and Mobile Radio Communications, 7 pages, 3 figures
summary: Reliable access selection in dynamic and heterogeneous indoor-outdoor environments is challenging because instantaneous radio measurements alone cannot capture future QoS degradation caused by mobility, blockage, traffic load, and resource competition. This paper proposes FedQoS, a federated QoS-risk learning framework for predicting the future reliability of candidate access links and supporting access-node selection without centralizing user-level network data. In FedQoS, each access node locally learns from its observed network logs, including radio, traffic, load, and service-context features, while a global QoS-risk predictor is trained through federated aggregation. The learned model estimates the probability of QoS failure for each candidate link, and the controller uses these risk scores to select reliable access nodes under dynamic network conditions. To evaluate the framework, we construct physics-based synthetic indoor-outdoor wireless datasets using the Sionna framework, covering normal traffic, mobility, event-driven congestion, and non-IID client observations. Simulation results show that learning-based access selection substantially reduces the QoS-failure rate compared with signal-based and historical-QoS heuristic methods. FedQoS achieves near-centralized predictive performance and provides clear reliability gains under mild non-IID data while remaining competitive under the more challenging severe non-IID condition. These results demonstrate the potential of federated QoS-risk learning for reliable, data-local access selection in dynamic wireless environments.

AI.tldr: FedQoS: federated QoS-risk learning for predictive access-node selection in dynamic wireless environments, achieving near-centralized performance while preserving data locality.
AI.motivation: Reliably selecting access nodes is hard due to mobility, blockage, traffic load, and resource competition; instantaneous radio metrics fail to capture future QoS degradation and user data privacy concerns; need privacy-preserving, scalable predictions under non-IID data.
AI.method: Each access node trains local models on local logs (radio, traffic, load, service context). A global QoS-risk predictor is trained via federated aggregation. The model outputs QoS failure probability for candidate links; a controller uses risk scores to pick reliable access nodes. Evaluation uses Sionna-based synthetic indoor-outdoor datasets with variations; non-IID settings.
AI.result: FedQoS reduces QoS-failure rate compared with signal-based and historical-QoS heuristics; achieves near-centralized predictive performance under mild non-IID and remains competitive under severe non-IID.
AI.conclusion: Federated QoS-risk learning is a promising approach for reliable, privacy-preserving access selection in dynamic wireless environments; it yields data-local learning with strong performance, validated on synthetic datasets.

title: CloSeR: Unified Relational Distillation from Closed-Set Teachers for Category Discovery
comment: Accepted as a conference paper at ECCV 2026
summary: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) is an intriguing open-world problem that has garnered increasing attention: given partially labelled data, the goal is to correctly recognize known classes while discovering coherent novel categories from unlabelled samples. Recent GCD methods typically adapt foundation models by jointly optimizing supervised classification and unsupervised discovery objectives on mixed labelled and unlabelled data. While effective, this coupled training can entangle closed-set recognition and open-set discovery, leading to objective conflict and biased predictions, and may disturb the semantic geometry of pretrained representations under limited labels and noisy pseudo-labels. We propose CloSeR, a simple plug-and-play framework that injects Closed-Set Relational knowledge into GCD training. CloSeR first builds a domain-adapted closed-set teacher by tuning lightweight block-wise adapters on labelled known-class data while keeping the foundation model backbone frozen, thereby preserving pretrained priors at low training cost. It then transfers the teacher's knowledge to downstream GCD via Unified Relational Distillation (URD), which distills complementary global sample-to-prototype relations to anchor known-class semantics and local sample-to-sample relations to preserve neighborhood structure, using separate feature pathways to reduce optimization interference. CloSeR is head-agnostic and readily integrates with both parametric and non-parametric GCD methods. Extensive experiments with DINO and DINOv2 backbones on six benchmarks (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, CUB, Stanford-Cars, and FGVC-Aircraft) show consistent gains over GCD baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Project page: https://visual-ai.github.io/closer/

AI.tldr: CloSeR introduces Unified Relational Distillation (URD) to Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) by injecting a closed-set teacher derived from lightweight adapters into pretrained backbones. It distills global sample-to-prototype and local sample-to-sample relations via separate pathways, achieving plug-and-play, state-of-the-art GCD across six benchmarks with DINO/DINOv2 backbones.
AI.motivation: GCD jointly optimizes supervised and unsupervised objectives on mixed data, causing objective conflict between closed-set recognition and open-set discovery and potentially distorting pretrained geometry, especially with limited labels and noisy pseudo-labels.
AI.method: 1) Train lightweight block adapters on labelled known-class data to create a domain-adapted closed-set teacher while freezing the backbone. 2) Apply Unified Relational Distillation (URD) to transfer teacher knowledge to GCD: (a) global relations via sample-to-prototype distillation anchoring known-class semantics, (b) local relations via sample-to-sample distillation preserving neighborhood structure. Uses separate feature pathways to reduce optimization interference and is head-agnostic, compatible with both parametric and non-parametric GCD methods.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, CUB, Stanford-Cars, FGVC-Aircraft with DINO and DINOv2 backbones show consistent improvements over GCD baselines and achieve state-of-the-art performance; project page provided.
AI.conclusion: CloSeR effectively mitigates the coupled training issue in GCD by injecting closed-set relational knowledge through a lightweight, plug-and-play URD framework, preserving pretrained geometry while enhancing known-class semantics and neighborhood structure, with broad compatibility across GCD methods.

title: Resilient Decentralized Wireless Federated Learning via Gradient Tracking with AdamW
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE Global Communications Conference (GLOBECOM 2026), IoT and Sensor Networks Symposium, 7 pages, 5 figures
summary: Wireless Internet-of-Things (IoT) edge networks require decentralized learning (DecL) methods that can operate reliably under both heterogeneous local data and communication-constrained wireless links. However, existing decentralized optimization schemes often incur substantial communication overhead and degraded performance when transmissions are constrained by strict airtime budgets, fading channels, and packet losses. This paper proposes QEF-GT-AdamW, a communication-efficient and outage-resilient algorithm for DecL over wireless communication (WCom) networks. The proposed method combines gradient tracking to mitigate the effect of non-IID data, AdamW-based adaptive optimization to improve training stability, and dual-stream biased quantization with error feedback to reduce communication payloads for both model and tracking exchanges. To address unreliable broadcast communication, the proposed framework further employs a local fallback strategy when scheduled packets are not successfully received. We explicitly model the effect of bandwidth, transmit power, airtime constraints, and fading channels on DecL performance, and establish convergence guarantees for the proposed algorithm under compressed and unreliable wireless communication. Experimental results on heterogeneous MNIST and CIFAR-10 settings show that QEF-GT-AdamW consistently improves robustness and convergence performance over representative DecL baselines while achieving favorable accuracy-communication trade-offs under limited wireless resources.

AI.tldr: QEF-GT-AdamW is a communication-efficient, outage-resilient decentralised learning algorithm for wireless IoT edge networks, combining gradient tracking, AdamW optimization, and dual-stream biased quantization with error feedback, plus local fallback, achieving convergence guarantees and better accuracy-communication performance under constrained wireless links.
AI.motivation: There is a need for decentralized learning in wireless IoT edge networks that operate under non-IID local data and strict communication constraints (bandwidth, airtime, fading, packet loss). Existing methods incur high communication overhead or fail to converge reliably under such constraints.
AI.method: Propose QEF-GT-AdamW: integrate gradient tracking to mitigate non-IID data effects; use AdamW-based adaptive optimization for training stability; apply dual-stream biased quantization with error feedback to reduce payloads for model and tracking exchanges; incorporate a local fallback strategy for unreliable broadcast; explicitly model bandwidth, transmit power, airtime, and fading, and prove convergence under compressed and unreliable wireless communication.
AI.result: Experimental results on heterogeneous MNIST and CIFAR-10 show that QEF-GT-AdamW improves robustness and convergence over representative DecL baselines and achieves favorable accuracy-communication trade-offs under limited wireless resources.
AI.conclusion: The framework delivers robust, efficient decentralized learning in wireless edge networks with provable convergence guarantees and practical performance gains under bandwidth and reliability constraints.

title: Unsupervised Anatomical Feature Learning via Diffusion Models: Enhanced Medical Image Segmentation with Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Submitted for peer review
summary: Acquiring pixel-level annotations for medical image segmentation is a severe bottleneck. Traditional U-Net architectures, while effective, learn local texture patterns and lack awareness of global anatomical structures, leading to boundary delineation failures in low-data regimes. This research paper proposes utilizing unsupervised Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) to extract anatomical features. We train a DDPM on 21 unlabeled abdominal CT scans to learn structural representations, transferring the encoder weights to a downstream segmentation task evaluated on the BTCV multi-organ dataset. Diffusion pretraining significantly improved liver segmentation: Dice increased from $0.75\pm0.36$ to $0.93\pm0.16$ ($p < 5.33\times10^{-26}$, 0.529 Cohen's d), Average Surface Distance (ASD) decreased by 66%, and 95th-percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95) reduced by 45%. For kidney segmentation, Dice improved from $0.90\pm0.19$ to $0.95\pm0.10$ ($p < 4.01\times10^{-11}$). Multi-organ pooled performance showed a 68% variance reduction and a 74% improvement in boundary precision (Dice $0.95\pm0.07$). Crucially, frozen encoder models retained > 80% of fine-tuned performance without exposure to segmentation labels, proving the existence of learned anatomical priors. In low-data scenarios, diffusion-pretrained models maintained robust performance with only 50% (Dice: 0.92 liver, 0.94 kidney), 25%, and even 10% (Dice: 0.89 liver, 0.71 kidney) of labeled data. Using unlabeled images for diffusion-based pretraining successfully embeds robust anatomical features prior to human supervision, transforming U-Nets into anatomy-aware systems.

AI.tldr: Diffusion pretraining on 21 unlabeled abdominal CTs yields anatomy-aware segmentation, boosting liver/kidney Dice and enabling good performance with limited labeled data by transferring encoder weights from a DDPM to a U-Net.
AI.motivation: Pixel-level annotation is expensive; traditional U-Nets rely on local textures and struggle with global anatomical structures, especially in low-data regimes. Unsupervised diffusion pretraining aims to learn structural anatomical priors.
AI.method: Train a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) on 21 unlabeled abdominal CT scans to learn structural representations. Transfer the encoder weights to a downstream segmentation task evaluated on the BTCV multi-organ dataset. Assess performance with Dice, ASD, and HD95, and examine low-data regimes (50%, 25%, 10% labeled data). Freeze encoder to evaluate retention of segmentation performance without labels.
AI.result: Liver Dice improved from 0.75±0.36 to 0.93±0.16 (p<5.33e-26; Cohen's d=0.529); ASD reduced by 66%; HD95 reduced by 45%. Kidney Dice improved from 0.90±0.19 to 0.95±0.10 (p<4.01e-11). Multi-organ Dice 0.95±0.07 with 68% variance reduction and 74% improvement in boundary precision. Frozen encoders retained >80% of fine-tuned performance without segmentation labels. In low-data regimes, with 50%, 25%, and 10% labeled data, Dice for liver/kidney remained robust (e.g., 0.92 liver, 0.94 kidney at 50%; 0.89 liver, 0.71 kidney at 10%).
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled diffusion pretraining embeds robust anatomical priors, transforming U-Nets into anatomy-aware systems and enabling strong segmentation performance with limited labeled data.

title: Reflection Steering: Disentangling Reflection from Reasoning in Activation Space for Token-Efficient Inference
summary: Large reasoning models often produce reasoning traces with verification, revision, and backtracking. When reflection merely re-checks established results, it wastes reasoning tokens and increases latency. Most existing reflection steering methods add a label-derived mean-difference direction across preset layers, but its entanglement with reasoning and length signals destabilizes the accuracy-efficiency trade-off. In this paper, we propose Reflection Steering, a training-free framework for controlling reflection-associated computation within LLMs by disentangling reflection-related activations from general reasoning. Specifically, we contrast reflective and non-reflective hidden states at each LLM layer, denoise the resulting reflection directions with PCA, and orthogonalize them against general-reasoning directions. To limit downstream amplification from early-layer interventions, we calibrate each layer across multiple intervention strengths on a small set, retain only stable layers, and apply bounded projection removal to their residual-stream activations. We conduct extensive experiments across two public benchmarks and three open-weight LLMs against state-of-the-art activation-steering baselines. Results show that Reflection Steering reduces reasoning tokens by 16.9% on average across six matched settings. Besides, our method further introduces a bounded reflection intervention-strength parameter $α$, enabling deployment-time adjustment to balance token savings, accuracy, and generation stability.

AI.tldr: Training-free Reflection Steering disentangles reflection activations from general reasoning in LLMs, using per-layer reflective state comparison, PCA denoising, and orthogonalization, with bounded projection and an adjustable alpha. It achieves a 16.9% average reduction in reasoning tokens and stable performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing reflection methods entangle reflection with reasoning and length signals, causing efficiency-accuracy trade-offs. A disentangled, data-efficient steering mechanism is needed to control reflection without degrading performance.
AI.method: For each LLM layer, contrast reflective vs non-reflective hidden states; derive reflection directions; denoise via PCA; orthogonalize against general reasoning directions; calibrate across multiple intervention strengths to identify stable layers; retain stable layers; apply bounded projection removal to residual-stream activations; introduce a deploy-time alpha parameter to adjust intervention strength.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on two public benchmarks and three open-weight LLMs shows average 16.9% reduction in reasoning tokens across six matched settings, outperforming state-of-the-art activation-steering baselines.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, controllable reflection mechanism that disentangles reflection from general reasoning yields substantive token savings while maintaining stability; PCA-based denoising, layer selection, and bounded projections mitigate entanglement and runaway effects, with an adjustable deployment parameter α.

title: Skeleton-based Zero-Shot Spatio-Temporal Action Localization via Weakly-Supervised Pretraining
summary: We propose a novel pretraining strategy for skeleton-based zero-shot spatio-temporal action localization to estimate unseen actions for person instances while overcoming high annotation costs for training via new target actions and pretraining using large-scale action scenery datasets. Specifically, our approach, termed Skeleton-Language feature Pooling Switching, introduces a weakly-supervised vision-language pretraining mechanism. This mechanism transitions pooling kernels from pretraining, which aggregates skeleton features at the video level and aligns them with each video's known action text embeddings, to the inference phase that computes instance-level features without training via target actions. Furthermore, we propose Scene-Mixed Discriminative Contrastive Learning to distinguish actions at the instance level within the combined scene through the MIL framework. Our experiments on four public spatio-temporal action localization and classification datasets demonstrate that the proposed method effectively addresses annotation limitations.

AI.tldr: A weakly-supervised vision-language pretraining framework for skeleton-based zero-shot spatio-temporal action localization, featuring Skeleton-Language feature Pooling Switching (from video-level to instance-level pooling) and Scene-Mixed Discriminative Contrastive Learning within MIL, achieving effective performance with reduced annotation cost on four datasets.
AI.motivation: To address the high annotation burden in spatio-temporal action localization and enable zero-shot recognition by leveraging large-scale action-scene data and cross-modal (vision-language) cues that align skeletal representations with textual action descriptions.
AI.method: 1) Skeleton-Language feature Pooling Switching: pretrain with pooling kernels that aggregate skeleton features at the video level and align with each video's textual action embedding; at inference, switch to instance-level pooling without training on target actions. 2) Scene-Mixed Discriminative Contrastive Learning: discriminates actions at the instance level within a mixed-scene context using a Multiple-Instance Learning (MIL) framework.
AI.result: Reportedly effective in mitigating annotation limitations, with experiments on four public spatio-temporal action localization and classification datasets showing positive results for zero-shot or low-annotation scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The approach presents a viable path to reduce labeling costs while enabling zero-shot spatio-temporal action localization for skeleton-based representations, validated across multiple datasets.

title: Interpreting Protein Language Model Embeddings via Orthogonal Projection for Protein Fitness Prediction
summary: Recently, there has been a growing adoption of protein language models (PLMs) in biomedical science. Their embeddings provide a rich numerical representation of protein sequences which achieve state-of-the-art performance on several downstream tasks including protein fitness prediction. However, PLM embeddings are not directly interpretable and, thereby, it remains unclear what features they encode. To gain insight into which biochemical properties of the protein are driving the prediction, we leverage an orthogonal projection technique that removes linear effects of known tabular features from embeddings and extend it to high-order and interaction effects. In this way, we remove the effects of interpretable biochemical features from PLM embeddings. In an ablation study, we show that this leads to a decrease in performance for a downstream classifier trained only on the embeddings to predict protein fitness. In an additional evaluation, we find that these biochemical features explain a substantial part of the variance in the predictions of this classifier. Hence, we can show that PLM embeddings encode patterns correlated with biochemical properties and quantify their contribution to predicting protein fitness. This computationally efficient approach is not limited to the features or embeddings considered here and is readily transferable to problem settings beyond protein fitness prediction.

AI.tldr: An orthogonal projection method strips known biochemical features from PLM embeddings to quantify their contribution to protein fitness predictions; removal reduces performance, and biochemical features explain a substantial portion of the variance, indicating PLMs encode biochemically relevant information. The approach is scalable and transferable.
AI.motivation: To interpret what biochemical properties are captured by protein language model embeddings and how those properties contribute to predictive performance.
AI.method: Apply an orthogonal projection to embeddings to remove linear and extended high-order/interactions with known tabular biochemical features; test via ablation and variance-explained analyses.
AI.result: Ablation reduces downstream performance when biochemical features are removed from embeddings; these features account for a substantial portion of variance in model predictions, indicating PLMs encode patterns correlated with biochemical properties.
AI.conclusion: PLM embeddings encode biochemically meaningful information; the projection-based approach provides interpretable attribution of this information and is adaptable to other problem settings beyond protein fitness prediction.

title: Difficulty-Aware Sample Allocation for Adaptive Data Augmentation in Semantic Segmentation
summary: Data augmentation is a standard component of modern semantic segmentation pipelines, but most augmentation techniques allocate transformations uniformly across training samples or adapt to a single difficulty signal such as loss. This ignores the fact that segmentation difficulty is multi-factorial, since ambiguous predictions, persistent optimization errors, rare classes, and complex object boundaries can each make a sample informative in different ways. This paper introduces Difficulty-Aware Sample Allocation (DASA), an architecture-agnostic framework that assigns stronger augmentation to samples estimated to be more difficult. DASA combines prediction ambiguity, training loss, class rarity, and boundary complexity into a normalized difficulty score, then maps that score to sample-specific augmentation strength during iterative training. Experiments on Oxford-IIIT Pet and binary Pascal VOC segmentation with U-Net, DeepLabV3, and SegFormer-B0 show that DASA improves over standard training and is competitive with or stronger than single-signal adaptive baselines. On Oxford-IIIT Pet, DASA improves DeepLabV3 from 0.633 to 0.740 mIoU. On binary Pascal VOC, DASA obtains the best foreground IoU for all three evaluated architectures. These results attest to the value of multi-factor difficulty estimation as a practical mechanism for directing augmentation where it is most useful.

AI.tldr: DASA is an architecture-agnostic framework that adaptively augments samples based on a multi-factor difficulty score, improving segmentation performance beyond uniform or single-signal augmentation strategies.
AI.motivation: Segmentation difficulty is multi-factorial and varying across samples; fixed or single-signal augmentation strategies fail to exploit the most informative samples.
AI.method: Compute a per-sample, normalized difficulty score from prediction ambiguity, training loss, class rarity, and boundary complexity; map this score to an augmentation strength; apply adaptively during iterative training across architectures (U-Net, DeepLabV3, SegFormer-B0) and datasets (Oxford-IIIT Pet, binary Pascal VOC).
AI.result: DASA yields notable gains, e.g., DeepLabV3 mIoU on Oxford-IIIT Pet improves from 0.633 to 0.740; on binary Pascal VOC, it achieves the best foreground IoU across all three evaluated architectures; outperforms standard training and is competitive with or stronger than single-signal adaptive baselines.
AI.conclusion: Multi-factor, difficulty-aware augmentation is a practical and effective mechanism for directing augmentation to the most informative samples, and DASA’s architecture-agnostic design demonstrates broad applicability in semantic segmentation.

title: Beyond Optimal Rates in Stochastic Optimization: Trajectory-Adaptive Stopping Rules
summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is typically analyzed at a deterministic horizon chosen before the algorithm is run, even though practical stopping decisions are made adaptively by inspecting the evolving trajectory. This mismatch creates a fundamental certification problem: fixed-time guarantees do not generally remain valid at data-dependent stopping times, while deterministic horizons derived from worst-case bounds can be highly conservative. We address this problem for strongly convex stochastic optimization by constructing fully observable, trajectory-adaptive upper confidence sequences for the squared distance of the last iterate to the optimizer and the suboptimality of a weighted average. These bounds hold simultaneously over time, attain the optimal $1/t$ decay rate up to iterated-logarithmic factors in the worst case, and adapt to the realized stochastic gradients, allowing SGD to stop as soon as a prescribed accuracy is certified without sacrificing statistical validity. Our approach treats the evolving SGD trajectory as a sequential experiment whose observations provide evidence about the unknown optimization error. To formalize this perspective, we develop new recursive confidence-sequence techniques and a general time-uniform empirical Bernstein inequality for adapted processes with time-varying conditional means and predictable ranges that may grow without bound. We further extend these confidence-sequence constructions to minibatch SGD, with the empirical Bernstein bounds exploiting the realized second-moment structure within each minibatch. Numerical experiments show that the resulting stopping rules can require several orders of magnitude fewer iterations than natural deterministic horizons.

AI.tldr: Trajectories-adaptive confidence sequences enable online stopping for SGD with strong guarantees, achieving near-optimal rates while reducing iterations.
AI.motivation: Fixed-horizon analysis of SGD misses practical adaptive stopping decisions; there is a need for online, data-dependent guarantees that certify optimization error as SGD progresses.
AI.method: Develop fully observable, trajectory-adaptive upper confidence sequences (UCS) for the squared distance to the optimizer and for suboptimality of a weighted average; establish time-uniform empirical Bernstein bounds for adapted processes with time-varying means and unbounded ranges; extend to minibatch SGD using batch-structure of second moments.
AI.result: The UCS bounds hold simultaneously over time and achieve the optimal 1/t decay up to iterated-logarithmic factors in the worst case; they adapt to realized gradients, enabling certified stopping without invalidating statistical guarantees; minibatch extension via realized second-moment structure; experiments show stopping can require orders of magnitude fewer iterations than fixed deterministic horizons.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled, data-driven stopping mechanism for SGD with strong theoretical guarantees and practical efficiency, extendable to minibatch settings.

title: LongVU-TTT: Causal Test-Time Training for Visual Resampling in Long Video Understanding
summary: Long-video MLLMs must model temporal change before a limited visual-token budget removes most frame evidence. We introduce LongVU-TTT, which inserts a convolutional Test-Time Training (TTT) resampler with causal fast-weight updates between the vision encoder and the LLM. Its grouped 2D fast weights adapt to each video and contextualize frame features before compression, while a hybrid uniform-and-change-aware selector retains explicit visual evidence for downstream reasoning. Under controlled conditions, TTT-Conv improves over TTT-MLP by up to +2.12 and bidirectional Mamba2 by up to +3.04 on MLVU, and it is stronger than attention- and fixed-state recurrent resamplers across three benchmarks. Analysis shows that the fast weights behave as a temporal aggregation state rather than a reliable long-horizon episodic memory: their benefit attenuates as evidence becomes more distant, motivating explicit frame retention. LongVU-TTT processes up to 512 frames before reducing them to 128 LLM frames and achieves competitive performance across five video understanding benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Introduces LongVU-TTT, a convolutional Test-Time Training (TTT) resampler with causal fast-weight updates between the vision encoder and the LLM for long-video MLLMs; shows improvements over TTT-MLP and bidirectional Mamba2 on MLVU and outperforms attention- and fixed-state recurrent resamplers across three benchmarks; processes up to 512 frames (reduced to 128 LLM frames) and achieves competitive results on five video-understanding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-video MLLMs must model temporal change under a limited visual-token budget, causing most frame evidence to be lost. The approach aims to dynamically adapt frame features and preserve explicit visual evidence to support downstream reasoning.
AI.method: Insert a convolutional Test-Time Training resampler with grouped 2D fast weights (causal updates) between the vision encoder and the LLM; use a hybrid uniform-and-change-aware selector to retain explicit evidence; process up to 512 frames, reducing to 128 LLM frames; compare against TTT-MLP and bidirectional Mamba2; evaluate against attention- and fixed-state recurrent resamplers; analyze the role of fast weights as a temporal aggregation state.
AI.result: TTT-Conv outperforms TTT-MLP by up to 2.12 and bidirectional Mamba2 by up to 3.04 on MLVU; is stronger than attention- and fixed-state recurrent resamplers across three benchmarks; LongVU-TTT achieves competitive performance across five video understanding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Fast weights function as a temporal aggregation mechanism with diminishing benefit for distant evidence, motivating explicit frame retention; LongVU-TTT can process long videos (512 frames to 128 LLM frames) and achieve competitive results, validating the resampling approach for long-video MLLMs.

title: Physics-Informed Foresight Pruning for Sparse PINN Solvers of Nonlinear PDEs
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 6 Tables. Submitted to the AI4S 2026 Workshop, Scientific Machine Learning track
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often rely on over-parameterized models to optimize coupled solution and differential-residual objectives, leaving unclear how much capacity is necessary and what pruning should preserve. We study foresight pruning at initialization for sparse PirateNet PDE solvers. Standard neural tangent kernel spectrum-aware pruning (NTK-SAP) aims to preserve output-side training dynamics but may overlook parameters whose main influence arises through derivatives in the governing equations. We introduce physics-informed spectrum-aware pruning (PI-SAP), which assigns saliency using sensitivity of the PDE residual. Experiments on the Gray-Scott equations, complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, Burgers' equation, and linear convection equation show that PI-SAP more consistently preserves Gray-Scott residual fidelity and is competitive under aggressive sparsity. However, no criterion is uniformly optimal across equations or sparsity levels. Small-batch PINN-NTK diagnostics further show that residual fidelity, solution accuracy, and kernel conditioning are distinct objectives, motivating pruning methods that explicitly balance solution-side and residual-side training dynamics during optimization.

AI.tldr: PI-SAP uses PDE residual sensitivity to prune PINNs at initialization, outperforming NTK-SAP in preserving residual fidelity under sparsity across several PDEs, but no universal optima; balancing residual and solution dynamics is crucial.
AI.motivation: Clarify the capacity needs of PINNs and how pruning should preserve physics-driven objectives; NTK-SAP may miss parameters whose influence is through PDE derivatives.
AI.method: Introduce PI-SAP by saliency based on sensitivity of the PDE residual; compare to NTK-SAP on Gray-Scott, complex Ginzburg-Landau, Burgers, and linear convection; evaluate residual fidelity, solution accuracy, and kernel conditioning.
AI.result: PI-SAP yields more consistent residual fidelity for Gray-Scott; competitive under aggressive sparsity; no single criterion is optimal across equations and sparsity levels; small-batch PINN-NTK diagnostics show residual fidelity, solution accuracy, and kernel conditioning are distinct objectives.
AI.conclusion: Pruning should explicitly balance solution-side and residual-side training dynamics; future work should develop multi-objective pruning strategies that jointly optimize these aspects during training.

title: MIMONet: Multi-scale Input and Multi-scale Output Network for Salient Object Detection
summary: The existing methods for saliency detection task focus on the application of multi-level features, aiming to take advantage of the respective strengths of high- and low-level features. However, because the inputs of these models are single-size images, their multi-level features have difficulty in learning the knowledge of size variations of salient objects. Object-scale variation learning has great potential for detecting multi-scale objects, which has not been fully explored by existing methods. To improve the recognition ability of a model for objects with different sizes, we are inspired by the image pyramid to propose a Multi-scale Input and Multi-scale Output Network (MIMONet). In MIMONet, we extract multi-level features for three images with different resolutions to form three encoder branches, and information will be exchanged between the branches. The advantage of this approach is that the features of one branch can learn the knowledge of target size variation from the features of the other two branches. In addition, we design a Multi-scale Perception (MSP) module, in which the input feature layer is divided into several sub-layers with different resolutions. Capturing the multi-level structure information of the objects in these sub-layers can make the objects more fully perceived. For network training, we propose a Joint Saliency Loss (JSL), which can constrain multiple saliency maps output by the network to identify the same foreground objects, and induce their boundaries to be preserved clearly. Experimental results show that MIMONet has stronger detection capabilities and harvests better evaluation scores on multiple datasets compared to existing models. The code of our model will be released.

AI.tldr: MIMONet is a multi-scale saliency detector that uses three encoder branches on different resolution inputs, with cross-branch information exchange, a Multi-scale Perception module that processes features at multiple resolutions, and a Joint Saliency Loss to align multiple saliency maps. It targets object-size variation and shows improved scores over baselines on multiple datasets; code will be released.
AI.motivation: Addresses the limitation that single-size inputs limit learning of object-size variations in saliency detection. Draws inspiration from image pyramids to learn scale-robust representations and improve multi-scale object detection.
AI.method: Three-branch encoder network processing three resolutions, with cross-branch information exchange; Multi-scale Perception module partitions the feature map into sub-layers at different resolutions to capture multi-level structure; Joint Saliency Loss penalizes discrepancies among multiple saliency maps while preserving boundaries.
AI.result: Empirical experiments report stronger detection performance and superior evaluation metrics on several datasets compared with existing models.
AI.conclusion: MIMONet effectively handles scale variation in saliency detection, leveraging cross-scale feature exchange and MSP with a joint loss; code release planned.

title: Beyond Scaling: Self-Evolving LLM Agents for Hardware Kernel Optimization via an Experience-Driven Workflow and Experience Graph Memory
summary: Hardware kernel optimization requires repeated compilation, correctness testing, profiling, and revision. LLM agents can automate parts of this process, and stronger foundation models, longer context windows, and longer execution horizons have improved optimization within individual tasks. These advances alone do not enable an agent to learn from completed optimization runs. Existing kernel-optimization agents seldom preserve a decision, its observed execution feedback, and the later decisions that use that evidence. Retaining every prior trajectory is also impractical because an expanding history competes with the current task for context. We present KOPE, an experience-driven framework for hardware kernel optimization. KOPE records optimization trajectories with correctness and performance feedback in Experience Graph Memory, then uses Active Context Management and Injection to retrieve relevant experience under a fixed token budget. The graph retains decision order, observed outcomes, and alternative branches, allowing evidence collected on the target hardware to inform later optimization steps and tasks. Under the same GLM-5.2 setting, the geometric mean of KOPE's per-operator speedups is $1.54\times$ that of CANNBot, the strongest competing baseline. In a complete 53-operator ablation, Active Context Management and Injection raises pass rate from 60.0\% to 84.6\%, increases the evaluator-reported positive-field geometric mean from 0.0382 to 0.0661, and reduces optimization token consumption from 15.9B to 1.113B tokens relative to passive agent-led context construction. Enabling Experience Graph Memory raises full-suite pass rate from 55.2\% to 84.6\% and yields a $1.43\times$ geometric-mean speedup on valid timing comparisons. These results support continual optimization through external experience while the foundation model remains fixed.

AI.tldr: KOPE introduces an experience-driven framework (KOPE) that uses Experience Graph Memory and retrieval-based context management to reuse optimization trajectories, achieving substantial speedups and higher pass rates over CANNBot, while reducing token usage and enabling continual optimization with a fixed foundation model.
AI.motivation: Existing hardware kernel optimization agents struggle to learn from completed runs because they do not preserve decision histories and suffer from limited, context-capped feedback, hindering continual improvement across tasks.
AI.method: KOPE records optimization trajectories with correctness and performance feedback in an Experience Graph Memory. It uses Active Context Management and Injection to retrieve relevant experience within a fixed token budget, preserving decision order, outcomes, and branches so past evidence informs future optimization. Evaluation is performed under GLM-5.2 with a 53-operator ablation comparing KOPE to CANNBot.
AI.result: KOPE achieves a 1.54x per-operator geometric mean speedup over CANNBot. In a 53-operator ablation: Active Context Management and Injection raise pass rate from 60.0% to 84.6%, increase evaluator-positive-field geometric mean from 0.0382 to 0.0661, and reduce optimization tokens from 15.9B to 1.113B. Enabling Experience Graph Memory raises full-suite pass rate from 55.2% to 84.6% and yields a 1.43x geometric-mean speedup on valid timing comparisons.
AI.conclusion: External experience memory with targeted context management enables continual hardware-kernel optimization with a fixed foundation model, improving correctness and efficiency across tasks.

title: InteractGesture: Progressive Chunk Guidance for Continuous Streaming Co-Speech Gesture Control
summary: Co-speech gesture generation has made significant progress toward realistic full-body motion from speaker audio, yet existing models lack fine-grained spatial controllability of individual joints. To address this, we introduce \emph{InteractGesture}, a model-agnostic, inference-time method for spatially controllable gesture generation. \emph{InteractGesture} guides target latent estimates of a diffusion sampler through a differentiable RVQ-VAE decoder, backpropagating spatial control gradients to adjust motion latents during sampling. A primary challenge in streaming co-speech generation is chunk-wise dependency: standard sequential inference freezes prior chunks, preventing spatial constraints in future chunks from adjusting preceding trajectories and causing boundary inconsistencies. To overcome this limitation, we propose \emph{Progressive Chunk Guidance}, a chunk-window strategy that maintains an active set of editable chunk latents with staggered delays, enabling spatial constraints to propagate gradients backward across chunk boundaries during streaming generation. Experiments on the BEAT2 dataset show that \emph{InteractGesture} improves multi-joint spatial control while preserving overall gesture quality. Furthermore, our approach supports diverse applications, including sparse joint positioning, dense joint trajectory control, and directional pointing. Our project page is available at https://exitudio.github.io/interactgesture-page .

AI.tldr: InteractGesture introduces a diffusion-based gesture generation method with per-joint spatial controllability, using a differentiable RVQ-VAE decoder to backpropagate control signals into motion latents. It addresses streaming chunk boundary issues with Progressive Chunk Guidance, enabling gradients to propagate across chunk boundaries for consistent motion. Evaluated on BEAT2, it claims improved multi-joint control while preserving gesture quality and supports various control applications.
AI.motivation: To enable fine-grained, spatially controllable co-speech gesture generation at inference time, addressing the limitation that existing models lack joint-level controllability and fail to propagate spatial constraints across streaming chunk boundaries.
AI.method: Utilizes a diffusion sampler guided by target latent estimates, refined through a differentiable RVQ-VAE decoder. Introduces Progressive Chunk Guidance with a chunk-window and editable latent sets, allowing backward gradient propagation across chunk boundaries during streaming generation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on BEAT2 shows improved multi-joint spatial control without sacrificing overall gesture quality. Demonstrates applicability to sparse and dense joint control and directional pointing.
AI.conclusion: InteractGesture is a model-agnostic, inference-time approach that enhances spatial controllability in co-speech gesture generation, particularly effective in streaming scenarios due to its progressive chunk guidance mechanism.

title: Individual Fairness in Hierarchical Clustering
summary: Hierarchical clustering produces ultrametric representations that impose strong global geometric constraints and may distort local similarities in ways that disproportionately affect individual data points. We study hierarchical clustering under an individual fairness requirement that bounds relative distortion within local $k$-nearest neighborhoods. We formulate this requirement as a feasibility problem over dominated ultrametrics and characterize the minimal multiplicative slack required for feasibility. We identify a sharp local threshold, prove stability under bounded perturbations, establish monotonicity in $k$, and show an intrinsic $Θ(\log n)$ separation between local and global realizability. Experiments on synthetic and real world datasets support our theoretical results.

AI.tldr: Study of hierarchical clustering under an individual fairness constraint that bounds local distortion within k-nearest neighborhoods by dominated ultrametrics; derives minimal slack for feasibility, a sharp local threshold, stability, monotonicity in k, and a Θ(log n) gap between local and global realizability; supported by experiments.
AI.motivation: Ultrametric hierarchies impose strong global constraints that can distort local similarities. The paper seeks a fairness-aware formulation that restricts distortion within local neighborhoods and analyzes its feasibility and limits.
AI.method: Formulate as a feasibility problem over dominated ultrametrics that bound relative distortion in local k-nearest neighborhoods; derive minimal multiplicative slack for feasibility; prove a sharp local threshold, stability under bounded perturbations, monotonicity in k, and a Θ(log n) separation between local and global realizability; corroborate with experiments on synthetic and real datasets.
AI.result: Characterizes when a hierarchy can realize local fairness constraints with minimal slack; identifies a sharp local threshold, proves stability, monotonicity in k, and a logarithmic separation between local and global realizability; empirical results align with theory.
AI.conclusion: Local fairness constraints yield tractable feasibility and reveal a fundamental separation between local and global realizability in hierarchical clustering; results provide guidance on how much slack is needed and how locality (k) affects realizability, with empirical validation.

title: Moving Beyond More Views: Redundancy-Aware Ego-Exo Fusion for Proficiency Estimation
summary: EgoExo proficiency estimation aims to assess action quality by integrating fine-grained motion cues from egocentric (1st-person) views with spatial context from multiple exocentric (3rd-person) views. Simply adding more exocentric views degrades EgoExo performance, as redundant or noisy perspectives dilute useful motion cues. Our analysis identifies two key causes: (1) Multiview redundancy - From the data perspective, certain views provide limited or noisy information, diluting discriminative cues; (2) Overfitting - From the feature perspective, conventional fusion increases representational complexity, causing the model to memorise view-specific patterns rather than learn generalisable representations. To address these issues, we propose two complementary modules: AdaMVS, which adaptively identifies and fuses the most informative view tokens under weak supervision from the data perspective, and VIB-GB, which combines Gradient Blending and Variational Information Bottleneck regularisation from the feature perspective to compress redundant signals and suppress overfitting during training. Experiments on EgoExo-4D and EgoExo-Fitness demonstrate that our method learns both which view to look at and how to fuse them, achieving new state-of-the-art results. Our source code is available at https://github.com/dx199771/AdaMVS

AI.tldr: Adaptive multi-view fusion for EgoExo that selects informative exocentric views and regularizes fused features to reduce redundancy and overfitting, achieving state-of-the-art results on EgoExo-4D and EgoExo-Fitness.
AI.motivation: EgoExo proficiency estimation combines egocentric motion cues with multi-view exocentric context, but adding more views can hurt performance due to redundancy and overfitting. The authors seek to identify which views are informative and how to fuse them effectively.
AI.method: 1) AdaMVS: adaptively selects and fuses the most informative view tokens under weak supervision from data perspective. 2) VIB-GB: a feature-level regularizer combining Gradient Blending with Variational Information Bottleneck to compress redundant signals and mitigate overfitting during training.
AI.result: The method achieves new state-of-the-art results on EgoExo-4D and EgoExo-Fitness datasets, demonstrating improved action quality assessment by learning which views to attend to and how to fuse them. Code released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive view-aware fusion and information-theoretic regularization jointly improve EgoExo proficiency estimation by addressing multiview redundancy and overfitting, suggesting that selective attention to views and compressed representations are key for robust multi-view fusion.

title: M-Fibration Theory with Applications to Neural Network Compression
summary: The purpose of this paper is to provide a general, comprehensive, theoretical framework that allows one to deal with fibrations on graphs labelled on a commutative monoid. This is a genuine extension of the theory of graph fibrations (as introduced in "Fibrations of Graphs" [Discrete Math., vol. 243, pp. 21-66, 2002]), that makes it possible to deal with weighted graphs, and also graphs labelled with other algebraic structures. The derived theory also lends itself naturally to consider approximate fibrations. As an example, we show how this framework can be applied to the compression of arbitrary neural networks (including CNNs), providing a strong theoretical underpinning to the recent results in "The role of fibration symmetries in geometric deep learning" [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA, vol. 123, no. 4, p. e2416552123, 2026]

AI.tldr: A general extended framework for graph fibrations with monoid-labeled graphs, enabling weights and various algebraic labels, including approximate fibrations, with application to neural network compression and connections to fibration symmetries in geometric deep learning.
AI.motivation: Extend and unify the theory of graph fibrations to labeled/weighted graphs and approximate versions, to provide theoretical underpinning for practical tasks such as neural network compression and symmetry-based geometric deep learning.
AI.method: Develop a comprehensive theoretical framework that generalizes fibrations over commutative monoids, formalizes approximate fibrations, and demonstrates the framework’s applicability to neural network compression.
AI.result: A broad, unified theory of fibrations for monoid-labeled (including weighted) graphs; can be specialized to neural networks and supports the analysis and design of symmetry-based compression techniques, aligning with recent geometric deep learning results.
AI.conclusion: The work generalizes graph fibrations to weighted/labelled graphs and approximate versions, enabling new analyses and applications in neural network compression and symmetry-guided geometric deep learning.

title: TDFNet: Tri-projection Deformable Fusion Network for Panoramic Salient Object Detection
summary: Recent years have witnessed the growing potential of panoramic salient object detection in robotic vision, virtual reality, and related applications. However, projecting spherical scenes onto 2D planes inevitably introduces geometric distortions, which fundamentally limit the effectiveness of existing projection-based methods. Specifically, Equirectangular Projection (ERP) suffers from severe polar stretching distortions, while cube map projection introduces discontinuities across cube-face boundaries, resulting in degraded feature discriminability and compromised geometric consistency. To address these limitations, we propose TDFNet, the first Tri-projection Deformable Fusion Network for panoramic salient object detection, exploiting complementary projection representations to alleviate geometric distortions and improve detection performance.Specifically, we design a cross-projection deformable attention (CDA) module that leverages spatial correspondences between different projections to construct geometry-aware sampling locations, guiding deformable attention for cross-projection contextual aggregation and enhancing robustness against projection-induced deformations. Furthermore, we introduce a latitude-guided fusion module, which utilizes spherical latitude priors to construct geometric confidence weights for adaptively balancing ERP and CMP features. Meanwhile, LGF incorporates distortion-reduced semantic references from Tangent Projection to achieve cross-projection feature refinement and spatial alignment.By constructing a three-branch encoding architecture based on ERP, CMP, and Tangent Projection, TDFNet simultaneously preserves global spatial continuity, local geometric details, and fine-grained boundary information.

AI.tldr: TDFNet: a Tri-projection Deformable Fusion Network for panoramic salient object detection that combines ERP, cube-map (CMP), and Tangent Projection with cross-projection deformable attention and latitude-guided fusion to mitigate projection distortions and improve detection accuracy.
AI.motivation: Panoramic scenes suffer from projection distortions when mapped to 2D planes (ERP polar stretching, CMP boundaries). Leveraging complementary projections and geometry-aware fusion can preserve spatial continuity and geometric details, improving salient object detection in panoramic vision.
AI.method: Three-branch encoder architecture over ERP, CMP, and Tangent Projection. A cross-projection deformable attention (CDA) module constructs geometry-aware sampling locations using cross-projection correspondences to fuse features across projections. A latitude-guided fusion (LGF) module uses spherical latitude priors to compute geometric confidence weights to adaptively balance ERP and CMP features. Tangent Projection provides distortion-reduced semantic references for cross-projection refinement and alignment.
AI.result: The abstract claims improved robustness to projection-induced distortions and enhanced detection performance by exploiting complementary projections, but no quantitative results are provided.
