Experimental results show that training a deep model on CO-AID can both predict defects in AI-generated images and optimize AI image generation, demonstrating its usability and effectiveness. The database and supplementary materials are available at: https://github.com/Future-IQA/CO-AID .

AI.tldr: Introduces CO-AID, a human-annotated dataset of compositional defects in text-to-image outputs, enabling defect prediction and prompt optimization.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art T2I models show systematic defects with complex compositional prompts. Quantifying and leveraging human judgments can diagnose and improve generation.
AI.method: Select 651 reference images across four categories (people, hand, object, scene); derive composition-focused prompts by editing ChatGPT-generated prompts; generate images with three T2I models; conduct a multi-label subjective study with 29 participants per image to annotate defect types and locations; assemble the CO-AID dataset with references, prompts, outputs, and defect annotations; train a deep model on CO-AID to predict defects and guide optimization of future generations.
AI.result: CO-AID enables defect prediction and prompt optimization; a deep model trained on CO-AID can predict defects in AI-generated images and help optimize generation; dataset and supplementary materials are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: CO-AID provides a practical resource to diagnose and mitigate compositional defects in T2I outputs, facilitating more reliable generation for complex prompts.

title: TailSFT: Filtered Fine-Tuning Improves Post-Training Performance
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training drives reasoning and agentic capabilities in modern AI systems, yet a growing body of work shows that it is most effective when used to fine-tune an already capable base model. We question whether existing pipelines yield models that are most suitable for reinforcement learning. Building on prior work highlighting the role of coverage and pass@K as predictors of post-RL performance, we design a simple modification to supervised fine-tuning, TailSFT, which filters out already fit sequences during training, thereby focusing learning on under-modeled regions, or the tail, of the data distribution. We justify and validate the design choices in TailSFT, particularly the specific filtering criteria, through a combination of controlled experiments and theoretical analysis. On OLMo-3 7B, TailSFT often improves pass@16 performance on math and coding evaluations, with gains up to 17% absolute, while incurring minimal computational overhead. These higher-coverage checkpoints consistently translate to up to 4% absolute pass@1 gains in subsequent GRPO runs, demonstrating that TailSFT checkpoints serve as better initializations for RL. We further introduce a lightweight diagnostic for identifying settings where TailSFT is most likely to help. More broadly, our results motivate a principled, stage-aware approach to model development, in which intermediate checkpoints are judged by how effectively they support subsequent training.

AI.tldr: TailSFT filters out already-fit supervised fine-tuning sequences to concentrate learning on the tail of the data distribution, improving RL readiness. It yields notable pass@K gains (up to 17% on pass@16) with minimal overhead, and translates to further RL gains (up to 4% pass@1) when used as initialization. It also introduces a lightweight diagnostic and supports a stage-aware, intermediate-checkpoint-centric development approach.
AI.motivation: Post-training RL performance correlates with data coverage and pass@K; however, standard pipelines may produce base models that are suboptimal for RL. The work seeks to precondition models for RL by emphasizing tail regions during supervised fine-tuning, potentially yielding better RL outcomes.
AI.method: Introduce TailSFT: during supervised fine-tuning, filter out sequences that are already well-fit, focusing training on under-modeled tail regions. Provide filtering criteria, justify them theoretically, and validate via controlled experiments. Assess impact on base-model quality (pass@K) and downstream RL performance (GRPO) on the OLMo-3 7B model; also propose a lightweight diagnostic to identify settings where TailSFT helps.
AI.result: TailSFT yields substantial improvements in high-coverage tasks: up to 17% absolute gain in pass@16 on math and coding benchmarks, with minimal computational overhead. The improved high-coverage checkpoints consistently translate to up to 4% absolute gains in pass@1 during subsequent GRPO RL runs. A diagnostic is introduced to identify favorable settings, supporting a stage-aware development approach where intermediate checkpoints are evaluated by their RL utility.
AI.conclusion: A principled, stage-aware approach to model development: intermediate supervised fine-tuning checkpoints should be judged by their effectiveness in enabling subsequent RL training, with TailSFT offering a simple, low-overhead method to steer learning toward under-modeled regions.

title: TAU-Agent: An Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Traffic Anomaly Understanding
summary: Traffic Anomaly Understanding (TAU) requires models and systems to detect, reason about, and explain anomalous events in transportation videos. To address this challenge, we propose TAU-Agent, an agentic retrieval-augmented framework for traffic anomaly understanding. Given a task query, a central retrieval agent orchestrates two visual perception tools, namely a Video Captioning Tool and an Open-Vocabulary Tracking Tool, to retrieve and select query-relevant evidence, including captions, temporal intervals, and object trajectories. The selected evidence, together with sampled video frames and the input query, is provided to a supervised fine-tuned vision-language model for final reasoning and answer generation. We evaluate TAU-Agent on both the in-domain and the out-of-domain benchmarks from the AI City Challenge 2026. TAU-Agent achieves scores of 0.6779 on Track 3, 0.3998 on Track 7, and 67.9275 on Track 8, ranking second, twelfth, and fifth, respectively. Code is available at: https://github.com/siri-rouser/TAU-Agent.

AI.tldr: TAU-Agent introduces a retrieval-augmented, agentic framework for traffic anomaly understanding that uses specialized perception tools to gather evidence (captions, intervals, trajectories) and a vision-language model to reason and answer.
AI.motivation: Traffic anomaly understanding requires not only detection and reasoning but also interpretability through evidence; existing methods often lack explicit retrieval of query-relevant evidence and cross-modal reasoning with structured outputs.
AI.method: A central retrieval agent coordinates two tools (Video Captioning Tool and Open-Vocabulary Tracking Tool) to extract captions, temporal intervals, and object trajectories relevant to the task query. This evidence, plus sampled frames, guides a supervised fine-tuned vision-language model to perform final reasoning and answer generation.
AI.result: On AI City Challenge 2026 benchmarks (in-domain and out-of-domain), TAU-Agent achieved 0.6779 (Track 3), 0.3998 (Track 7), and 67.9275 (Track 8), ranking 2nd, 12th, and 5th, respectively. Code is available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that retrieval-augmented, agentic architectures can improve traffic anomaly understanding by producing query-relevant evidence and leveraging a vision-language model for reasoning, with competitive performance across multiple tracks; future work could explore more diverse evidence, better open-vocabulary reasoning, and robustness to domain shifts.

title: Learning from waste: Machine Learning for health risk prediction and computer vision-based sorting in Ghana
summary: The inappropriate disposal of solid waste remains a significant public health and environmental concern worldwide, including in Ghana. Poor sanitation and improper waste management practices contribute to substantial economic costs and avoidable deaths annually. In 2022, a field study in Atonsu, Kumasi, Ghana, reported a community-perceived relationship between household waste disposal and illness patterns, but only through descriptive analysis without quantitative validation. This study extends that investigation using two data-driven approaches. First, a Random Forest classifier was developed to predict illness categories using waste disposal practices and demographic survey data. On a held-out group of respondents who reported illness (N=69), the model obtained a macro F1 score of 0.63, with disposal method emerging as the most important substantive predictor of illness type. Second, a MobileNetV2 image classification model enabled automated waste sorting via visual recognition, achieving 88.2% accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.87 on the test set (N=415). The vision-based approach offers an affordable, camera-driven alternative to complex multi-sensor systems, making it highly suitable for resource-constrained settings. Taken together, the findings provide quantitative evidence for a community health relationship previously documented only qualitatively. They demonstrate the potential for automated waste-sorting in low-resource environments. Importantly, the results illustrate that technological performance alone does not guarantee public health improvements; effective institutional support and implementation are equally necessary.

AI.tldr: Quantifies a community health link between waste disposal and illness in Ghana and demonstrates a low-resource mobile vision solution for automated waste sorting, with implementation caveats.
AI.motivation: To move from qualitative observations of waste–illness associations to quantitative evidence and to explore affordable waste-sorting technology suitable for low-resource settings.
AI.method: Two data-driven approaches: (1) Random Forest classifier predicting illness category from waste disposal practices and demographic data (held-out illnesses, N=69; macro F1=0.63; disposal method most important predictor). (2) MobileNetV2 image classifier for automated waste sorting (test set, N=415; 88.2% accuracy; macro F1=0.87).
AI.result: RF model indicates disposal method as a key predictor of illness type; vision model achieves high accuracy and macro F1, suggesting feasible automated sorting in resource-constrained environments.
AI.conclusion: The study provides quantitative support for a community health relationship related to waste disposal and demonstrates potential for low-resource, camera-based waste sorting. However, technological performance alone is insufficient to guarantee health benefits; effective institutional support and implementation are essential.

title: Auditable CT Phenotyping Through Report-derived Radiological Observations
summary: Medical image foundation models can predict clinical phenotypes from computed tomography (CT), but strong performance leaves open whether they read disease-specific findings or shortcuts that correlate with the diagnosis. We tested this in 221 electronic-health-record (EHR) phenotypes using Auditable CT phenotyping (ACT), built on report-derived radiological observations. We trained ACT on 38,317 patients, mined 376,194 observations and evaluated it in 25,183 held-out patients. ACT exceeded five vision-language baselines on zero-shot annotation, and CT-CLIP across 221 phenotypes from unseen CT pulmonary angiography, both under zero-shot scoring (0.651 versus 0.572) and under linear probing (0.709 versus 0.662). Reading each probe exposes what accuracy conceals: only 97 observations occupy the 221 rank-1 positions, and one phrase describing aortic and coronary calcification ranks first for 20 phenotypes, including osteoporosis, urinary tract infection and major depressive disorder. Restricting the bank to clinician-specified evidence redirects those probes onto phenotype-related observations in 86 phenotypes at no accuracy cost (0.751 versus 0.741). Accurate CT-based EHR phenotyping can therefore rest on observations that are not valid evidence for the coded phenotype and that ACT can identify and intervene on.

AI.tldr: Auditable CT phenotyping (ACT) uses report-derived radiology observations to phenotype 221 EHR phenotypes from CTs, outperforming vision-language baselines; many top cues are non-phenotype evidence, but restricting cues to clinician-specified evidence preserves accuracy.
AI.motivation: Determine whether CT-based phenotyping relies on disease-specific findings or shortcuts by auditing which observations drive predictions across many phenotypes.
AI.method: Train ACT on 38,317 patients with 376,194 mined observations; evaluate on 25,183 held-out patients; compare zero-shot and linear-probing performance against five vision-language baselines and CT-CLIP on unseen CT pulmonary angiography; analyze top-ranked observations and the effect of restricting the observation bank to clinician-specified evidence.
AI.result: ACT outperformed five vision-language baselines in zero-shot annotation; CT-CLIP achieved higher performance on unseen data in both zero-shot scoring (0.651 vs 0.572) and linear probing (0.709 vs 0.662). Only 97 of 376,194 observations appear in rank-1 for 221 phenotypes; a single observation about aortic/coronary calcification ranks first for 20 phenotypes, including osteoporosis, UTI, and major depressive disorder. Limiting the observation bank to clinician-specified evidence maintains accuracy (0.751 vs 0.741) while redirecting probes to phenotype-relevant observations in 86 phenotypes.
AI.conclusion: CT-based EHR phenotyping can rely on observations that are not valid evidence for the coded phenotype; ACT can identify and filter these spurious probes, enabling more reliable alignment between observations and true phenotypes without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Drift-Aware Multimodal User Representation Learning via Multi-Scale Temporal Modeling and Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Understanding user preferences from noisy and temporally evolving social media behaviors is fundamentally challenging due to interest drift, where user preferences shift across time and exhibit both multi-scale temporal patterns and diverse co-existing interests. To address this, we propose DUMoE, a unified framework for drift-aware multimodal user representation learning. Our model consists of (i) a temporal dynamics-aware backbone that captures and integrates static profiles, short-term behavioral signals, and long-term dependencies into a coherent representation, and (ii) a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) interest adapter that disentangles multiple latent interests via expert specialization and adaptive routing. Each expert models a distinct interest subspace, while a gating network dynamically selects and aggregates a sparse subset of relevant experts for each user. To enable stable and effective optimization, we further introduce a three-stage training strategy that decouples backbone learning, expert specialization, and gating optimization. Extensive experiments on real-world social media datasets show that DUMoE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both user interest prediction and interaction prediction tasks.

AI.tldr: DUMoE proposes a drift-aware, multimodal user representation learning framework that combines a temporal dynamics backbone with a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) interest adapter, plus a staged training strategy. It aims to capture static profiles, short- and long-term behaviors, and multiple latent interests under interest drift, achieving state-of-the-art performance on interest and interaction prediction tasks in real-world social media data.
AI.motivation: User preferences in social media are noisy and temporally evolving due to interest drift, exhibiting multi-scale temporal patterns and overlapping interests. A unified model should integrate static profiles, short-term signals, and long-term dependencies while disentangling multiple latent interests.
AI.method: 1) Temporal dynamics-aware backbone that fuses static profiles, short-term behavioral signals, and long-term dependencies into a coherent representation. 2) Sparse MoE interest adapter that assigns distinct latent-interest subspaces to experts; a gating network selects a sparse subset of experts for each user via adaptive routing. 3) A three-stage training strategy to decouple backbone learning, expert specialization, and gating optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world social media datasets show that DUMoE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both user interest prediction and interaction prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: DUMoE offers a unified, drift-aware framework for multimodal user representation that can capture dynamic interests through specialized experts and adaptive routing, supported by a stable, staged optimization procedure and strong empirical performance.

title: 4DGS-WAM: Bridging Past and Future with an Object-Centric World Action Model based on 4D Gaussian Splatting
comment: This is a work in progress
summary: Current world action models (WAMs) typically operate on 2D visual data. These models can achieve exceptional visual quality, but they lack explicit spatial structure for individual objects and repeatedly process redundant background content. Although point clouds can represent the world in 3D space, they can be difficult to align and accumulate across viewpoints. In this paper, we leverage an explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) representation that separately models dynamic objects and the static background of a scene. For dynamic objects, we use a policy model to predict future actor actions and a world model to predict transformations of their observed Gaussian splats. The static background need not be regenerated for future states, as much of it has already been observed in past frames. This forms an object-centric world action model, which we name 4DGS-WAM. It lifts 2D observations into a persistent 4D representation so that previously observed static content can be reused during future prediction. Future-state extrapolation can then focus on modeling the evolution of dynamic objects. Experiments on KITTI-MOT evaluate short-horizon prediction and past reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Proposes 4DGS-WAM, an object-centric world action model that uses 4D Gaussian splatting to separate dynamic objects from the static background, reusing observed background to improve short-horizon prediction and past reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of explicit object-level spatial structure in 2D world action models and the inefficiency of processing redundant background data; leverage a persistent 4D representation to align, accumulate, and reason about dynamic objects across viewpoints.
AI.method: Represent the scene with 4DGaussian Splatting (4DGS) that separates dynamic objects and static background. For dynamics, employ a policy model to predict future actor actions and a world model to predict transformations of observed Gaussian splats. The static background is not regenerated each state and is reused from past observations. The approach lifts 2D observations into a persistent 4D representation, focusing future prediction on dynamic object evolution. Validation on KITTI-MOT for short-horizon prediction and past reconstruction.
AI.result: Demonstrates feasibility of an object-centric 4D representation (4DGS-WAM) that enables background reuse and targeted dynamic-object extrapolation; evaluated on KITTI-MOT with short-horizon prediction and past reconstruction tasks.
AI.conclusion: An explicit 4D object-centric world action model effectively separates static and dynamic content, enabling reuse of observed background and more efficient prediction of dynamic object evolution, as evidenced by KITTI-MOT experiments.

title: EXAONE Tabular 1.0 : Technical Report
summary: EXAONE Tabular is a compact tabular foundation model family for classification and regression via in-context learning, producing predictions without dataset-specific gradient updates. Pretrained exclusively on a synthetic structural-causal-model (SCM) prior, its central contribution is an architecture-centered redesign of tabular in-context learning. Rather than compressing features into a fixed row embedding before a separate row-level learner, EXAONE Tabular interleaves feature-axis attention within each item with support-conditioned item-axis attention within each feature at every Transformer layer, mediated by item-summary and feature-summary tokens. Across four public benchmarks, EXAONE Tabular combines strong predictive performance with high efficiency. On TabArena, its 20.81M-parameter classification model ranks first overall, surpassing tuned ensembles and 4-hour AutoML pipelines, while regression reaches the performance regime of the 1.64B-parameter TabFM at roughly 1/11 the inference cost. On BCCO and TALENT, EXAONE Tabular ranks second in classification and first in regression. On ScoringBench, it achieves the best mean rank for both point-estimation and predictive-distribution quality, leading the $R^2$, RMSE, and CRPS evaluations. Together, these results establish EXAONE Tabular as a state-of-the-art compact tabular foundation model family, combining strong predictive performance across classification, point regression, and probabilistic regression with an efficient model design.

AI.tldr: Compact tabular foundation model (EXAONE Tabular) uses architecture-centered interleaved attention for in-context learning, pretrained on a synthetic SCM prior, achieving state-of-the-art performance with high efficiency across classification and regression tasks.
AI.motivation: Develop a compact, gradient-free tabular foundation model that attains strong predictive performance via an architecture redesign in place of gradient updates, leveraging synthetic causal priors to guide learning.
AI.method: Redesign Transformer architecture to interleave feature-axis attention within each item with support-conditioned item-axis attention within each feature at every layer, using item-summary and feature-summary tokens; pretrain on a synthetic SCM prior; evaluate on TabArena, BCCO, TALENT, ScoringBench; compare against ensembles and AutoML pipelines.
AI.result: On TabArena (20.81M parameters), ranks first overall; regression performance approaches the 1.64B-parameter TabFM at ~1/11InferenceCost; on BCCO and TALENT, ranks second in classification and first in regression; on ScoringBench, achieves best mean rank for point-estimation and predictive-distribution quality across R2, RMSE, CRPS.
AI.conclusion: EXAONE Tabular is a state-of-the-art, compact tabular foundation model family that delivers strong predictive performance across classification, point regression, and probabilistic regression with efficient design.

title: Less Contouring, More Accuracy: Lesion-Guided ROI Deep Learning for Ovarian Ultrasound Classification
comment: Submitted as a research article. The manuscript contains figures, tables, and supplementary material
summary: Ovarian lesion classification using transvaginal ultrasound remains challenging due to overlapping imaging characteristics and the dependence on expert interpretation. This study investigates whether lesion-guided region-of-interest (ROI) deep learning can achieve competitive diagnostic performance while reducing the annotation burden associated with pixel-level lesion segmentation. Two publicly available ovarian ultrasound datasets were evaluated: the Multi-Modality Ovarian Tumor Ultrasound (MMOTU) dataset for eight-class classification and the Ovarian Ultrasound Dataset (OUD) for binary classification. Four strategies were compared under a unified framework: global image-based deep learning, lesion-guided ROI-based deep learning, lesion contour-based deep learning, and contour-based radiomics with machine learning classifiers. Four deep learning architectures, MaxViT-Tiny, Swin Transformer, EfficientNet-B7, and ResNet18, were evaluated. Radiomics models were developed using support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, and artificial neural network classifiers, with ANOVA-based feature selection applied for the lower-sample OUD dataset. The lesion-guided ROI strategy achieved the strongest overall performance, with MaxViT-Tiny obtaining 93.10% accuracy and an AUC of 0.99 on MMOTU and 97.56% accuracy and an AUC of 0.99 on OUD. The contour-based approach achieved comparable accuracy but required substantially higher annotation effort. These findings demonstrate that lesion-guided ROI deep learning provides an effective balance between diagnostic performance and annotation efficiency, offering a practical approach for scalable AI-assisted ovarian ultrasound analysis

AI.tldr: Lesion-guided ROI deep learning on ovarian ultrasound improves classification performance while reducing annotation burden compared to contour-based segmentation; achieves near-state performance on two public datasets using MaxViT-Tiny.
AI.motivation: Accurate OC lesion characterization is challenging due to overlapping imaging features and reliance on expert interpretation; reducing pixel-level annotation could lower burden and accelerate AI-assisted workflow.
AI.method: Compared four strategies (global image DL, lesion-guided ROI DL, lesion contour-based DL, contour-based radiomics) across four architectures (MaxViT-Tiny, Swin Transformer, EfficientNet-B7, ResNet18) on MMOTU (8-class) and OUD (binary). Radiomics used SVM, KNN, ANN with ANOVA feature selection for OUD.
AI.result: Lesion-guided ROI approach yielded the best performance: MaxViT-Tiny achieved 93.10% accuracy and AUC 0.99 on MMOTU; 97.56% accuracy and AUC 0.99 on OUD. Contour-based methods matched accuracy but required substantially more annotation effort; global-image DL and radiomics underperformed relative to ROI DL.
AI.conclusion: Lesion-guided ROI DL offers a favorable balance between diagnostic accuracy and annotation efficiency, supporting scalable AI-assisted ovarian ultrasound analysis.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Aggregation in Semi-Supervised Federated Learning with non-IID Data
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, ICASSP 2026 - 2026 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables distributed training of machine learning models while preserving data privacy. However, FL struggles with heterogeneous, non-IID client data distributions, resulting in sub-optimal and biased global models. In this paper, we propose pFedMARL, a novel approach leveraging Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) with Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) to dynamically adapt aggregation strategies in FL settings. Our method employs a server-side agent adjusting client contributions to optimize global model robustness and client-side agents balancing global and local updates to personalize models effectively without pre-training. We demonstrate superior performance of pFedMARL for training a semi-supervised audio spectrogram transformer, matching or outperforming FedAvg, Ditto, and local training approaches across multiple non-IID scenarios and in the presence of adversarial clients. Our results indicate that pFedMARL actively improves accuracy, robustness, and fairness, making it suitable for real-world deployments.

AI.tldr: Proposes pFedMARL, a MARL-based dynamic aggregation approach for federated learning (FL) to tackle non-IID data. It uses server-side TD3 to adjust client contributions and client-side agents to balance global/local updates for personalization, without pre-training. Demonstrates improved performance on a semi-supervised audio spectrogram transformer, matching or beating FedAvg, Ditto, and local training across non-IID and adversarial scenarios, with enhanced accuracy, robustness, and fairness.
AI.motivation: FL suffers from heterogeneous, non-IID client data which biases the global model; static aggregation like FedAvg fails to adapt to heterogeneity and adversarial participants.
AI.method: A two-level MARL framework: a server-side agent dynamically adjusts client contributions (aggregation weights) using TD3; client-side agents balance global vs local updates to personalize models; no pre-training required; evaluated on a semi-supervised audio spectrogram transformer across multiple non-IID settings and in the presence of adversarial clients.
AI.result: pFedMARL achieves accuracy, robustness, and fairness improvements, matching or outperforming FedAvg, Ditto, and local training across various non-IID scenarios and adversarial conditions.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, MARL-guided aggregation in FL can enhance robustness and personalization without pre-training, making FL more viable for real-world deployments, particularly for semi-supervised audio tasks.

title: PANDA - Prototype-Anchored Alignment for Partially Unpaired Multimodal Learning, with Applications to Alzheimers MRI and TCGA Pathology
summary: Multimodal medical prediction often faces incomplete pairing: auxiliary modalities with complementary signal are available for only a subset of subjects (or none) and cannot be assumed at deployment. We introduce PANDA (Prototype Anchored Data Alignment), a two-stage framework that transfers auxiliary information to a primary-modality model without auxiliary inputs at inference. Stage 1 learns a shared embedding from the paired subset and estimates class prototypes from auxiliary modalities; Stage 2 trains the primary encoder on all subjects using cross-entropy plus alignment to the frozen prototypes. Because supervision is defined at the class-prototype level, PANDA accommodates arbitrary pairing rates, including zero subject overlap. We evaluate PANDA on two applications. On a 1,021-subject multi-scanner ADNI cohort, we perform AD/CN classification with three auxiliary modalities at distinct pairing rates: tabular scores (44.8%), FDG-PET (18.7%), and external handwriting kinematics (0% overlap). Relative to the same-backbone MRI-only baseline, PANDA attains AUC 0.868 +-0.020 (+7.9pp) and reduces 1.5T CN false positives by 24.3pp; on a fully trainable Conv5-FC3 backbone it reaches AUC 0.893 (best overall). A pairing-rate ablation shows that the joint anchor remains within seed noise from 75% to 5% pairing. On TCGA-Lung survival prediction from whole-slide images with RNA-seq as auxiliary data, PANDA improves over WSI-only on 2-year OS (AUC +3.5pp) and Cox PH (C-index +9.0pts) and outperforms full-fusion training, which underperforms WSI-only, while requiring no RNA at inference; wide confidence intervals on this smaller cohort keep the gains below conventional significance. Overall, PANDA provides a deployment-oriented mechanism for leveraging incomplete auxiliary modalities to improve primary-modality prediction.

AI.tldr: PANDA enables learning from incomplete auxiliary modalities in multimodal medical prediction by a two-stage approach that transfers auxiliary information into a primary-modality model at deployment when auxiliary inputs are unavailable or only partially paired.
AI.motivation: Multimodal predictions often suffer from incomplete pairing between the primary modality and auxiliary modalities. At deployment, auxiliary data may be missing or unavailable, necessitating a method to leverage auxiliary information without requiring it during inference.
AI.method: Stage 1 learns a shared embedding from the paired subset and estimates class prototypes from the auxiliary modalities. Stage 2 trains the primary encoder on all subjects using cross-entropy loss plus alignment to the frozen class prototypes. Supervision is defined at the class-prototype level, allowing arbitrary pairing rates, including zero overlap.
AI.result: On ADNI (1,021 subjects): improved AD/CN classification with three auxiliary modalities across pairing rates; AUC improvements up to +7.9 percentage points over MRI-only baseline; reduced CN false positives; Conv5-FC3 backbone achieves best AUC of 0.893. Pairing-rate ablation shows joint anchor remains within seed noise from 75% to 5% pairing. On TCGA-Lung (RNA-seq as auxiliary): AUC for 2-year OS improved by +3.5pp; Cox PH C-index improved by +9.0 points; outperforms full-fusion training and MRI-only in some respects, with no RNA at inference; confidence intervals wide due to small cohort.
AI.conclusion: PANDA offers a deployment-oriented framework to exploit incomplete auxiliary modalities for improved primary-modality prediction, robust to varying pairing rates, including zero overlap.

title: Geometry-Constrained Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: Learning Edge Geometry via Banach Duality
summary: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) replace fixed activations in deep architectures with learnable univariate edge functions, making the choice of edge parametrisation central. Existing variants rely on fixed bases such as splines, polynomials, or Fourier features, which impose a function-space geometry before data are observed. We introduce geometry-constrained KANs, a family of edge activations derived from Banach duality maps in which the geometry itself is learned through a scalar exponent $p > 1$ per edge. This exponent controls the qualitative response: sub-Euclidean values produce sharp, threshold-like behaviour reminiscent of the $\ell_1$ (LASSO) geometry, $p = 2$ recovers the linear regime, and larger values produce flatter responses near the origin. Across 50 symbolic-regression targets ($40$ from the AI Feynman benchmark plus $10$ synthetic stress tests), geometry-constrained KANs match or beat every fixed-basis baseline on median NRMSE (Banach-KAN $0.030$, tying Chebyshev and improving on splines); on average rank Banach-KAN is best on the $18$-equation core ($2.00$) and statistically tied with the strongest spline on the full benchmark ($2.32$ vs. $2.34$). The clearest gains appear under measurement noise: as $σ$ grows from $0$ to $1$, $\ell^p$-KAN degrades only $3.7\times$ -- below even a cross-validated spline ($\approx 11\times$) -- while an unregularised spline degrades $21.6\times$; Banach-KAN degrades $8.8\times$, comparable to a tuned spline but far more stable than the unregularised one. Banach-KAN also takes the most per-equation wins in the small-sample regime, with fixed-basis models catching up only as the training set grows. Learned exponents provide an interpretable, relative signal: at a fixed initialisation they reveal a consistent, target-dependent geometric ordering across equation families and input dimensions.

AI.tldr: Geometry-constrained KANs (Banach-KAN) learn edge-wise p-geometry via Banach duality, improving symbolic regression robustness and interpretability relative to fixed-basis activations.
AI.motivation: Remove pre-imposed function-space geometry by using learnable edge exponents p>1 that shape edge activations; allow data to determine geometry per edge.
AI.method: Introduce geometry-constrained KANs with per-edge exponent p>1 controlling response; learn p alongside network; evaluate on 50 symbolic-regression targets (AI Feynman + synthetic tests); compare against fixed-basis baselines (splines, polynomials, Fourier); analyze performance under noise; assess interpretability of learned p.
AI.result: Banach-KAN achieves median NRMSE 0.030 (ties Chebyshev, better than splines); best average rank on 18-equation core (2.00); near-best on full benchmark (2.32 vs 2.34); under noise, degradation with sigma from 0 to 1 is 3.7x for ell^p-KAN vs 11x for cross-validated spline; unregularised spline degrades 21.6x; Banach-KAN degrades 8.8x; more per-equation wins in small-sample; exponents provide interpretable, target-dependent geometric ordering across equation families and input dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Learning per-edge p yields a flexible, interpretable geometry that adapts to data, delivering robust, competitive performance in symbolic regression and noise regimes, with advantages in small-sample settings and clear interpretability of edge geometry.

title: FRAME: separating sampling variation from representational cause in medical imaging fairness
summary: Subgroup performance differences are the standard evidence for fairness bias in medical imaging, and the usual response removes the demographic information that a model encodes. Here we introduce Fair-model Reference And Mechanism Evaluation (FRAME), a two-step framework for auditing such a claim. The first step derives a fair-model reference, the distribution of the difference under exact fairness at the observed subgroup sizes. In the second step, we test the remainder with two operators in representation space. One operator cannot change a within-group ranking by construction. Across 702,206 images and 36 encoders, the reference accounts for a median 41% of the reported race difference and 22% of the age difference. Injecting demographic decodability leaves the remainder unchanged, while entangling the group with the disease direction raises the race difference from 0.077 to 0.118. No intervention we tested changes the remainder more than a change of random seed does. Those interventions reduce a difference at the operating point and leave the within-group ranking difference at a median of 0.000. Applied to 89 differences in 9 published studies across 6 medical imaging modalities, the reference accounts for a median 25% of a rate difference and 70% of a difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Image-text pretraining instead raises worst-group performance by about 0.05. Applying FRAME before choosing an intervention could distinguish differences that need a mechanistic explanation from differences compatible with sampling variation at the current cohort sizes.

AI.tldr: FRAME is a two-step fairness auditing framework for medical imaging: derive a fair-model reference under exact fairness at observed subgroup sizes, then test the remainder with two representation-space operators. It shows that the reference explains a substantial share of observed race/age differences across a large dataset, while most remaining differences are not easily reduced by common interventions. It generalizes across modalities and encoders and can help distinguish sampling variation from true mechanistic biases.
AI.motivation: To diagnose whether subgroup performance differences attributed to fairness are due to sampling variability or to true model bias, rather than simply removing demographic information. FRAME provides a diagnostic tool to separate the portion of disparity explainable by sampling from the remainder that may require mechanistic intervention.
AI.method: Two-step FRAME: (1) derive a fair-model reference distribution under exact fairness at the observed subgroup sizes; (2) test the remaining disparity with two representation-space operators—one that preserves within-group ranking, and another that entangles the group with the disease direction. Evaluate on 702,206 images across 36 encoders; further apply to 89 differences in 9 published studies across 6 modalities.
AI.result: The fair-model reference accounts for a median 41% of race difference and 22% of age difference in the main dataset. Injecting demographic decodability leaves the remainder unchanged, while entangling group with disease direction raises race difference from 0.077 to 0.118. Interventions did not shift the remainder more than random seed changes. FRAME applied across 89 differences shows the reference accounts for a median 25% of rate difference and 70% of AUC difference; image-text pretraining raises worst-group performance by ~0.05.
AI.conclusion: FRAME provides a principled auditing framework to distinguish sampling variation from disparities that require mechanistic explanations. Using FRAME before interventions helps identify which differences merit mechanistic investigation versus those compatible with sampling variation at current cohort sizes, with demonstrated robustness across modalities and encoders.

title: Canalization Before Generalization: Grokking as a Dynamical Probe
summary: For overparameterized neural networks, many solutions can fit the training data equally well while behaving very differently on unseen samples. Grokking separates training fit from visible generalization, providing a window for studying how this selection develops during training. We sweep short, fixed-duration weight-decay (WD) pulses across this plateau and measure how they shift later generalization time. Across three grokking tasks, these shifts are unordered early in the plateau but later form a stable dose ordering, with stronger WD increases leading to earlier generalization and stronger WD decreases leading to later generalization. This ordering emerges before visible generalization in all three tasks. Meanwhile, test-loss barriers between perturbed and baseline generalization checkpoints collapse toward zero while the ordered timing effects persist. We call this combination of increasingly constrained solution selection and persistent dose-ordered timing sensitivity the canalization of function selection.

AI.tldr: Weight-decay perturbations during grokking reveal a dose-ordered timing effect on generalization, forming a robust canalization of function selection prior to visible generalization.
AI.motivation: To understand how, in overparameterized networks, selection among many trainable solutions that fit the data evolves during training, particularly during grokking when generalization emerges after training fits fade, and how perturbations influence this process.
AI.method: Systematic application of short, fixed-duration weight-decay pulses across the grokking plateau across three tasks, measuring how these perturbations shift the time to generalization and how their effects organize (unordered early, ordered later).
AI.result: Early training shows unordered effect of WD pulses; later, a stable dose ordering emerges: larger WD shifts lead to earlier generalization, smaller WD shifts lead to later generalization. This ordering appears before visible generalization. Test-loss barriers between perturbed and baseline generalization checkpoints collapse toward zero while timing effects persist.
AI.conclusion: The observed combination of increasingly constrained solution selection and persistent dose-ordered timing sensitivity constitutes canalization of function selection, indicating robust, ordered shaping of which solutions generalize despite many fit solutions.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Latent Diffusion Models for Faithful Super Resolution
summary: The perception-distortion trade-off poses a fundamental challenge in single-image super-resolution (SR). Although diffusion-based SR methods excel at generating perceptually realistic images, achieving high fidelity remains a key limitation. Recent advances in diffusion-based SR have shown promise in improving fidelity, but these methods often compromise perceptual quality due to their high reliance on a high-fidelity image. To address this, we introduce UGDiff, a novel diffusion guidance paradigm designed to further improve the perception-distortion balance. In particular, we first estimate the reconstruction uncertainty of the latent features corresponding to a high-fidelity image. This uncertainty is then used to guide the diffusion process to selectively restore high-frequency details in high-uncertainty regions, while preserving fidelity elsewhere. Furthermore, our guidance method adaptively identifies the high-uncertainty regions by considering not only the estimated uncertainty but also the posterior variance of the diffusion sampler at each timestep. This relaxes the reliance on the high-fidelity image in the later stages of sampling, thereby achieving a better perception-distortion balance. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method performs favorably against state-of-the-art diffusion-based SR methods.

AI.tldr: UGDiff introduces a diffusion-guided SR framework that uses reconstruction uncertainty and diffusion-sampler posterior variance to selectively restore high-frequency details in high-uncertainty regions, reducing reliance on high-fidelity references to improve the perception-distortion trade-off.
AI.motivation: To address the perception-distortion trade-off in single-image super-resolution (SR). Diffusion-based SR methods provide perceptual realism but often sacrifice fidelity; existing approaches rely heavily on high-fidelity images, hindering balance. A need exists for guidance that preserves fidelity while enhancing perceptual quality.
AI.method: Estimate reconstruction uncertainty of latent features corresponding to a high-fidelity image, then guide the diffusion process to selectively restore high-frequency details in high-uncertainty regions. The guidance adaptively identifies high-uncertainty regions by jointly considering the estimated uncertainty and the posterior variance of the diffusion sampler at each timestep, reducing reliance on the high-fidelity image in later sampling stages.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that UGDiff achieves favorable performance against state-of-the-art diffusion-based SR methods, validating its effectiveness in improving the perception-distortion balance.
AI.conclusion: UGDiff provides a principled diffusion-guidance strategy that concentrates restoration on uncertain regions while moderating dependence on high-fidelity references, leading to improved perception-distortion trade-offs in single-image SR and strong empirical results.

title: Learning Continuous Regional Temperature Fields with Lead-Time and Resolution Queries
summary: Accurate regional near-surface temperature forecasting is fundamental to short-range weather services and downstream risk assessment. Existing deep learning-based regional forecasters commonly produce a fixed set of future frames on a prescribed grid, limiting their use when forecast products must be evaluated at query-dependent lead times or display resolutions. To overcome these fixed-output constraints, we formulate regional T2M forecasting as query-conditioned continuous spatiotemporal temperature field evaluation and propose the Continuous Spatiotemporal Temperature Forecaster (CSTF), a neural field that turns forecast lead time and output resolution into explicit queries when evaluating 2-m temperature (T2M). Specifically, CSTF first encodes multivariable ERA5 histories into latent meteorological states and then decodes T2M as a coordinate-based field. Accordingly, spatial location, forecast lead time, and output resolution are introduced as queries, enabling standard hourly forecasts, intermediate lead-time diagnostics, and resolution-controllable outputs within a unified field-evaluation framework. Furthermore, to maintain coherence across flexible field queries, we design spatial-gradient, temporal-difference, and scale-consistency objectives that regularize regional thermal structures, lead-wise evolution, and cross-resolution agreement. Experiments on the Southeast China 0-6 h ERA5-Land benchmark demonstrate that CSTF achieves the best aggregate deterministic skill, including a 17.0 percent reduction in Bias, with global-scope diagnostics further illustrating flexible lead-time and resolution-controllable inference.

AI.tldr: A neural-field CSTF framework enables query-conditioned, continuous spatiotemporal forecasting of 2-m temperature (T2M) with flexible lead times and resolutions, achieving state-of-the-art deterministic skill and reduced bias on a Southeast China ERA5-Land benchmark.
AI.motivation: Current DL regional forecasters output fixed sets of future frames, limiting evaluation for query-dependent leads and resolutions. A continuous, query-driven forecast framework can provide flexible, coherent outputs and facilitate diagnostics across lead times and resolutions.
AI.method: CSTF encodes multivariable ERA5 histories into latent meteorological states and decodes T2M as a coordinate-based field. Spatial location, forecast lead time, and output resolution are treated as explicit queries. The framework includes spatial-gradient, temporal-difference, and scale-consistency objectives to regularize spatial structures, lead-time evolution, and cross-resolution agreement.
AI.result: On the Southeast China 0–6 h ERA5-Land benchmark, CSTF achieves the best aggregate deterministic skill and reduces Bias by 17.0%. Global diagnostics demonstrate flexible lead-time and resolution-controllable inference.
AI.conclusion: A unified field-evaluation approach enables accurate, flexible, and coherent regional T2M forecasts across arbitrary lead times and resolutions, with improved bias and competitive skill.

title: UltraPIPS: Improving model perception in B-mode ultrasound with foundation models
summary: In medical imaging, it is common to use learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) to compare images semantically in feature space. Although backbones pretrained on natural images are widely used for LPIPS computation, B-mode ultrasound images possess distinct speckle patterns and acoustic-specific image statistics that are fundamentally different from natural images and even from other images in radiology. Consequently, we propose that domain-specific models are needed to measure perceptual similarity in ultrasound data, a finding which is not necessarily the case for other imaging modalities. We compare LPIPS metrics across downstream tasks like classification, segmentation and reconstruction using natural image, medical generalist and ultrasound backbone models and show that selection of LPIPS backbone is a non-trivial design choice. In particular, the ultrasound backbone models were more correlated with downstream performance of supervised models than classical and natural image models, and optimization of the LPIPS loss with an ultrasound backbone achieved a strong balance between reconstruction quality and realism. Our code is available at https://github.com/talg2324/UltraPIPS and introduces the UltraPIPS library, a set of LPIPS metrics based on the open-source foundation models analyzed in this paper.

AI.tldr: Ultrasound-specific LPIPS backbones improve perceptual similarity measurement and downstream task performance; UltraPIPS library provides ultrasound-domain LPIPS metrics.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound images have unique speckle patterns and statistics not well captured by natural-image LPIPS backbones; domain-specific perceptual metrics may better align with clinical signal semantics and improve downstream tasks.
AI.method: Systematically compare LPIPS metrics across backbones trained on natural images, medical generalist data, and ultrasound data across tasks (classification, segmentation, reconstruction); quantify correlation with downstream performance; optimize LPIPS loss with an ultrasound backbone; introduce UltraPIPS library.
AI.result: Ultrasound backbones show higher correlation with downstream performance than natural-image or generalist models; optimizing LPIPS with an ultrasound backbone yields a balance between reconstruction quality and realism; code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific LPIPS backbones are beneficial for ultrasound; UltraPIPS provides tailored perceptual metrics and demonstrates improved alignment with downstream tasks.

title: VINCENT: Validated Interaction Network for Cross-drug Explanation of Therapeutics
summary: Drug synergy prediction estimates whether two drugs produce a stronger joint effect than expected from their individual activities. For drug combination discovery, a single synergy score is often not enough: researchers also need to know which molecular regions jointly drive the prediction. We study motif-pair synergy explanation, which identifies pairs of chemically coherent regions, one from each drug, that jointly contribute to predicted synergy. Existing interpretable synergy models expose atom- or substructure-level signals, but their explanations are built into the predictor architecture, and none validates cross-drug region scores under repeated perturbations or feeds that evidence back to refine the explanation. A reliable motif-pair explanation should instead be chemically coherent, perturbation-stable, and aligned with predictor behavior. We introduce VINCENT (Validated Interaction Network for Cross-drug Explanation of Therapeutics), a post-training framework for a fixed interaction-aware synergy predictor. VINCENT extracts atom-pair evidence from attention and gradient signals, groups atoms into chemically coherent motifs, and validates candidate motif pairs through repeated local perturbations. The validated evidence is fed back to refine motif assignments, yielding explanations that satisfy these three criteria. On a 25-pair literature-annotated subset, VINCENT achieves a mean motif recall of 0.826 (95% CI: 0.78-0.87), compared with 0.49-0.66 for baselines. Across all 71 test pairs, its validated interaction scores yield a TP/TN separation of 3.36. These results show that closed-loop perturbation validation recovers literature-supported molecular regions more accurately than existing alternatives while producing cross-drug interaction scores that better reflect predictor behavior.

AI.tldr: VINCENT is a post-training framework that explains cross-drug synergy by identifying motif-pair explanations, validated via perturbation, yielding coherent, stable, and predictor-aligned evidence.
AI.motivation: Provide robust, chemically coherent, perturbation-stable explanations for cross-drug synergy predictions, addressing limitations of architecture-embedded explanations and lack of cross-drug validation.
AI.method: A fixed interaction-aware synergy predictor is used. VINCENT extracts atom-pair evidence from attention and gradients, groups atoms into chemically coherent motifs, and validates candidate motif pairs through repeated local perturbations. Validated evidence is fed back to refine motif assignments in a closed loop.
AI.result: On 25-pair literature-annotated data, mean motif recall is 0.826 (CI 0.78–0.87), outperforming baselines (0.49–0.66). Across 71 test pairs, validated interaction scores achieve a TP/TN separation of 3.36.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop perturbation validation improves recovery of literature-supported molecular regions and yields cross-drug interaction scores that better reflect the predictor's behavior.

title: StreamPI: Streaming Multimodal Temporal Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated effectiveness in robot manipulation, yet state-of-the-art models such as pi0.5 operate under a single-frame paradigm, limiting their ability to retain past observations and develop precise spatial perception. In this paper, we propose StreamPI, a streaming multimodal temporal modeling framework that equips single-frame VLA with temporal reasoning capability without introducing any additional parameters. One core design is instruction-anchored temporal modeling. It treats each (visual observation, language instruction) pair as an atomic temporal unit: bidirectional attention within each pair enables cross-modal fusion, while causal attention across pairs preserves autoregressive streaming inference. This ensures the language instruction serves as a persistent semantic anchor throughout task execution. To bridge the gap between synchronous training and asynchronous real-robot deployment, we introduce a andom-interval streaming training strategy: a proper inter-frame interval (e.g., every 3 frames) enables faster and smoother action execution. Beyond this, randomizing the interval further improves robustness to frame-timing perturbations, supporting asynchronous deployment in practice. Furthermore, by leveraging the length extrapolation capability of the LLM backbone, StreamPI seamlessly inherits pretrained single-frame weights and supports flexible single-frame and multi-frame inference. Experiments on real-robot tasks spanning memory-dependent and precise perception scenarios, as well as the simulation benchmark LIBERO, demonstrate that StreamPI outperforms pi0.5 across diverse tasks.

AI.tldr: StreamPI adds temporal reasoning to single-frame vision-language-action (VLA) models without extra parameters by instruction-anchored streaming; it outperforms pi0.5 on real-robot and LIBERO benchmarks and enables robust asynchronous deployment.
AI.motivation: Single-frame VLA models struggle to retain past observations and achieve precise spatial perception, hindering long-horizon tasks and robust real-world deployment. There is a need to incorporate temporal context while preserving parameter efficiency and leveraging pretrained language models.
AI.method: Propose StreamPI: a streaming multimodal temporal modeling framework. Treat each (visual observation, language instruction) pair as an atomic temporal unit. Within each pair, bidirectional attention fuses visual and textual modalities; across pairs, causal attention enables autoregressive streaming inference. The language instruction acts as a persistent semantic anchor. Introduce randomized-interval streaming training: use a proper inter-frame interval (e.g., every 3 frames) to align with real-time execution; randomize intervals to improve robustness to frame timing perturbations for asynchronous deployment. Leverage the length extrapolation capability of the LLM backbone to inherit pretrained single-frame weights, supporting both single-frame and multi-frame inference.
AI.result: Empirical results on real-robot tasks (memory-dependent and precise perception scenarios) and the LIBERO simulation benchmark show StreamPI outperforms pi0.5 across diverse tasks.
AI.conclusion: StreamPI enables temporal reasoning in VLA without adding parameters, bridging synchronous training and asynchronous deployment. It is robust to frame-timing perturbations, benefits from pretrained LLM backbones, and demonstrates strong generalization to real-robot and simulation tasks.

title: CEDAR: Controlled and Event-Driven Demand Forecasting via Residual Decomposition
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Published in KDD 2026
summary: Forecasting in large-scale e-commerce marketplaces is increasingly required to support planning: merchants need to evaluate sales outcomes under future action sequences such as budget schedules, rather than passively predicting what happens next. However, most existing time series forecasting (TSF) approaches remain inherently passive. Even when incorporating operational decisions as auxiliary covariates, they typically optimize for correlation-based extrapolation under historical policies. This design suffers from autoregressive inertia and conflates endogenous market evolution with decision-induced transitions, leading to policy-insensitive rollouts and unreliable counterfactual analysis. To bridge this gap, we propose CEDAR (Controlled and Event-Driven Demand forecasting via Action-aware Residual decomposition), a two-stage framework for robust decision-conditioned simulation. In Stage I, an Action-Interleaved Transformer learns controllable action-conditioned state transitions for rollout under planned interventions. In Stage II, a Residual Correction Module leverages external event signals and LLM-assisted text representations to align noisy event descriptions with product context and correct event-driven deviations. Our study is enabled by a large-scale real-world dataset from Alibaba 1688, comprising approximately 32 million product trajectories with paired state-action sequences and aligned event signals. Extensive offline experiments and online controlled experiments in production demonstrate that CEDAR consistently improves simulation accuracy over strong TSF baselines and delivers practical gains for real-world budget planning.

AI.tldr: Two-stage action-conditioned forecast framework (CEDAR) enabling decision-conditioned simulation in large-scale e-commerce by modeling controllable action-conditioned state transitions and residual event corrections, improving rollout accuracy and budget planning.
AI.motivation: Passive time series forecasting models fail to separate policy-induced transitions from endogenous market evolution, hindering reliable counterfactuals and planning.
AI.method: Stage I: Action-Interleaved Transformer learns controllable action-conditioned state transitions for planned interventions. Stage II: Residual Correction Module uses external event signals and LLM-derived text representations to align event descriptions with product context and correct deviations.
AI.result: Offline experiments and online controlled experiments on Alibaba 1688 dataset (≈32 million trajectories) show improved simulation accuracy over strong TSF baselines and practical gains for budget planning.
AI.conclusion: CEDAR provides robust decision-conditioned simulation for large-scale marketplaces, demonstrating viability and benefits of a two-stage action-aware framework for planning under interventions.

title: MyoMechanix: Biomechanically-Grounded Compositional Skilled Activity Understanding and Coaching
summary: Existing action quality assessment (AQA) datasets and methods rely primarily on visual inputs such as RGB and pose, overlooking physiological dynamics such as muscle mechanics and often modeling actions as monolithic patterns. These limitations hinder fine-grained, biomechanically grounded feedback. We introduce MyoMechanix, a multimodal ecosystem for weight-loaded actions that aligns motion with muscle activity. Expert-annotated, it contains 7,500+ samples of 20 actions from 38 subjects, with synchronized multiview RGB video, 3D pose, sEMG, and additional physiological signals, forming the largest multimodal AQA benchmark to date. We further construct the Fitness Knowledge Graph (FKG), which organizes expert annotations into structured relationships among actions, phases, key steps, errors, and corrective feedback, enabling compositional scoring and interpretable assessment. Building on these representations, we develop CUBIST (Compositional Ontological Reasoning Engine), which performs decomposition-analysis-recomposition for fine-grained error attribution and feedback generation. We also establish MyoMechanix-AQA, MyoMechanix-VideoQA, and a novel MyoMechanix-Video2EMG task. Experiments show that multimodal sensing and structured representations improve performance, interpretability, and error attribution, with CUBIST achieving state-of-the-art results; VideoQA enhances language-grounded action understanding; and Video2EMG suggests video-based alternatives to costly EMG sensing. MyoMechanix advances skilled activity understanding toward biomechanically grounded, multimodal, and compositional reasoning for Physical AI applications in fitness, rehabilitation, healthcare, and machine learning. Project page: https://haoyin116.github.io/MyoMechanix/

AI.tldr: MyoMechanix introduces a multimodal, biomechanics-grounded framework for action quality assessment (AQA) in weight-loaded actions, combining synchronized video, pose, sEMG, and physiological signals with a structured ontology (FKG) and a compositional reasoning engine (CUBIST) to enable interpretable, granular feedback and new QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Current AQA datasets rely mainly on visual cues and treat actions as monolithic patterns, ignoring muscle dynamics and biomechanical structure, which limits fine-grained feedback and interpretability.
AI.method: Collect and annotate 7,500+ samples of 20 actions from 38 subjects with synchronized multiview RGB, 3D pose, sEMG, and additional physiological signals. Build the Fitness Knowledge Graph (FKG) to organize annotations into relationships among actions, phases, steps, errors, and feedback. Develop CUBIST for decomposition-analysis-recomposition to attribute errors and generate feedback. Define MyoMechanix-AQA, MyoMechanix-VideoQA, and MyoMechanix-Video2EMG tasks.
AI.result: Multimodal sensing and structured representations improve performance, interpretability, and error attribution. CUBIST achieves state-of-the-art results; VideoQA enhances language-grounded understanding; Video2EMG provides insights into video-based EMG alternatives. Establishes the largest multimodal AQA benchmark to date and a robust knowledge graph for compositional reasoning.
AI.conclusion: MyoMechanix advances skilled activity understanding toward biomechanically grounded, multimodal, and compositional reasoning, with broad applications in fitness, rehabilitation, healthcare, and ML-based Physical AI.

title: How Edge of Stability Hinders SCAFFOLD in Federated Optimization
summary: In federated learning, it is well known that heterogeneous data can (in theory) slow down optimization, and much effort has been directed at designing optimization algorithms that are unaffected by data heterogeneity, such as the SCAFFOLD algorithm. Yet, despite strong theoretical guarantees, SCAFFOLD does not usually outperform the much simpler FedAvg in practice. In this work, we propose that this gap is due to the presence of Edge of Stability (EoS) and progressive sharpening in federated optimization, supported by extensive empirical probing. First, we find that EoS-like dynamics occur with both FedAvg and SCAFFOLD under a variety of architectures and hyperparameters. We observe that the equilibrium value of the sharpness is inversely proportional to the learning rate (as in GD), and interestingly, the degree of data heterogeneity (but not the number of local steps) also affects the equilibrium value. Most importantly, we observe that SCAFFOLD's ability to estimate the gradient of the global objective is severely degraded at the EoS, as measured by the correlation between sharpness and SCAFFOLD's error in estimating the global gradient along the optimization trajectory. This suggests a mechanism for SCAFFOLD's lackluster performance in deep learning: with high sharpness at the EoS, SCAFFOLD cannot reliably estimate the global gradient.

AI.tldr: Federated learning exhibits Edge of Stability (EoS) and progressive sharpening, with EoS-like dynamics in FedAvg and SCAFFOLD. Equilibrium sharpness scales inversely with learning rate and is influenced by data heterogeneity (not by the number of local steps). At EoS, SCAFFOLD's global-gradient estimation deteriorates, suggesting a mechanism for its weak practical performance compared to FedAvg.
AI.motivation: Explain the gap between strong theoretical guarantees for federated optimization methods (e.g., SCAFFOLD) and their practical performance by investigating Edge of Stability and progressive sharpening effects under data heterogeneity.
AI.method: Extensive empirical probing across architectures and hyperparameters to measure sharpness dynamics, equilibrium sharpness vs learning rate, influence of data heterogeneity, and correlation between sharpness and SCAFFOLD's global-gradient estimation error.
AI.result: EoS-like dynamics are observed for both FedAvg and SCAFFOLD. The equilibrium sharpness is inversely proportional to the learning rate; data heterogeneity affects this equilibrium; the number of local steps has little effect. SCAFFOLD’s ability to estimate the global gradient degrades at EoS, evidenced by reduced correlation between sharpness and its gradient estimation error.
AI.conclusion: EoS and progressive sharpening provide a plausible mechanism for the underwhelming practical performance of SCAFFOLD in deep learning, since high sharpness at the EoS impairs reliable global-gradient estimation and may explain the theory-practice gap in federated optimization.

title: A Visual Dependence-Aware Framework for Multimodal Unsupervised Continual Post-Training
summary: In this paper, we explore a novel task of Multimodal Unsupervised Continual Post-Training (MU-CPT), enabling deployed MLLMs to continually evolve from streaming unlabeled data. Existing unsupervised post-training methods for MLLMs typically optimize target tokens uniformly, overlooking their heterogeneous visual dependence (VD). However, we reveal that token-level VD is crucial for MU-CPT. Specifically, its structural distortion serves as an indicator of cross-modal catastrophic forgetting, and its inherent heterogeneity acts as a compass to guide new-task learning. Leveraging this property, we propose a Visual Dependence-Aware (VDA) framework with two main components. First, Visually Constrained Optimal Transport (VC-OT) formulates the VD structural distortion of old-task VD during new-task learning as an optimal transport problem to mitigate cross-modal forgetting. By designing a region-aware ground cost and a dependence-stratified transport penalty, it prevents global shifts in visual focus while strictly prohibiting visual reliance from degenerating into language bias. Second, Visually Modulated Adaptation (VMA) exploits VD heterogeneity to emphasize visually grounded new-task learning, promoting new-task plasticity. Together, our method simultaneously maintains old-task stability and new-task plasticity during challenging MU-CPT. Extensive experiments under our MU-CPT setting validate the effectiveness of VDA.

AI.tldr: MU-CPT with Visual Dependence-Aware (VDA) framework, using VC-OT and VMA to stabilize old tasks and adapt to new tasks in MU-CPT.
AI.motivation: Token-level visual dependence causes cross-modal forgetting in unsupervised post-training; VD heterogeneity can guide learning.
AI.method: VC-OT: optimal transport aligning old-task VD with new-task learning via region-aware ground cost and dependence-stratified penalty. VMA: uses VD heterogeneity to bias learning toward visually grounded aspects.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show VDA improves stability-plasticity trade-off in MU-CPT, outperforming baselines.
AI.conclusion: VDA enables simultaneous old-task stability and new-task plasticity in unsupervised continual post-training for MLLMs.

title: A General-Purpose Molecular Foundation Model Transfers Across Diverse Olfactory Tasks
summary: Foundation models have transformed molecular property prediction, yet it remains unclear whether a molecular foundation model, fine-tuned on a single canonical olfactory prediction task, can learn representations that transfer across diverse machine olfaction problems. We investigate this question by fine-tuning Uni-Mol2 on the GS-LF benchmark for multi-label odor descriptor prediction and evaluating the resulting model, without additional deep-learning training, on four complementary downstream settings: cross-dataset odor descriptor prediction, odorous-versus-odorless classification, enantiomer evaluation, and odor mixture discriminability. The fine-tuned model matches or exceeds the performance of the state-of-the-art olfaction-specific baseline on the primary GS-LF benchmark and consistently transfers across these downstream evaluations. The enantiomer analysis further shows that three-dimensional molecular representations distinguish mirror-image molecules in a way that two-dimensional graph models fundamentally cannot, although accurately predicting the perceptual consequences of stereochemistry remains an open challenge. Together, these results support a train-once, transfer-across-tasks paradigm for machine olfaction and suggest that chemically pretrained molecular representations provide a strong foundation for transferable olfactory prediction.

AI.tldr: A single-task fine-tuned molecular foundation model demonstrates transferable olfactory predictions across multiple tasks, supporting train-once transfer in machine olfaction.
AI.motivation: Assess whether a molecular foundation model pre-trained on one olfactory task can generalize to diverse olfactory problems without additional training.
AI.method: Fine-tune Uni-Mol2 on the GS-LF multi-label odor descriptor task and evaluate zero-shot transfer to four downstream settings: cross-dataset odor descriptor prediction, odorous-vs-odorless classification, enantiomer discrimination, and odor mixture discriminability, comparing against olfaction-specific baselines.
AI.result: The fine-tuned model matches or exceeds the state-of-the-art on GS-LF and transfers consistently to downstream tasks; three-dimensional molecular representations distinguish enantiomers beyond 2D graph models; predicting perceptual outcomes of stereochemistry remains challenging.
AI.conclusion: Supports a train-once, transfer-across-tasks paradigm for machine olfaction; chemically pretrained molecular representations provide a strong foundation for transferable olfactory prediction, though stereochemical perceptual mapping remains an open challenge.

title: RefVideo-6M: A Reliable Reference-Based Dataset for Instructional Video Editing
summary: Recent advances in video editing have been largely driven by large-scale instruction-based datasets. However, existing datasets still suffer from two critical limitations. First, target videos are commonly produced by automatic editing models, which may introduce visible artifacts and unreliable supervision signals. Second, most public datasets rely primarily on textual instructions, while lacking visual references that are crucial for precise, identity-preserving, and controllable editing. To address these limitations, we introduce RefVideo-6M, a large-scale reference-guided editing dataset containing 5 million video editing samples and 1 million image editing samples. To ensure reliable supervision, our dataset uses a construction pipeline that treats artifact-free real videos as editing targets and generates quality-filtered input conditions with multiple editing experts. In addition, it provides approximately 6 million visual references, covering diverse reference types and editing scenarios, thereby enabling models to learn fine-grained visual correspondence beyond text-only instructions. Based on RefVideo-6M, we further train a reference-guided video editing model, Ref-MoT, to evaluate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed dataset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RefVideo-6M provides substantially more reliable supervision than existing datasets and enables the training of powerful editing models with improved visual quality, controllability, and reference consistency. The open-source dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/RefVideo6M/RefVideo6M.

AI.tldr: RefVideo-6M is a large-scale, reference-guided video/image editing dataset (5M video edits, 1M image edits) built on artifact-free real videos with multiple expert-generated inputs and ~6M visual references, enabling reliable supervision and fine-grained visual correspondence for editing models like Ref-MoT; claims improved quality, controllability, and reference consistency, with open-source release.
AI.motivation: To overcome two limitations in existing instruction-based editing datasets: (1) use of artifact-prone automatic editing targets, and (2) reliance on text-only instructions lacking visual references for precise, identity-preserving edits.
AI.method: Construct a pipeline that treats real, artifact-free videos as editing targets and generates high-quality, input conditions via multiple editing experts; assemble ~6M visual references of diverse types and editing scenarios; train a reference-guided video editing model (Ref-MoT) to evaluate dataset effectiveness.
AI.result: Experiments show RefVideo-6M provides substantially more reliable supervision than existing datasets and enables training of editing models with improved visual quality, controllability, and reference consistency.
AI.conclusion: RefVideo-6M offers a scalable, high-quality resource for reference-guided editing and supports training effective models like Ref-MoT; the dataset is open-sourced for community use.

title: Towards A Unified Information Bottleneck Framework for Time Series Explanations
summary: Explaining deep learning models operating on time series data is crucial in various applications that require transparent and interpretable insights into model behavior. {Existing explanation methods generally fall into two categories: attribution-based explanations, which identify the temporal regions most responsible for a prediction, and counterfactual explanations, which reveal how an input should be modified to alter the model's decision.} {Despite valuable insights, these two fields are largely studied independently. This disconnect leaves attribution methods lacking causal validation, while counterfactual methods suffer from severe instability, producing adversarial-like noise instead of meaningful explanations.} In this work, we revisit time-series explainability from an information-theoretic perspective and show that existing explainers are vulnerable to trivial solutions and distributional shifts. To address these limitations, we propose a unified objective function for explainable time series learning that bridges attribution and counterfactual reasoning within a single framework. Building upon the Information Bottleneck principle, our formulation explicitly prevents trivial explanations and out-of-distribution counterfactuals. {Based on this objective function, we introduce {\modelname}, a novel explanation framework that learns a parametric transformation network to construct explanation-embedded instances, where preserved information yields attribution explanations and controlled information removal produces stable counterfactual explanations.} We evaluate {\modelname} on synthetic and real-world benchmarks against state-of-the-art baselines. Extensive quantitative and qualitative results show that {\modelname} consistently outperforms competing methods, yielding faithful attributions and stable counterfactual explanations.

AI.tldr: Unified information-theoretic framework for explainable time-series learning that unifies attribution and counterfactual explanations via the Information Bottleneck (IB). Introduces a transformation network to embed explanations; claims superior fidelity and stability over baselines on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: Explainability in time-series is split into attribution (identifying influential regions) and counterfactuals (how to change inputs to alter decisions). Each faces issues—attribution lacks causal validation; counterfactuals can be unstable and generate adversarial noise. A unified, causal-valid framework is needed to ensure faithful and robust explanations.
AI.method: Formulates a single objective based on the Information Bottleneck to prevent trivial explanations and out-of-distribution counterfactuals. Proposes a parametric transformation network ({modelname}) that yields explanation-embedded instances: preserved information yields attribution signals, while controlled information removal yields stable counterfactuals.
AI.result: Evaluations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show the proposed approach consistently outperforms baselines in both attribution fidelity and counterfactual stability, with both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments supporting its efficacy.
AI.conclusion: A unified IB-based objective successfully bridges attribution and counterfactual reasoning in time-series explainability, producing faithful attributions and robust counterfactuals, and improving over state-of-the-art methods.

title: Forecasting Multiple Observables with SCROLL: Score-Trained Uncertainty for Stochastic Dynamics
comment: preprint for of the submitted paper
summary: Forecasting a stochastic dynamical system rarely means a single number: one wants several observables---future state, threshold event, regime label---each with its own likelihood. Standard multi-task recipes balance per-task losses, tuned or learned.
